en: Preface to the *Brief Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, composed by Master Siqi, Grand Master of the Transmission of the Teachings and Ordination Platform, conferred the purple robe, of Wumen. What is it that cultivates the person?

It is nothing other than the precepts and discipline (*śīla-vinaya*). What is it that harmonizes the mind? It is nothing other than Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodhi*). At the outset, one is strictly adorned with...

The Vinaya ultimately reveals Perfect Enlightenment (*Samantabhadra-vijñāna*), and both of these were transmitted to me, a humble person, by the late Great Master Jinghui (whose name was Shanzheng). Having followed what I heard from his gate, I have concurrently lectured on their essential tenets;
in my later years, I took Perfect Enlightenment as my primary teaching, and thus I shall now expound its chapters and verses.

The *Brief Commentary* (Lüeshū) in two fascicles and the *Brief Sub-commentary* (Lüechāo) in six fascicles by Chan Master Guifeng Dinghui: the commentary serves to clarify the sutras, while the sub-commentary serves to clarify the commentary;
they investigate the profound and seek out the hidden, with concise language yet vast meaning, thus providing a complete exposition.
The Preface by Prime Minister Pei: Master Dao Gu’s tradition has continued down to the present day;

among those who drive their arguments today, there are none who do not take this compendium as their guiding compass. I, Siqi, am ignorant and dull-witted, yet I have fortunately been granted this teaching.

I shall stand in awe of the sacred words, fearing they might be confused like water and cranes, and I am deeply concerned that transmitters might err like the characters "lu" and "yu. Therefore, I consulted with the Dharma Master Zhongxi of Wulin.

I have consulted various original texts and authoritative commentaries, following the principle of honoring the ancient while disparaging the modern, and I have privately considered the intent behind the historical omission of certain passages.
Having established a definitive draft for the purpose of carving it into print, my disciple Zizhang has diligently modeled the wooden printing blocks; with great effort, he has wielded his brush.

Whether this is right or wrong, if it is not right I shall delete it, and if it is right I shall preserve it; thus I have returned to the fundamental source and subsequently committed these words to writing.
May those who perceive the world not condemn me for failing to carry forward my intent;
if they instead embrace my intent, then the Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment will shine forth without end, and Guifeng’s commentary will guide beings to the utmost limit. At that time—

On the day of the full moon in the month when the handle points to the Beak of the Bird (the constellation Kṛttikā) in the year of Xinsi, the second year of the Kangding era of the Imperial Song dynasty,
I, the śramaṇa Zongmi of Guifeng Hermitage, respectfully preface this first fascicle of the *Brief Commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, extracted from the Great Commentary.

Regarding the two fascicles of the *Jiangshi lueshu* (Brief Commentary on the Explication), there are two parts: first, the title; second, the main text. First, the title, which has two sections: first, indicating the general title; second, identifying the author. Second, the main text, which has three sections: first, a general exposition of the broad outline;

second, the specific exegesis; third, the concluding summary. In the first section, the general exposition of the broad outline, there are three parts: first, revealing the principle; second, clarifying the practice; third, the conclusion. In the first part, revealing the principle, there are two sections: first, demonstrating the essence of the awakened mind; second, explaining its function. In the first section, demonstrating the essence of the awakened mind, there are two parts:

first, distinguishing its essentials; second, providing a detailed analysis. In the first part, distinguishing its essentials, there are two sections: first, pointing toward the source of the mind by way of the fruit-virtue; second, citing analogies. In the first section, pointing toward the source of the mind by way of the fruit-virtue, there is one part: citing analogies.
Regarding the phrase "Sū, Yuán-hēng, etc.," this is merely citing the virtue of the Qian hexagram from the *Zhouyi* as an analogy.

However, among the customs venerated by this nation, the various classics reach their pinnacle in the *Zhouyi*, and all things reach their ultimate in the Way of Qian. (Of the myriad things in the world, none surpass Heaven and Earth;

therein, they are unified by Earth and Heaven. Since Heaven is honored and Earth is humble, and the Way of Qian represents Heaven, it is taken as an analogy. Since the standard for emulation lies within the Confucian tradition, the Confucians are cited here.

I have studied the Way of what is known to reach the principle of awakening through analogy, so that it may be clearly understood. Having already transformed the customs of Confucian scholars, the grasses of the common people now bend of their own accord.
Other metaphors are too numerous and fragmented to be compared with the True Dharma; its primary manifestation of the virtue of *Qian* (Heaven) is found herein.
Now, since "Original, Penetrating, Favorable, and Correct" (*Yuán-héng-lì-zhēn*) are the four virtues of *Qian*, I shall first clarify these four virtues.
First, the Way of Qian is revealed; "Qian" is the name of a hexagram, specifically the very first hexagram of the *Zhouyi*.

(The hexagram *Qian* is thus the beginning because all things originate from *Qian*; hence the *Xici* says: "Qian knows the Great Beginning; Kun completes the creation of things. It is called a "hexagram" (*gua*) because the *Yiwei* states:
"Hexagram means 'to hang' (*guà*)," meaning that objects are suspended and displayed for people to see; thus it is called a hexagram. However, this refers only to the form of two lines.

Although the qi of yin and yang has not yet formed the images of the myriad things, the hexagrams cannot be established unless there are three lines to symbolize the Three Powers (the Heaven, Earth, and Human).
Only when the images of Heaven, Earth, Thunder, Wind, Water, Fire, Mountain, and Lake are depicted can they be called hexagrams;
thus the *Xici* says, "When the Eight Trigrams are arrayed, their images are contained therein. However, with these initial three lines, [the essence of] the myriad things is already present.

Because the transformations and applications were not yet fully exhausted, it was further doubled to produce six lines, thereby encompassing the forms and images of the myriad things and exhausting the capacities of heaven and earth;
thus, the hexagram is formed. This hexagram of Qian is fundamentally intended to symbolize Heaven, which is constituted by the accumulation of all yang qi;
therefore, all six lines of this hexagram are yang lines (one long line constitutes a yang line; two short lines facing each other constitute a yin line).
Since this [the hexagram Qian] already represents Heaven, it is not called "Heaven" but rather "Qian.

"Heaven" (Tian) is the name for a fixed essence, whereas "Qian" is a designation for both essence and function (that is, the function of the essence). Thus, the *Saying on the Hexagrams* states: "Qian is vigor. This means that the essence of Heaven takes vigor as its function.
The Sage composed the *Yi* fundamentally to instruct people, desiring them to model themselves after the function of Heaven rather than [merely its essence].
The essence of Heaven is therefore called *Qian* (the Creative), rather than being called "Heaven" itself.
That Heaven takes vigor as its function—its ceaseless revolution and its inexhaustible responsive transformations—is the natural principle of Heaven;

thus, the Sage should model himself upon this spontaneity in conducting human affairs, responding to things and accomplishing tasks with unceasing activity, remaining ever-vigilant day and night without a moment's slackening.
It is for this reason that the celestial phenomena are used to instruct people in affairs; thus the Great Image says: "The movement of Heaven is vigorous" (*tian xing jian*).

"Movement" (*xing*) refers to motion; "vigorous" (*jian*) is a term for strength. This is the natural image of Heaven. Among all things that possess vigor, there is inevitably decline and weariness; yet Heaven travels one degree each day.

This refers to the movement of the celestial body, which proceeds day and night without ceasing, completing its cycle and beginning again, never failing or retreating. Liu Biao said: "Thus, 'Heaven' (*tian*) is the name for the substance (*ti*), while 'Vigorous' (*qian*) is the name for the function (*yong*); this is its definition."

"The superior man, in accordance with this, exerts himself without ceasing" (because he uses the image of the hexagram to encourage himself and must not stop, it is called "firmness"). The *Wenyan* says: "The Master composed the *Wenyan* to explain the main text of the *Zhouyi*.
Hereafter, it explains the character 'Qian' [Heaven]: 'Qian initiates and is able to benefit the world with its beautiful benefits;

that it does not speak of what it benefits—how great it is! It further says: 'How great is Qian! It is firm, strong, correct, and balanced; it is pure, complete, and refined. Because it occupies the position of honor, it stands above all other hexagrams."

The beginning of this [treatise] constitutes the initial principle of the *I Ching* (having concluded the explanation of the character *Qian*). As for "Great, Success, Advantage, and Persistence" (the text appearing in the hexagram’s *ci*), although the functions and applications of *Qian* are manifold, they are subsumed under these four virtues;
therefore, these are selected. The *Zi Xia Zhuan* states: "Great means the beginning; success means penetration; advantage means harmony; and persistence means rectitude.
This means that the virtue of this hexagram possesses the nature of pure yang, and by its very nature, it is able to initiate the birth of yang energy.

The myriad things attain flourishing and success; it can cause the natures of things to be harmonious so that each has its own benefit, and it can also cause things to be firm, steadfast, and correct;

therefore, it is called the Four Virtues. This means that the Sage should likewise model himself after this hexagram to practice the Way of Goodness, nourishing the myriad things as the Primordial (Yuan), and should also bring the myriad things together through auspicious and beautiful matters.

It causes things to open and flow, thereby constituting *heng* (pervasive success). Furthermore, it should employ righteousness to harmonize the myriad things so that each attains its own principle, thereby constituting *li* (benefit).
Its pattern should be firm and steadfast in managing affairs so that all things attain their proper correctness, thereby constituting *zhen* (correctness).
For this reason, the Sage models himself after Qian and practices these four virtues; thus it is said: "Great, pervasive, beneficial, and correct. — Wenzi.

The commentary states: (The following section discusses the four virtues of Qian. As for the substance of Qian, it is the function of Heaven; the transformation and evolution of Heaven and Earth occurs spontaneously, arising from non-being to being. Heaven is originally without intention; how could it deliberately create the names "Original," "Beneficent," "Advantageous," and "Correct"?

It is simply that the Sages attributed these matters to them, designating this spontaneous efficacy as the four virtues of Heaven. They transmitted this teaching to those below so that future rulers of men might model themselves on what Heaven does; thus, the four virtues were established to provide instruction. "Originality is the foremost of the good. (The *Zhuangzi* says:
"The original virtue of Heaven begins by giving birth to the myriad things. Among the great forms of goodness, none is greater than bestowing life, such as the grace of parents.")

The reason the gravest [offense] arises precisely from this body is that its kindness must not be left unrequited; thus, among the three thousand categories of the five punishments, no crime is greater than filial impiety. Conversely, the blessing of requital through filial piety is likewise the greatest in the world. Therefore, the most filial of all ages have been able to move Heaven and shake the earth.

From this, one knows that that which can produce human life is the highest and supreme good in the world. Thus, Buddhist teaching says: "Building a thousand Buddha-stupas is not equal to saving the life of a single person.

Although all things each have their own place of origin, if one traces them back step by step to the very beginning, one finds that Yang (the Creative) is the primary source of birth. Therefore, Qian (Heaven) is given the name Yuan (the Origin). Thus, one knows that Yuan is the foremost of all goodness. *Heng* (Pronouncement/Success) signifies excellence.
"Meeting" (hui) means that Heaven can penetrate and harmonize all things, causing them to gather together; thus it is so called. "Advantage" (li) is the harmony of righteousness;

Heaven can benefit all species, each attaining its proper suitability and achieving concord. "Constancy" (zhen) is the backbone of affairs; Heaven can, through the qi of central correctness, bring all things to completion, each attaining its own support and sustenance. Master Zhuang’s intention in these four phrases is to clarify the virtue of Heaven:

"Origin" (yuan) is the beginning of things and corresponds to Spring; "Pervasion" (heng) is penetration and corresponds to Summer; "Advantage" (li), as the harmony of righteousness, corresponds to Autumn—since in Autumn things are completed and each accords with its suitability; and "Constancy" (zhen), as the backbone of sustenance, [corresponds to Winter].

At this time, the storage of winter provisions is completed and all affairs are settled. Among the five elemental energies (*pañca-mahābhūta*), only the energy of Earth (*pṛthivī*) is yet deficient; for Earth presides over the four seasonal energies, and it is because the circulation of these four energies cannot be sustained without Earth.

These four energies are none other than the four seasons. From this point onward, it clarifies how the person emulates the celestial operation of these four virtues: "The gentleman embodies benevolence (*ren*); being benevolent, he is like Spring. He is sufficient to lead others;

by embodying the Way of benevolence, extending universal love, and bestowing life, he is sufficient to be honored as a leader among men—this is the emulation of Heaven’s primal virtue (*yuan*). His auspicious assemblies are sufficient to harmonize with ritual (*li*); his benefiting of things is sufficient to accord with righteousness (*yi*). [All these are...]

It may be known from this that "uprightness and firmness are sufficient to manage affairs" (meaning that being upright and firm allows things to be completed and ensures all matters are successfully handled).

When a noble person practices these four virtues—Greatness (*yuan*), Benevolence (*ren*), Pervasiveness (*heng*), Propriety (*li*), Benefit (*li*), Righteousness (*yi*), and Uprightness (*zhen*)—and since wisdom is required for the practice of these four matters, the *Qian Zuodu* states that the two elements of water and earth both incorporate both faith (*xin*) and wisdom (*zhi*).

Therefore it is said: "The Great Ultimate of Qian brings about prosperity, benefit, and uprightness. This concludes the statement made by King Wen when composing the *Yi*, intended to have the noble person emulate it; yet, practicing these four virtues results in a merit equal to that of Heaven. It is not... [the text ends].

The Sage cannot be equated with what is merely called the "Junzi" (Noble Person). This is because while the feudal lords, dukes, and high ministers are all expected to practice these virtues, the Sage alone is able to establish them at their ultimate perfection;

others act according to their respective capacities, and thus each has its own degree of attainment. Since the hexagram Qian (Heaven) takes Heaven as its image, these four virtues are all considered the virtues of Heaven. However, when Yin and Yang conjoin and the two images complement one another, both are capable of possessing virtue; it is not the hexagram Qian alone. Therefore, within the other hexagrams there are also these four virtues.

Yet, because the four virtues of the other hexagrams are all inferior to those of Qian, they each contain supplementary wording—as in the hexagram Kun, which says, "Kun: Yuan, Hong, Li, Zhen; it is advantageous for the female horse to maintain constancy. The hexagram Qian simply speaks of the four virtues directly and says nothing more, in order to manifest the four virtues of Qian.

Virtue is that which encompasses all things. Now, those who use *Qian* (Heaven) as a metaphor for the Buddha do so because *Qian* signifies ceaseless movement and activity—the quintessence of Yang energy—and is not of the same nature as Yin, which is solid and still;
likewise, the Buddha is awakening, which is the wisdom of *bodhi*, and is not of the same substance as *nirvāṇa*, which is solid and quiescent.
Furthermore, the four virtues of *yuan*, *li*, *heng*, and *zhen* are used as metaphors for the four qualities of permanence (*nitya*), bliss (*sukha*), selfhood (*ātman*), and purity (*śubha*).

Although the functions of the Great Ultimate (Taiji) and the Yang are vast and manifold, benefiting all things under heaven without limit, the virtues of its substantial reality consist only of these four;

thus, it fully possesses the Five Constant Virtues (the five constants being benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness). "Originality" (Yuan) is benevolence; "Pervasion" (Heng) is propriety; "Benefit" (Li) is righteousness;

and "Correctness" (Zhen) is trustworthiness. The four virtues taken together are named wisdom. As assigned above, since it fully possesses the Five Constant Virtues, it completely encompasses the core of the Confucian tradition. It also fully possesses the Five Elements: Originality is wood, Pervasion is fire, Benefit is metal, and Correctness is water; earth [is inherent therein].

Because the King [of the seasons] encompasses the four seasons, he synthesizes the four virtues; since these are complete with the five elements, they exhaustively include the arts of yin-yang, divination, auspiciousness, and calamity. Because they possess the four seasons, they encompass one full cycle of the heavens (the zodiac), as assigned above.
The virtues of the Buddha are likewise: although they are immeasurable and boundless, his virtues of substantial reality are likewise only four.
Because of these four, he far transcends the realms of ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, and those of the two vehicles, as explained extensively below. Furthermore, "Gān" (乾) is the general name.
The "Original" (Yuan) and other attributes are distinct virtues; apart from these individual virtues, there is no separate substance of Qian. The Buddha and the four virtues are analogous to this.
The commentary begins with "originating in the One Qi" (One Vital Breath), which investigates the source from which the virtues of this Way of Qian derive.
Originating in the One Qi—this "One Qi" is that upon which the Dao relies, the root of Yin and Yang and of Heaven and Earth. It means that when the Way of Heaven has not yet...
Before the division of yin and yang had dissolved, and prior to the existence of heaven, earth, people, and things, there was only the single, pure primordial qi.
Thus, the *Yi Gouming Jue* states: "That which existed before heaven and earth were divided is called 'one qi' (it is called 'one' because the two—yin and yang—had not yet been divided).

The *Jingming Kai Shu Xu* states: "The single qi was shrouded in obscurity, and black and yellow [the colors of heaven and earth] were not yet distinguished. The *Huayan Xu* states: "At the very beginning of the commencement of creation, the Way of Heaven had not yet been divided. Within this state, transformation subsequently arose.
The Five Transitions (*wǔyùn*)—the term "transition" (*yùn*) refers to the movement of numbers, meaning the alteration of time; it takes the sense of "change" (*yì*) from the *Zhou Yī*—are:

Taiyì (Great Simplicity), Taichū (Great Commencement), Taishi (Great Beginning), Taisu (Great Coarseness), and Taijí (Great Ultimate). When the phenomena of qi and form have not yet been differentiated, it is called Taiyì (this is the very first root of the single qi).

When the primal qi (*yuánqì*) first sprouts, it is called Taichū. When there is the tip of qi and form, it is called Taishi. When form undergoes transformation and possesses substance, it is called Taisu. When substance and form are already [manifested]...

"Equipped with" refers to the transformation of the Great Ultimate (Tàijí) into five; therefore, it is called the "Five Movements" (wù yùn). (From the Great Ease [Tàyì] it transforms into four, and including the original source itself, they are called the Five Movements.
The *Huangting jing* says: "Diverse paths meet in one, returning to the essential end. Liangqiuzi’s commentary states: "They all return to the One Qi.

Thus, the ultimate teachings of both Confucianism and Daoism both take the One as their source. Furthermore, the *Huangting jing* says: "The five elements push against one another, yet their great convergence..."
Furthermore, it is said that "The One" as a thing cannot be fully seen at once. Zhuangzi says, "When one penetrates the One, all things are completed.

He also says, "That from which the One arises is the One, yet it is not yet manifest" (Guo Xiang’s commentary states: "The One is the beginning of existence, the most subtle. Because it is the most subtle, it has not yet taken on the physical forms of principles.

That from which the One arises arises from the Ultimate One; it does not arise from nothingness. That which is not nothingness is the profound and subtle primordial pneuma [qi]"). The *Xici* says, "Of all things under heaven..."

"Movement is fundamentally one. All that is referred to as "one" here refers to *qi* (vital energy). (However, because it is profound, mysterious, and without form, it is called "one"; thus, when Kong [Qiang] explained "one yin and one yang," he said:
"It is void and non-existent, and cannot be distinguished, therefore it is called 'one'"). Therefore, Laozi says: "The profound *qi* serves as harmony" (He Shanggong says:

"Within all things there is primordial *qi*, by which they attain harmony and softness"). Master Zhaor says: "Primordial *qi* is contained within the Great Image; the Great Image is hidden within the Perfect Circle."

Form is the spirit that animates things; within this spirit there is a deity, and within the deity there is a body. The hexagram Qian (Trigram of Heaven) contains the line: "The hidden dragon does not act;
the yang energy is below. The commentary on this states: "The imagery of this single line specifically clarifies the natural qi of Heaven.
Furthermore, the Wenyan (Explanatory Words) says: "The hidden dragon does not act; the yang energy is concealed and stored. This explains the first nine (the first line).
Furthermore, because it refers exclusively to *qi* (vital energy) as the fundamental basis, it is said that "it begins with the One Qi" (concluding the commentary on the *Sūtra*).

Regarding the passage "Constant Joy" (*nitya-sukha*) and below, the two [phrases] correctly clarify the following: although the Buddha’s virtues are immeasurable, these four are specifically pointed out for five reasons:
first, because they are the virtues of the Buddha’s actual substance; second, to distinguish them from the false attachments of ordinary beings regarding permanence.
First, it overturns and refutes the four inversions—such as the impermanence held by the Two Vehicles; second, it is the ultimate fruit of the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness;
third, although the Buddhas have taught immeasurable Dharma-gates, they ultimately do so to manifest this very point;
fourth, the Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa between the four pairs and eight types of trees at the Śāla grove during the second month.
It is solely to manifest this principle that the "attributes of the substantial reality" are first mentioned. The *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states:
"Regarding the self-nature and characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā*), all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas possess neither increase nor decrease.
From the very beginning, its nature has been spontaneously fulfilled with all meritorious qualities; that is to say, its self-nature possesses the great light of wisdom."
Because it clarifies the meaning [of reality], up to the meaning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* and is also called the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata.

Second, regarding the distinction from ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles: because ordinary beings are deluded regarding their own *tathāgatagarbha*, the *dharmakāya*, and *tathatā* as being fundamentally permanent, blissful, self, and pure, they falsely conceptualize the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as being permanent, blissful, self, and pure.

Therefore, in various sūtras, the Buddha instructs the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity, the contemplation of suffering, the contemplation of impermanence, and the contemplation of non-self in order to counteract the grasping at the five aggregates of birth-and-death as permanent, blissful, self, and pure (the above concludes the refutation of the four inversions of permanence, etc., held by ordinary beings).

However, he has not yet revealed the permanence, bliss, self, and purity of the *dharmakāya* which is the object of delusion; thus, although śrāvakas and others receive these teachings and practice accordingly, [they do not realize the ultimate truth].
Even those who have individually realized the fruits [of the path] remain deluded regarding the Dharma-body’s four virtues, such as permanence.

For this reason, the Buddha extensively refuted this view within various Mahāyāna sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Thus, the second fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Sentient beings are likewise;
covered by afflictions and ignorance, they give rise to perverted minds, conceiving of self where there is no self, permanence where there is impermanence, and purity where there is impurity."
To reckon purity as suffering and to regard it as being shrouded by afflictions—though one gives rise to such a notion, one does not comprehend its true meaning.
It is like a drunken man who perceives a non-turning state as turning. (The above is the correct refutation of the two vehicles’ four inversions, such as impermanence.
"Self" is the meaning of the Buddha; "permanence" is the meaning of the Dharma-body; "bliss" is the meaning of Nirvana; and "purity" is...
The Meaning of the Dharma (Correctly Revealing the Four Virtues of Reality): "O bhikṣus, why do you say that there is a notion of self (*ātman*) that transmigrates through birth and death?

If you say that you also cultivate the three notions of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, these three types of cultivation lack true meaning [as they are merely a summary of the impure, yet spoken of as three for the sake of emphasizing the most prominent]. I shall now explain the three superior methods of cultivation: regarding what is suffering, one reckons it to be pleasure."
To perceive pleasure as suffering is an inverted dharma; to perceive the impermanent as permanent and the permanent as impermanent is an inverted dharma;
to perceive the non-self as self and the self as non-self is an inverted dharma; to perceive the impure as pure and the pure as impure is an inverted dharma.
One who possesses such four inverted dharmas does not know how to correctly cultivate all phenomena.
(Above this, the fourfold inversion of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles is concluded. In the world there is permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
in the supramundane there is also permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Worldly dharmas have words but no meaning; supramundane dharmas have both words and meaning. Why is this?
Because worldly dharmas involve inversion, one does not know their true meaning. What is meant by "meaning"? That which is called "selflessness" is the meaning.
That which is the self of birth and death is called the Tathāgata; that which is impermanent refers to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; that which is permanent is the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata;
that which is suffering refers to all non-Buddhists; that which is bliss is Nirvāṇa; that which is impure is conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*);
and that which is pure is the true Dharma possessed by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—this is called being non-erroneous. Because it is non-erroneous...

Therefore, know the words and know their meaning. If you wish to distance yourselves from the four inversions, you should understand that [the Buddha-nature] is thus permanent, blissful, self, and pure (and so forth).
You all should know that the previously practiced perception of impermanence is not the ultimate reality.
It is, for example, like a group of people bathing in a great pond during springtime who lose a lapis lazuli gem; they all enter the water together to search for it.
In search of this treasure, they vied with one another to seize tiles, stones, grass, wood, sand, and pebbles;
each thought they had found a lapis lazuli gem and joyfully carried it out, only to realize it was not the real thing. At that time, the true jewel remained still within the water.
A wise man, employing skillful means, entered the water calmly and slowly, and immediately obtained the pearl. You bhikṣus should not practice in such a manner.
You have practiced the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity as being the ultimate truth;
you should now skillfully learn expedient means and constantly cultivate the perceptions of permanence, self, bliss, and purity in every situation.

Furthermore, you should know that the four types of perceptions previously cultivated were all inverted; those who wish to attain the true reality and cultivate various perceptions should act as follows.

The wise person skillfully extracts the precious jewel, namely the conceptions of self, permanence, bliss, and purity. (This above section, employing both dharma and metaphor, contrasts the four inversions of the two vehicles to further manifest the four virtues.

Below, the śrāvakas challenge the Buddha regarding his prior teaching of the dharma of non-self; the Buddha uses the analogy of the old physician who used milk and the new physician who forbade it, yet later used it again, to illustrate how the non-Buddhists speak of a self, while the Tathāgata refutes the self and then speaks of a self.
The subsequent dharma-parallel states: You should know that the Tathāgata is likewise; having appeared in the world, he subdues the heterodox physicians and non-Buddhists who proclaim—

Regarding the statement that there is no self, person, sentient being, or life-span: when non-Buddhists speak of a "self," it is like insects eating wood until the shapes of characters happen to form.
Therefore, the Buddha proclaimed "no-self" in order to discipline living beings and because he knew the proper time [to teach].

As for those who say there is a self, it is like a skilled physician who knows well the nature of milk; it is not like the "I" or "self" imagined by ordinary people, nor is it like what some call the "Great Self."
Whether it be the size of a thumb, a mustard seed, or a mote of dust, the Tathāgata says that I am not like these at all.
Therefore, he says that all phenomena are without self; yet in truth, they are not without self. What is this "self"?
If a phenomenon is real, true, permanent, sovereign, a refuge, and its nature is unchanging—this is called the self. You should cultivate this fifth [dharma].
The scroll also says: Furthermore, liberation is called "not empty. It is like a jar containing water, wine, ghee, honey, or the like;
even if it lacks water and so forth, it is still called a "water-jar," a "wine-jar," and so on. Liberation is likewise; one cannot say it is empty or non-empty.

"Empty" refers to the absence of the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*) and all afflictions (*kleśa*). [If one considers] all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*) as being like a jar, then without the water, it would be empty.
That which is called "neither empty nor non-empty" refers to the true, virtuous form—eternal, blissful, self, and pure;
it is immovable and unchanging, like the color, fragrance, flavor, and touch of that jar. In the seventh fascicle, the *Tathāgatagarbha-parivarta* also states:
The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "Regarding the four inversions: to give rise to the perception of suffering within what is not suffering—that which is 'not suffering' is named the Tathāgata."

The perception of suffering refers to [the thought]: "The Tathāgata is impermanent and subject to change; having abandoned this body of suffering, he has entered nirvāṇa" (and so forth). [The other three perceptions are treated similarly. It is said:

"In the world it is said that there is no Buddha-nature in the self, but the Buddha-dharma within the self is itself the Buddha-nature" (and so forth). "The Tathāgata is not the physical body of impure food and afflictions.
Kāśyapa said: "From this day forward, I have finally attained right view. Prior to this, we were all called people of false views. (Based on Kāśyapa...)

Master Ye’s statement—that the view of non-self is a false view and the view of self is the correct view—is as follows: Later he further says that teaching sentient beings first to cultivate the view of non-self is for the purpose of eliminating the various deluded views of the world; for the conception of a self is false and not real.

It is like a woman who applies a bitter medicine to her breast so that her child will not drink from it (because the child must avoid milk when taking medicine for an illness). Later, she washes the breast so that the child might drink, yet the child hesitates and does not drink. [Thus it is said.]
It says: "I now also speak of the Tathāgatagarbha... (and so forth). Furthermore, in the thirty-seventh fascicle, it says:
"The Lion’s Roar [Sūtra] states that all phenomena are entirely impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure; it speaks only of the Tathāgata as permanent, blissful, self, and pure.

Based on the numerous repetitions cited above, one knows that permanence, bliss, self, and purity are the ultimate, true virtues of all Buddhas. Throughout the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* as a whole, from beginning to end, these four textual characteristics are extensively analyzed; they are most extensive among all the Mahāyāna teachings of ultimate reality.

The same applies to the vehicle (*yāna*); it is cited here specifically because the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* represents the ultimate consummation of the teachings, wherein provisional means (*upāya*) are subsumed into the reality (*bhūtārtha*).

Thus concludes the preceding explanation of the second intention, which reverses and counters the two sets of four inversions (*viparyāsa*). Third, regarding the ultimate fruit of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*):

"four" refers to contemplating the body as impure, contemplating feelings as suffering, contemplating the mind as impermanent, and contemplating phenomena as selfless. (These four aspects [of practice] appear below in the "Universal Eye" chapter, within the section on the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.)

Regarding the "power of mind" mentioned in the commentary, it is examined and explained briefly as follows: the antidote to the four perversions such as the notion of purity (this applies to the cultivation of both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna).
Furthermore, the *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Contemplate the body as ultimately empty; contemplate feelings as empty internally and externally;

contemplate the mind as non-existent; contemplate phenomena as being merely names. (The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains this in the same way. This serves as the antidote to the four perversions such as the notion of impurity (this is cultivated exclusively by those of the Mahāyāna). These constitute two sets of four perversions.
Once [the body] has been dispatched, its own essence is revealed as being endowed with true reality, permanence, bliss, self, and purity;

therefore, it is called the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya (as in the passage from the *Awakening of Faith* cited previously). Thus, it is said to be the "ultimate fruit. Tiantai says: "Deeply contemplating the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is itself sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);

there is no need for other expedient means, as the capacities [of beings] differ. Therefore, he speaks of the other categories (the "other categories" referring to the four right efforts, etc.), based upon the four foundations of mindfulness.
Since the "foundations" (āyatana) serve as the antidote to the four inversions, their meaning does not differ from the four contemplations discussed in the preceding section;

however, because the four foundations of mindfulness are the foremost among the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and constitute an essential gateway for practice—such that all sentient beings, from the ordinary person to the sage, across both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, cultivate them without exception—the Tiantai school has a separate four-fascicle text on the foundations of mindfulness. Therefore...

As the Buddha, at the time of his parinirvāṇa, left this final exhortation to his disciples, instructing them solely to practice in accordance with this [teaching] (the details of this exhortation are explained extensively in the Introductory Section below), it is for this reason that it is separately designated as a distinct section.
△ Fourth, although all Buddhas have taught immeasurable dharma-gates, they ultimately do so to reveal this very [truth].
As stated in the verse on the fifth stage, the Stage of Ultimate Perfection (*niṣṭhāgata-bhūmi*), within the five stages of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*: "This is precisely..."

The untainted realm is inconceivable (general heading): it is wholesome (*śubha*, meaning pure), eternal (*nitya*, meaning constant), blissful (*sukha*, meaning joy), and liberation (*vimukti*, which is also purity).
This great Muni is named the Dharma-body (*ātman*). Regarding the fifth point, "The Tathāgata was between the *śāla* trees for two months," etc., the thirtieth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Good son, for these reasons, I am here between the twin *śāla* trees."
The Great Master’s Lion’s Roar—this "Lion’s Roar" is named the Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Noble son, those who are "twins" in the east destroy impermanence and attain permanence; and so on, up to those who are "twins" in the north, who destroy impurity and attain purity.
Noble son, herein these sentient beings, for the sake of the twin trees, protect the śāla grove so that outsiders cannot enter.

If people were to take its branches and leaves, cutting and destroying them, I too would act in this same way for the sake of four dharmas, causing my disciples to protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
What are these four? They are permanence, bliss, self, and purity. These four trees are presided over by the Four Heavenly Kings;
I, as the Four Kings, protect and uphold my Dharma. Therefore, it is therein that I enter parinirvāṇa, O son of good family.
The flowers and fruits of the twin *śāla* trees are ever-luxuriant and constantly able to benefit immeasurable sentient beings;
I am also like this, constantly able to benefit śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. "Flowers" is a metaphor for me; "fruits" is a metaphor for bliss.
For this reason, I shall enter great parinirvāṇa here between these twin *śāla* trees. Śāriputra said: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata..."

For what reason is it that the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa in the second month? Good son, the second month is the month of spring warmth, when all things grow and flourish, flowers and fruits bloom in splendor, and the rivers overflow with water.
At this time, sentient beings frequently give rise to the notion of permanence;
therefore, in order to shatter such minds of sentient beings, it is said that all phenomena are universally impermanent, while only the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and unchanging.
In the first month of winter, men are withered and emaciated, and none find joy in them; yet in the harmonious moisture of spring, all people cherish and love it.

To shatter the worldly pleasures of sentient beings, [the Buddha] expounds upon eternal bliss. (The preceding has already explained "bliss"; hereafter, by analogy, he explains "self" and "purity. It is the same for self-purity:
in order to shatter the worldly notion of self and the worldly notion of purity, the Tathāgata speaks of the Tathāgata’s true self and purity, saying: "The second month."
The "not delighting in winter" is a metaphor for the two kinds of *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata, which the wise do not find joyless;

the "entering *nirvāṇa* at the end of the second month" is a metaphor for the wise who cherish and delight in the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity (from this it is known that the Buddha’s passing away in the second month symbolizes permanence, bliss, self, and purity). Thus, the two sets of four inversions (*viparyāsa*) comprise eight inversions in total. Regarding these four...

Since the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) possesses two levels—both essential nature and phenomenal characteristics—it remedies the eight inversions and thus constitutes eight practices.
These ultimately lead to Buddhahood and are termed the "eight virtues. Specifically, the four virtues of the Dharma-body, such as permanence and so forth, are the virtues of reality;

the manifestation of the four virtues of the form-body, such as impermanence and so forth, are the virtues of expedient means (e.g., manifesting impurity by accepting Yaśodharā, manifesting suffering by receiving the golden spear, concealing the eight masteries to manifest non-self, and descending to be born).

[This refers to] the cessation of the manifest, which is impermanence. Therefore, Tiantai said that the four states of withering and four states of flourishing of the twin *śāla* trees precisely represent this.

(The terms "withering" and "flourishing" were established by Tiantai; the text is found in a separately translated version of the scripture. This refers to the form of *dharmatā*. (Speaking according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:

It is truly not pure, yet ordinary beings reckon it as pure—this is called perversion. It is truly not impure, yet the followers of the Lesser Vehicle reckon it as impure—this is also called perversion.
Now, observing that the category of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is itself emptiness, and since within emptiness there is no purity, how could there be defiled attachment?

Thus, the ordinary person’s inversion of purity regarding the *smṛtyupasthāna* of form is shattered, and the category of form is realized as provisional. Through the wisdom of the provisional, it is eternally pure; how could one stagnate in emptiness and grasp at nihilistic extinction by claiming that form is impure?
This is called the two vehicles’ inversion of purity regarding the *smṛtyupasthāna* of form, which is shattered, and the observation of the original limit of form is thereby accomplished.
Neither empty, nor provisional, nor pure, nor impure—this is called the Middle Way. Because the Buddha manifests this principle, he enters *parinirvāṇa* in the middle;

the other three [categories] follow this pattern (one should apply this analogy to the contemplation of sensation, mind, and dharmas as suffering, impermanence, non-self, and so forth). Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha possesses] permanence and the other [three virtues].
However, since these four true virtues are fully present and their meanings differ across the various aforementioned categories, the Commentary enumerates them all in detail, stating: "The Buddha..."

This is its virtue. The commentary states that "based upon one mind" refers to the passage on the four virtues of *tathatā* (Suchness) from the *Awakening of Faith*, which establishes the section on the "Principles" (*lìyìfēn*) where the Master posits "one mind" as the fundamental basis.
Within this, there are two gates: the "Mind-as-Suchness" (*xīn zhēnrú*) and the "Arising-and-Ceasing of Mind" (*xīn shēngmiè*).
The Mind-as-Suchness possesses the four virtues, such as permanence; within the Arising-and-Ceasing of Mind, [the aspect of] the beginning...
Fundamental non-duality constitutes ultimate awakening; this is also the intent of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and other texts.

Thus, one knows that the perversion [of delusion] and the constant [nature of reality], and so forth, are all inseparable from the one mind. The boundless virtues of the Buddha likewise have nothing that is not the one mind.

This is explained at length in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, specifically in the "Praise Verses of the Yama Heaven" chapter, as well as in the initial section on the various manifestations within the "Chapter on Samantabhadra" in this commentary.
All give rise to the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment; this may be verified and described by referring to what is stated in the text.
The commentary specifically addresses the second [section], which clarifies how cultivating the mind achieves its resultant virtue. First, it provides an analogy from the Way of Heaven (*qiandao*):
since the four virtues begin with the One Qi, the cultivation and refinement of the Daoist gate focuses exclusively on the One Qi. As a Daoist scripture says: "Focus the qi to reach..."

Rouyi said: "The primal qi is the spontaneous Great Way; its nature is fundamentally still and silent, and because it is supple and weak, it is able to give rise to movement (as Laozi says, 'stillness is the lord of agitation') and is able to give rise to strength and hardness (and again it says, 'the supple overcomes the hard; the weak overcomes the strong').

Because commoners cannot remain still and silent, nor maintain suppleness and weakness, they deviate from the Way; they cannot preserve their life-span, they cannot accomplish myriad affairs, and they cannot achieve anything."
A ruler of men brings harmony to the world (hence Laozi says: "The violent and overbearing do not die a natural death"; "To be wealthy and noble yet arrogant is to bring calamity upon oneself";

"A whirlwind does not last all morning"; and "Chasing after hunting excites the mind to madness"). Therefore, the person who has attained the Way focuses their will upon stillness and the ultimate softness—the primal qi (as the Master said:
"Be intent upon the Way"). In harmony with the spontaneous Great Way, they apply themselves diligently to its practice and preserve the feminine.

Maintaining weakness with unceasing continuity (therefore, the *Laozi* instructs one to act without relying on it, lead without presiding over it, blunt the sharp and untangle the complex; know the white but maintain the black; do not boast, do not claim merit; appear as if clumsy and slow of speech; embrace the One as a model for the world;

and be like water, which dwells in places loathed by the masses, or like an infant who has not yet begun to smile—all of the above are excerpts from the *Daodejing*. The general principles of both Confucianism and Daoism are likewise so; they need not be cited in full detail).

When the efficacy [of practice] is manifest and culminates in suppleness, it is called "accomplishing the Way" (*chengdao*). (At the time of completion, one returns to the original Way; therefore, the *Daodejing* says:)

Now, all things are in constant flux, yet each returns to its root; returning to the root is called stillness; stillness is called the restoration of the mandate; the restoration of the mandate is called the eternal. It is further said that one returns to the Infinite (wuji). This is like the Buddhist concept of returning to the origin and restoring the source as the ultimate fruit.
When the Way is perfected, one can preserve longevity and accomplish all affairs, nurturing all things. Having conformed to the Way of Qian (Heaven), each thing rectifies its own nature and destiny;
preserving and harmonizing the Great Harmony constitutes "beneficial and firm" (li zhen). Therefore, Laozi says: "The most supple thing in the world..."
It gallops across the most solid things in the world; furthermore, it explains that where there is emptiness, there is utility. By disregarding the body, the body is preserved;

because it never seeks greatness, it is able to achieve greatness. The *Zhouyi*, in the hexagram Qian (Humility), states that humility is like water which can flow downward, and thus the hundred rivers flow into it to form the great ocean. The *Xisheng jing* says that nothing is more yielding and weak than [this].
Among all things, nothing is more yielding and weak than the Dao. It is because the Dao is yielding and weak that it envelops heaven and earth and penetrates through the myriad things.
Is it not the case that while the yielding gives rise to the firm and the weak gives rise to the strong, no one in the world can know the root from which they arise?
(The root is yielding and weakness. According to the various passages cited above, it is said that the Dao is ultimately yielding and weak; therefore—

Now it is said that by concentrating the vital breath (*qi*), one attains suppleness. (Concentrating the vital breath refers to practicing cultivation to attain suppleness for the sake of achieving the Way; this is precisely clarified below when it says "cultivate the single mind to achieve the Way," which corresponds to this passage, differing only in wording.
As for what is called "the One": if we discuss its fundamental nature, it is the primordial breath (*yuanqi*); because it has not yet differentiated between clarity and turbidity, it is called "One.
If we speak in terms of refinement through practice, it is the harmonious breath (*heqi*), referring to the method of fetal breathing (*taixi*) which is continuous and subtle.

If one maintains a state that neither indulges nor suppresses, severing all conditioned activities and ceasing the machinations of the mind, so as to merge with the primordial *qi* and remain free from being too hurried, too slow, too coarse, or too deep—this is called "harmonious *qi*" (*heqi*).

Because the yin *qi* and yang *qi* are harmoniously integrated and non-dual, it is called "one. Thus, the *Daode jing* says: "The profound *qi* serves as harmony" (attaining a harmony of *qi* that is supple, like marrow within the bones). It further says:
The valley spirit does not die; this is called the Mysterious Female (the Yin). The gate of the Mysterious Female is called the Root of Heaven and Earth.

Subtle and continuous, it seems to exist, yet its use never exhausts itself. It is further said: "Can one embrace the One and not depart from it? (The 'One' is the vital essence of the Grand Harmony produced at the beginning of the Dao.

Can one concentrate the breath until it reaches suppleness? (Master He Shang Gong’s commentary states: 'To concentrate the vital essence so that it is not disordered, then the physical form will respond to things with flexibility and compliance. Can one be like an infant?"

Furthermore, it says: "To employ the mind to drive the vital energy (qi) is called 'stoutness' (*jiāng*). When the mind is focused and unified, the spirit-energy (*shénqì*) is substantial within; this is called 'weakness and suppleness. To employ the mind to drive the vital energy causes the harmonious breath (*héqì*) to depart from the center;

this is called 'stoutness and overbearing' (*jiāngliáng*). The commentary explains: "The upper term 'supple' and the lower term 'stout' can be explained in contrast to gain and loss. As stated above, to deviate from the Dao and be stout is one thing, while to accord with the Dao and be supple is another.

This is what is meant by "deep roots and firm stems" (where people take the vital energy as the root and the essence as the stem). Furthermore, it says: "Heaven attained the One and became clear," and so forth [referring to the passage: "Earth was tranquil, the spirits were efficacious, the valleys were full, the myriad things were born, and the lords and princes were set right"].

Therefore, the sage embraces the One as a model for the world. As Zhuangzi says: "Unify one's nature (for if it is embellished, it becomes dual); nourish one's vital energy (not allowing the mind to direct it);

harmonize one's virtue (not allowing external things to separate one from one's nature). The *Neijing Jing* of the *Huangting* says: "Divergent paths meet at one point (all returning to the single vital breath); returning to the essential, one's will culminates in the One.
Before long, one ascends to the void (if one studies the Way with single-mindedness and shares the same substance as the void, then the state of a transcendent can be attained). It further says:

"In the *Zhengyi*, the inner flower is contained and thus fills [the body] (by preserving the Correct and guarding the One, the spirit and breath flourish). Master Zhaoming said: 'Guarding the True and restraining the One, one is not stained by external things;
how could there be any loss in this Great Unity of pure emptiness? The *Commentary on the Appended Phrases* says: 'As for Qian, when it is still, it is focused;
when it moves, it is direct' (directness is correctness). The explanation states: All the passages cited above pertain to the gates of cultivation in Confucianism and Daoism, focusing on..."

To take the breath as the essential and subtle meaning [is the method]; (those footnotes are all from their respective original commentaries: the commentary by He Shang Gong on the *Laozi*, that by Guo Xiang on the *Zhuangzi*, that by Han Kangbo on the *Xici*, and that by Liangqiu Zi on the *Huangting Jing*).

Commentary: First, a general introduction; second, the correct elucidation of the virtues of the Buddha-fruit. Since these virtues are fundamentally rooted in the one mind, if one does not cultivate the one mind but instead cultivates separately, how could one achieve the Buddha-way?
It would be like polishing a brick to produce a clear mirror or smelting iron to obtain true gold—it is impossible.
Therefore, the Great Master Qingliang taught that the myriad practices are all inseparable from the mind; it is simply a matter of awakening to it.
To realize that what appears to one’s own mind is ultimately pure is the perfection of the myriad practices within a single thought-moment.

That the mind does not arise is *śamatha* (calm abiding); knowing that it does not arise is *vipaśyanā* (insight). Not being conditioned by the myriad objects is *tyāga* (renunciation); the non-arising of delusion is *śīla* (precept); settling the mind in the principle of reality is *kṣānti* (patience);
the uninterrupted continuity of the mind is *vīrya* (diligence); the essence of the mind being free from thought is *dharma* (the teaching). This is the mind—

Original enlightenment is the Buddha; the non-contradiction of essence and attributes is the Sangha. Because the Six Perfections and the Three Jewels are unified within the one mind, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"When Bodhisattvas cultivate all Buddha-dharmas, purify all Buddha-fields, accumulate sublime practices, and discipline sentient beings, up until the attainment of great bodhi, none of these are apart from the mind. Therefore, one should assist one's own mind with wholesome dharmas.
One should make one’s own mind firm through diligence; one should make one’s own mind expansive through patience; one should bind one’s own mind to purity through the realization of wisdom;
one should make one’s own mind clear and sharp through insight; one should develop one’s own mind through the sovereign power of the Buddha;
one should make one’s own mind vast and equal through the Buddha’s equanimity; and one should examine one’s own mind with the illumination of the Buddha’s ten powers. Furthermore—
It is said that a Bodhisattva should know that their own mind is constantly and at every moment attaining perfect enlightenment as a Buddha. Why is this?
Because all Buddhas and Tathāgatas attain perfect enlightenment without departing from this very mind; as it is with one's own mind, so it is with the minds of all sentient beings.
Based on the aforementioned passage, we know that to achieve the Way of Buddhahood, one must necessarily cultivate the "one-mind" (ekacitta). As for the term "one":
The Treatise states: "The True Suchness of the mind is precisely the essence of the Great Universal Dharma-gate of the Single Dharma-realm;

that is to say, the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished. This universal mind of the total characteristic permeates both ordinary beings and sages, and because it does not differentiate between cause and effect or defilement and purity, it is called "one."

The phrase "the mind that is the essence" (*śūcitta*) refers to the following eight points which correctly reveal [the nature of the mind]: First, the general enumeration: "Mind" refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*, the intrinsically pure mind (*svabhāva-viśuddha-citta*).
Generally speaking, there are four types of "mind," each with distinct Sanskrit terms and different translations:

1. *Hṛdaya*: This refers to the physical heart, the lump of flesh. 2. That which is named "mind" due to its cognitive deliberation (*ālambana-manasikāra*): This refers to the eight consciousnesses, as all of them possess the capacity for cognitive deliberation.

Because it takes itself as its object, it is called *saṃcita* (accumulated); this refers to the mind that arises from accumulation, namely the eighth consciousness, because it gathers all seeds and gives rise to active manifestations (*pravṛtti*).
Fourth, *kharatva* (solidity) refers to the "firm and solid" mind; it is this which is being discussed here.

The commentary states that "profound emptiness" (*chōng-hū*)—the latter two characters directly manifest this profundity—is deep and mysterious. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra Preface* says, "Vast and profound, profoundly harmonious," and also says, "It encompasses and contains what is profoundly deep.
The commentary further notes that because it is profoundly deep and broadly inclusive, the *Laozi* says, "The Way is profound and yet when used it is never exhausted;
it is empty, for it has no substantial form. Thus, as for being "wondrous," it is stained yet unstained, like a lotus flower which—though [growing in the mud]...
Because it is not defiled by the mud, it is likened to the Sublime Dharma (*saddharma*). Tiantai’s commentary explains that there are ten meanings of "sublime" (*miao*).
In the *Tianchang Shu*, the commentary on "sublime" states: "That which is neither coarse nor sublime is alone named the 'Ultimate Sublime'. Therefore, the subsequent text says:

"The various illusory transformations arise from the Tathāgata’s Perfectly Awakened Sublime Mind. "Pure" (*cui*) means refined and pristine; "brilliantly manifest" (*binghuàn*) refers to all [phenomena] being thus.

The characteristic of ultimate clarity is one of brilliant and radiant manifestation; thus, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* Commentary’s Preface, in describing the "Gate of Subtle Interpenetration and Stable Establishment" among the Ten Profound Gates (*daśa-gambhīra-mukha*), states: "They manifest simultaneously in brilliance, like mustard seeds in a jar.
This intends to convey a state that is vividly distinct and free from confusion. The *Analects* says, "Brilliant indeed are its patterns," and the commentary explains: "Huan means bright."

Regarding "spiritually luminous" (*lingming*): if one were to speak merely of "luminosity," it would not distinguish it from the light of the sun and moon; therefore, the term "spiritual" (*ling*) is used.

The intended meaning is that the luminosity of the mind is such that there is no phenomenon it does not know, yet it is free from discrimination; there is no phenomenon it does not manifest, yet it is free from differentiation.
It is profoundly spiritual, divine, tranquil, and penetratingly clear; thus it is called "spiritually luminous. It is precisely this spiritual luminosity that shines forth with brilliance.
Brilliantly radiant.
The commentary states that "without going" means that the three vertical [dimensions] are free from both going and coming;

this refers to the fact that this mind does not migrate forward toward the past limit, nor does it come from the future limit, nor does it abide in the present. That which abides in the present consists of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Because it is the Dharma, the *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) states: "Abiding indicates that this dharma has temporary utility.

Now, this is not like that, for this true mind is without marks and lacks the distinction between subject and object; thus, it cannot be perceived in the present. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"It is only by way of enumeration that one speaks of the three periods of time; it does not mean that bodhi has past, future, or present. This is truly because bodhi is also...

Being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it is identical to the true mind (*tathatā-citta*); therefore, it does not belong to the three periods of time. If one considers the characteristic of bodhi itself, it has a beginning but no end.

How could one avoid [the problem of] the initial limit being darkly pervasive throughout the three limits? It is because it does not belong to the three limits that it is universally pervasive in all of them.
Furthermore, the reason why the visual consciousness of today cannot see the forms of yesterday is that whatever forms are perceived, they all fall into [the category of conditioned phenomena].

The past has already passed away; now, because the true mind does not follow the shifting of phenomena toward the past, within this present moment, it can clearly manifest the images of all phenomena of the future limit, and it can also pre-manifest the phenomena of the future with distinct clarity.
Although it thus penetrates the three periods of time, when sought within those three periods, it is entirely unobtainable. This is because... [it is] without object.
Because the manifested objects of the three periods of time are known to be indivisible, they are said to be "dark" (*ming*). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) pervades all places; all sentient beings and lands throughout the three periods of time are entirely contained within it, without exception.
Furthermore, no form or characteristic can be apprehended. The first three phrases apply universally across the three periods, while the final phrase refers to dark, seamless integration.
The commentary states that "neither within nor outside" and "pervasive horizontally" means it is neither within nor outside. There are two intentions behind this:
first, it does not exist within the body, in between, or outside the body. If it were within the body or in between, it would have a specific location;
if it were outside the body, it would not be my mind. Since none of the three—body, sense-object, or consciousness—can be apprehended, how could there be "inside," "outside," or "in between"?
"Non-dual" means that this mind is neither of the two extremes of existence or non-existence; because the two external extremes have been discarded, the middle way also vanishes.
Thus it is neither middle nor extreme—it is the absolute, numinous mind. This "non-middle" does not mean that it is not the middle; rather, it means that it is not [limitedly defined as] the middle.
As for "non-external," it does not mean that it is not external; rather, it means that it is not [limitedly defined as] external.
It is not that one who penetrates the ten directions externally has a mind that is present in some places and absent in others;

because it has no place of presence, it has no place of absence, and thus it penetrates the ten directions. Regarding the two characters "penetrating" (dòngchè), their general meaning does not differ.

However, when contrasted with the term "mystically penetrating" (míngtōng), the syntactic force of the two phrases differs slightly: it means to be transparently and thoroughly permeated without obstruction.

The fact that [the term] "pervasive" (*biàn*) is not used here is intended to clarify that it refers to a definitive, total pervasion of the entire substance, rather than being a casual or expedient expression.

Furthermore, although the terms "mysterious" (*míng*) and "penetrating" (*dòng*) are each mutually abbreviated within their respective phrases, both are fully present; thus, it is not precluded from also stating, for example, "mysteriously communicating with the ten directions" (*míng tōng shīfāng*) or "penetratingly comprehending the three periods of time" (*dòng chè sānjiè*).

The commentary states that "below 'non-extinction' [it refers to] the five truly constant [factors] which are neither born nor extinguished. This is because the true mind is unchanging, and thus it is neither born nor extinguished.

The *Awakening of Faith* says: "That which is called the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished. However, regarding this non-birth and non-extinction, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are not the same:

the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) has no substance and thus can be born and extinguished; the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) is such that it is born yet not born, and extinguished yet not extinguished.

The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) exists as its own essence from the beginning; it does not depend on new production, but remains ultimately and eternally constant throughout the limits of the future, never ceasing or perishing. It is precisely this that is "neither produced nor destroyed by nature.

Unlike the former two natures, if the three natures are considered in relation to one another according to their respective characteristics, then the phenomena of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) are falsely produced and falsely destroyed, whereas the perfected nature...

The true mind is neither arising nor ceasing. Dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) has two aspects: its appearance is identical to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), thus appearing to arise and appear to cease;

its essence is identical to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), thus being neither arising nor ceasing. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "All phenomena are without arising; all phenomena are without ceasing," and so forth.
This is because dependent nature lacks a separate self-nature and is therefore entirely identical to the perfected nature. Thus it is taught in all Mahāyāna sūtras.
That all phenomena (*dharmas*) are neither born nor extinguished, but are quiescent and eternally abiding—all such meanings refer to this. How could they be harmed by the four mountains?
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 29, states: "As I previously told King Prasenajit: 'Great King, suppose there were a trusted person of yours who came from each of the four directions, each saying:

"Great King, four great mountains are coming from the four [directions]...'"* (The text continues with the description of the king's fear and the Buddha's reassurance)."* (Note: The provided source text is incomplete; the translation reflects the available portion.)

"Your Majesty, these are about to come and harm the people; if Your Majesty hears this, what plan will you devise? The King said, "World-Honored One, even if they were to come, there would be no place to escape;
I can only focus my mind on upholding the precepts and practicing generosity. I then praised him, saying, "Excellent, Great King!
What I call the 'four mountains' are precisely the birth, aging, sickness, and death of sentient beings. Birth, aging, sickness, and death constantly come."

Regarding the phrase "how can all people [be harmed]": Great King, you do not cultivate giving and precepts; how is it that you now cause harm? This is because the sutra states, "desiring to harm the people.
If one follows the phrasing of the sutra, the standard expression would be "birth, old age, sickness, and death constantly come to harm all people.
In this case, one should instead say: "How could the four characteristics possibly harm them? This interpretation is also applicable.

Regarding "separation from nature" (*li-xing*) in the six lines below: "separation from nature and separation from characteristics" means that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are empty—this is "nature," as in "form is itself emptiness.
"Phenomena arising through conditions" refers to "characteristics," as in "emptiness is itself form.
Now, although the True Mind is empty and contains not a single thing, its essence is not empty; therefore, while it is "separated from nature," it follows conditions to manifest as all things.

The various phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) do not have form as their essence; because they are free from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and free from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are called the Middle Way and true reality (*tattva*).
How could the five colors cause blindness? "How" means that the five colors can indeed blind; as the *Daodejing* says:

"The five colors cause the eyes to go blind" (if one covets lust and delights in beauty, it injures the vital essence and leads to loss of sight). "The five sounds cause the ears to go deaf" (if one delights in listening to the five sounds, then...).

When the breath departs, the mind can no longer hear the sound of silence. Regarding the five colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and black—and the five musical notes—gong, shang, jiao, zhi, and yu—the text cites these as the primary colors and primary tones;
all others may be understood by analogy. Now, the meaning of this commentary is as follows:
that which can cause blindness through color can only blind the consciousness that perceives color. The true mind, being free from marks, does not engage with color.
Regarding that, how could one be blind? When facing forms, form is itself emptiness; who then could be blind?

In the Way of the Teachings, taking non-being and stillness as the Way and forgetting emotions and severing wisdom as cultivation, one regards forms and listens to sounds as being blind and deaf, thereby losing the Way.
Now, the true mind is detached from nature and does not stagnate in empty nothingness; therefore, when seeing forms and hearing sounds, sound and form cannot blind it.
To obscure it is like a mirror clearly manifesting forms; what could obscure its clarity?

In the section on the "seven unchanging states" arising from the preceding, within each of the two pairs of four-line sets, the first line indicates the principle (*dharma*) and the second line clarifies it through analogy.
Because sentient beings have been drifting and drowning in beginningless birth and death, they are like a stream that is boundless and bottomless.
Therefore, just as the ocean is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), Nirvāṇa is the "Heavenly One" (*deva*) who transcends to the further shore;

thus there is the expression "the Heavenly One of the Shore. As for the "Black Dragon Pearl" (*li-zhu*): beneath the chin of the black dragon is a bright moon-like jewel whose radiance is transparent and penetrating.

Although it is within the ocean, its radiance does not perish. This is unlike a lamp or candle, which perishes upon entering the water; yet, while this pearl cannot illuminate the entire ocean, [Nirvāṇa] does so.
Because all things within it are [identical], it is called the "Solitary Radiance. Although sentient beings dwell amidst birth and death, this luminous mind is never obscured;

yet they are deluded and do not realize it. Because they do not realize it, they cannot penetrate all things. It merely illuminates its own essence, standing alone like a solitary pearl radiating light.
Thus, Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty composed the inscription for the Great Master Bodhidharma to express this intended meaning.
It is said that within the vast ocean there is a pearl of the black dragon, white as a hair-tuft, which neither heaven can see nor man can recognize;
my Great Master has obtained it. "Cang" (Calm Sea) describes the depth, breadth, mystery, and distance of the water; "tian" (Heaven) describes its azure hue, its loftiness and remoteness.
To "sit upon the shore of Nirvana" means that Nirvana—here translated as "Perfect Quiescence"—is the emptiness of all dharmas.
The mind is fundamentally without thought; it merges into the single true essence (*dharmatā*), which is without distinction.
Because it is free from the clamor and agitation of birth and death, the true mind is perfect and entirely quiescent. To "sit" (*ju*) means to dwell in a state of composure and ease.

Therefore, people of the time all referred to arrogance and haughtiness as "haughty sitting. The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "From afar he saw his father sitting upon a lion throne, with a precious desk supporting him..."
Zu Kuo said: "If it were not for the Master who is the Transformation Lord of the Lotus Treasury, who could occupy its source? 'The cassia wheel' refers to the moon;
because there is a cassia tree within the moon, it is called the 'cassia wheel. 'The azure sky' refers to a clear autumn night when there are no clouds or mist, so that only the azure color is seen.
This is like the Sky of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-dhātu*), which, being free from the clouds and mist of all delusions and karma, is thus metaphorically called the 'azure sky.'"
When all phenomena are empty and quiescent, the fundamental awakening of the mind—the great wisdom-light—shines universally throughout the Dharma-realm, free from all discrimination;
thus it is said to be "solitary and radiant. Like the moon in the clear blue sky, there is nowhere it does not illuminate.

Therefore, when the mind is perfectly still, it is like the moon in the heavens, unlike a pearl in the sea. Furthermore, as previously stated, the term "solitary" refers only to the state of delusion.

It is able to illuminate itself but cannot universally illuminate all things; thus it is now called "solitary. This refers to the clear autumn sky where only the moon universally illuminates the world, while stars, lamps, and candles are all unsuitable as analogies.
Such wisdom, which is identical to the essence [of the mind], cannot be compared to the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādikṣaṇika-bodhi*) that functions through opposition.
"Great indeed!"—the following eight instances of "Great indeed! are words of reverent admiration, following the stylistic conventions of the *I Ching* (Book of Changes).
Sometimes they appear above the object of admiration, such as: "Great indeed! The Primordial Purity of Qian; all things receive their beginning from it," and "Great indeed!
Qian! It is firm, vigorous, central, and correct; its essence is pure and refined. Sometimes they appear below the object of admiration, as in: "Qian initiates... and so forth.
"It is able to benefit the world with beautiful benefits without speaking of what it benefits—how great this is! It is also said, "The principle of responding to the times is how great it is!
Furthermore, the *Xici* says, "Exalted virtue and great enterprise reach the ultimate! These are all such examples. Now, combining these two perspectives, I shall briefly describe this mind:
vertically exhausting the three periods of time and horizontally pervading the ten directions; among all phenomena, there is nothing that it does not encompass.
Because its thorough penetration and exposition are inexhaustible, he concludes with a eulogy, saying, "How great it is!

Furthermore, wishing to describe below the nature and characteristics of this mind that gives rise to the myriad dharmas—its unimpeded, profound, and vast virtue—he marks the beginning with the eulogy, "How great it is!
The phrase "the source of all dharmas" precisely clarifies that this mind does not abide in its own nature, but arises in accordance with conditions throughout the world.
This refers to all phenomena, both defiled and pure. For now, we shall first clarify how delusion regarding this true mind results in the formation of out-flowing (sāsrava) defiled dharmas;

subsequently, based on the commentary text that follows, we will reveal that this mind—in its state of being free from inversion—is inherently endowed with ocean-like meritorious qualities and wondrous functions, where essence and characteristics are non-obstructive, and is fundamentally an out-flow-free (anāsrava) dharma. First, regarding the "defiled": although all sentient beings...

This inherently pure mind has, since beginningless time, been deluded and remained unaware of itself (this refers to "fundamental non-awakening" in the *Śāstra*, which is synonymous with "independent ignorance" (*mūla-avidyā*) in the sense of being deluded regarding Reality;

as the *Śāstra* says: "Because one does not know the Dharma of True Suchness as it truly is," etc.). Consequently, one falsely identifies the four elements and the objects of discursive thought as one's own body and mind (as stated in the subsequent text:
"Falsely identifying the four elements," etc.). Thus, there arise successively the primary and secondary branches, and the secondary and tertiary branches, each arising in its own right. First:
First, due to fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), various afflictions (*kleśa*) arise; second, due to afflictions, various karmas are created;
third, due to the maturation of karma, one undergoes the various retributions of birth and death within the six realms.

The *Buddhanāmasūtra* states that "independent ignorance serves as the seed of affliction," and further says: "These three obstacles are mutually dependent; it is because of affliction [that the other two arise]."
Because one gives rise to evil karma, and by virtue of the causes and conditions of that evil karma, one obtains bitter fruits. First, regarding those who give rise to afflictions from ignorance:
to briefly explain the coarse characteristics of these afflictions, they are simply greed, hatred, and delusion.
