The Āgamas and other sūtras of the Hīnayāna constitute the second period; therein, based on the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature), the emptiness of all phenomena is taught, yet the *paratantra* (dependent) and *pariniṣpanna* (perfected) natures are not yet said to exist—this is called the "Teaching of Emptiness," namely the various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras.

During the third period, the Mahāyāna of the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena) is taught, wherein the emptiness of objects and the existence of the mind are established; this is called the "Middle Way Teaching."

The *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other such sūtras belong to the fourth period, in which the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are revealed to all sentient beings, and the three vehicles are unified into a single vehicle;
this unification of provisional means into the ultimate reality is called the teaching of "converging in the same destination," namely the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

The fifth period consists of the teachings spoken at the time of his imminent entry into nirvāṇa, wherein it was declared that all sentient beings, even down to the icchantikas, possess Buddha-nature.
All those with a mind will certainly attain Buddhahood; that which is named the teaching of "permanence, bliss, self, and purity" (nitya-sukha-ātma-śubha) is the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Because it brings a single class of practitioners to fulfillment from beginning to end, it is collectively termed the "Gradual Teaching.

Regarding the phrase "emptiness and existence manifest alternately," "alternately" means in succession. This refers to [the treatment of] the self and dharmas, mind and objects, or the ultimate and conventional truths, whether presented sequentially or...

At the same time, they mutually manifest the meaning of the emptiness and existence of all phenomena. Furthermore, regarding the objects and mind of the initial [teachings], there are two pairs of emptiness and existence: first, in the teachings of the first period, both object and mind exist;
second, in the teachings of the second period, both object and mind are empty (the former two are sequential and mutual).

Third, in the teachings of the third period, the object is empty while the mind exists (simultaneous and mutual). As for the distinction between the ultimate and conventional truths, it is as follows: *Note: The original text contains a structural outline regarding the three periods of teaching and their respective presentations of emptiness and existence.*
The "four propositions" refer to the teaching of the second period, which holds that conventional existence is empty of true reality;

and the teachings of the fourth and fifth periods, which hold that conventional existence is empty while true reality exists (because they refute the worldly permanence, bliss, self, and purity, yet reveal the supramundane permanence and so forth). Thus, the Sūtra says: "That which is empty is saṃsāra; that which is not empty is nirvāṇa.

Regarding the teaching of the third period, the four levels of the two truths are viewed in relation to one another as alternating between emptiness and existence. When the teachings of the second and third periods are compared, the "true reality" of the second period [is seen as empty by the standard of the third].

Regarding the third period, where both the conventional and the ultimate are empty, there are likewise four propositions concerning the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*) based on their presence or absence:

First, in the teachings of the initial period, those of the *deva* and *manuṣya* vehicles hold that both self and phenomena exist. Second, in the intermediate period of the Mahāyāna, both self and phenomena are empty.

Third, in the initial stage of the Hīnayāna, the self is empty while phenomena exist. Finally, in *nirvāṇa*, the self exists while phenomena are empty. [That sutra refutes the Hīnayāna notion of non-self and explicitly explains the ultimate truth.]
Therefore, in the preceding section, there were ten pairs concerning both emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence (*bhāva*), which were presented alternately by way of both phenomena (*dharma*) and time;

thus it is said they "alternately manifest" one another. (Although the relative opposition of emptiness and existence is discussed further below, those who lack the power of mind need not be recounted here. Regarding the determination of depth and shallowness in the various teachings that speak of emptiness and existence:
for example, when speaking of external objects, if one compares the first and second periods of the teaching, one exists while the other does not.

Regarding the profundity and shallowness of the two emptinesses (*śūnyatā*), if one speaks of the dependent origination (*paratantra*) of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), there are two pairs:

first, the comparison between the teachings of the second and third turnings; second, the comparison between the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Among these, the latter is shallow and the former is profound.

Third, when comparing the first, third, fourth, and fifth [turnings], the former is existent and the latter is empty, such that the latter is profound and the former is shallow. If one speaks of the self (*ātman*), when comparing the first and last [turnings], the former is empty and the latter is existent.
The emptiness [taught] here is shallow, while that which follows is deep; all other instances of emptiness and existence, whether deep or shallow, should be understood by this analogy.

Consequently, various teachings may either refute existence and praise emptiness, or disparage emptiness and praise existence. Without grasping this intent, it is difficult to understand the sacred words.

Regarding the statement "the two truths are suddenly non-dual," this reveals the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the Middle Way. There are two explanations for the ultimate truth: first, their mutual integration.

In clarity, the ultimate (paramārtha-satya) and the conventional (saṃvṛti-satya) are mutually identical and non-dual; this is precisely the primary meaning (paramārtha). Thus, the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* states:

"Regarding the truths, they are always two (the ultimate and the conventional); regarding their realization, they are always one (the ultimate is identical to the conventional, and the conventional is identical to the ultimate).

To penetrate this non-duality of truth is to enter the primary meaning. As an ancient said: "The two truths are neither separate nor dual; they are eternally divergent yet never distinct; they are two yet always a unity."

The "obliteration of both the manifest and the hidden" means that it is neither true nor conventional, but is simply the numinous mind (therefore, Tiantai says it is "simultaneously illuminating and simultaneously negating");

this refers to the phrase below, "the profound numen is beyond all dependence. Furthermore, regarding "neither true nor conventional," there are two meanings: first, because they mutually negate one another.

This means that because the conventional is identical to the true, the conventional is obliterated; and because the true is identical to the conventional, the true perishes. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "In non-existence there is no existence."
Neither duality nor non-duality exists; all three periods of time are empty—this is the Dharma of all Buddhas.
Because it reveals the essence, when one says it is not "true," it means it is neither true nor false; it is likewise neither mundane nor supramundane.
Since it is neither of those two, it is the luminous essence itself, profound, subtle, and wondrously mysterious, beyond the reach of thought. Therefore, it is so described.

The "insentient spirit" (*lingxin*) is absolute and beyond dependence. To explain this extensively, one should consult the third section of the *Xuantan* (Prolegomena), specifically within the discussion on the fivefold distinctions of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as contrasted with the School of Characteristics (*xiangzong*).
Therein, the analogies of the mirror and its reflection, as well as the principles regarding the contemplation of the absolute insentient spirit, are set forth.

Furthermore, regarding the "mutual negation" (*shuangmin*), this merely negates the "truth" (*zhen*) that is opposed to the conventional; it does not negate the essence of truth itself, and thus it may also be termed [the ultimate].
Because it is not the two truths and is beyond all dependence, an ancient said: "A pair of solitary wild geese fly high, sweeping the ground;
two mandarin ducks stand alone by the edge of the pond.

[The Commentary] Now, below this, the second section separately sets forth the purport of this sutra, which has three parts. First, the establishment of the fundamental principle (*mūla-tattva*): Now that the one *piṭaka* of scriptures...
There are no teachings other than the sudden and the gradual; we shall now each point to their respective categories.

As for the gradual, it begins at the Deer Park and ends at the Crane Grove, spanning the three periods and five phases from beginning to end. It gradually leads one class of practitioners from start to finish;

therein, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa* assemblies bring provisional teachings back to the ultimate reality. This is the final teaching within the gradual Mahāyāna. As for the sudden...
Second, the sudden mode of teaching (*ikāya*) consists of two types: first, the sudden teaching according to the nature (*dharmatā*), which refers to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

At the time of his initial attainment of Buddhahood, the Buddha taught the principles and phenomena, their root and branches, their beginning and end, and their cause and effect all at once, exhausting the ultimate principle and fully realizing the nature. Second, the sudden teaching according to capacity, which refers to those of superior faculties who are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) complete in their potential;
for them, he suddenly points directly to the absolute, non-relative Middle Way and true nature, which differs from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Mahāparinirvāṇa* sūtras and their like.
There are three [teachings] that may be sublated and provisional means that may be reconciled;

yet, when the single true nature of awakening is revealed—namely, in over forty scriptures such as the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra*, the *Vajrasamādhi-sūtra*, the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, the *Samantaprabhā-garbha-sūtra*, and the *Mahāyāna-śrī-mahā-saṃnipāta-parivarta-bodhicitta-prakṛti-prabhāsvara-viśuddhi-sūtra*—they all speak little of phenomenal circumstances and directly expound the true nature, the principle, and the wisdom. This is because there are no [provisional] "three carts," "removal of filth," or "false city" [expedients].
Because it takes as its object that which can be realized, this sutra is indicated as belonging to the category of the Sudden;

however, this is the Sudden in terms of revealing the essence according to the capacities of beings, not the Sudden in terms of the formal mode of transformation. Since it is not a gradual teaching, it does not belong to the three periods or five periods.

Regarding the "Land of Tranquil Light" (*śāntaprabhāsa-kṣetra*): Master Tiantai established four lands: (1) the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages (also called the Land of Transformation); (2) the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder;

"Entering the Great Radiant Treasury of Supernatural Powers (*abhijñā-mahāprabhā-kośa*), in the right reception of samādhi (*samādhi-samāpatti*)," and so on, up to "conforming to non-duality.
Therefore, this is the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhā-bhūmi*). Regarding the phrase "the single source of ordinary and holy beings," the text says: "The light of all Tathāgatas..."

The Venerable Abbot [comments]: (Since all Buddhas are identical in this regard, it is the Dharma-nature land, which is also the Self-Enjoyment Land; for in this school, principle and wisdom are not distinct. He further states: "This is the ground of pure awakening of all sentient beings.

In the commentary, the section beginning with "Mañjuśrī" has two parts: first, the introduction; second, the exposition of the main teaching. Regarding the first, "True Faith and Understanding": *Mañjuśrī* is the correct Sanskrit name for Wen-shu (文殊);
the meaning of its name and virtues is explained in the commentary below. In the commentary, the term "Mahāsattva" refers to the Dharma...

Regarding the phrase "the Great Being (Mahāsattva) of the body," the commentary begins by inquiring into the cause of the original arising (*mūla-utpāda*). "Original" (*chuàng*) here carries the meaning of "the very beginning.
There are two senses to this "original": first, that before the various bodhisattvas had questioned Mañjuśrī, he was asked first; since no one had previously asked this, it is called "original.
Second, the matter being questioned is the primary and essential doctrine to be understood at the very outset within the stages of the Buddha-dharma.
Prior to this Dharma, there is no further meaning of the Buddha-dharma’s cause and effect that could serve as the essential point for its initial arising;
therefore, the commentary states that "the original arising" refers to the very first mind arisen from the original cause.

Other meanings should be sought in the lower sections of the commentary, such as the *Awakening of Faith*, the two types of awakening (*bodhi*), the arousal of the three minds, the cultivation of the five practices, and the *Avataṃsaka*’s Sudhana, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*’s Dharma-practice, and so forth.
Regarding the term *bhagavat*, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: "Thus have I heard: at one time, the Bhagavat...
The commentary explains that the word *bhagavat* operates according to six meanings: first, the meaning of sovereignty; second, the meaning of brilliance;
third, the meaning of majesty; fourth, the meaning of renown; fifth, the meaning of auspiciousness; and sixth, the meaning of nobility. As it is said in a verse:
It is said: "Mastery, brilliance, majesty, renown, glory, and nobility—one should know that these six distinct meanings are collectively termed *Bhagavān*.
Since all Tathāgatas possess all of these in every respect and are never separated from them, the Tathāgata is called *Bhagavān*. What is the meaning of this? It refers to..."

Because the Tathāgata is forever unbound by any afflictions, he possesses the sense of mastery; because he has been refined and tempered by the fiercely blazing fire of wisdom, he possesses the sense of brilliance;
because he is adorned with the thirty-two excellent major marks, he possesses the sense of majestic dignity;
because all supreme qualities are perfected and there is nothing he does not know, he possesses the sense of renown throughout all worlds.
Because he is constantly approached, served, and praised by all, he possesses the meaning of auspiciousness;
because he always exerts skillful means to benefit and bring peace to all sentient beings without weariness or negligence, he possesses the meaning of nobility.
"Supreme" (*śrī*) refers to the most venerable and the ultimate honor. Furthermore, just as the myriad subjects serve the king, and the king serves the Supreme Deity (*Īśvara*).
"Supreme God" (Shangdi) refers to the Heavenly Lord (Devendra). All the heavens, as well as the worthy and holy ones of the Three Vehicles who revere the Buddha, also serve the Buddha.

The Buddha is the most honored among all sages, just as the moon is supreme among the stars, the ocean is supreme among all streams, and the Buddha is supreme among all sages; therefore, he is called the "Most Honored One" (Zhizun).
In the commentary (*shu*), the term "firstly" (*shouti*) means to raise up at the beginning. "Ultimate fruition" (*jiujing guo*) refers to the direct answer within the sutra.

The initial heading states: "Good sons, the Unsurpassed Dharma King possesses a great *dhāraṇī* gateway named Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), from which flow forth all pure *tathatā*, *bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, and the *pāramitās*, thereby instructing bodhisattvas.
Regarding this designated "Perfect Enlightenment," its grand status resides in the essence of the fruition; as it pervades both the defiled and the pure, it is here referred to as "unsurpassed."

Regarding the passage in the *Dharmarāja-sūtra* which states that "beginningless illusory ignorance is all established from within," if one discusses this "within," it refers to the One Mind, the Great Position (*mahāsthāna*).

Because this [One Mind] is present in the causal stage and permeates both the defiled and the pure, it is designated as "the mind of sentient beings. Its explanation possesses the two meanings of awakening (*bodhi*) and non-awakening (*abodhi*).
What is called "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*) refers to the fusion of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) with original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), wherein initial and original awakening are not distinct.
The second is called "Ultimate. The Commentary states: "One who illuminates this true essence" refers to the Scripture’s passage:

"All Tathāgatas, regarding the ground of their original practice, all rely upon the pure aspect of awakened awareness (the illuminating wisdom) that perfectly reflects (the true essence being illuminated).

Only by permanently severing ignorance do they attain the Buddha-way" (this simultaneously indicates the meaning of extinguishing the form of dreams below, thereby establishing the causal basis). Regarding the phrase "extinguishing that form of dreams," the Scripture asks: "How is it that there is no..."?
The commentary states: "It is clear that all sentient beings, from time immemorial...
(as previously cited)... even this ignorance has no real substantial body. It is like a person in a dream; while dreaming, it is not non-existent, yet upon waking, nothing can be found.

(The 'dream-form' is a metaphor for ignorance. Now, by means of this metaphor, the cessation of the dream is revealed; this corresponds to the preceding illumination of the True, which constitutes the cause for returning to the origin. The sub-commentary asks: "Knowing there is no self or person, who is it that receives [the retribution]?"
The *Lunzhuanzhe jing* (Sūtra on the One Who Transmigrates) states: "One who cultivates Perfect Enlightenment knows that [transmigration] is like a flower in the sky;

thus there is no transmigration, nor is there a body or mind that undergoes birth and death. Because it is not produced, it does not exist. Because its fundamental nature is non-existent, [birth and death] are inherently absent from the beginning. (The phrase "because it is not produced" refers to the method of breaking [delusion] through non-production; "because its nature is non-existent" means that the self-nature of birth and death is originally non-existent.)

The commentary on the section beginning with "Various kinds" has three parts: first, the general clarification of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*); second, the cultivation and realization for those of superior faculties;

and third, the specific explanation of the perfection of contemplation. Regarding the phrase "various illusory transformations, etc.," this answers the inquiry of Samantabhadra concerning the fundamental application of the mind in cultivating contemplative practice.
That is to say, Samantabhadra asked: "One who cultivates the Mahāyāna, upon hearing this Perfect Enlightenment..."
How does one practice? (This inquiry arises by examining the faculties. If those sentient beings know that [all things] are like illusions, then body and mind are also illusions;

how can one use illusion to further cultivate illusion? (The question: "Illusion within illusion—what is there to cultivate? If the nature of all illusions were utterly extinguished, then there would be no mind;

who would then be the practitioner? (The question: "If it is total annihilation, who practices? The above points show that the characteristics of understanding and practice are contradictory. If one does not fundamentally practice, then delusive thoughts will arise.
"How is the mind liberated? (This addresses the fault of failing to practice. The Buddha answers:

"The various illusory transformations of all sentient beings are all produced from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*vimala-bodhi*), just as flowers in the sky arise from space. (This establishes the fundamental meaning. Commentary:

"When illusion is exhausted and enlightenment is perfected" contains two layers of meaning: the first refers to the principle of applying the mind as taught in the Chapter on Samantabhadra; the second refers to... [the Chapter on Samantabhadra].
In the chapter on the eye, when one engages with objects through contact and applies the mind for a long duration, one correctly accomplishes the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Regarding the first point, the Sūtra says: "Although illusory flowers may perish, the nature of emptiness is not destroyed; the illusory minds of sentient beings likewise depend upon illusion for their cessation. When all illusions are extinguished, the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*) remains inactive.

The Awakened One is also like this: up to the point where one knows that illusion is itself detachment, no further expedient means are required;

once illusion is detached from, it is awakening, and there is no gradual progression (only when one proceeds in this way without stagnation can it be called the exhaustion of illusion). Later, regarding the explanation within the section on "Correct Cultivation," in the "Universal Eye" chapter, the Buddha says:
"If new learners among bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the末法 (final age) desire to seek the Tathāgata’s pure, perfect, and awakened mind..."

One should maintain right mindfulness and distance oneself from all illusions. First, relying on the Tathāgata’s practice of *śamatha*, one should firmly uphold the precepts, settle the assembly, and sit in meditation within a quiet chamber.
One should constantly contemplate that this body is a provisional combination of the four great elements;

when the sense organs, their objects, and the conditions for perception are each separated, what is conventionally designated as "mind" ultimately does not exist. Thus, the illusory body, the illusory mind, and the illusory objects, even up to the extinction of these illusions, are all non-existent.
"Furthermore, they are extinguished"—this refers to the two characters "illusion-exhausted" (huàn-jìn) in the Commentary. Because illusion is extinguished, that which is not illusion does not cease;

Regarding the phrase "the mind of the Commentary penetrates and the Dharma is pervasive," the Sūtra says: "This Bodhisattva and sentient beings of the final age realize the extinction of all illusions."
Because it is a reflection, at that moment one immediately attains the manifestation of directionless purity and boundless space through awakening;

The commentary on the fundamental mind begins with the second section, which investigates and explains the source of delusion. First, regarding the initial two phrases:

Therefore, the Tathāgata further explained that one has been a Buddha from the very beginning; that the ordinary beings of the ten directions have fundamentally realized the Way of Buddhahood, yet subsequently gave rise to ignorance.
He asked, "When could all Tathāgatas ever again give rise to any afflictions? Thus, the present summary of the Buddha’s response states, "The mind is fundamentally the Buddha," and so forth.

As the Treatise says: "What is called the meaning of awakening refers to the essence of the mind being free from thought. This state of being free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space; it is precisely Suchness."

Therefore, it is said: "By means of thought, one drifts and sinks. To "drift" means to temporarily emerge among humans and devas; to "sink" means to fall into the three evil realms. Since the essence of the true mind is itself the Dharma-body, it is appropriate to refer to it as either "mind" or "body. Thus, the treatise titles the section "The Essence of Mind is Free from Thought," and concludes with: ...the essence of mind is free from thought. It is not that there is no thought, but rather that thought does not arise. Why? Because the essence of mind is originally free from thought. If thought arises, it is like waves on water; if thought ceases, it is like still water. Although there is arising and ceasing, the essence of mind is neither born nor extinguished. Why? Because the essence of mind is originally free from thought. If one realizes this, one attains liberation. If one does not realize this, one is bound by delusion. Therefore, the sūtra says
This is precisely the Dharma-body; however, this body is not a physical form, and the mind is not discursive thought. Therefore, one is fundamentally a Buddha.
If one falsely identifies with physical forms and discursive thoughts, then both body and mind become obscured—just as Master Sengzhao said, "hidden within the shell of the physical form.

Thus, the Buddha replied: "From beginning to end, there is arising and ceasing, gathering and dispersing, starting and stopping; these states continue in succession, revolving and returning in a cycle."

All various acts of grasping and rejecting are entirely within saṃsāra; to attempt to discern perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) without having escaped saṃsāra is for that nature of perfect enlightenment to likewise undergo cyclic flow.
It is like moving one's eyes, which causes the still water to appear to shake; or like fixing one's gaze while the fire-brand wheel appears to revolve;

"If even [the mind] cannot be attained, how much less so the defiled mind that revolves in birth and death, which has never been purified?

To contemplate the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment and yet not turn back from it—therefore, you have given rise to the three delusions" (the meaning of this and so forth is as explained in the sub-commentary).

These points are precisely the same as what is stated in the *Treatise* regarding "beginningless, moment-to-moment succession," and so on. Regarding the phrase "The shore does not actually move," the *Mìfǎn jīng* (Secret Translation Sutra) says:

As a boat moves, the shore appears to shift; this illustrates that the mind is truly the Buddha, yet through delusion it seems like a sentient being. The shore is actually stationary, yet because the boat moves, it seems to turn.
Thus it is said: "It rushes and gallops. "Rushes" (*mù*) means to gallop; "gallops" (*zòu*) refers to the swift pace of a horse. Both "rushing" and "galloping" are signs of rapid running;
the meaning of the response through this metaphor is already clear. How much more so for the metaphors of empty flowers and gold ore?
Regarding the metaphor of the sudden removal of delusion so that the void no longer produces flowers, the Sūtra says:

"For example, when one with a cataract sees illusory flowers in the sky, if the cataract is removed, it cannot be said that 'this cataract has been extinguished' or 'when will these cataracts arise again'? Why?
Because the two phenomena of the cataract and the flowers do not exist in mutual dependence. It is also like the illusory flowers in the sky; when they vanish into the void, [they leave no trace]."
One may ask: when will these empty flowers arise again? For what reason? Because emptiness is fundamentally without flowers; they are neither produced nor extinguished.
This metaphor illustrates that the sudden awakening to the essence of the mind is Buddha, for it is the self-realization that one is fundamentally without discursive thought.

Thus, the preface’s intent is to state that delusive rulership is suddenly eliminated. Regarding the phrase "gradually exhausted" in the commentary: it means to realize that [delusion] is fundamentally non-existent.
This metaphor illustrates gradual cultivation. As the Sūtra says: "Good son, it is like refining gold ore; gold does not exist apart from the refining process.

Once it has become gold, it does not revert to ore, even after an infinite amount of time, for the nature of gold is indestructible. A verse states: "Gold exists because it is not [merely] refined," and so forth.
To apply this to the teaching: the wondrous, perfect, and enlightened mind (*bodhicitta*) of all Tathāgatas is fundamentally devoid of the attainment of *bodhi* or *nirvāṇa*.
The Buddha’s cycle of saṃsāra is such that even what is attained by the śrāvakas does not reach the level of direct realization;

how much less can the境 (object) of Perfect Enlightenment be fathomed by a conceptual mind? It would be like attempting to burn Mount Sumeru with the light of a firefly, or even worse, seeking a fruit of emptiness through such efforts.
Furthermore, the passage concerning "refining ore" is precisely the section from Maitreya’s chapter that severs the root of saṃsāra. This is it.
The metaphors used here to explain the principle of the method for severing [defilements] are precisely those found in the subsequent commentary;
I shall now summarize the preceding and following sections to describe them as "gradually exhausting the source of craving. As for the subsequent section:

"All sentient beings, from the beginningless past, because they possess various forms of affectionate attachment and greedy desire, undergo saṃsāra, even to the point of creating the karma for the hells of evil ghosts."

Virtuous humans and devas alike do not achieve sainthood; rather, by overturning two kinds of obstacles, they reveal the five natures, all of which are within saṃsāra (the above constitutes the source of craving;

from here below is the gradual severance). If sentient beings give rise to a superior resolve toward Great Perfect Enlightenment, they should make great vows and practice in accordance with those vows to gradually sever all obstacles.
When the obstacles are exhausted and the vows fulfilled, they shall ascend to the pure state of liberation.
The Dharma Hall is the realm of the wondrous adornment that realizes Great Perfect Enlightenment (*mahāpariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
Regarding the first phrase of the second section—“Discerning the stages of realization according to their positions”—the Sūtra states:
“The self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment is neither nature nor non-nature; it exists by following the arising of all natures, yet it is without grasping and without realization regarding reality.”
Within these marks, there are in reality neither Bodhisattvas nor sentient beings. Why is this? Because both Bodhisattvas and sentient beings are all illusory transformations;

since illusory transformations perish, there is no one who attains realization. For example, the visual faculty does not see itself. The nature of the self is inherently equal, yet there is no one who is equal.
Regarding the commentary on "wisdom appearing as though having gradations": sentient beings are deluded and inverted, and have not yet been able to eliminate [this state]. One.

Furthermore, if there is a person whose toil and anxiety are forever severed, they shall attain..."

The purity of the *dharmadhātu* is itself an obstacle to pure understanding; because it constitutes a self-obstruction, one lacks mastery over perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) [the stage of the Ten Faiths].

Although the obstruction of understanding is severed when one perceives that understanding is an obstacle, one still lacks mastery because one dwells in the perception of enlightenment, whereby the very awareness of enlightenment becomes an obstacle [the stage of the Sages].
Therefore, both "illumination" (*āloka*) and "awareness" (*bodha*) are termed obstacles; for this reason, the Bodhisattva constantly awakens without abiding in either illumination or awareness.
That which illuminates is simultaneously quiescent and extinguished, like one cutting off one’s own head;

when the obstruction is extinguished by the obstruction, the obstruction is severed and extinguished, and there is no longer any obstructing thing (the Stage of the Sage). All obstacles are then ultimately realized as awakening;

whether it be mindfulness or loss of mindfulness, there is nothing that is not liberation, including formation and destruction, up to the ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm that clearly perceives all phenomena as being like empty space (the Stage of Fruition). △ Commentary and Elucidation.

Regarding the two types of deluded minds mentioned below, the *Sūtra on Sudden Enlightenment* states: "All Bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age, at all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts;

The "All-Knowledge" (the fruition-wisdom that is perfectly luminous).
The commentary states: "Suddenly emerging" refers to the second [section], which specifically clarifies the cultivation and realization of those of middling and inferior faculties.

Just as touching its hair follows the will of the driver—(the remaining passages concerning old age, sickness, and death, which correspond to skin, flesh, and bone, are all to be understood by this analogy)—the driver’s training of the horse is not invariably certain, whereas the Buddha’s training of sentient beings is invariably unfailing; therefore, I am called the "Tamer of Men" (Puruṣadamyasārathi).

Regarding the "Precious Means of Cultivation," within the treatise it is stated that upon the arousal of the mind and the commencement of practice, a question is raised:

The answer is: "It is like a great maṇi jewel whose essential nature is luminous and pure, yet which possesses the impurities of ore."
Just as a person who merely contemplates the nature of a jewel, yet fails to polish and refine it through various skillful means, will never attain its purity;
so too, although the *tathatā* (suchness) of sentient beings is by nature empty and pure, it is defiled by immeasurable afflictions (*kleśa*).
If a person merely contemplates *tathatā* without practicing various forms of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), they likewise shall not attain purity, because these defilements are immeasurable and pervasive.
Because all phenomena are such, one cultivates all wholesome practices as an antidote;

if a person practices all wholesome dharmas, they naturally accord with the *tathatā* (suchness) because wholesome dharmas externally oppose false defilements while internally conforming to *tathatā*.

Since intention is exhausted through images and images are manifested through words, one attains the images and forgets the words, and attains the intention and forgets the images; this is like [forgetting] the snare.
This is because when one has caught the rabbit, one forgets the trap; when one has caught the fish, one forgets the decoy.
Thus, words are the traps for images, and images are the decoys for meaning. To cling to words is not to grasp the images;

"It is not its image" means that while speech arises from the image and speech is preserved within it, what is thus preserved is no longer the original speech. The commentary explains:

It is forgetfulness. (The Way of the *Yi* is profound and mysterious; its ultimate principle is difficult to comprehend. (The Sages observed the Three Powers (*sancai*) and established images; they doubled them to form the sixty-four hexagrams. When both [the image and the meaning] are forgotten, they are unified. Therefore, one may take various categories to form its images and combine meanings to serve as its evidence.

If the meaning lies in strength, why must it be a horse? If the category lies in docility, why must it be an ox? If the hexagram-line coincides with docility, why must it be the Kun hexagram to represent an ox?

If the meaning corresponds to strength, why must it be the Qian hexagram to represent a horse? The function of the image arises according to the meaning; it does not remain stagnant in a single direction, for the matter is such.

They penetrate through myriad transformations: although Qian is associated with the horse, it does not exclusively define hardness by means of the horse; although Kun is associated with the ox, it does not solely define compliance by means of the ox. Why must one insist on the horse and the ox? Those who are deluded discuss them with such fixation that they become stuck on the hexagrams. Thus, the deluded fix the horse upon Qian;
yet when one examines the text and scrutinizes the hexagram, if there is a horse but no Qian, then false explanations proliferate and become difficult to enumerate.

This means that those who are deluded insistently identify the horse as Qian and the ox as Kun; however, when examining the text and scrutinizing the hexagram to grasp its imagery, if there is a horse but no Qian, or an ox but no Kun, this constitutes an irrationality.
How extreme is this perversity! How profound is the error! It is truly difficult to record. Since the *hùtǐ* (reciprocal body) is not fixed, one proceeds to the *guàbiàn* (change of hexagrams);

To violate principle and deviate from the fundamental tenet—taking images based on the *hùtǐ* and seeking meanings through the *guàbiàn*, skillfully deducing the six positions and curvingly matching them to the Five Elements—this is indeed to lose the original source while increasing artificiality and deception. While Duke Huan was reading a book in the hall above, Lún Pián was planing wheels in the hall below.
Setting aside his mallet and chisel, he ascended and asked Duke Huan, "May I venture to ask what it is you are reading? The Duke said, "The words of the sages. Lún Pián said, "As for the sages—"
Duke Huan said, "He is already dead. The wheelwright replied, "In that case, what Your Majesty reads is but the dregs of the ancients.
Duke Huan said, "When I read books, how can a wheelwright dare to criticize me? If you have a reason, it shall be acceptable; if you have no reason, you shall die.
The wheelwright said, "I observe my own work as a craftsman: if I carve a wheel too slowly, it feels easy and pleasant, but..."
If it were too tight, the wheel would be painful and would not fit; if it were too loose, it would not fit.

By being neither too fast nor too slow, he attained mastery with his hands and responded with his mind, such that his mouth could not describe it. There was a subtle principle (shu) existing between them;
I, your servant, could not explain it to my son, and my son likewise could not receive it from me. Thus, at the age of seventy, I am still old at the wheelwright's bench.
(This statement means that things each have their own nature, and that teaching is of no benefit. The ancients and that which they could not transmit have died with them;

yet all you read, O Lord, is merely the dregs of those ancients. (The affairs of antiquity perished along with antiquity itself; even if something were transmitted, how could it make the ancient present?

Since the ancient is no longer present and current affairs have already changed, one must abandon learning, follow one's nature, and transform with the times, and only then will one arrive at the goal.)

From that time on, I have become so absorbed in their study that even now I do not know whether I practiced them in a previous life or what karmic conditions led to this;

Several people who encountered this discourse likewise held no differing views; it was as if a firefly were trying to burn Mount Sumeru (as the latter part of the sutra states:

This is truly because this sutra fully embodies the three schools of Dharma-nature, Dharma-characteristics, and the refutation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), as well as the two traditions of the Northern and Southern [Ch'an] and the Sudden and Gradual, while further aligning with the Chan gate and being complete in its perfection, just like the *Avataṃsaka*.

(Zongmi) remarked that those who find the gateway to awakening and cultivation are difficult to encounter; he therefore devoted himself to refined study and profound reflection without ever growing weary.

Later, while investigating the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and Chengguan’s *Extensive Commentary*, he traced the origins to their conclusions. He further read through the entire Tripiṭaka, consulting, inquiring, discussing, and deliberating upon everything he had heard and studied.
As he perused each text, he compared them in detail with the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (Yuánjué jīng), examining both their fundamental principles and their specific applications.
Seeking its essential meaning, in the first month of the eleventh year of the Yuanhe era, while at Zhiju Monastery on Mount Zhongnan, he categorized the text to establish its framework;
subsequently, while reciting the Tripitaka and consulting various commentaries, he searched for and extracted their meanings, compiling them into two volumes.
Later, upon returning to the capital, he would privately consult them whenever he had the opportunity.

Later, realizing that the conditions for transformation were such that my labors and anxieties would be too great, in the first month of the first year of the Changqing era, I withdrew once again to the Grass Hall Temple on Mount Zhongnan.

Secluding myself to contemplate the void and strike at the silence, I drafted this commentary based on my own ignorance; by the summer of the third year, the work was finally completed.

Furthermore, the phrase "the Way is not a constant Way" is from the *Daode Jing* (though when lecturing, it is sufficient to cite only the first two lines, even though the full passage is provided below). It says:

The Way that can be spoken of (the Way of the correct teachings of the scriptures and arts) is not the eternal Way (it is not the Way of natural longevity; the eternal Way should be like nurturing the spirit through non-action, settling oneself in non-activity, containing the radiance, concealing the brilliance, extinguishing traces, and hiding the extremities—only then can it be called the Way).
The name that can be named (the name of wealth, honor, and high status surpassing the world) is not the eternal name (it is not a name that is naturally and eternally present;

the eternal name is like an infant before it can smile, or an egg before it has divided, like a fine jade within stone or a bright pearl inside a clam—though brilliant within, it appears dull and foolish without). Thus, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
The phrase "immediately entering nirvāṇa" refers to the verse spoken by the fourteen rākṣasas: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are the nature of arising and ceasing.

When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss. The *Yijue* (Explanatory Key) to that sutra states: "Regarding the meaning of emptiness taught by the World Hero endowed with the Ten Powers:
the five aggregates and all conditioned phenomena arise from causes and conditions; when conditions depart, they immediately cease. This is the first line of that verse.

The first two lines concerning "all conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskāra*) and so forth constitute the gate of *pravṛtti* (evolution). For that which arises must necessarily cease; having ceased, it arises again.

This cycle of cessation and arising—where there is no cessation and no arising—is the bliss of *śānti* (quiescence). The latter two lines, stating that "arising and ceasing have ceased, and quiescence is bliss," refer to the Great *Nirvāṇa*, the gate of *nivṛtti* (reversion).
Furthermore, the first half-verse refutes the past misconception of permanence, thereby eliminating the view of eternalism.
The latter two lines refute the former inversion of impermanence, thereby eliminating the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, the first half [of the verse] states that arising and ceasing are empty in their entirety, while the latter speaks of the characteristic of *nirvāṇa* as being without self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Regarding the commentary on the passage:

"Now, knowing that the mind is the Buddha-mind, one will certainly become a Buddha"—this is because the mind realized as neither arising nor ceasing is termed "original enlightenment" (*mūla-avabodha*), which is entirely [the Buddha-mind].
The minds of all Buddhas take this as their foundation; through the certainty of practice, one attains Buddhahood.
Indeed, there are many scriptural passages concerning the statement that "one's own mind is the Buddha," such as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Chapter on the Manifestation [of the Tathāgata], which says:

"One should know that in every thought-moment of one's own mind, a Buddha is always attaining perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Buddha praises Cunda, saying his mind is identical to the Buddha-mind; this is its definitive meaning.
The phrase "one shall become a Buddha" is also entirely a passage concerning *nirvāṇa*. The text states: "All who possess a mind will certainly become Buddhas";
therefore, it is said thus. [Commentary:
