Regarding "all-aspect knowledge" (sarvajñatā): in the state of Buddhahood, it is called *sarvajñatā* in Sanskrit, which in the Tang language means "all-aspect knowledge.

However, according to scriptures such as the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, three types of knowledge are fully present: namely, all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), path-knowledge (*mārgajñatā*), and all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
The first belongs to the Śrāvakas, the second to the Bodhisattvas, and the last to the Tathāgatas. When the term "all-aspect knowledge" is used here, it is intended to encompass all [three].

Regarding the "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*): although the Tathāgata encompasses both of the preceding two [knowledges], he is distinguished from the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas by being designated as the most supreme.

Since one who has cultivated extensive learning reaches all things and is endowed with the knowledge of all modes is alone named a Buddha, the cultivation of the cause must necessarily rely upon extensive learning;
this is especially so since the scriptural text of the third stage (*bhūmi*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* specifically emphasizes extensive learning.

This serves as the initial gateway to the practice of a bodhisattva; through five successive stages of investigation, it is shown that the practice of delivering sentient beings begins with extensive learning (*bahuśruta*).

As that text states: "A bodhisattva, thus wearying of and detaching from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), takes pity on all sentient beings, recognizes the superior benefit of the knowledge of all-knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*), and desires to rely upon the wisdom of the Tathāgata to rescue and deliver them."
He gives rise to this reflection: "These sentient beings have fallen into the midst of the great suffering of afflictions;
by what skillful means can they be rescued and established in the bliss of ultimate nirvana? He then thinks:

"To deliver sentient beings and establish them in nirvana, one must not be separated from the wisdom of unobstructed liberation (the mastery over both the provisional and the ultimate, free from the two obstacles, which is the skillful means for ultimately gathering in and sustaining sentient beings)."

The wisdom of unobstructed liberation is inseparable from the realization of all phenomena as they truly are (to realize all phenomena as they truly are means that "as they truly are" is the *dharmatā*;

by virtue of this, one is able through skillful means to sever delusions and give rise to activity). The realization of all phenomena as they truly are is inseparable from the light of wisdom consisting of the practice of non-practice and non-arising practice (wisdom takes non-practice and non-arising as its characteristic mode of practice).
The light of wisdom consisting of the practice of non-practice and non-arising is inseparable from the definitive skillfulness of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Wisdom (the mastery of entering and emerging from meditative concentration without being bound by it); skillful mastery of dhyāna and definitive wisdom that does not depart from skillfulness (because one does not grasp at the characteristics of what is heard);

extensive learning (this refers to the wisdom of hearing; because it gives rise to the preceding wisdoms of reflection and cultivation, etc.; if explained in forward order, then through extensive learning one gives rise to the wisdom of dhyāna, through the wisdom of dhyāna one gives rise to the wisdom of non-arising, and through the wisdom of non-arising one awakens to the nature of phenomena;

by awakening to the nature of phenomena, one spontaneously advances with stillness and illumination flowing as one, which is called Buddha-wisdom, capable of delivering and liberating all sentient beings). The Bodhisattva observes and understands in this manner.

Having understood this, he redoubles his diligent pursuit and cultivation of the True Dharma; day and night he aspires only to hear the Dharma, to delight in the Dharma, to rejoice in the Dharma, to rely on the Dharma, to follow the Dharma, to understand the Dharma, to accord with the Dharma, to reach the Dharma, to abide in the Dharma, and to practice the Dharma.

Thus, the Bodhisattva diligently seeks the precious wealth of the Buddha-Dharma without any stinginess; he perceives no object whatsoever as difficult to obtain or worthy of high esteem, except for [the Dharma].
Because they conceive the thought that a person capable of preaching the Dharma is difficult to encounter, there is no internal or external wealth they cannot relinquish;
there is no act of reverence they cannot perform; there is no pride they cannot abandon; there is no service they cannot provide;
and there is no hardship they cannot endure. If they hear even a single verse of the Dharma not previously heard, their hearts give rise to joy.

Suppose someone were to say: "If one can purify the bodhisattva practice through even a single verse of the Dharma not yet heard, then one would rather enter a fire-pit seven fathoms deep—even if it meant forfeiting the three thousandfold world-system filled with the seven treasures, as well as the rank of a wheel-turning monarch, Śakra, or Brahmā.

Thus seeking the Dharma, one contemplates and practices according to what has been heard, even to the point of reflecting in a secluded place that the Buddha-dharma is attained only by practicing exactly as taught. It is not [attained] otherwise.

It is merely by verbal recitation that one can attain purity (hereafter it is said that one attains the four dhyānas and eight samādhis, etc.). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* also states: "Through much hearing one can know the Dharma;

through much hearing one can leave behind transgressions; through much hearing one abandons what is meaningless; through much hearing one attains the wisdom of nirvāṇa. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:

"Those with much hearing but no wisdom, and those with wisdom but no hearing, both fail to know the true mark (*dharmatā*). Only when one possesses both wisdom and much hearing does one finally know the true mark."

One who possesses neither learning nor wisdom is a "bull among men. It is said that when the mind-ground opens and becomes clear, this is the gate of sudden enlightenment (*tongwu*), which is precisely the possession of wisdom.
Therefore, the present statement regarding the cultivation of extensive learning describes the gate of gradual cultivation (*jianxiu*).

Furthermore, the tradition concerning the encounter with the *rākṣasa* on the road also illustrates the benefit of extensive learning. As the "Chapter on the Inquiry into Wisdom" (*Wenming pin*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "It is not only by..."

The statement that "one who is well-versed in the teachings can enter the Dharma of the Tathāgata" clarifies that the fault lies in not severing the afflictions, rather than disparaging extensive learning;
the phrase "not merely" intends to encourage one to practice in accordance with what has been heard.
The commentary states: "Therefore, he again travels" clarifies the gradual cultivation that follows. Regarding the phrase "therefore, he again":

although it was previously stated that the "ground of the mind has opened and the sky of principle is bright," because the causes for attaining Buddhahood depend upon extensive learning, one must still "travel.
"Traveling to a hundred cities" means wandering through kingdoms and towns to visit spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and seek instruction in the Dharma-gates.

The phrase "going to visit" refers to the words from the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* concerning the Buddha dispatching messengers to inquire after his illness; each instance says, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
This is currently based on the actual text of the scripture, combined with the practice of using diagrams to illustrate the sequence of visits to the various seats;
thus, it is called "going to visit. As for the "hundred cities," this refers to the journey of the youth Sudhana through the hundred cities in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
He traveled southward in search of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), passing through one hundred and ten cities; here, he speaks only of the general number.
Regarding the phrase "sitting to explore the various scriptures," this means that while on his way seeking the Dharma, he would immediately consult and examine the canonical teachings as he went;
thus, "sitting" is intended here as a counterpart to "traveling. (Zongmi) Among the Buddhist scriptures encountered during this journey, there were none that he did not explore.

I have examined and read these works; furthermore, at Zhiju Temple on Mount Zhongnan, I vowed not to descend the mountain until I had completed a full recitation of the Tripitaka over a period of three years.
Only after fulfilling this vow did I descend to Yunju, Caotang, Fengde, and other temples, where I spent another three and a half years.

These were all occasions for seeking out the holy teachings; other instances occurred from time to time in various places and cannot be recorded in detail. This has been from the age of seventeen or eighteen until the present day.
Because his daily practice was never interrupted, it is said that he "probed the multitude of scriptures.

Regarding the fact that his lectures were authorized by the masters of the five schools despite being of inferior rank, there is an ancient tradition that in Puzhou there was one who did not permit Tai, and in Zizhou there was one who did not permit Zhao;
they were men of superior virtue and intelligence who refused to allow them to lecture, whereas I [did].

I, a person of the dregs of the ignorant, have had a slight karmic affinity from previous lives; having searched through the commentaries and sub-commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, I have gained a faint glimpse of its outlines.
When I had not yet seen the lineage of the author of these commentaries, while I was in Xiangzhou and the Eastern Capital, I previously ventured to lecture upon them twice.

My conduct appeared similar to that of the ancient masters, yet because the worthy and the foolish were not of one mind, it is said that my practice was "spurious. The use of the word "although" (*suī*) clarifies that there was indeed [a basis for this].
Receiving [the teachings] was not merely a matter of listening; therefore, it is followed by the statement, "He studied under Master An.

This refers to the fifth year of the Yuanhe era, when he first lectured on [the text] once in Xiangzhou, and in the sixth year, he lectured in the Eastern Capital (the details of these events may be found in the Preface to the Commentary, as described therein).
Subsequently, he entered the Upper Capital to attend personally upon the Master for several years, seeking instruction. During the first two years, by day...

At night, he did not leave his companions; although he traveled between various monasteries to lecture and transmit the teachings, whenever he encountered doubts, he went back and forth to consult them without ceasing.

When people spoke of "Master An," they were referring to Dharma Master Dao’an, who was the one venerated by the world at that time. Thereafter, contemporaries all said: "If one’s learning does not take Dao’an as its master, its meaning will not withstand scrutiny.
As for those who humbly receive [his teachings] like I do, they are as numerous as those who enter the Way. This was during the days in the Eastern Capital.

During the course of a lecture, a disciple named Taigong severed his arm as an act of devotion to celebrate the Dharma. The Retainer (Liu Shou) submitted a formal petition to the Secretariat for a decision;

in this document, it was stated: "Regarding the disciples under the Huayan school, we fear that the Chancellor may inquire into the identity of the author of the commentary and whether he is still alive.

Since the author has not yet been personally identified, we fear he might not acknowledge [the work]. We have therefore drafted this memorial to detail the twenty fascicles of the commentary that we have received and understood."

Regarding the section on the "Major Sections of the Middle Joints" (*Chung-gwŏn kyŏng-daebu gyeongmun pinhoe*) in the *Hyeokse-maek* (Blood Vessels) spanning seven or eight sheets, the junior master Hyeon-gwi and Ji-hui submitted a memorial to the Chief Lecturer to clarify that his exposition was not reckless.
The Chief Lecturer responded with a series of letters, instructing them: "I have received your letter and understood the purport of the Great Teaching.
Your account of the sincere resonance of the *Ch’oen* and *Jwan* [scriptures] is truly moving; I have taken it to heart. I myself shall propagate [this teaching]."
Some heard it directly from his own lips (listening in person), while others received it through successive transmission (having heard it at the seats of various *śāstrins* at the gates).

It has filled foreign lands (this commentary circulated in both the two kingdoms of Silla and Bohai). Yet, as for Confucius parting his carriage-canopy with Zhongni and Boya severing the strings of his zither—both being stories of ancient worthies whose hearts met and who were "knowers of sound"—since this meaning follows [the preceding], the word "yet" (*rán*) is used here to separate them.
Even so, it still relies upon form and sound (the intent is: although the profound Way may be attained through spiritual resonance, it nonetheless relies upon form and sound).

"Without having seen my form or heard the sound of my preaching the Dharma, you have grasped my intent, surpassing those of antiquity. (This means that one transmits and attains the essential purpose without meeting face-to-face;

it signifies that one has attained the profound essence of the Great Teaching, which lies beyond the realm of signs and forms. "Your intent is like my own mind" (*yōu* means "resembling"; it means that your understanding does not differ from mine). "There has never been such a thing before" (this is precisely the expression clarifying how one surpasses antiquity). The commentary states:
The phrase "now, having received [your grace]" (*tāomù*) and so forth refers to the meaning of the words within this letter, as it says in the letter:
My mind is as my heart; feeling a sense of profound sorrow, I have now spoken thus. To receive such words is for me to express my humble sentiments.
Having been so generously granted this seal of approval, though my draft is flawed, it shall truly be the seal of a "True Son of the Wheel-Turning King.
As stated previously: "It is not by relying on sacred power alone, but must depend upon past causes; you should comfort yourself as a True Son of the Wheel-Turning King."
This can be illustrated by an analogy. The commentary states: "To say 'it is appropriate' is also my own admission of my own shallowness and inferiority; it is not within my lot.

To claim such words would be empty and erroneous. The "True Son of the Wheel-Turning King" refers to the metaphor cited in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* regarding how a Bodhisattva of the Ten Stages receives their position, just as a Wheel-Turning Sage-King has a thousand sons, among whom the eldest son born of the principal queen is selected.
A single person is now receiving consecration to succeed to the rank of a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin). Regarding the Master’s use of this matter:
"turning the wheel" refers metaphorically to the position of a Wheel-Turning King, while in terms of the Dharma, it refers to succeeding to the position of turning the Wheel of the Dharma.
Just as in the successive generations of the Chan Patriarchs, one person succeeds as the legitimate heir, the term "true son" refers to one who is like the son of the principal consort.
Regarding the seal of "birth," the colophon of the manuscript states: "If one were to obtain even a single face of this seal, what further addition would there be to its liberating resolution?
Should one suddenly encounter obstacles, one need only achieve mental resonance with the profound ultimate; how could mountains, rivers, forms, or sounds possibly create a separation?"

In the sub-commentary (*shu*), the third section of the first part—“Encountering Again”—explains the intent of composing this commentary in three points. First, regarding “the arousal of the mind to propagate the Dharma”:

the phrase “encountering again a close friend” employs the parable of the “Tying the Jewel” from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, specifically the chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples, to express the present meaning by way of understanding and receiving the prophecy.
That sutra says: “For example, there was a man who went to the house of a close friend and became intoxicated with wine.”
At that time, while he was lying down, a close friend, having business with the authorities and needing to depart, tied a priceless jewel inside his garment and gave it to him before leaving.
The man, intoxicated and asleep, was completely unaware of this.

Having risen and wandered on, he reached another country where, for the sake of food and clothing, he sought them with great effort and underwent immense hardship; yet if he obtained even a small amount, he considered it sufficient.
Later, a close friend saw him and said these words: "Alas, O man! Why do you toil for food and clothing to such an extent?

Long ago, I wished to let you enjoy the five desires at will; on a certain month and day, I tied a priceless jewel inside your garment, which remains there even now, yet you were unaware of it and instead sought your own livelihood through hardship and anxiety."

"How extremely foolish you are! You may now trade this jewel for whatever you require; it shall always fulfill your wishes so that you lack nothing. This lower teaching can be understood through its correspondence.
The commentary states: There are two explanations regarding the "tied jewel. First, according to the explanation based on the formation of karmic conditions (*kṣaṇa-bandhana*):

perfect understanding is the jewel, and the preaching [of the Dharma] is the tying. The perfuming of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*) within the mind of afflictions is the intoxicating liquor, and the five destinies (*pañca-gati*) are the vessel.
Seeking happiness, one exerts effort through hardships to realize a minor nirvana; not seeking the great fruit, one considers a small gain sufficient.

Later, hearing the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra is like encountering a close friend who reveals knowledge and vision, thereby obtaining the jewel. By means of the cause, the fruit is easily attained, and all that is desired is obtained.
Second, explaining this in terms of the original, true nature: it was as if a pearl had been tied [to one's clothing] in the past; thus, it is originally possessed.
In the past, when the deluded mind heard [the teaching], it did not awaken; it immediately claimed, "I was entirely unaware," thereby forming a firm seed.
It is like being bound and unable to realize the fundamental substance, as if [the substance] were within one's clothes. Because one has previously heard the Dharma, one seeks virtuous blessings;

because one is conditioned by the necessities of food and clothing, there is hardship. Now, encountering this primary condition once again, it acts as a kinsman and friend. The rest is largely the same as explained previously.
However, at the time this person was entrusted with the jewel, he had already met his close friend for the first time;
therefore, when the friend later saw him and spoke these words, it constituted their second meeting. I am likewise so:

by verifying the present event against its past cause, I know for certain that in a previous life I heard the teachings of the Master of the Commentary, and thus upon hearing them now, I immediately understood.
Therefore, it is said that they have met again. Regarding the phrase "even more deeply moved by the Buddha’s grace" (*mí gǎn fó ēn*): *mí* (彌) carries the meaning of "profound.

This means that prior to the lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, whether through reciting or listening, whenever he encountered passages in the scriptures describing the profundity of the Buddha’s grace, he would rejoice in having heard the Dharma and feel gratitude for the Buddha’s kindness.
Now, because he has met a virtuous friend who personally lectures the *Avataṃsaka*, his feelings of gratitude are even more profound.

In the profound vision of this school, one perceives the traces of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who, over many kalpas, underwent ascetic practices to extensively protect the Great Dharma and compassionately pity sentient beings;
furthermore, one realizes that the flavor and meaning of the Great Teaching are boundless.

Were it not for Śākyamuni’s descent into the world to appear and expound this gateway, by what means could I have reached this stage? Therefore, my gratitude is ever more profound and ever more deep. This has been long explained in the *Sūtra-ṭīkā*.
"Alas, being solitary and poor, I shall now set forth the gift of Dharma. All that follows is for the purpose of repaying the Buddha's kindness; thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Even if one were to carry [the scriptures] upon one's head for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, and use one's body as a seat throughout the trichiliocosm, if one does not transmit the Dharma to transform sentient beings, in the end there would be no way to repay his grace.
"Alas" (*kǎi*) is a silent sigh of lamentation. "Solitary and poor" refers to the third stage (*bhūmi*) in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

The Sūtra says: When a Bodhisattva perceives that the wisdom of the Tathāgata brings great benefit and perceives the faults and afflictions of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*), they give rise toward sentient beings to ten kinds of compassionate mind.
That is to say, seeing all sentient beings as solitary and without reliance, they give rise to a compassionate mind.

(In the world, one who has no father while young is called "solitary" (*gu*), and one who has no son while old is called "lonely" (*du*). Now, because these sentient beings are distantly separated from the compassionate Honored Ones, the Buddhas, they are "solitary" above; and because they do not benefit living beings below, having no disciples, they are "lonely. Upon what else could they rely? Seeing...

He gives rise to a heart of compassion for all sentient beings who are impoverished and destitute—[being] "impoverished" because they lack merit and wisdom; "destitute" because even when they have obtained [something], they are never satisfied;

and "in need" because they cannot practice fewness of desires and instead seek further; and "lacking" because they do not know contentment with what they have obtained. Furthermore, the *Pañcamabhūmi* states: "This Bodhisattva reflects:

'These sentient beings undergo such suffering, being solitary, destitute, and oppressed by hardship, without rescue and without refuge. (Regarding the term "solitary": if one thing is not obtained, then everything is as if lost; thus, "solitary" implies that even within a single thing, nothing is obtained.)

"Everything is for the sake of reaching the ultimate. Regarding the phrase "about to present the gift of Dharma" (*fashī*), "about to" (*jiāng*) means "desiring," and "presenting" (*chén*) refers to the act of setting forth or arranging.
As for the "gift of Dharma" (*fashī*), it means employing a pure mind free from the defilement of seeking fame or profit to bestow the Dharma upon others;

hence, it is called the gift of Dharma. The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (Pusa jie xu) states: "The two gifts of wealth and Dharma are equal and without distinction. Furthermore, the *Mahādharmolkā-dhāraṇī* says: [text continues].
The Sūtra says: "For example, it is like a merchant who seeks profit through his wealth; as the months and years pass, his storehouses become filled and he is able to provide relief to many people.
If he does not engage in trade, his wealth and profit will not increase, and later, encountering famine, he will lose his family estate.
The teacher of the Dharma is also like this: he should constantly proclaim the teaching without ceasing or becoming lax; if he constantly proclaims the Dharma, then the Dharma..."

It increases the benefit for humans and devas; yet if one does not proclaim the Dharma, it will decline and perish. (Furthermore, there are three differences between the two types of giving—material and Dharma:

first, material giving comes to an end as it is given more, whereas Dharma-giving only increases as it is given more; second, material giving results in worldly retribution, while Dharma-giving results in supramundane merit; third, material giving accomplishes the form-body, while Dharma-giving accomplishes the Dharma-body.)
The commentary collects the latter two [sections] to clarify that the composition of various commentaries serves as the necessary conditions for this present commentary;
this is to clarify the matter of the "Dharma-gift" (*dharma-dāna*), meaning that one composes named teachings to instruct future generations so that the seed of the Buddha may not be severed.

As for collecting the *Prajñā[pāramitā]*, it is because one sees that *prajñā* destroys [false] characteristics and is the mother of all Buddhas; since the Patriarchs have praised it deeply, [the author] therefore... [uses] the original [text].

In the fourteenth year of the Wadō era, at Kōfuku-ji Temple, he collected the commentaries on the treatises of Asanga and Vasubandhu, such as those by Dayun, and compiled their essential subtleties with the annotations of Master Hui-zhao and others to explain the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He produced one volume of commentary (*sho*) and one volume of sub-commentary (*shō*).
His commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was so comprehensive because he perceived that the Dharma of the *Avataṃsaka*, which accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), is vast and expansive.
This vast and profound [teaching] is truly worthy of veneration; yet because its literary expression is rich and its meaning so expansive, scholars find it difficult to discern its limits.
Consequently, those who focus merely on excerpts and commentaries become confused regarding the intent of the sūtras, leading later generations to treat the Great Sūtras with contempt.

Some say that those who lecture on the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Nirvāṇa* are merely "reciters of sūtras," while others call them "rollers of sūtras. Thus, in the second year of the Changqing era, at Nanshan...

At Fǎngdé Temple, [the Master] arranged the key points and thematic threads from the commentary (*shù*) to run through the entire text of the sutra, so that the lecturer might focus their mind on memorizing the sutra text in order to explain it according to this commentary;
this was completed in five fascicles and titled *Huáyán Lúnguàn Shū* (The Commentary on the Thematic Threads of the Avataṃsaka).

Regarding the "summarizing the *vinaya*": because he had extensively investigated the great *vinaya-piṭaka*, the five sections of the Vinaya, and other texts, he listened to [lectures on them] four times.
Upon examining the new chapters, I observed that the Vinaya texts are voluminous and the matters they enumerate are repetitive; some are customs of India that have no relevance to this land.
Because the transmitters have indulged in such profuse layers of phrasing, practitioners are unable to discern the essential points for actual practice.
Consequently, during the summer of the third year of the Changqing era, while listening at Fengde Temple, I selected [the following].
In compiling this sub-commentary on the Vinaya texts, I have extracted and summarized those essential practices for practitioners to employ, intending to guide and lead those following the Way;

thus, it has been condensed into three volumes. This commentary elucidates the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*), which is the fundamental tenet and the guiding principle of the Buddha’s teachings.

However, as the various treatises are vast and the interpretations of different masters diverge, students tend to focus their efforts merely on becoming thoroughly familiar with the volumes, verses, and phrases.
Having realized through the investigation and reflection of his own mind that the designations of "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra) are merely the manifestations of his own mental consciousness,
he then, from the winter solstice of the fourteenth year of the Yuanhe era until the spring of the fifteenth year,

excerpted the essential and pure orthodox meanings from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and its commentaries at Xingfu Temple and Baoshou Temple in the Capital, composing a commentary on the thirty verses of the root text.

Comprising two fascicles, it elucidates and clarifies the essential tenets of the Vijñaptimātra school, making it easy for people to perceive the principle that all phenomena are nothing but one's own mind;
therefore, it is called "The Elucidation of Vijñaptimātra."

The commentary states: "The following three sections correctly describe the original intent; the original intent lies in the *Awakening of Faith* (*Yuanjue*). Within this, there are two parts. First, an analogy is presented:
suppose a person with an illness goes to a great physician's house. They should simply seek a prescription for their own specific ailment and purchase medicine to compound it.
They must not, upon seeing thousands or tens of thousands of scrolls of medical texts, greedily attempt to read them from beginning to end to distinguish between them."
In such cases, one’s illness increases and the body perishes before the reading is complete. It is like a person who enters the ocean to gather priceless jewels;

yet within the great ocean there are immeasurable treasures. If one sees them and immediately seizes them, or hears their names and immediately seeks them out, then with white hair at the end of one's life, one dies in the midst of the sea.
On what day shall one return to Jambudvīpa to relieve poverty? One should simply seek [the essential].
As soon as one obtains the maṇi jewel, one may take it back home, and naturally, the myriad treasures and ten thousand precious things will be fully provided.

Why is this so? "Maṇi" is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "wishing-fulfilling. Whatever wealth, treasures, clothing, food, drink, or various other items one desires in one's mind, this jewel can produce them.
Because they are obtained according to one's wishes, it is called "wishing-fulfilling. △ Commentary on the Visualization.

Now, as for the two dharmas mentioned below, should one wish to propagate and elucidate the Dharma-gates, there is nothing more supreme than the *Avataṃsaka* for discerning their essential subtlety and its perfect, definitive meaning.
This has been judged by the Tripitaka masters of both the Western Regions and this land throughout past and present to be the most complete, as described in the preface of the relevant commentaries.
Nevertheless, the volumes are vast and the principles are manifold; thus, those of beginner capacity find it difficult to enter.
Next, it is difficult to enter [this teaching], for just as one cannot seek all the rare treasures within the great ocean simultaneously, so too this sutra does not allow for gradual entry;

rather, through the single path, one enters all at once, where appearances merge into the nature, thought ceases, and the whole is perfected in reality. Even images are empty, and that which is manifested by awakening is fully revealed.

Because awakening is perfect and luminous, the ice of afflictions melts away, and its wondrous function and divine efficacy can be attained in a single lifetime. Thus, it was previously said: "within the ocean."
First, one seeks the fulfillment of wishes. "Rich in Text" refers to the eighty fascicles; "Broad in Meaning" refers to the five cycles of cause and effect, the five teachings, and the ten mysteries.
"Sincerity" means reality; "Yielding" means deference. "The Flower Ornament" (Saṃpuṣpita) refers to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and others, which point to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as the *Saṃpuṣpita Sūtra*.
This means that the myriad practices that evoke their fruits are like all the various flowers produced by heaven and earth. All...
His virtue adorns his person like gold, jade, silks, and brocades, and because it encompasses all manner of flowers, it is called "miscellaneous. The meaning is this:

if one considers the richness and breadth of its textual and doctrinal content, one truly knows it cannot surpass the *Avataṃsaka*; yet if one takes its direct pointing to the essence of the awakened mind to introduce those of sudden enlightenment who are beginners, it is not as effective as the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Śūraṅgama-samādhi*).
Therefore, he applied himself with great diligence and focused his partial aspiration on propagating this [text], which was his original intent.
It is indeed so.
For this reason, I have consulted the four commentaries below and composed this sub-commentary (*shu*) on the sutra.

Its foundation began in the spring of the eleventh year of the Yuanhe era at Zhiju Temple on Mount Nan, where I categorized the text with my brush and collated the meanings of the four commentaries to compile this work.
I consulted the two-volume *Siji* (Private Notes) to evaluate the scriptural text for the sake of those engaged in Chan studies.
In the second year of the Changqing era, I revised it at Caotang Monastery into a commentary (*shu*), opening up dozens of topical sections (*zhangmen*).

It was not until the autumn and winter of the third year that the work was finally completed. Regarding the various treatises mentioned, they include the *Qixin lun*, the *Weishi lun*, the *Baoxing lun*, and the *Foxing lun*.
This includes the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and so forth.

Regarding the "hundred schools," it refers to the commentaries and sub-commentaries of various masters, as well as all treatises, admonitions, discourses, hymns, and eulogies that have been composed—including their established doctrines and formal arguments. I have searched exhaustively for those works that are essential and currently in vogue;
having examined them in detail and read them repeatedly, I have compiled them here. I have compared this work against those others, turning over the pages again and again to ensure thoroughness.

One should investigate the flavor and intent of the teachings and carefully evaluate their merits and defects, following the example of Nan Rong, who recited the lines of the "White Jade Disc" three times.
As for the "White Jade Disc," the *Mao Shi* states: "The flaw in a white jade disc may yet be polished away, but the flaw in these words cannot be remedied.
When Nan Rong read this chapter, he repeated the lines over and over again to demonstrate his intention and to urge caution in speech.
Regarding the sharpening of one's tools, the *Analects* states: "The artisan who wishes to do his work well must first sharpen his tools.

This clarifies that because I wished to compose this commentary on the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra*, I have for over a decade first studied various teachings to sharpen my wisdom and broaden my learning before finally composing this commentary.

Yet it is not lacking. Furthermore, the momentum of its prose follows the introduction to the "Monthly Ordinances" (*Yueling*) in the *Liji*, which states: "Your servants reverently receive the imperial decree;

we have exerted our utmost thought and refined our studies, yet we feel ashamed that we lack the ability to expound upon it fully. We have mistakenly been entrusted with the responsibility of this discussion.

The subsequent two lines—"The meaning encompasses both nature (*xing*) and characteristics (*xiang*), and includes both sudden and gradual [teachings]"—precisely clarify the distinctions of the meaning. "Nature and characteristics" refers to the two...

The six sections below, beginning with "Shule Cheng," conclude the preceding and introduce the subsequent, meaning they summarize the intent of the Great Commentary (*Da shu*) and give rise to the intent of the Abridged Commentary (*Lü shu*).

The text consists of two parts; the first part concludes the three-fascicle Great Commentary, comprising approximately two hundred and ten sheets of paper, which has already been transmitted to diligent students.
Since the completion of the commentary, about three years have passed; there are currently approximately one hundred students who have practiced it, and seven or eight who have lectured upon it.
All of these individuals were formerly practitioners of Chan principles or lecturers on the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, and each of them currently transmits the work.
Because one maintains [this practice] without ceasing, it is called "strenuous study" (*qiángxué*).

The meaning of "strenuous study" refers to having sharp faculties and a keen nature, a spirit that is refined, vigorous, courageous, and firm—described as "granting him progress, not granting him retreat. The text refers to the *Liji* (Book of Rites), which says:
"Study strenuously and wait for questions. I am now employing this expression; the current sense is that only those of such a class of strenuous study [are qualified].

Although one is able to transmit the Great Commentary, there may still be those whose aspirations for its study are present yet whose faculties are somewhat inferior and whose strength is insufficient to sustain it;
for them, one should further abridge and simplify the essentials so as to reach them.

Although this intention is contained within the subsequent text, since the preceding section has already included the sense of "arising" (the transition from the former to the latter), it is said here that "the preceding is concluded and the subsequent is generated."
The commentary on the two preceding sections is briefly outlined in three parts. First, regarding the capacities of those for whom the teaching is intended:

since the dispositions of learners differ, there must be both extensive and concise teachings to suit them; otherwise, the teaching would not suffice. Those with superior faculties constitute the "superior grade," while those with middling or inferior faculties constitute the "middling and inferior grades.
For now, we shall speak in terms of one class of learners who are capable of study; therefore, all three grades are indicated.
If these grades were to be categorized in detail and fully encompassed, there should also be nine grades ranging from the highest-of-the-high (*uttamottama*) to the lowest-of-the-low (*adhamādhamā*).

Regarding the phrase "the faculties, aspirations, and dispositions differ": the first clause explains superiority and inferiority in a vertical sense, while the second clause describes distinctions in a horizontal sense.

"Faculties" (*indriya*) refers exclusively to the faculty that initiates the Noble Path; "aspirations" (*chanda*) refers to the desire for [practice]; and "dispositions" (*gotra*) refers to the spiritual lineage—these are the three meanings.
Because they are distinct from one another, they are called "horizontal. These are the objects of knowledge for three of the ten powers (*daśabala*).

First is the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties (*indriya*), which refers to the five faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; because these exist in the grades of superior, medium, and inferior, they are termed "superior and inferior.

Second is the power of knowing various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*), also known as "resolute belief" (*adhimukti*), which refers to aspiration or desire. That is to say, if it arises from others...

Faith is considered its precursor. The various superior inclinations (*adhimukti*) of love and delight—classified as inferior, middling, or superior—are also called "desire" (*chanda*), meaning the wish, longing, or fondness for something;
for example, some may crave wealth and profit, while others prefer fame, meditative concentration, or wisdom, each differing according to their type.

Subsequently, there is the power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*dhātu-jñāna-bala*). "Element" (*dhātu*) refers to one's innate nature (*prakṛti*), meaning that one may possess the nature of the One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, the Four Vehicles, or the Five Vehicles.
The various categories, such as those dominated by greed, hatred, or delusion, up to the eighty-four thousand types of conduct, are termed "diverse natures" (*nānā-dhātu*).

This "nature" is itself the seed; "inclination" (*chanda*) refers to its actual manifestation (*samudācāra*). All of the above is based on the explanations found in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other treatises.

The Commentary: Now, regarding the following two sections which formally describe that which is capable of being [the object of] this commentary, the first two phrases state the intent. "Fa" (法) means rule or standard;

Taking that as the rule and emulating it, I have made the great commentary correspond to the small.
The commentary states that [the Dharma] bends and curves according to the capacities of sentient beings, causing them all to awaken and achieve the Buddha-way;
thus it is said, "It follows those curves to bring them to completion. Therefore, the *Xici* (Appended Statements) says: "The *Yi* accords with Heaven and Earth;

therefore it can encompass and interweave the Way of Heaven and Earth" (as in observing the celestial patterns above and examining the terrestrial principles below, etc.). This continues until: "It encompasses the transformations of Heaven and Earth without exceeding them, and bends and curves to bring all things to completion."

"Things are encompassed without omission" (Han Kangbo’s commentary states: "To 'encompass' means to model oneself after Heaven and Earth and fully complete their principles; to 'perfectly accomplish' means to respond to things by following transformations, not being restricted to a single direction;

thus, all things shall obtain what they require"). Now, the present commentary explains: this meaning clarifies that the Sage models himself on Heaven and takes Earth as his law to sustain the myriad things;

therefore, each may follow its own kind and universally receive benefit. Thus it is said, "He perfectly accomplishes them according to their ease and simplicity," which precisely elucidates this point.
The intent of this summary is to be concise and easy to understand; therefore, it is said to follow what is "easy and simple" (*yìjiǎn*).
This passage on "ease and simplicity" also appears in the *Xīcí* (Appended Statements). Its meaning explains that the Way of Heaven and Earth is extremely easy and extremely simple:

they transform through non-action (*wéiérhuà*), accord with the nature of things, and thereby accomplish their great achievements. That text states: (The text actually occurs before the section on "curving and completing," but I have cited it here together with the commentary so that you may understand its principle yourself. Qian.

it does not toil, yet it excels at completing; therefore, they are called "Ease" and "Simplicity. Being easy, it is easy to know; being simple, it is easy to follow. Being easy to know, there is affinity; being easy to follow, there is achievement.

(Because it accords with the nature of all things, it is said there is affinity; because it penetrates the wills of the world, it is said there is achievement. Having affinity, one may endure long; having achievement, one...

One who possesses the virtue of ease and simplicity can achieve enduring and expansive merit. That which is enduring is the virtue of the worthy person; that which is expansive is the enterprise of the worthy person.

(Heaven and earth are easy and simple, yet all things each carry their own form; the Sage does nothing, yet all quarters each fulfill their own enterprise. When virtue and enterprise are complete, they enter into the realm of physical forms;

therefore, the virtue and enterprise of the worthy person are so designated. Through ease and simplicity, the principles of the world are attained. (The principles of the world all proceed from ease and simplicity, such that each attains accordance with its own position and station. Explanation.
It is said that once one has conformed to the Way of Heaven and undergone transformation, it is easy and simple. Thus, the *Daode jing* states:
"The Great Way is very easy to practice, yet no one in the world is able to practice it," and it further states: "The Great Way is very level (*yi*, meaning 'even'), yet people prefer the shortcuts.

Therefore, we know that one need only seek the intent of the scriptures in a single direction, interpreting them directly in accordance with principle; there is no need for extensive expositions of the various schools' elaborate descriptions of names and characteristics.

"Then it would be easy and simple. [The questioner asks: "Regarding the extremely profound meanings of the Dharma, which are difficult to understand and difficult to enter, how can you say they are easy? [The answer is:

"To accord with the Buddha’s skillful means (*upāya*) and virtuous merit, enabling one to attain easy understanding within the teachings that are difficult to understand—this alone is called 'skillful exposition.
How could that which causes people to fail to understand or comprehend through its composition or oral delivery be called 'sublime' (*miao*)? Therefore, Upagupta..."

When this Dharma was preached, hundreds of thousands of millions of beings who heard it all attained realization; so it was with Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, and so it was within the assembly of the Buddha.
Those who now boastfully claim that what is difficult to understand is profound and subtle are of a class that obstructs the Path.

Thus one should know that there are teachings that are profound and subtle yet easy to understand, and there are those that are coarse and shallow yet difficult to understand, as well as those that are shallow [yet easy].
The *Yi* (Book of Changes) contains profundities that are difficult to fathom; such differences arise from the skill or lack thereof in one’s exposition.

For instance, in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*, Huixiu attained a profound understanding after hearing Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras only once, yet he did not comprehend the Vinaya even after hearing it thirty times.
How could one then claim that the Vinaya section is more profound than the sūtras and śāstras? Since you already recognize this, why do you not simply compose a concise version?
Why does this commentary provide an extensive exegesis before directly explaining the scriptural text? Does it not state in the preceding line that "the faculties, desires, and natures differ"?
It is simply because commentaries on the gradual stages of names and characteristics have already circulated throughout the world;

since certain individuals stubbornly cling to what they previously heard and reject this [teaching], I have therefore opened this chapter to explain each point in accordance with the truth, leading them back to the single ultimate.
For those who do not cling [to elaborate commentary], this essential abridgment allows them to enter directly; it is the Dharma that completes what was left incomplete without omission.
The sub-commentary further searches for the refined essentials and provides direct annotations to the root scripture:

it straightforwardly expounds the meaning of the root text’s own doctrine to dissolve its textual difficulties, annotating each section beneath the relevant passage so that readers may easily perceive the meaning and avoid having to consult the scripture separately.

I have sought out the structural divisions of this original commentary; although there was a brief summary of the topical gates preceding the text, eight of the ten sections found in the *Great Commentary* (Dàshù) have been deleted here, which is why it says, "further searching for the refined essentials."

The "Sū" (Commentary) and "Shu" (Exposition) herein constitute the three lower sections, which establish their benefit. The teachings spoken by all Buddhas are fundamentally for the purpose of elucidating the mind;
since the mind possesses immeasurable gates of meaning, they are explained and clarified through successive stages, thereby forming various categories of phenomena.

Scholars who merely follow the words and follow the meanings become confused regarding the fundamental mind that is to be elucidated. Therefore, I now point toward the mind at every stage, so that scholars may, in each instance, [return to it].

When investigating the meaning of the various matters, one finds that the two views regarding the mind—as set forth in the thousand chapters and ten thousand phrases of the Vinaya section—are all contained within the gates of practice.

Therefore, those who compose commentaries and deliver lectures merely list the phrases at length and extensively generate interpretations of their meanings; this causes students to greedily seek out the literal phrasing and become deluded regarding the actual conduct of the precepts.

Consequently, the Master of the Nanshan Commentaries (Daoxuan) excised the redundant and supplemented the omissions, so that students may immediately apply themselves to the facts and the reality of the practice.
Since the present practice and intention are likewise identical to that, it is said that "phenomena are themselves the mind.
However, while the Vinaya regulations for body and speech clarify only their outward conduct, the current cultivation of concentration and wisdom aims at attuning the mind;

thus, whereas that [text] says "phenomena are themselves conduct," this [text] reverses that to say "phenomena are themselves the mind. Regarding "daily increase and daily decrease," the *Laozi* states: "In learning, there is daily increase."

"One diminishes daily for the sake of the Way. Now, borrowing the meaning of that expression, "diminishing daily" refers to severing delusions, while "increasing daily" refers to accomplishing wisdom;

diminishing daily refers to severing evil, while increasing daily refers to cultivating goodness. Thus, diminishment is for the purpose of departing from faults, and increase is for the purpose of accomplishing virtues.

The Commentary, about to explain the following two sections, provides an annotated exposition by opening with the chapters. First, it lists the names of the chapters. Regarding the "Analysis in Ten Sections":
the first eight are thematic gateways (*arthamukha*), while the final two constitute the actual explanation, as the title of the Sūtra itself belongs to the main text.

Nevertheless, these ten sections arise in a systematic sequence. First, concerning the "Causes and Conditions" (*nidāna*): Now, the words of the Sage are not in vain; their utterance must necessarily have a cause.
How could this be the same as the base and ignorant who, without cause or reason, impulsively seek to clarify the sacred scriptures? First, one must understand the origins [of the teaching];
therefore, the "Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching" follows. Once these causes and conditions are revealed, there is a teaching that arises;

though the teachings are immeasurable, they do not transcend the two or three baskets (*piṭaka*), nor the various vehicles (*yāna*) of the Great and Small Vehicles, nor the twelve divisions of the scriptures. One must know which basket and which vehicle this sutra belongs to.

Regarding the classification by which [this text] is subsumed: as for the threefold subsumption under the divisions of the *pitaka* (collections) and *yāna* (vehicles), all such divisions of *pitaka* and *yāna* encompass both provisional (*neyārtha*) and ultimate (*nītārtha*) teachings.
One must know whether this scripture is ultimate or provisional; for the judgment of what is provisional and what is ultimate requires authoritative evidence.
This is especially so because the traditions of the various masters of the final age in India and China—who composed treatises and commentaries—differ in their fundamental tenets.

Fifth, having received [the teaching] through the distinction between the provisional and the real regarding these four points, one has already distinguished that this sutra belongs to the category of the definitive (real) teaching;
however, as it is not yet known how the scope and depth of the meaning elucidated by this sutra are defined, it is followed by the section on "The Profundity of the Scope.

Sixth, having understood that the meaning of the sutra is extremely profound, one still does not know what kind of faculties and capacities are capable of receiving this Dharma; therefore, the next section clarifies this.
Sixth, although the profound meaning is known to be intended for those of sudden capacity (*tun-jī*), it is not yet known what constitutes the essence of the scriptures that express it;

therefore, next, the nature of the expressive vehicle is clarified. Seventh, while the profundity and subtlety of both the words and their meanings are understood, it is not yet determined what the primary tenets and aspirations therein are; therefore, next, the general and specific principles and purports are clarified.

Eighth: Although the general principles of the textual meaning have already been discussed in the preceding seven sections, and although the distinction between the means of expression (*vyañjaka*) and that which is expressed (*vyaṅgya*) ultimately pertains to the doctrinal system (*śāstramata*), one attains the intended meaning through these expressions;
yet once the meaning is attained, the expressions must be forgotten. In the cultivation of the mind through this forgetting of expressions, there are both sudden and gradual approaches.

How, then, are the skillful means for entering realization through these sudden and gradual methods? Therefore, the next section distinguishes the stages of cultivation and realization. Ninth: The Essential Meaning.
Having introduced the general intent, I shall now explain the meaning of the text. First, I clarify the title because it encompasses meanings that are difficult to conceive;
therefore, this is followed by the "General Explanation of the Title. As for the ten [sections], although their general intent is known, they are difficult to understand from the text alone.

To ensure that the distinct categories of meaning are made manifest through the brush and ink, and so that the essence of the fundamental principles appears within the scriptural passages, this is followed by the "Detailed Interpretation of the Textual Meaning."
The Commentary begins with ten sections of sub-commentary following the chapters. First, regarding the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching (*śāstrasyotpatti-pratyaya*):

Now, the term "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) has both general and specific meanings. The general meaning is that "cause" (*hetu*) refers to the causal basis and "condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to the contributing factors;
both carry the sense of "the reason why. Their intended meaning does not differ, as it is like saying, "For what cause did he do such a thing? or "By what condition did he do such a thing?"

Regarding the two points mentioned above, generally speaking, the force of their terminology is the same; however, the distinction lies in the fact that the former refers to *upakāra-pratyaya* (auxiliary conditions) while this refers to *hetu-pratyaya* (causal conditions), such that the former is a direct cause and the latter is an indirect condition.
Now, when this commentary speaks of "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*), it carries the previous general meaning without distinguishing between direct and indirect.

If one were to follow the previous explanation, it would be acceptable to say that "repaying the cause" constitutes the cause and "repaying the request" constitutes the condition; nevertheless, the fundamental intent of this commentary is simply...

A general investigation into the causes and conditions by which the Tathāgata, through various circumstances, expounds all the teachings. This section has two parts; first, the general introduction, and second, the specific explanation.

Regarding the first, the explicit revelation of the causes and conditions: When the Buddha was on the path of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), he cultivated his conduct and made vows, aspiring to attain Buddhahood, preach the Dharma, and deliver sentient beings.
Now, as he turns the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*), he fulfills the practices and vows of his causal ground. As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "The Buddha Vairocana..."
The vow-power pervades the entire Dharma-realm; within all lands, he constantly turns the unsurpassed wheel. Regarding the commentary on the request:
when the Buddha first attained the Way, Brahmā King, Śakra Devendra, and others requested him to turn the Wheel of Dharma. As the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"At that time, the various Brahmā Kings, the various Śakras, the World-Protecting Four Heavenly Kings, and Maheśvara joined their palms in reverent salutation."

When the Buddha was formally requested to turn the wheel of Dharma, he accepted that request; thus, beginning at the Deer Park and ending at the Śāla Grove over a period of forty-nine years, he expounded various sūtras and teachings to deliver sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "expounding the principles to deliver beings": he taught the vehicles of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha) to reveal the principle of the emptiness of persons through the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and so forth; he taught the Mahāyāna to deliver ordinary people and non-Buddhists.
The teaching reveals the principle of the two emptinesses to deliver those of the Two Vehicles, as well as ordinary beings and non-Buddhists of superior and middling faculties;

it expounds the One Vehicle teaching to reveal the ultimate principle of the three truths, the three virtues, the dharma-realm, and the dharma-nature, thereby delivering those of the Two Vehicles, provisional-vehicle bodhisattvas, and a class of ordinary beings of the highest-faculty type.
Thus, it is said that "it reveals the principle to deliver sentient beings. (The commentary states: All...

"By this" means that all the teachings of the Buddha throughout his lifetime arose and were disseminated in the world through the fulfillment of these intentions, such as repaying causes and conditions.
*Commentary:* If one traces back [the origin], the following two points specifically address the Buddha’s intention:

first, if one relies on the resonance of the capacities of sentient beings, many conditions are complete; when these conditions converge, he responds to their requests and speaks the teachings that are to be spoken. Furthermore—

The three vehicles differ in their depth and shallowness; however, speaking directly from the Buddha’s original intent, he acted solely to reveal and manifest the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision for the sake of sentient beings, and for no other purpose. As the *Lotus Sūtra* states:
"All Buddhas appear in the world for the sake of one great causal event. The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, desire to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision..."

Because they have attained purity, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world; they appear in the world desiring to reveal to sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, even unto leading them into the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach and transform only Bodhisattvas;
all that they do is for a single purpose, which is solely to reveal and awaken sentient beings through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. Śāriputra, it is thus with the Tathāgata.
It is solely for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle that he preaches the Dharma for sentient beings; there is no other vehicle, whether dual or triple.
The teaching of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions is likewise. Thus, one knows that the Buddha’s intention is solely for the One Vehicle.

As for the "two distinct [teachings]," this refers only to the specific causes and conditions for the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) and does not refer to other sūtras; hence it is called "distinct. (Section Ten)

First, to reveal that the practice of causes has a foundation: the practice of causes consists of the various *pāramitās* and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharmas*) which assist the path.
To say it "has a foundation" means that all such causal practices are established as actual practice only through the realization of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*);
only then can they be called the "True Cause. Therefore, Mañjuśrī requested the World-Honored One to explain the pure dharmic practices of the Tathāgata’s stage of causality.
The text points to the awakened mind as the root of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), stating that the *pāramitās* and other virtues flow forth from perfect awakening (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).
It further states that the original ground of practice for all Tathāgatas relies entirely upon the aspect of pure, universally illuminating awakening.

Moreover, it explains that all sentient beings mistakenly identify the four great elements and their objects of discursive thought as their own body and mind, while also teaching that ignorance is fundamentally empty.

The wisdom that can comprehend this is likewise unattainable; the meaning of this entire chapter is to bring about the realization that one’s own mind is originally perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*), fundamentally devoid of such phenomena as ignorance, afflictions, and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
It is for the purpose of revealing this fundamental basis of practice that this sutra is taught.
Regarding the second section of the commentary, "The Extinction of the Characteristics of the Fruit":

this means that when bodhi and nirvāṇa are extinguished—that is, when they are seen as being nothing other than the pure nature of awakening (bodhicitta)—only then does one attain the ultimate fruit, which is without beginning or end, neither increasing nor decreasing. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"In the wondrous, perfect, and enlightened mind of all Tathāgatas, there is originally no bodhi and no nirvāṇa; there is also no becoming a Buddha, nor..."
It is said that attaining Buddhahood, as well as birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa, and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and all Buddhas, are equally like the appearance of flowers in the sky.
It is further said that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like a dream from yesterday. The passages cited above all serve to obliterate the dual characteristics of the fruits of *bodhi* and nirvāṇa.
The commentary states that "originally there is no *bodhi*" and so forth; this explains the obliteration of the characteristics of the fruit. Therefore, [there is] none.
The preceding and following sections all explain and establish the perfection [of the teaching].

This means that Bodhi has no beginning and afflictions have no end, which differs from the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school’s view that Bodhi has a beginning and afflictions have an end. As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

"The mundane is not destroyed, and the supramundane is not exhausted; there is neither increase nor decrease. And as the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "All ordinary beings, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas..."
All Buddhas are without increase or decrease; they are not born in the past limit nor do they perish in the future limit, but are ultimately eternal and constant.

From the very beginning, their nature has been spontaneously fulfilled with all merits—namely, that their own essence possesses great wisdom-light and so forth, even being called the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata. (Thus we know that only that which is inherently possessed by nature constitutes the true fruit. This is the ultimate fruit.

When one realizes that both birth-and-death and nirvana, as well as afflictions and bodhi, are equally unattainable and does not grasp at these two characteristics, one penetrates to the heart of empty stillness and numinous awareness.
Since this very heart of awareness is originally empty and still, and its original knowing and perceiving is fundamentally bodhi and nirvana, it is called the "ultimate fruit.
Thus, a sutra says: "Because the three matters are perfectly realized, it is named 'ultimate.'"
Nirvāṇa (the ultimate state of nirvāṇa); it is also said that "all obstacles are themselves ultimate awakening" (the ultimate state of bodhi).

It is further said that "if the obstacles of phenomena and principle have been eternally severed and extinguished, one enters the subtle and perfect *bodhicitta* of the Tathāgata" (this refers to that which has been thoroughly reached as described above), which is the fulfillment of bodhi and great nirvāṇa (both of which are ultimate). It is also said that "bodhi and nirvāṇa flow forth [from this]" (these... [etc.])
All the gates are ultimately the two fruits; because they accord with the essence of awakening, they are all ultimate. Regarding the commentary on "decisive discernment" (*viniścaya*) and so forth:

It refers to the selection and rejection of biased views.
Some people exclusively claim that [the nature] is originally perfect and true, requiring no cultivation or practice;

others exclusively claim that one realizes truth by severing obstacles, extinguishing the state of an ordinary being to become a sage. Therefore, it is said: "The definitive discernment of awakening and cultivation," etc. (Note:
