because one suddenly realizes that body, mind, and sensory objects are all empty, one does not cling to various marks (*nimitta*) and does not realize a "mind-nature," for the mind-nature is fundamentally unmoving.

Furthermore, because one suddenly realizes that the merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are fully present, one accords with them in every thought-moment; this is called "conforming to the Way. This is due to having awakened to it previously.
Therefore, one must understand [the sequence]. Regarding the commentary’s statement, "First cultivation, then awakening," etc., this refers to the subsequent correspondence.

That is to say, because all conditions are suddenly severed (as detailed in the passage cited above), the ground of the mind opens up; since the faculties and aspirations are superior, this differs from the aforementioned sudden cultivation followed by gradual awakening.
The note states that "cultivation is like taking medicine" means taking a potent medicine all at once; "awakening is like the illness [subsiding]."
"Removing" means that one suddenly breaks into a sweat, and all four limbs and hundred joints become light and cool at once.

One does not take the sense of a gradual recovery as the awakening, because the awakening occurs later; therefore, it must be understood in terms of realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). Furthermore, this realization and understanding are without two distinct characteristics.

In the commentary, "cultivation" and "awakening" are simultaneous, while "realization" and "understanding" are sequential. This means taking non-characteristic (*animitta*) as cultivation and clarity as realization.
Awakening is wisdom; it is function. Cultivation is concentration; it is essence. Heze said: "To realize essence within function is self-knowledge.

This is an excerpt from the commentary on the *Zhiguan* (Stopping and Contemplation), intended to guide the mind toward the essentials. In full, it states: "If one is without mind regarding forgetting and illumination, then all burdens are cast off;
if one follows the natural flow with tranquil awareness, then all practices arise. Here, we have taken only the first phrase of each pair for our purpose.

The Essential Points of Mind for One Enlightenment and One Cultivation: It is also said that when not a single thought arises, the boundaries of past and future are severed (this is sudden cultivation);
when the luminous essence stands alone, self and others are both thus (this is sudden enlightenment). Heze said:

"When one does not deliberate at all upon good or evil, under these words, thoughts and conceptions are spontaneously cut off" (cultivation); "when there is precisely no thought or conception, the mind already knows itself" (enlightenment). This commentary provides a comprehensive explanation and realization.
This has two meanings: first, as explained above, both realization (*pratyakṣa*) and understanding (*adhigama*) are without dual characteristics;
thus both are pervasive, meaning that realization is itself understanding and understanding is itself realization. Second, it may refer to either realization or understanding:

the sudden comprehension and the sudden cessation constitute understanding-awakening (*adhigama-bodha*), while the sudden exhaustion and the sudden awareness constitute realization-awakening (*pratyakṣa-bodha*), like awakening from a great dream.

It is called "sudden awakening" because dreams must necessarily end all at once (as explained in detail below according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*). The Commentary states: "If [the mind] is originally endowed... This is the eighth pair.
It concludes by saying "comprehensively understanding," which refers to realization (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*); this also contains two meanings as previously stated.

The first meaning can be understood; the latter meaning should now be explained. Regarding the exegesis, one takes only the untainted original awakening (*anāsrava-mūla-bodhi*) as enlightenment, without adding further cognitive activity.
The mind that has realized [this] takes only the merits inherent in the nature as its practice, rather than waiting for the cessation of the mind to constitute practice.

In the commentary, the characters "drinking" (yǐn) and "attaining" (dé) are both metaphors corresponding to this; when explained in terms of realization (*pratyakṣa*), it refers to the moment when initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) merges with the fundamental [awakening], such that there is no distinction between them.
Thus, the Huayan school speaks of the "newly accomplished ancient Buddha" and the "anciently accomplished new Buddha," which constitutes accomplishment.
At that time, one perceives only the original, original reality and does not see the marks of constant renewal;

since both awakening and cultivation are thus, the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra states that at the moment of attaining Buddhahood, one must be of the same essence as all sentient beings and attain realization together with them.
Furthermore, the teaching that "attainment and non-attainment are without distinction" is precisely because one does not grasp at the illusory marks of new attainment.
The sub-commentary (*shu*) explains that this refers to the three assemblies following the "Perfect" [Assembly] in this sutra. The text consists of headings and explanations;

within the explanations, one should extract the corresponding meanings from the section on the "Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching" and from the subsequent passages where the text is analyzed (*xiao-wen*). I shall not repeat those descriptions here.

However, what is referred to as "realization" (*zheng*) in this context simply takes the time when the practice corresponds to contemplation (*guan-xing*); what is perceived through direct perception (*xian-liang*) at that moment is itself termed realization.
To realize [the truth] does not necessarily require the fruit of sainthood.
The commentary states that the following three points resolve potential objections. Specifically, there may be an objection stating:

"Since the provisional and the real were already extensively distinguished previously, and the teachings of sudden and gradual were fully explained, why are they being stated again now? It is for this reason that these points are provided as a resolution.
The commentary states: "If one obtains the lower four [stages], they are all established as concentration and wisdom (samādhi-prajñā).

This means that because concentration and wisdom have three distinct natures—*savikalpa* (with activity), *nirvikalpa* (without activity), and their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)—both the sudden and gradual approaches are correspondingly appropriate.

Thus, Heze [Shenhui] spoke of three types of the Threefold Training. Regarding the three types of *savikalpa*: they refer to "not committing any evil," and so forth (*etc.*). Regarding the three types of *nirvikalpa*: [they refer to... (*etc.*).

The non-arising of deluded mind is *śīla* (precept), which is the absence of greed, hatred, affliction, jealousy, and so forth. The original absence of deluded mind is *samādhi* (concentration), which is the absence of discursive thought and cognition.

Knowing that the mind is without conceptualization is *prajñā* (wisdom), which does not fall into the emptiness of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). These three self-natures are called emptiness, stillness, and illumination (corresponding respectively:

emptiness corresponds to *śīla*, as it signifies the departure from the four marks and the severance of the hundred negations; the other two may be understood accordingly). What is called "delusive thought" is wisdom without concentration. What is called "non-" [is]...
"The reporter lacks the concentration of wisdom. This refers merely to being in a state of profound obscurity where there is no discernment, resulting in the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*);
it is not that the indeterminate is defined solely by its failure to distinguish between good and evil.

As for the phrase "examine and cultivate it," the intent of this section lies in practice rather than in mere intellectual understanding; therefore, it exhorts one to "cultivate" it rather than "study" it. This is the eighth [section].

This is narrated based on the "Gate of the Profundity and Shallowness of Cultivation and Realization" within the ten gates of the *Huayan shu xuantan* (Prolegomenon to the Avatamsaka Commentary) composed by Master Qingliang under imperial decree,
as well as the Chan gates of the various schools and the essential Chan teachings of the various sutras.
The Sub-commentary on the Brief Commentary of the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, Scroll Four;
The Sub-commentary on the Brief Commentary of the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, Scroll Five.
Extracted from the Great Commentary by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Mount Guifeng.
○ Ninth: General Explanation of the Title of the Scripture. The Commentary (Sūtra) has two parts. First, the direct explanation of the title of the scripture.

It is called a "general explanation" because the title encompasses the entire text; hence it is termed "general. The text has three sections. The first five lines of the commentary above correspond to the Dharma and its meaning. Regarding "Dharma and its meaning":
whenever one wishes to understand a sutra or śāstra, one must first clearly identify the Dharma and its meaning, relying upon the Dharma.
When the meaning is understood, the meaning itself becomes clear; when the meaning illuminates the Dharma, the Dharma itself becomes manifest.
Nowadays, those who listen and study seek only the literal meaning and do not investigate the essence of the Dharma, nor do they examine what kind of Dharma this meaning belongs to.
As for those who practice Chan, they merely wish to recognize a single dharma; once it is recognized, they stop, no longer investigating or refuting the fundamental source of all Buddhas.
Since this treatise provides an exposition on the nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*) of the Bodhisattva, I shall now correlate it in full.

Within the treatise, wishing to reveal the profound and hidden principles of the Mahāyāna’s nature and characteristics, it first introduces these two treatises, stating: "The Mahāyāna generally consists of two kinds:
first, phenomena (*dharma*); second, meaning (*artha*). 'Phenomena' refers to the One Mind; 'meaning' opens into the Three Greatnesses. This is precisely identical to the present case.

(The Treatise says: "That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings; this is the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind" [this is the name for *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* when it is entangled in defilements]).
However, all the various differentiated meanings and principles of the Mahāyāna taught by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are explained solely in reference to the fundamental mind (*mūlacitta*);

there has never been a single dharma taught apart from this fundamental mind. Therefore, the Treatise says: "Based upon this mind, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed" (the "mind" here is precisely the mind of sentient beings). [The Sage...]

Since we manifest based on this mind, we should seek it within this very mind and not seek it within words or language. Now, within these eleven characters of the sutra’s title, there are two layers of Dharma-meaning; they are to be correlated with the text as follows:
in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra-vyākhyā*, "Perfect Enlightenment" (*yuánjué*) refers to the Dharma.

At the beginning of the main teaching, the Buddha himself established the fundamental principle, positing only Perfect Enlightenment (as the text says: "The Unsurpassed Dharma King has a Great Dhāraṇī-gate called Perfect Enlightenment, from which all things flow forth," etc.). This is the intermediate section.

In this commentary, the preceding section introduces the subsequent one; the title and the conclusion specifically point to and expound only upon *yuanjue* (Perfect Enlightenment), and do not further mention *dafangguang* (Mahāvaipulya).

(The text says: "When the Tathāgata cultivated *yuanjue* during his causal stage," and again, "Having heard of this *yuanjue*, how should one practice? and also, "All manner of illusory transformations arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of *yuanjue*.

Following these textual patterns, there are three to fifty such sections. The sub-commentary states that "*dafangguang*" refers to the "meaning" (*yi*), which corresponds to the "essence, characteristics, and function" (*ti-xiang-yong*) of the *Qixin lun* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith).
The character "Great" (*dà*) is as explained below. The six characters following the commentary [in the *Śū*] correspond to the "Dharma-meaning" (*fǎyì*) within the "expressive medium" (*néngquán*).

Among these six characters, the first five—referring to the comparison with various sutras, the praise of this sutra’s superiority, and their synthesis into a title—belong collectively to the category of the expressive medium.
However, from the perspective of the intended meaning (*yòngyì*), one should understand that this entire scripture, the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra*, is [the Dharma-meaning].
Among the Sūtra Piṭaka, this refers to the sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). The single character "sūtra" (經) precisely designates this entire collection of names, phrases, and syllables;
therefore, it corresponds to the Dharma, which is the teaching (*deśanā-dharma*).

In the commentary on the sutra, there are two sections below that mark the extensive [explanation] while preserving the abbreviated [statement]. Regarding the five names, the marking of the extensive is as follows:
in the *Pravartana* (Circulation) section, the text states: "The name of this sutra is *Mahāvaipulya Samantabhadra-bodhi-citta*; it is also called *Sūtra of Definitive Meaning*;
it is also called *Secret King Samādhi*; it is also called *Tathāgata’s Decisive Realm*; it is also called *Tathāgatagarbha Self-Nature Differentiation*."

The alternative interpretation is as follows: the title at the beginning of the *Śāstra* commentary is abbreviated to "Only Two" (*wei er*). The fundamental tenet (*zongben*) is Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanjue*), which is the essence of the Dharma;

its function (*tiyong*) is Great Vaipulya (*dafangguang*), which is the meaning (*yi*) of the Dharma. Therefore, it is called the "vastness of the Dharma and its meaning" (*fayi zhi hong*; *hong* means great). Regarding the "guiding line" (*gang*): a guiding line is that upon which a net depends.

As the *Book of Documents* says, "If the net is on the guiding line, there will be order and no confusion. "Confusion" (*wen*) means disorder. This "explanation" (*quan*) refers to the *Sūtra*, which is speech; it encompasses both the purport (*zhi*) and the merit (*gong*).

"Virtue" (*de*) refers to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), which is the "image" (*xiàng*); the words of definitive meaning distinguish this [sūtra] as superior to other sūtras. "Brightly" (*jiǎo*) signifies ultimate clarity;

"mirror" (*jìng*) means that which can discern the beautiful from the ugly and the good from the bad. This serves as a metaphor for how this sūtra can serve as a standard to determine the heterodox from the orthodox, the Great from the Small, and the provisional from the real.
The phrase "the details are exhaustive below" (*shù shì zhōu xià*) doubly concludes the intent regarding both the extensive and the abbreviated [versions].
The commentary on the three "Greats" and below explains the text according to its sections: first, the explanation of the five characters that are the subject matter;

second, the explanation of the first three characters and the subsequent two characters; third, the explanation of the three "Greats. First, the general heading: "Great" (Dà) refers to the essence-nature (*tattva*) of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*);

"Square" (Fāng) refers to the qualities and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of Perfect Enlightenment; "Vast" (Guǎng) refers to the functional activity (*karma*) of Perfect Enlightenment; therefore, they are called the "Three Greats. [Commentary begins: Regarding "Great" (*Dà*), etc., below...

Second, the citation and explanation of the three [sections]: first, the explanation of the term "Great" (*mahā*) in the *Śāstra*. Regarding the title of the *Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas of the Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyāna-śata-dharma-viśada-mukha-śāstra*), its commentary states:
"The term 'Great' has the sense of distinguishing from the 'Small,' while 'Vehicle' (*yāna*) is named for its function of conveying [beings].
Therefore, it is stated as such. The commentary first addresses "all dharmas," which refers to the humans and animals spoken of in the two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism.

The myriad things, including plants and trees, take Heaven and Earth as their origin; yet Heaven and Earth themselves take the primordial, undifferentiated One Qi (chaotic single breath) as their ultimate source.
Therefore, the title "Yuanshi" (Primordial Beginning) was established. Furthermore, Laozi said: "There was something formless and complete, born before Heaven and Earth. Master Yansheng said:
"Heaven, Earth, humans, domestic animals, and the myriad things all arise from chaos. What is clarified by the present orthodox teaching is that [it is] Heaven... [text truncated].
The lands, people, and animals are the results produced by individual karma; both that which is produced and that which produces it arise from the transformations of one's own deluded consciousness.

Thus, deluded consciousness is primary. Since this deluded consciousness exists because of the迷失 (delusion) of the Perfectly Awakened True Mind (*pariniṣpanna-tathatā*), the Perfectly Awakened Mind is primary.
Therefore, the subsequent scripture states: "All manner of illusory transformations arise from the wondrous mind of Perfect Awakening. This leads to...
Space, too, is a transformation of consciousness; one should know that only Perfect Enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-vidyā) is the primary meaning, and thus it is said to "precede all dharmas.
If one considers the non-obstruction between the fundamental and the derivative, or the harmonious integration of the true and the false, there is neither before nor after.
However, from the perspective of delusion regarding the truth giving rise to falsehood, and the fundamental giving rise to the derivative, it is said to "precede all dharmas. This is the meaning.
The sequence of their manifestation does not correspond to the sequence of their temporal arising; it is because they are foremost that they are called "Great.
This is like a person who is the eldest being called "great" because they were born first; it does not refer to physical stature when speaking of large and small.

Regarding the citation from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, this is an invocation of the sūtra to prove the meaning of permanence, which is the meaning of "Great. "Permanence" refers to the vertical dimension, exhausting the beginning...
This refers to the third chapter of that sutra, the "Chapter on the Merits of the Name," where the Buddha told Kāśyapa: "This sutra is named the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.

Its opening words are excellent... (and so forth), up until: "That which is called 'Great' (*mahā*) is designated as 'Eternal' (*nitya*), just as the eight great rivers all flow back to the great ocean...
(and so forth). Here, we take only the character "Great" (*mahā*) and interpret it in terms of its unchanging essence.

Therefore, it is named "constant" (*nitya*), because its nature is inherent and not something produced by construction. Thus, Master Daosheng’s commentary states: "If one seeks its ultimate course, it is that which I have only now realized.
It is not that there is illumination in the present; rather, illumination does not reside in the present. This means that nothing precedes it, and thus it is 'Great.
Since it is called 'Great,' it is for this reason termed 'constant. Regarding the term "transverse" (*heng*) in the commentary, this explains "greatness" in terms of its spatial dimension.
Regarding the statement "The *Śūramgama-samādhi-sūtra* further says," this refers to the fifth chapter of that sūtra, the "Tathāgatagarbha" (Rulai xing pin), which states: "The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
'That which is called "great" has a nature as vast and expansive as empty space. Furthermore, it has another meaning, namely, the twenty-third [chapter], which says:
'For example, empty space' is a metaphor for true liberation (*bhūtavimukti*), and true liberation is precisely *nirvāṇa*."

△ Regarding "the meaning of 'method' (*fang*)": the following two [sections] explain the character "method," and the text is explicit. △ Regarding "the meaning of 'vast' (*guang*)": the following three [sections] explain the character "vast.
As for the phrase "originally possessing sands of eons of faults and so forth," this refers to what the *Śāstra* says: "From the very beginning, its nature is spontaneously fulfilled with all merits;
that is to say, its own essence possesses the meaning of great wisdom-light" (and so forth), up until it is fully endowed.

Because there are meanings of delusive defilements exceeding those of the sands of the Ganges, and because this meaning corresponds to them, when the nature of the mind is unmoving, there are manifested the meanings of the characteristics of all pure merits exceeding those of the sands of the Ganges (as each is paired with its opposite, both defilement and purity exceed the sands of the Ganges). The commentary states:

it is now changed to "dust-sands" (*chen-sha*) for two reasons: first, to avoid the imperial taboo; second, because the number is even more extensive—referring to the dust motes scattered throughout the world.

The realms constitute the dust; each particle of dust constitutes a single function of virtue, which is why it is said to be "many. As for the sands, this refers to the number of all the sands within the Ganges River.
The Commentary states that "they arise secretly and respond subtly" because, even within the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), these wondrous functions are not entirely absent;
however, since ordinary beings do not realize them in their daily activities, they are described as "secret" and "subtle. Thus, the Treatise says: "They are able to give rise to all things."

Because it is the cause and fruit of mundane and supramundane goodness (and because unwholesome states contradict reality and are thus what is to be remedied, they do not function as such). Question: If that is so, then one should be separated from reality. Answer: Because of delusion regarding reality, one cannot be separated from reality;

because it contradicts reality, [the unwholesome] does not function [as a cause]. Since it also gives rise to mundane goodness, it is not the case that ordinary beings lack it. Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says:
"In the minds of Bodhisattvas and all sentient beings, there is always, at every thought-moment, a Buddha attaining perfect enlightenment. (The commentary on this passage is missing.)

Regarding that which has rest and exhaustion, when discussed in general terms, its function is inexhaustible; it does not distinguish between ordinary beings and sages, but simply takes this virtue as inherently existing within the nature.

If one approaches it from the perspective of the stage of sagehood, as stated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Great Parinirvāṇa can establish great meanings, such as containing Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed, and so forth, concluding: "Good son, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in the Great Nirvāṇa..."
Because it can manifest various and immeasurable supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*), it is therefore called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Question: The title of the *Avataṃsaka* also speaks of "Mahāvaipulya"; how do these two differ? Answer: They are the same when categorized according to the three great natures (*trividha-mahātmya*);
they differ when their meanings are explained according to their respective schools. In the *Avataṃsaka-śāstra*, "Mahā" is explained as: "All marks and functions are identical with the Truth."

Because its nature is eternally pervasive, to uphold it is to uphold both nature and characteristics; endowed with the ten gates of the Mysterious Portal (*daśa-guhya-mukha*), one is able to generate understanding regarding each and every phenomenon.
Thus, Master Zang expounded the meaning of the hundred gates within a single atom, composing two fascicles in summary.
In its broadest sense, it is able to encompass and pervade all things—characteristics are identical and characteristics enter one another in infinite layers, each corresponding to every other.
This similarity and difference can be understood.

Regarding the phrase "The Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment," the following two sections explain the essence of the Dharma. First, within the initial section, there are two parts: first, the single sentence that formally introduces the topic;

second, the passage beginning with "If not... which serves to clarify and point out the essence. Thus, one should know that what has been discussed hitherto refers only to the vast, encompassing, and sustaining nature of Perfect Enlightenment.

The commentary on "equal, vast, and perfect" (等也疏圓者) provides the formal explanation of the latter two [phrases], as fully detailed in the preceding commentary on the passage from the Preface concerning "pervasive and pure" (彌滿清淨).
The commentary on "therefore, the treatise" (疏故論下) cites scriptural evidence to prove the meaning that awakened illumination is free from all conceptual discrimination.

The commentary on "the explanation says" (疏釋曰下) clarifies the stages [of realization], showing that the expression "free from thought" (離念) does not depend upon the attainment of a saintly stage. The commentary on "therefore we know" (疏故知下) provides the final interpretation.
The establishment [of this meaning] follows the commentary; the six proofs below demonstrate that its significance does not differ from what was stated in the introduction.
However, regarding this *Perfect Enlightenment* (*Yuanjue*), its name varies according to the specific school within the various sūtras.

In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is designated as "Buddha-nature" (*foxing*) because one realizes and cultivates this nature—which inherently exists within the bodies of ordinary beings—and thereby certainly attains Buddhahood. In the *Lotus Sūtra*, it is designated as... [the text here appears to be truncated].
It is praised as this single Dharma that carries sentient beings to the place of treasure, for other vehicles cannot do so and all other dharmas are inferior;
therefore, it is called the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna) and the Wondrous Dharma. Regarding the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti), it refers only to those who abide in this nature (*dhātu*);

their spiritual transformations are immeasurable, beyond what can be discussed by speech or conceived by the mind, and are thus called the "Inconceivable Liberation. Regarding the Vajra, it refers only to this.
Because its nature manifests the capacity to destroy afflictions, it is called *prajñā*; other categories may be understood accordingly.

These are all distinctions within the gate of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). This is truly because, while the functions of the spirit are manifold and vast and sublime virtues are boundless, they cannot be designated as such;
thus it is directly titled "The Gate of Perfect Enlightenment Chan. It is detached from [other designations].
The contemplation of non-contemplation is likewise intended here to sweep away traces and block off errors;

however, as it is a transmission from mind to mind through secret instruction rather than a matter discussed in written documents, I shall now briefly address it by means of formal words to distinguish it.

The Commentary (*śūtra*)—or [the sub-commentary]—uses four characters or one character for the lower section, while two characters are used for the first section as a general heading to indicate the meaning of the Dharma.
It states that "only awakening (*bodhi*) is the Dharma. For instance, although the worldly void (*ākāśa*) can also be all-pervasive, only spiritual awakening has no equal in the world;
therefore, only this is the Dharma. Thus, in the Sūtras, it is sometimes simply said that "awakening pervades the ten directions," and it is also said that "it is spoken of based on illusion."
Awakening is also called illusion; if one says that awakening exists, one has not yet departed from illusion, and the same applies to saying that awakening does not exist.
Furthermore, it is said that "all is awakening," and it is said that "all are in accord with awakening.

It is also said that they are "not awakening" because those who are able to enter do so by entering through what is not awakening. Moreover, it is said that one realizes awakening and enters parinirvāṇa.

It is said that this is called "conforming to pure awakening" (*viśuddha-bodhi-anuloma*). Furthermore, the phrase "with a mind of pure awakening" appears in all three contemplations; such passages are not few.
Since it is not definitively stated that [this refers to] the Perfect [Teaching], and the single character "awakening" (*jue*) remains unchanged, one knows this is the Dharma-method.

Moreover, the character "perfect" (*yuan*) is a semantic term, as is clear from the subsequent explanation. The intent of the *Sūtra* commentary (*shu*) states that the following two sections cite the Dharma to explain the meaning. The first four characters cite [the Dharma].
The remainder of the Dharma is the explanation of the meaning. Within the text, these four characters are explained through three layers of relative correspondences.
Regarding the three layers of alternating correspondences: "vast" (1) corresponds with "three," and "square and round" (2) corresponds with "four"; hence they are called "alternating.
As for the explanation of these alternations, it is to take "essence and function" as one pair and "principle and phenomena" as another pair. This is the principle.

This is the definitive source of the school’s tenets; it should be called "Rectitude" (*fangzheng*). This is the reason for the explanation; it should be called "Perfection" (*yuanman*), and thus it is taken as the counterpart.

The commentary (*shu*) may also be understood through the following two pairs in sequence: that is, binding the four characters together to form a single pair of "Essence" (*ti*) and "Function" (*yong*).
Furthermore, regarding the three [characters] above and below, they form a pair of "General" (*zong*) and "Particular" (*bie*); the term "three characters" refers to the particular.

The three great meanings are essence (ti), characteristic (xiang), and function (yong). The intent of the passage from "The meaning clarifies" (*yi ming yi xia*) onwards is to manifest the general and specific aspects by means of the dharma-meaning (*fa-yi*).

It states that "awakening" (*jue*) is that which possesses (*neng ju*), while the "three greatnesses" (*san da*) are that which is possessed (*suo ju*); the complete sufficiency of these three is what constitutes "perfection" (*yuan*).
The commentary (*shu*) indicates that the following three lines are a general praise and conclusion, which can be understood accordingly.
In the commentary following this, the second section explains the six characters that serve as the expressive medium (*abhidhāna*). First, regarding the assignment [of these characters], it says:

"To refer generally to all sūtras" means that among the three piṭakas, this is the Sūtra Piṭaka (*sūtrapiṭaka*). The intent is that this *Awakening of Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyāna-śrīmālā-siṃhanāda*) is a sūtra of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) within the Sūtra Piṭaka;
it is not praised as being among the other two piṭakas. The cited text states: "The eyes," which is the explanation.
The title of this section means "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*). Since "eye" (*cakṣus*) carries the sense of opening, resolving, manifesting, and illuminating with clarity, the commentary [states]:

"Regarding the *sūtra*... and so forth. This is the second part, the actual explanation, which consists of three sections. First, the explanation of the three characters: this meaning was already fully presented in the second section, the "Gate of the Compendium of the Pitakas," where its interpretation concluded;

That is to say, because it is a definitive explanation (*juézhé shuō*), it is not a concealed or indirect teaching. (If one were to speak only of the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing, that would conceal the true reality of emptiness; if one were to speak only of non-self, that would conceal the characteristic of the true self;

if one were to claim that all is empty and that this alone constitutes the ultimate path, that would conceal the characteristic of the numinous awareness of fundamental wisdom and the infinite virtues inherent in its nature. Therefore, these are not definitive. Conversely, those that are the opposite are called "definitive meaning" (*lǐoyì*). This is the ultimate teaching. It is an exhaustive explanation.

Therefore, it is not a teaching given with intentional ambiguity (saṃdhāya-bhāṣita). [The Buddha’s original intent in saying "no-self" was to secretly reveal true self; in saying that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, he secretly revealed the nature-virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

in saying that all things are empty, he secretly revealed the original enlightenment of True Suchness. Fearing that people might become attached by following the words, he merely quelled their conceptual thoughts; thus, it is not the ultimate teaching. It is a teaching of explicit revelation, not a teaching of concealed implication.

[Every provisional teaching spoken by the Buddha contains the true and ultimate Dharma, but because it did not explicitly state it, it is called "concealed. Now, because the perfect and pure enlightened nature is made manifest, it is called "explicitly revealed."]

The profound and wondrous principle melts and fuses the myriad phenomena of the phenomenal world—both defiled and pure—into a single-flavored dharma.
It is like casting millions of golden vessels and images in a blazing furnace, reducing them all to a single flavor of gold.

Furthermore, the infinite varieties of differentiated wisdom are subsumed within the wisdom of the single true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), just as the hundreds of rivers and ten thousand streams are gathered into the great ocean.
It flows into one great ocean, while the rest are all visible.

Furthermore, regarding the "Great Jewel" section below, the second part provides an explanation according to the teachings (*jiao*). Based on the cited scriptural passage, the initial "Buddha" first raises the inquiry, followed by the self-citation and explanation.
Within this self-citation and explanation, the definitive and non-definitive (*nītārtha* and *neyārtha*) are clarified in contrast, consisting of four pairs; however, each...

Regarding those whose understanding of the characteristics of practice is not yet complete, much corresponds to the definitive teachings (*nītārtha*) within the Dharma-characteristics schools (*lakṣaṇa-yāna*) of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;
that which accords with the Dharma-nature school (*dharmatā-yāna*) corresponds to the Final Teaching (*paryanta-yāna*) and the Sudden Teaching (*tada-yāna*).

For now, I shall point out how this sutra accords with the Buddha’s own judgment regarding definitive teachings, thereby establishing its title and simultaneously distinguishing it from the non-definitive teachings (*neyārtha*); let this be examined in detail.
Regarding the first pair mentioned therein, that which is called "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*) refers to the single Piṭaka of the Hīnayāna, which teaches only conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Although it speaks of the Four Noble Truths, when compared to True Suchness (*tathatā*), these still constitute conventional phenomena. Furthermore, many sūtras and śāstras of this school primarily teach the conventional while rarely teaching the ultimate (*paramārtha*);
this clearly demonstrates that they are of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). As for that which is called "ultimate," it is based on...
In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, there are four layers of the two truths, totaling eight truths. The first truth is exclusively conventional and not ultimate;
the final truth is exclusively ultimate and not conventional. What is called "ultimate of the ultimate" (*paramārtha-paramārtha*) is precisely *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (Perfect Enlightenment).
As stated in the subsequent text: "From *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* flow forth all pure *tathatā* and *nirvāṇa*. That which flows forth is likewise a provisional establishment (*prajñapti*).

In contrast to this, True Suchness (tathatā) constitutes the second conventional [truth]. Within the second pair, those that speak of karma and afflictions are also teachings on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-dharma*).
Among the extensive explanations in the teachings on characteristics, there is not even one percent that speaks of the true nature (*dharmatā*);

these are spoken from the perspective of the majority and belong to the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). As for what is said regarding the exhaustion of afflictions and karma, it also accords with this sutra, which states: [text continues]
It is said that ignorance is eternally severed; furthermore, it is stated that this ignorance has no real substance.

It is also said that knowing these to be like flowers in the sky means there is neither cyclic existence nor a body and mind undergoing birth and death—this is the meaning of the exhaustion of afflictions and karma.

Regarding the third pair, the mention of "detachment and renunciation" and so forth refers precisely to the school of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka-yāna*). Within the Dharma-character school (*dharma-lakṣaṇa-vāda*), regarding...
The severing of hindrances, the realization of truth, and the transformation of consciousness into wisdom are likewise of this same category.

Regarding the statement that "birth and nirvāṇa are non-dual," this sutra teaches that both nirvāṇa and the various illusory transformations are born from the awakened mind; that these two dharmas share the same source is precisely the meaning of non-duality.
Furthermore, it says that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like a dream, and that one neither loathes birth-and-death nor craves nirvāṇa.

The *pātra* and other such items are all likewise so. Regarding the "various distinctions of phrases and sentences" mentioned in the fourth pair, this refers to the specific determinations of the Dharma-character school (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) concerning the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and so forth.

As for the statement that it is "profound, difficult to see, and difficult to awaken to," it is difficult to see because differentiation is itself non-differentiation. This sutra speaks of "the mind of deliberation."
To attempt to fathom Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti-nirbhāsa) is like trying to burn Mount Sumeru with a firefly’s glow; it can never catch fire.

This is precisely the meaning of its being difficult to see and difficult to realize. Therefore, the Commentary concludes by judging that these all correspond to Perfect Enlightenment. Since this was the Buddha’s own selection, one should not harbor doubts.

In the sub-commentary (*śūtra*), the section following "the three below" explains the character *jing* (sūtra), stating that "as explained above" refers to the explanation within the section on the "inclusion of the Tripitaka.

The sub-commentary poses a question regarding the "three below," which serves to resolve two types of objections. First, the direct resolution of the intent of the question is as follows: [The objection] is understandable. The answer states:

"In contrast to praising the general, one praises the particular. "General" refers to the single *Sūtrapiṭaka*; "particular" refers to the individual sūtras, each of which is distinct. Now, one is praising this particular [sūtra].

One part consists of those sutras of definitive meaning within the Sūtra Piṭaka, such as when praising an eminent person by saying, "This person is among men," or when extolling the Buddha as the "God among Gods" (Devātideva), and so forth;
this can also be understood from the examples provided in the second section below of the Commentary.

Regarding the second section, the specific explanation of the translation, the *Shu* (Commentary) states: "Juejiu" (Awakening and Saving). This Tripiṭaka Master took "compassion and wisdom" as his name.

"Jue" (Awakening) refers to awakening to [truth], and "jiu" (Saving) refers to saving those who are deluded. Furthermore, "Jue" means awakening to the Dharma, and "jiu" means saving the world (as the verse of salutation in the *Qixin lun* refers to the Buddha as the "Savior of the World").
This means that because he awakens to the true Dharma and saves the deluded masses of the world, he is named Juejiu. [The commentary notes: North India.

As for the country of India, there are five regions: the four directions and the center; this [region] is the north. Regarding India and Kaśmīra, the Chinese names have not yet been fully standardized.

As for Baima Si (White Horse Monastery), during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Later Han dynasty, the Indian monks Mokṣala and Dharmaratna arrived at the capital of Luoyang carrying scriptures on white horses.
The Emperor ordered the construction of a monastery to repay the kindness of the white horse; this was the Tianzhu Monastery (India Monastery).
The patriarchs of the Lower Temple (Gembō-ji) resided in the Old Capital (Kyōto), some twenty li or more to the east of the present capital; I have also visited there myself.
Regarding the original arrival of the white horse and the Sanskrit scriptures of Matanga and Dharmarakṣa, the details are as extensive as described in other fascicles.
As for the one commentary (*sho*), its catalog states it consists of twenty-eight sheets, or perhaps one or two fascicles; the catalog does not record the year or month [of its composition].

It is said that this sutra was recently produced, though it is not certain which year; however, with the intention of propagating the Way, one’s primary concern should be to discern the false from the genuine.

Since the true exposition is unerring, why should one insist on knowing the specific year and month? (The above is the original text. Critique: I maintain that simply stating "the year and month are not recorded" suffices;
why must these additional words be added? Therefore, the commentary states: "The year and month are not recorded. (From the *Longshu*).
Regarding the "Collection" (*Ji*), there is an interpretation stating that the Great Emperor Gaozong ascended the throne as the Flying Dragon and ruled the world during that year.
This account is likely erroneous; I have seen it stated elsewhere that the year of Chángshòu was the era of Empress Zetian, yet even now I am not certain of its precise source.
I shall await further investigation and verification, as detailed in a separate record, though I do not know what kind of catalog or compendium that is.

I have examined all available records and found an interpretation stating that the Venerable Dharma Master Chengyi was of the Huangfu clan of Jingzhao, while the śramaṇas Fan, Fuli, Huaisu, and others were responsible for the oral transmission, transcription, and dictation. How can it be that half [the names] appear in this biography while the other half appear in that chart?
It may be that they were simply unknown; one must not arbitrarily give rise to divergent theories. The commentary by Dharma Master Jianzhi identifies the person who presided over the translation.
The year and month are identical to those in Zanghai’s commentary; the only difference is that it specifies "the Tripiṭaka Master from Kaśmīra of India.

Furthermore, I saw a copy of the *Niyuan jue jing* among the miscellaneous scriptures at Fengde Temple. It was many years old and extensively damaged by insects, with most of it already torn and decayed;
only the last two or three sheets could still be deciphered. At the end, it says: "The twentieth year of Zhenguan..."
In the year of Dīngwèi, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month (Jǐhài), being the fifteenth day after the first day of the moon (Yǐyōu), this was completed at the Bǎoyún Monastery in Tánzhōu.
The śramaṇa Lóuhòutánjiàn served as the scribe for the translated words; the disciple Jiāng Dùnkè verified the text;
the Great Virtuous Zhīxī, Fǎqì, Huìquán, and Bǎozhè verified the meaning and principles. However, as these matters were not yet fully detailed or certain, there may be some inaccuracies.
These were previously translated, but because they could not be presented for imperial review, they remained in the south and did not enter the Northern Canon;
otherwise, this would be a case of fraud and error.

Because it is comprehensive, there is the "Introductory Section" (also called the "Distinct Introductory Section," as each sutra has its own distinct one), such as those in the *Vimalakīrti*, the *Ratnacchattra*, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* regarding the light from the brow-hair.

In this present sutra, however, the text combines these without division; therefore, it is said that they are present here. This means that when the Buddha enters [samādhi] below, both types of introductory sequences are manifested.
[Commentary: Now, to specifically clarify the "Section on Certifying Faith," the words "Ānanda asks questions" refer to wisdom.

The second treatise states: At the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the grove of twin śāla trees at Kuśinagara, he lay down with his head toward the north, intending with single-minded resolve to enter nirvāṇa.

Because Ānanda had not yet eliminated his personal affection and was not free from desire, his mind sank into an ocean of grief from which he could not emerge on his own. At that time, the Elder Aniruddha spoke to Ānanda, saying:
"You are one who guards the treasury of the Buddha's Dharma; you should not, like an ordinary person, sink into an ocean of sorrow.

All conditioned phenomena possess the characteristic of impermanence; do not be distressed. Furthermore, the Buddha first entrusted the Dharma to you, yet now, in your distress, you are losing that which was entrusted to you.
Therefore, you should ask the Buddha: after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, upon what shall we rely to practice the path, and whom shall we take as [our teacher]?"
The Master spoke harshly to Canda, saying, "How shall you dwell together? What words should be placed at the beginning of all sutras?
Regarding such various matters of the future, one should ask the Buddha. Having heard these words, Ānanda’s heart was distressed;

after he had recovered slightly and regained his mindfulness through the power of the Way, he asked the Buddha about them. The Buddha told Ānanda (summarizing the gist of what was said): "After my parinirvāṇa, you [disciples]..."

One should dwell in accordance with the four foundations of mindfulness (contemplating the body as impure, contemplating feelings as suffering, contemplating the mind as impermanent, and contemplating phenomena as non-self), taking the precepts as one's teacher.
When silently excluding monks of evil character, the initial formula of the compiled scriptures always states: "Thus have I heard:

at one time the Buddha was in a certain kingdom, city, mountain, or forest, together with a multitude of followers. Therefore, it is said that the Buddha commanded this to be placed [at the beginning]. If one wishes for a detailed explanation:

I have examined the *Dachao shu* (Commentary on the Great Collection), which also addresses the severing of doubts and clarifies the Buddha’s intention for establishing these words. There are three such intentions:

first, the severing of doubts. This refers to when Ānanda ascended the seat at the time of the council intending to proclaim the Dharma-piṭaka, his physical marks and signs suddenly became identical to those of the Buddha, causing the assembly to give rise to three doubts:
first, the doubt that the Buddha had arisen once more to preach the Dharma; second, [the doubt that it was] from another world-system...
When the Buddha arrived, Ānanda had three doubts; as soon as he turned to become a Buddha and uttered the words "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), those three doubts were instantly severed.

Since it is said that [the Dharma] was heard from the Buddha, it is clear that he himself was not the Buddha. (The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha cites the Vinaya as saying this; this applies generally to the phrase "Thus have I heard. Second, to quell disputes:
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that if one does not attribute the words to having heard them from the Buddha and instead claims they were composed by oneself, disputes will arise.

Because this treatise has arisen, the [previous] formulations are now set aside. Since "I" follows what was heard, and what was heard comes from the Buddha, the subtle tracks transmitted through the generations have not been interrupted (this restricts "I heard").
Because the three are distinct from the heterodox, the scriptures of non-Buddhists all establish "Āyu" at the beginning as an auspicious invocation (this restricts "Thus").

Answer: The Great Sage established his teachings through many gates of provisional and ultimate truth;

Regarding the body’s reliance on the four lands, concerning the *dharmatā-kṣetra* (Dharma-nature land), the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"It is solely by means of the pure *dharmadhātu* that the *dharmakāya* is constituted, and it is likewise by means of *dharmatā* that its land is constituted. Although their nature is of a single flavor, they are divided into two based on the characteristics of the body and the land.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also says: "The *svabhāvakāya* relies upon the *dharmatā-kṣetra*; although this body and land [are non-dual]..."

The essence is without differentiation, yet it belongs to the Buddha (the body) and the Dharma (the land), because their natures and characteristics differ. (As the *Cien* commentary states: "The Dharma-nature belonging to the Buddha is the Dharmatā-kāya; the Dharma-nature belonging to the Dharma is the Dharmatā-bhūmi. It is said thus because 'nature follows the differentiation of characteristics.

The intention of this master [Kuiji] is that what belongs to the Buddha is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), while what belongs to the Dharma is the nature (*dharmatā*'). Master Qingliang, relying on the school of the ultimate teaching (*paramārtha-yāna*), explains: "Because the Buddha possesses the meaning of awakening (*buddhi*), it is called the Buddha-land (*buddha-kṣetra*);

because that which lacks the meaning of awakening merely maintains its own nature (*svabhāva*), it is called the Dharma. This is also as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: among sentient beings it is called Buddha-nature (*tathāgata-garbha*), and among insentient things it is called Dharma-nature. Regarding the statement that "nature and characteristics differ," this refers to the body and the land.

If categorized by their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there are two distinctions; however, if categorized by their underlying nature (*svabhāva*), there is no difference. Now, because this undifferentiated nature conforms to differentiated characteristics, it is said that "nature varies according to characteristics.
This is precisely what was cited previously from the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*. The treatise continues: "This Buddha-body and its land are both not subsumed under form (*rūpa*).

Although their dimensions—whether large or small—cannot be described, yet according to phenomenal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), their measure is boundless. (Regarding the three bodies and three lands, since their phenomena are already boundless, how could their characteristics and nature have limits? It is, for example, like empty space pervading all things."

"Every place" (since it is like empty space, it pervades both the realms of form and non-form) is also as stated in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*: "The physical marks of Samantabhadra’s body are like empty space;
they abide in accordance with the Truth, not within a land. (*Śāstra*, 2). Regarding the Enjoyment Land (*saṃbhoga-kṣetra*): this land of the Enjoyment Body further has two types.
First, the Self-Enjoyment Body abides in the Self-Enjoyment Land. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "That is to say, the Perfect Mirror..."
The pure consciousness associated with wisdom, through the accomplishment of causes and conditions for the dull and pure Buddha-fields of self-benefit cultivated in the past,
transforms continuously from the moment of initial enlightenment until the end of the future into purely pure Buddha-fields that are boundless,
perfectly circular, and adorned with various jewels; the Body of Self-Enjoyment constantly dwells therein, and just as the Buddha-field is pure, so too is its measure.
Because each of his sense faculties and marks of excellence is produced by boundless and limitless roots of goodness, his merit and wisdom—

though not being material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and thus cannot be described in terms of shape or magnitude— are nevertheless said to pervade all places, based on what he has realized and the body upon which he relies.
This same applies to the Body for Others' Enjoyment (*parasaṃbhogakāya*), which also relies on its own land, namely, the Land of Equality.

Through the power of great wisdom and compassion, and by virtue of the causes and conditions for benefiting others cultivated in the past, he achieves a pure Buddha-field that is untainted and purely immaculate.

This field manifests according to what is appropriate for Bodhisattvas dwelling in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). As described in the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, each stage has its own specific measure and scope (the first stage perceives only the sign of a hundred-petaled lotus, while the third stage perceives a trichiliocosm).
He transforms it into a pure land that may be small or large, inferior or superior, changing from one state to another as circumstances require.

The body of enjoyment for others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) abides by depending [on the *dharmakāya*], and the dimensions of this dependent body are likewise without fixed limit. As for the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it depends on the transformation land (*nirmāṇabhūmi*).

This refers to the wisdom that accomplishes activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), which, through the power of great compassion and the causal conditions of the pure and impure Buddha-lands cultivated for the benefit of others in the past, achieves accomplishment.

(This is because within the transformation lands there are both pure and impure areas, unlike the lands of enjoyment for others; therefore, they are described as "pure and impure. The lands of enjoyment for others consist of the dharma-joy.)

Because it increases, it is similar to the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (self-enjoyment body); although it preaches the Dharma, because its supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) increase, it is designated as "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*). This is explained in detail in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*.

According to the suitability of sentient beings who have not yet ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*), it manifests as a Buddha-field that may be pure or defiled, large or small, changing and shifting from one state to another.

The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Buddha dwells in reliance upon this; the dimensions of the supported body are likewise without fixed limit. [The commentary states: "If one opens..."—this refers to opening [the gates].
Regarding the three [categories] being reduced to four meanings as explained above in the *Daocao* (Great Commentary), the "unification of the two" refers to further binding the four into two.
Among the various sutras and śāstras, there are instances where these two types of "two" are first subsumed into "pure" and "impure.
There are many reasons for this; first, while the preceding three are entirely pure, the fourth contains both pure and impure aspects, meaning that three and a half categories are pure.

Regarding the classification of lands as either impure or pure: the first three are pure because they are the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* (Enjoyment by Others) lands where the two obstacles are partially severed and True Suchness is partially realized;

thus they are named "pure. The Transformation Lands (*nirmāṇakāya-bhūmi*) are all impure; even if they possess the seven treasures, because they are inhabited by defiled sentient beings, they are not pure lands.
The latter two are both impure. As the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra) states: "The Three Sages and Ten Saints dwell in the retribution of their fruits; only the Buddha [is truly pure]."
One person asks: "If Master Geng says that all that has form is defiled and that which is formless is pure, then only the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) would be pure.

If this were so, how could the *svasaṃbhogakāya* realm be called defiled? This is because it is identical in essence with true nature (*tathatā*) and cannot be described in terms of its size or dimensions;
thus, it is subsumed under the category of purity. Briefly stated, the latter two [realms] encompass the former four as both nature and characteristics.
There are two gates: first, that the *dharmatā* (nature of reality) constitutes the essence (*svabhāva*), while the other three are all aspects (*lakṣaṇa*);

second, that the self-enjoyment land (*svasaṃbhogakāya-bhūmi*) is identical with true nature and may thus also be called "essence," while the other two are merely "aspects. The Great Commentary (*Mahā-ṭīkā*) states following this: "To say they 'fuse into one' differs from other schools;

for in [this teaching], whether it be the two lands of purity and impurity as essence and aspect, or the three or four lands, there is nothing that is not fused and subsumed—this is precisely the Lotus [Sūtra]."
Because of the intent of [the masters such as] Yan and this sutra, it is said that [this teaching] differs from other schools. △ Commentary:

Now, the following two points integrate the many aforementioned varieties into a state of neither being identical nor different. This integration is performed because the preceding classifications of opening and closing were not fixed (as the *Great Commentary* cited above states:

"integrating them into one" refers to identity; "listing many varieties previously" refers to difference; now they are neither identical nor different). However, the original text by Master Zhuang of Dong'an contains three phrases, which are not present here.
There is the "phrase where the substance is not established. Qingliang added this phrase to form two pairs: namely, that the realms of purity and defilement are neither identical nor different;
that the single principle has but one flavor and cannot be said to be different; that their nature is darkly identical to emptiness and cannot be said to exist;

and that they are established according to conditions and cannot be said to be non-existent. Now, "one" is used to negate difference, and "non-existence" is used to negate existence. However, in his commentary...
Regarding "one," this is also based on principle; in reality, the meaning of "one" has two aspects: first, based on principle; second, based on phenomena. As for the first, based on principle:
the pure lands of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions all equally exist and cannot be said to be non-existent; because they can be termed "one," the commentary states, "negating through form," etc.
However, while the four propositions were briefly cited above, if one strictly refutes the fault of being exclusively [one-sided], then in reality, it is both different and identical.
Identity is both existence and non-existence; if they mutually negate one another, then both unity and difference vanish, and both existence and non-existence become quiescent.

If they are perfectly interfused and unimpeded, then identity is multiplicity and multiplicity is identity, non-existence is existence and existence is non-existence, multiplicity is the multiplicity of the one and the one is the one of the many; thus, existence and non-existence are the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle.

The non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (shishi wuai) arises from this layering of the one and the many; thus, in every single atom within the Flower Treasury World-Ocean described in the Great Sutra, the entire Dharma-realm is perceived.
*Commentary:* The preceding section on "Ordinary Beings" concludes with three continuous passages that connect the preceding and following sections, as is easily understood from the text.
In the Sutra, regarding the assembly of those who share the same essence (*tongti fazhong*), the initial general heading states: "Bodhisattvas. To speak fully, this is *bodhisattva*. This...

"Bodhi" is translated as "Awakening" (jue), and "sattva" is translated as "sentient being" (youqing). There are three explanations for this: First, the explanation in terms of the object (*ālambana*):
This refers to the objects of both compassion and wisdom. That is to say, one cultivates wisdom seeking Bodhi, while exercising compassion to transform sentient beings.

Second, the explanation in terms of the mind: This refers to those who possess the awakening of realization. It means that at the initial stage of the path, there is sudden awakening (*tongwu*), and prior to the stages (*zhudi*), there is analytical contemplation (*biguan*).

Regarding the "realization" (*abhisamaya*) upon entering the stages (*bhūmi*): although it is called "the awakening of clear comprehension," this is not a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound—meaning that "clear comprehension" is itself "awakening"—and it is spoken of in this way specifically to distinguish it from the fruit of Buddhahood.

The same applies to the term "sentiment" (*qing*) used below. As for other forms of discursive thought (*ālambana-citta*), although they involve understanding prior to the stages, they do not constitute realization;
thus, the mind during the post-meditative state (*vyutthāna*) upon entering the stages is characterized by sentimental deliberation.

From the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, because the three subtle [defilements] have not yet eliminated their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), the third [category] is explained in terms of subject and object.

However, since the aforementioned [explanation] concerns that which is sought and that which is transformed—both of which are objects of opposition rather than one's own essential substance—it was called "objects" (*viṣaya*).

Now, it is explained in terms of one's own subject and object; that is to say, Great Bodhi is that which is sought, and one's own mind is that which seeks. Regarding the phrase "the Great Dharma," etc.:
The *Lotus Sūtra* states that one will "certainly preach the Great Dharma" and further says to "expound the meaning of the Great Dharma.

The subsequent passage speaks of sentient beings in the final age who are about to give rise to the great mind (*mahā-citta*), seeking spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and practicing the path of great cultivation for the sake of the two benefits (*dvaya-artha*). That which realizes the Great Way is the awakened nature of True Suchness (*tathatā-bodhi-svabhāva*).

If explained in terms of stages (*bhūmi*), "faith" refers to the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), and "understanding" refers to the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*). The "arising" [of the mind] refers to...
That is to say, the mind of the great vows of the ten dedications realizes the path of seeing, practices the path of cultivation, and proceeds through the stages from the eighth bhūmi upward,
flowing spontaneously and without effort into the ocean of sarvajñā.
In the commentary on the individual listings within the Sūtras: "The Sage has no name; names are established for the sake of things. As Zhuangzi says: "The Perfected Man (zhìrén) has no self;
the Divine Man (shénrén) has no merit; the Sage (shèngrén) has no name. Now, although he has no name in terms of benefiting sentient beings, we have provisionally established a name for him.
"Mostly based on his conduct and virtues" means that this is not an exhaustive definition; it implies there are also those who possess the nature [of Buddhahood], such as Maitreya.

They also have causes for their names, such as Vasubandhu and others who were so named because they sought a deity; and they also have causes based on their parents, such as Śāriputra among the śrāvakas.

Nevertheless, those whose names are established primarily based on their conduct and virtues are the majority. Question: Since all bodhisattvas possess the virtues of conduct based upon which these names are established, why are they distinguished?
Answer: It is said that they are designated individually according to what is appropriate to their specific capacities (yogyatā). This refers to the suitability of the faculties (indriya-yogyatā).

Because the manifestations they represent differ from one another, they are said to be "a thousandfold distinctions" and so forth. For example, observing their voices and attaining liberation through them is named Avalokiteśvara;
having compassion for sentient beings is named Sadāprarudita; raining flowers from the hand is named Puṣpahasta, and so on.
Furthermore, as a verse in a sutra says: "Insatiable great compassion never abandons"—this is seen as the Bodhisattva Vajraprema (Vajra-Love).
Those who praise even small acts of goodness are the Vajrasādhu Bodhisattvas; those whose non-abiding generosity is like space are the Vajraratna Bodhisattvas, and so forth.
These twelve great beings are the leaders among the hundred thousand [bodhisattvas], representing twelve sections of the Dharma.
They serve as the primary interlocutors for each respective gate, because—

Because those with a beginner’s mind have dull faculties and do not yet understand how to seek instruction, the Bodhisattva, out of compassion, raises their doubts to pose questions (this clarifies the intent behind questioning despite already having some understanding).
△ Commentary: Now, each [section] is explained individually according to its expressed meaning (*so-ch'uan*). Regarding the term "punning interpretation" (*chuan-tso*):

Kong Anguo, in his commentary on the *Analects*, states that when Confucius was in Chen and longed for home, wishing to leave, he said, "My own community (*wu-pang*)... (referring to the *Hsiang-t'ang* chapter).

"My son, you who are madly intent on advancing toward the Great Way have engaged in reckless fabrication and forced interpretation to compose this literary work, yet you do not know how to properly fashion its structure;
I shall return to fashion it myself. [The commentary on] "Wondrous Head" (*Miaoshou*) and so forth: Now, Mañjuśrī is the Sanskrit term;
its vulgarized form is *Manjusiri*, which translates as "Wondrous Head" (*Miaoshou*). According to the Huayan school, this Bodhisattva...
The syllable *sa* represents three dharma-gates: first, it signifies the mind capable of faith;
thus, in the "Chapter on the Ten Faiths" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, ten bodhisattvas all share the name "Head," such as Bodhiruci (Jue-shou) and others, and Mañjuśrī is precisely this "Wondrous Head.

The *Sūtra on the Samādhi of Observing All Dharmas* calls him Puguang (Pǔshou), the *Amoghapāśa Sūtra* calls him Ruru (Róushou), and the *Anantamukha Sūtra* refers to him as [the one of] infinite gates.
The *Sūkṣma-rahasya-sūtra* states that "Gentle Head" (*Maitreya*) contains the character for "head" (*mūrdhan*), signifying that faith is the head of all practices and all virtues.

As for the second name, "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (*Mañjuśrī*), the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* says: "Because all those in the world who draw near, make offerings to, and praise him are called Wondrous Auspiciousness.
Paramārtha explains: "Because he is eternally tranquil and impartial toward both enemies and kin."

"Benefiting others without causing harm or affliction is called Mañjuśrī" (as cited in the *Commentary on the Sūtra of the Superior Birth*). This explanation by the Three Holy Ones expresses the understanding that is able to give rise to practice and vows.
Immediately following this, the three names are explained: "Mañjughoṣa" (Wonderful Virtue) signifies the great wisdom capable of realizing ultimate truth.
Many sūtras refer to him as a "Dharmarāja-putra" (Son of the Dharma King), because, like a crown prince, he is without equal or peer; the text of the present sūtra abbreviates this title.
The meaning is broad, yet it is explained in a single location because Mañjuśrī already encompasses these three meanings;

therefore, it is said that he represents faith-understanding (*adhimukti*), wisdom (*jñāna*), and realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*), as stated in the *Tri-samaya-darśana*. Since Mañjuśrī represents the understanding that gives rise to practice and vows, he is here called "Wondrous Auspiciousness" (*Mañjughoṣa*).
"Auspiciousness" is precisely the practice arising from understanding. The text of the *Tri-samaya-darśana* explaining this follows immediately below. [End of] Commentary.△ Sūtra.
