therefore, they are called "merits. Thus, the *Śāstra* states: "If the mind has movement... [and so on]. In the subsequent portion of the *Śāstra*:

The preceding text states: "Because all dharmas are fundamentally mind-only and truly devoid of thought (this cites the principle that is misunderstood), yet there is a deluded mind that, through non-awakening, gives rise to thought and perceives various objective realms;
therefore, it is called ignorance" (this refers to the arising of delusion from the True, meaning the subtle and coarse defiled minds, the non-awakening of both root and branch).

Being about to explain the pure, one first cites the defiled in contrast to reveal it—the subsequent phrases follow this pattern. How is it revealed? As stated below: "The non-arising of the mind-nature is itself Great Wisdom."

Because it has the meaning of the light of wisdom (*prajñā-āloka*), [it is as follows]: since the arising of thought is precisely non-enlightened ignorance (*avidyā*), its non-arising is the luminous wisdom of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).

If the mind gives rise to views, then there is the characteristic of non-seeing (deluded vision is not all-pervasive); if the nature of the mind is free from views, this is the meaning of universally illuminating the *dharmadhātu* (true illumination is perfect and bright).

If the mind has movement, it is not true cognition; conversely, this reveals that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is unmoving. It has no self-nature (clarifying that deluded defilement has no substance; conversely, this reveals...).

Revealing the intrinsically pure mind as being neither permanent, nor blissful, nor self, nor pure (this clarifies that the four delusions are false; conversely, it reveals the four virtues of *tathatā*). Regarding "feverish affliction" (*paritāpa*):

because various delusions burn the mind, it is extremely feverish and afflicted; therefore, *tathatā* is said to be cool (*śītala*). Regarding "decay and change" (*vipariṇāma*): false defilements undergo transformation, which conversely reveals that *tathatā* does not decay or change. Thus, one is "not sovereign" (*asvatantra*); because one is bound by the fruits of karma, this reveals the sovereignty of *tathatā*.
As stated above, these are the meanings of being cool, immutable, and sovereign. Furthermore, [the mind] possesses even more than sands of the Ganges in number of false defilements.

Because this meaning corresponds to that meaning, when the nature of the mind is without movement, there is the manifestation of the characteristics of all pure merits and virtues exceeding the sands of the Ganges (as each is paired with its opposite, both defilement and purity exceed the sands of the Ganges).

If the mind arises and one further perceives prior dharmas as objects of recollection, then there is deficiency (seeking through the deluded mind and external thoughts is insufficient). Such immeasurable merits of pure dharmas are, in essence, one.

When the mind has nothing further to contemplate, it is therefore fulfilled (the nature of pure virtue is full and requires no external seeking); this is called the Tathāgata-garbha of the Dharma-body. The commentary states:
"Once the mind moves, there are the delusions and defilements as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; when it does not move, there are the meritorious virtues as constant as the sands of the Ganges.
It further says: "Such virtues are precisely the One Mind. Thus we know that there is no separate dharma that flows out from within. [End of] Explanatory Notes.
Regarding "outflows" (*āsrava*), all treatises state that when afflictions (*kleśa*) manifest, they cause the mind to flow and disperse in a continuous stream; thus, they are termed "outflows.
Just as a leaking vessel or a leaking house is deeply loathsome, defiling, and extensive in its damage, they are censured for their faults and established under the name "outflows.

There are three types: namely, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*, the afflictions of the desire realm), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*, the afflictions of the two upper realms—so called because they have no further objects of perception and thus retain their original names), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).

Regarding the outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava)—which is not designated by other dharmas to manifest the essence of its own activity—it is held that in the Dharma-nature school (*dharmatā-yāna*), fundamental non-enlightenment (*mūla-abodhi*) along with the three subtleties and six coarsenesses constitute the dharmas of outflow.

These do not differentiate between the distinctions of the three realms nor the differences between seeds and manifestations, because when deluded they are entirely defiled and when enlightened they are entirely pure, having no inherent nature. Nevertheless, the Sūtra states: "All things are pure; this is purity."

The categories of dharmas exceed the sands of the Ganges; for now, I shall briefly cite four examples—such as *tathatā* (true suchness)—to represent the remainder. That is to say, *tathatā* is the universal characteristic and the fundamental basis, while the other three are its particulars. Among these, *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* are the fruits, and the *pāramitās* are the causes. These encompass all pure phenomena without exception; therefore, this Great Commentary cites only these [four]. Regarding this passage: "The categories of dharmas exceed the sands of the Ganges" means that the various classifications of dharmas are more numerous than the grains of sand in the river Ganges. "For now, I shall briefly cite four examples—such as *tathatā*—to represent the remainder" means that although the categories of dharmas are vast, I will provisionally list four items, beginning with *tathatā*, to serve as representatives for all others. "That is to say, *tathatā* is the universal characteristic and the fundamental basis" means that *tathatā* is the general characteristic common to all phenomena and serves as the root from which all things arise. "While the other three are its particulars" means that the remaining three—*bodhi*, *nirvāṇa*, and the *pāramitās*—are specific instances derived from that foundation.

"Among these, *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* are the fruits, and the *pāramitās* are the causes" means that within these four, *bodhi* (enlightenment) and *nirvāṇa* (liberation) constitute the results, whereas the *pāramitās* (perfections) constitute the causal practices. "These encompass all pure phenomena without exception" means that these four categories fully include every dharma belonging to the realm of purity. "Therefore, this Great Commentary cites only these" concludes that for these reasons, the *Great Commentary on the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* selects only these four items as representative examples.

Each of the four dharmas has its own chapter; for each dharma there are four sections: first, the explanation of the name; second, the determination of the essence; third, the categories; and fourth, the functional activity.
Although these are not explicitly set forth here in brief, they are nonetheless contained within them; it is merely that the number of sections may be reduced.
In the sub-commentary on the *Awakening of Faith*, the second section explains *tathatā* (suchness) in three parts: first, the explanation of its name; second, the brief explanation, which states:

"Regarding 'perfect awakening' (*yuanjue*) and so forth," this refers to the direct pointing to the meaning of the sutra. Regarding "it is called 'true' (*zhen*)" and so forth, this is further explained by means of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only).
The text is found in the ninth fascicle of that treatise, where the root verse says: "This ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena is also precisely suchness (*tathatā*), which is eternal."
Because it is according to its nature, this is the true nature of *vijñapti-mātra*. The prose commentary provides a full explanation, which I shall now cite briefly.
Of the seven phrases in the prose, the first two distinguish [the nature from] the contaminated (*sāsrava*), also called the "imagined" (*parikalpita*), because contaminated phenomena are false.

The next two phrases distinguish [it from] the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), also called the "dependent" (*paratantra*), because the transformations of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing are conditioned phenomena. The final three phrases explain that verse.
The fourth phrase also says "in all states," which refers to the four characteristics of conditioned phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava*), the three periods of time, and so forth.
"Constantly as its nature" means it does not change; "hence" is the concluding particle. That treatise states in full: "Because it is always as its nature, it is called *tathatā* (Suchness).

(In this [text], we follow the abbreviated version which contains only the single character "hence"). △ In the commentary, following "Furthermore, True... and below, there are two points of detailed explanation. It says: "Falsehood is... and so on, which is for now...

"Explaining 'not true' and 'not suchness' (the text below says: "Now, being free from these [distinctions], the reverse is precisely Suchness"): regarding 'tutenague-suchness' and so forth—tutenague has its own substance and is not false, but because it is not gold, it is called counterfeit.
A reflection corresponds to the characteristics of the object and is not deceptive, but because it lacks a real substance due to conditions, it is called illusory.
'Speaking horizontally of their respective differences' means that the sense-object of form differs from sound, fragrance, and so on."

The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) differs from sensation, perception, and so forth; craving and other afflictions differ from faith and other wholesome states; hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals differ from humans and devas;

the Sahā world differs from the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*); and the mental objects of *śrāvakas* differ from those of *bodhisattvas*, and so on—even up to the eighty-odd categories in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, all of which are distinguished by being simultaneous yet different. As for what is called "vertical" transformation (*pariṇāma*), it is as follows:

"Like last year, this year is old within the mirror"—this and other [passages] such as "summer differs from spring," "gaining the new while forgetting the old," and "if the cause is pleasure, etc."—the Commentary now explains below that there are no longer the four faults mentioned above, thereby establishing the meaning of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
That is to say, this "substantial entity" is the true essence of mind (whereas previously, based on *vijñapti-mātra*, it was merely said: "this reality is merely...").

The term "non-falsehood" (*amṛṣā*) has not yet revealed its essential nature (*svabhāva*); now, pointing to this very essence as being real, the commentary designates it as a "detailed explanation. The intent is as follows: the essence of mind (*cittatattva*) is the *dharmin* (the subject), and that it is truly real is the *sādhyadharma* (the predicate). If one were to take "True Suchness" (*tathatā*) as the *dharmin* to serve as the prior subject, that would merely be a redundant statement; for since True Suchness also carries the meaning of being unchanging and non-false, how does it differ from the word "real"? Furthermore, these [terms] are divided into horizontal and vertical aspects, each having two meanings;
because each is distinct, the principle is inexhaustible and the significance is endless—hence it is called "detailed. Regarding "in the future, etc.": today’s space is like yesterday’s.
Regarding the phrase "the space within form is like... it means that the space inside a kitchen is like the space inside a hall.
"The true aspect (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is not false and resembles [it]" is the formal conclusion of the name *tathatā* (Suchness).
That is to say, "like" (*tathā*) has the meaning of resemblance or identity; the intent is to state that this and that are alike only in this mind-nature. This refers to a person of virtue.
The Buddha-nature of those who resemble evil people is like the Buddha-nature of the present;

the Buddha-nature from time immemorial is identical to the Buddha-nature of ordinary beings, and the Buddha-nature of the Two Vehicles is the same as that of humans, devas, and Bodhisattvas—all are explained in this manner.
Only this can be called the true characteristic (*tathatā*), for it is not different by so much as a hair’s breadth; therefore, this reality is named "Suchness" (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, there is nothing else that can be truly similar or identical in nature.

Even if there were a person whose own brother was very similar to him, if one examines it closely, they cannot be said to be exactly alike; there would inevitably be some slight difference in length, size, or other characteristics.
If this were not so, how could one ever mistake one's own wife? This applies even to worldly objects.

Among each and every category of form, none is exempt from having minute particles of weight, lightness, size, or quality—whether large or small, good or bad—and ultimately there is nothing that is entirely identical [to another].
Thus we know they are all false semblances; as for "false semblance," it means that one does not attain true suchness (*tathatā*).

Since ancient times, the traditional interpretation of the character *ru* (如) has merely stated that it signifies the meaning of profound stillness and immovability, but it has never pointedly explained its etymological derivation.

Regarding the character "ru" (如): it is the character for this country [China], yet I have not examined where in the *Shuowen*, *Erya*, *Yupian*, or *Qieyun* and other such works it is glossed as "profound stillness and immovability" (*zhanji budong*).

Therefore, one knows that it is precisely because the nature of the awakened mind is entirely as it is among ordinary beings and entirely as it is among sages, and entirely as it is within the state of cause and entirely as it is within the state of fruit—being thus both horizontally and vertically—that it is "profound" (*zhan*).
However, the meaning of "immovable" (*acala*) is not its definitive definition. When asked about this, the Great Master of Heze said:
"Everyone takes the similarity between two things to be 'suchness' (*tathatā*), whereas I take the absence of any similar thing to be it.

If you now explain *tathatā* by means of a definitive similarity, does this not contradict that teaching? The answer is: it is precisely the same as this; therefore, it was stated above that "beyond this, there is nothing further."

Regarding the principle that "likeness is like-ness," since it is said that there is no substance to likeness, one knows that only the Buddha-nature of ghosts and hells and the Buddha-nature of humans and animals are truly identical in their true aspect.
The Great Master distinguished among people, saying: "When two things are similar, they are called 'like' (ru)";
this is also as explained above. Even when close brothers are similar, in the end they cannot be entirely identical down to the slightest fraction.
It appears so; let the wise examine it closely. The preceding section has finished explaining the names. ▲ The *Śāstra* states: "The following two [sections] set forth the essence (*svabhāva*).

in the Emptiness school (Śūnyatāvāda), it is mostly defined in terms of the two abandonments—namely, realizing that the afflictive and cognitive obstructions are fundamentally empty, which is itself called the "two abandonments. Abandonment is itself Bodhi, for there is no separate Bodhi. Thus, a sutra states:

"Afflictions are themselves Bodhi, because they do not undergo change. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (Compendium of the Great Vehicle) identifies these two wisdoms and two abandonments as the essence of Bodhi.

The "Dual" refers to the schools of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇa) and Emptiness (Śūnyatā). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that both the realization of bodhi and the severance of afflictions are termed "bodhi";

this combines the two aforementioned schools. Regarding the Dharmatā school, the commentaries on the wisdoms of *yathābhūta* and *yathāvastu* explain these three in terms of the respective wisdoms possessed by those of the Three Vehicles.

Furthermore, the commentaries on the *Awakening of Faith* discuss original enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣā-jñāna*), initial enlightenment (*ādikṣānti-jñāna*), and ultimate enlightenment (*niṣṭhā-jñāna*). These four [points] constitute the analysis.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* explains that through four grades of wisdom— lower, middle, upper, and supreme—

one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and accordingly attains the bodhi of the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva, and Buddha, as well as the four types of wisdom-bodhi,

such as the Great Perfect Wisdom (the four wisdoms have already been explained in the "Chapter on the Pure Land"). Regarding the commentary and the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 58, states:
1. Bodhi of the Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-bodhi*): Because one generates the mind for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* amidst immeasurable births and deaths, it is called "Bodhi";

this is a case of referring to the fruit within the cause. 2. Bodhi of Subduing the Mind (*citta-damana-bodhi*): It refers to severing all afflictions (*kleśa*), subduing that mind, and practicing the various *pāramitās*.
3. Bodhi of Illuminating the Mind (*citta-avabhāsa-bodhi*): It refers to contemplating the Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
The discernment of the true mark of all dharmas through the distinctions of root and branch, general and specific, is called the *prajñāpāramitā*.

By attaining the power of skillful means within this *prajñā*, one does not cling to *prajñā* itself; one beholds all Buddhas of the ten directions, attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), exits the triple world, reaches *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), and sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) for the sake of the fivefold unsurpassed bodhi.
"Having severed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If we follow the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, this is endowed with ten kinds [of qualities], as explained in the fifty-first and fifty-ninth fascicles; fearing prolixity, I shall not enumerate them here.

'The commentaries all subsume these' means that the various types are summarized to constitute the essence. [The commentary] below "the causes being perfected" (in the phrase *yinyuan*) clarifies the third point: the activity and function (*karmopayoga*). It says:

The "Boundless" (Ananta) is able to sever the two hindrances, realize the two emptinesses, and seal all capacities of sentient beings (as stated in the "Appearance Chapter" of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "All minds are universally pervasive like scrolls of scripture within dust motes," and also:

"Bodhi universally seals all mental activities; therefore, Perfect Enlightenment is called 'Immeasurable"). It manifests the myriad phenomena (capable of manifesting and generating the bodies, lands, and reflections of wisdom, etc.), encompassing both movement and stillness, and penetrating cause and effect.

The Commentary: Below this, four sections explain *nirvāṇa*. First, regarding the explanation of the name: as for "quiescent extinction" (*śānti-nirvāṇa*), that treatise (the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*, composed by Master Sengzhao) states:

"In the language of Qin it is called 'unconditioned' (*asaṃskṛta*) and also named 'extinction and deliverance' (*parinirvāṇa*). 'Unconditioned' is taken from the sense of emptiness and stillness, being wondrously transcendent of the conditioned;
'extinction and deliverance' means that the great afflictions are forever extinguished and one has transcended the four currents. This, indeed...
This is the ultimate destination of mirror-images and the profound abode where all designations are severed.

What is now called "nirvāṇa" (寂滅)—where "quiescence" (*ji*) refers to the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang dynasty and "extinction" (*mie*) refers to the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva—was thus stated by Master Sengzhao: "The truth of the exhaustion of *nirvāṇa* (泥洹盡諦) does not merely mean the exhaustion of fetters;
rather, because birth and death are forever quiescently extinguished, it is termed 'exhaustion'. This is as explained in the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

All [masters], including Daosheng, Sengzhao, and Master Huiyuan, correctly translate it as "extinction" (*mie*). Furthermore, among the Four Noble Truths, it is designated as the "Truth of Extinction" (*nirodha-satya*);

therefore, we here briefly adopt the term "extinction. Regarding the frequent occurrence of various terms in the commentary, masters such as Daosheng and Huiyuan explain them as "non-arising," "non-acting," "non-emerging," "signless," "inexhaustible," or "quiescent. The commentary generally translates [the term] as "perfection" (*yuan*).
The term "Quiescence" (Ji) was translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Tang Dynasty. Because its meaning is complete and perfect (*yī-zhōu-yuán*), it is called "Total" (*zǒng*).

The *Shū* (Commentary) states that from "Awakening" (*jué*) downward, it explains the aforementioned meaning of being "complete and perfect," which constitutes the second section: the determination of the essence (*chūtǐ*). To speak of the actual reality, the nature of awakening (*jué-xìng*) is itself quiescence;

this is the essence. Taken collectively, the three virtues (*sāndé*) constitute the essence. Since the three virtues are the nature of Perfect Awakening and that nature is quiescence, it is so described.
The three virtues of parinirvāṇa are *mahāprajñā*, *vimukti*, and *dharmakāya*. That which is stillness within illumination is *prajñā*;
that which is illumination within stillness is *vimukti*; and the essence of both stillness and illumination is the *dharmakāya*.

These three are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither merged nor separate, like the letter ‘I’ in the Sanskrit word for Brahmā; this constitutes Great Nirvāṇa, as explained at length in that sutra (the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*).

Thus, these three [purity, bliss, and permanence] derive their names from the inversion of the three types of defilement (*saṃkleśa*). By inverting afflictions (*kleśa*), one attains prajñā (for afflictions are themselves bodhi);

by inverting karmic bonds (*saṃyojana*) and karma, one attains liberation (*vimukti*); and by inverting the body that is the basis of suffering, one attains the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) (for the essence of mind is free from thought and is the fundamental Dharma-body).

Therefore, the three defilements are themselves the three virtues of intrinsic purity; it is only because of the apparent difference between delusion and awakening that they are said to be mutually inverted. If one considers them according to the Dharma...

Among the six types of unconditioned phenomena (*asamskṛta-dharma*), there is *tathatā* (which is the "nature-purity" mentioned below), *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (where "discernment" [*pratisaṃkhyā*] refers to the act of selection and "cessation" [*nirodha*] refers to the severance of defilements;

it is the ultimate truth manifested when untainted wisdom arises and severs all obstructive defilements—this is the "purity through expedient means" mentioned below). The commentary (*śāstra*) at II.3b3 distinguishes two types: first, nature-purity (because its nature is fundamentally pure);

second, purity through expedient means (because it is manifested through cultivation via expedient means). Third, there is the single *svabhāva-nirvāṇa* (which encompasses both the defiled and the pure; this is the aforementioned nature-purity).

Second is true *nirvāṇa* (which is the aforementioned purity through skillful means; having realized the innate purity of one's original nature through the cultivation of skillful means, this constitutes "true"). Third is *nirvāṇa* by response (after realizing the truth, manifesting entry into extinction according to the capacities of beings to benefit them;

this is "response. Thus, both the realization of truth and the responding to beings are the purity through skillful means). Fourth is the fourfold [classification]: first, self-nature purity (the self-nature of *tathatā*, which pervades all ordinary beings and sages);

second, *nirvāṇa with remainder* (i.e., *tathatā* emerging from the obstacle of afflictions); third, *nirvāṇa without remainder* (i.e., *tathatā* transcending birth and death; if the above two are taken together, they apply to all three vehicles).

The four abodes of non-abiding (the *tathatā* emerging from the cognitive obstacles, supported by compassion and wisdom, and thus not abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa) are called "abodes of non-abiding" because they are possessed exclusively by the Buddha alone. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "All sentient beings possess the first;

those of the two vehicles who have attained no-more-learning may possess the first three; only the World-Honored Buddha can be said to possess all four. The commentary (*śāstra*) likewise includes these as its concluding summary. [The text continues: "Therefore, below [the phrase] 'that'... This fourth section clarifies the functional activity (*karman*).
Part one points to *nirvāṇa* and provides a general explanation. The word "therefore" (*gù*) serves as a proof that establishes what was previously stated.
The term "comprehending" (*she*) means to step upon the momentum to clarify its function; it skillfully causes the textual flow and its underlying structure to remain connected.

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the two lines following "flowers": this section from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* provides a distinct analysis. Now, taking the essential meaning, I shall briefly cite the text. This has two uses, which are divided into two parts:
first, the use of manifesting the true Nirvana as a real benefit. The text states: "O Son of the Buddha, the Tathāgata does not [act] for the sake of Bodhi..."
Sākyamuni taught that all Tathāgatas enter ultimate *nirvāṇa* (yet he did not teach eternal extinction for the sake of the two vehicles);

nor did he manifest such events to them (his final passing at the Twin Śāla trees was for the sake of ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle—this is to distinguish [them from] those who have severed [defilements like] ashes). Why is this?

It is because he desires to cause them to see all Tathāgatas as eternally abiding before them (causing them to see, in accordance with reality, that their own *saṃbhogakāya* is identical to the *dharmakāya*, eternally abiding before them). Within a single thought-moment, they see the past and the future...

"All Buddhas of the past and future appear with their physical bodies (rūpakāya) complete, just as they do in the present" (meaning that because the application [of the Buddha] across the three periods of time is seen to be likewise eternal, it is therefore "as in the present").

The commentary states: Because one perceives the eternally abiding *nirvāṇa*, one sees the Tathāgata as eternally abiding and perfect; this is precisely the actual function (*prayojana*) of *nirvāṇa*.

The sub-commentary (*śāstra*) explains that this is merely to manifest the functional utility of the *nirvāṇa* of response (*nirmāṇa-nirvāṇa*) for the sake of the two lower vehicles, yet the Lotus Sutra...
The *Yanjing* (Śrīmālā-sūtra) explains that there are ten gates regarding nirvāṇa; what was cited above is the second gate, "The Perfection of Virtuous Functions.
The present passage is the third gate, "Entering and Exiting while Remaining Constantly Tranquil. It states:

"O Son of the Buddha, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, appear in the world in order to inspire joy in sentient beings, and they manifest nirvāṇa in order to inspire longing and devotion in sentient beings."

In reality, the Tathāgata neither appears in the world nor enters into parinirvāṇa. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata eternally abides in the pure *dharmadhātu*, manifesting parinirvāṇa in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
The commentary explains: This clarifies that *nirvāṇa* is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and yet not non-active.
Because it is not non-active, it is able to accomplish great deeds; it is not obstructed by appearing and manifesting traces for the sake of birth, nor does it cease its traces.

Because extinction is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), its essence is eternally serene. When it manifests its traces, it is "with remainder" (*sa-upādiśeṣa*); when it ceases its remaining traces, it is "without remainder" (*an-upādiśeṣa*).

Thus, "remainder" and "without remainder" are merely provisional designations used in response to sentient beings; how could they be used to obstruct the sun of the Buddha's meaning with the traces of his various manifestations?
The phrase "under the sun of the Buddha" refers to the fourth chapter of that scripture, the "Gate of the Non-transmigration of Waning and Waxing. That sutra states in full: "The Buddha..."
"Son, it is like this: when the sun rises and shines universally upon the world, its reflection appears in every vessel of pure water;
it pervades all places without coming or going. Yet, if even one vessel is broken, the reflection does not appear.
Son of the Buddha, what do you think? Is the non-appearance of that reflection the fault of the sun? He replied, "No, it is not. It is simply due to the brokenness of the vessel."
Just as the sun has its eclipses, so too is the sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom; it universally manifests throughout the entire dharma-realm without before or after.
Within the vessel of the pure minds of all sentient beings, there is no Buddha who does not appear. If the vessel of the mind is constantly pure, one will always see the Buddha-body;
if the mind is turbid or the vessel is broken, then one cannot see him. The commentary states: "The image is not mine; it arises from that vessel."
If the mind that waxes and wanes is not born of the self, how could it universally manifest before and after? If the vessel of precepts is broken, on what can the water of concentration rely?
If the vessel of bodhi is broken, how can the water of wisdom remain still? Without precept, concentration, and wisdom, by what means can one see the Buddha?

The Commentary states: "The following five [sections] explain the *pāramitās*. The commentary provides both general and specific explanations of the names. Within the specific explanation of the names, it already encompasses the other three sections:
essence (*svabhāva*), function (*vṛtti*), and categories (*prabheda*). The text is divided into two parts: first, a general explanation of the names;

second, the formal explanation of the text, which is easy to understand. The Commentary states: "Now, [the author] generally anticipates and addresses an objection. The objection runs as follows: "According to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the Mahāyāna..."
The teaching is based on the principle of ultimate reality, which states that sentient beings are inherently quiescent and are originally *nirvāṇa*;

they do not undergo further extinction. How, then, can it be said that one departs from this state to arrive at that? Is this not the same as the fault of longing for and loathing [existence] found in the Hīnayāna? Therefore, we now harmonize these views:

while the teaching speaks of "reaching the other shore" in terms of delusion and awakening, the commentary (*śū*) briefly explains the distinction between the names of the latter two [stages]. There is indeed a difference.
The six perfections, five perfections, ten perfections, and eighty-four thousand perfections—these various numbers are all different types.

As for their remaining essence and function, each shall be explained according to the text. This is divided into four parts. First, regarding the six perfections: the first point takes wisdom as the final member.

As for the "six obscurations" and the "six types," the texts are all found in the *Śāstra* (the *Buddhagotra-śāstra*), which are precisely the passages from the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*; however, here we take only the general meaning.

Briefly cited from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "Within the dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*), profound understanding manifests (this is *understanding*). One practices the cultivation of detachment from signs (this is *conduct*).

Because one knows that the essence of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) is devoid of stinginess and greed (this is *understanding*), one accordingly practices the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) (the same applies to the following five).

Because one knows that the dharma-nature is unstained and free from the faults of the five desires (this is *understanding*), one accordingly practices the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*)."
Because one knows that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is without suffering and is free from anger and affliction, one practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) in accordance with it;
because one knows that the nature of phenomena is without the characteristics of body or mind and is free from indolence, one practices the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) in accordance with it;
because one knows that the nature of phenomena is eternally settled and its essence is without distraction, one practices the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā) in accordance with it.
Because one knows that the essence of the Dharma-nature is luminous and free from ignorance, one practices in accordance with the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Regarding these six types of commentaries, only their names have been listed; now each shall be explained individually: "Generosity" (*dāna*) refers to bestowing what one possesses upon others;

"Ethical Discipline" (*śīla*) means preventing wrongdoing and ceasing evil; "Patience" (*kṣānti*) means being able to receive all dharmas without yet having forgotten them; and "Diligence" (*vīrya*) means refining the mind regarding the Dharma.

Diligent application directed toward attainment is the mind of progress (*vīrya*); mental tranquility is *dhyāna*; and discerning through investigation is *prajñā*. Regarding the other two gates of essence and function:
since it is said that the nature (*dharmatā*) is free from stinginess and greed, etc., for generosity and the others, this nature constitutes the essence.

Because practicing the six perfections in accordance with this nature brings them all to fulfillment as *pāramitās*, this conformity to nature constitutes the function. [End of] the second section following the commentary on "Bodhi" (Enlightenment).

Regarding the statement that "wisdom is the foremost mother of all Bodhisattvas and Buddhas," this is a specific praise of wisdom (prajñā). As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says, "The perfection of wisdom is the mother of Bodhisattvas," and as the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts state, she is the "Mother of Buddhas.

Regarding the phrase "the primary provision for awakening" (*bodhi*), "awakening" refers to *bodhi*, and the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are the provisions for *bodhi*; among these, wisdom is the first.

These five refer to the [first] five perfections, such as giving (*dāna*), while the "remainder" refers to the final four among the ten perfections. As for "direction" (*diś*), it refers to the directions.

Regarding the statement that "the powers of aspiration and the wisdoms are all comprised within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)," etc.: it is because they are due to wisdom, and because all ten are subsumed under the perfections.
The prose commentary (*bhāṣya*) on that treatise explains: "Why is this? Because Prajñā is foremost, being the most excellent.
Just as among all the sense organs (*indriya*), the eye organ is the most excellent; just as among the parts of the body, the head is the most excellent; so too among all the perfections..."
Because the Prajñāpāramitā is the most supreme, it is likewise so; because the Prajñāpāramitā is the most supreme, it serves as the primary provision (*sambhāra*), and so forth.

Furthermore, it is the essence of the cause for the purification of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala-pariśuddhi*) among all the pāramitās—because through wisdom one does not conceive of a self, does not conceive of a recipient, and does not conceive of the fruit of giving—and because it is not shared with the two vehicles (*yāna*), there is nothing superior above it.
Because it is that which should be known, this wisdom reaches the further shore of all things (and so forth). The text is extremely extensive and cannot be cited in its entirety.
As for the inclusion of other categories, the five [perfections] are established through wisdom; thus, wisdom is their function, while the other five are its auxiliaries, and wisdom is their essence.

△ In the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*, the latter two of the five perfections are combined into one—the gate of śamatha-vipaśyanā—merging concentration and wisdom into a single category. The remainder...
This can be understood as explained above. △ Regarding the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Commentary on the Thirty Verses), after the six [perfections], four more are added:

namely, seventh, skillful means (*upāya*; method and expediency); eighth, aspiration (*praṇidhāna*; longing and desire); ninth, power (*bala*; invincibility); and tenth, knowledge (*jñāna*; decisive discernment according to reality).
Regarding the ten obstacles and ten suchnesses, they are as explained in the usual commentaries and will appear later as well. These ten pāramitās are universal because...
The Great Bodhicitta constitutes its essence (*tattva*), while that which assists in subduing obstacles and assisting in realization constitutes its function (*vṛtti*).
As for the specific details, as explained in the Dharmalakṣaṇa school, each has its own essence and function; however, the text is too voluminous to be recorded here.

*Commentary:* If one summarizes the four [categories] below, the eighty-four thousand delusions are the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), and their awakening is the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*.
The meaning of "sweetness" as being the opposite [of bitterness] is as explained above in the *Awakening of Faith* regarding the passage on the "flowing forth of all pure dharmas.
As for the "essence and function," the essence is taken collectively as awakening, while the function of each is the ability to overturn defiled dharmas.
The commentary on the meaning of the phrase "as explained below" refers to the "Chapter on the Universal Eye."

The commentary clarifies the sixfold analysis of the preceding and following sections to generally manifest the functional activity. Regarding the phrase "the Dharma which is the teacher of all Buddhas," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma. Because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal.

Thus concludes the general explanation of the four gateways of pure dharmas that flow from the Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). All other untainted (*anāsrava*) and similar dharmas should be understood by analogy with this. This means:
Perfect Enlightenment is fundamentally without bondage, which is precisely what is called liberation; it is fundamentally without the three poisons, which are the roots of the three virtues;
it is fundamentally without doubt and turbidity, which is pure faith, and so forth, up to being fundamentally without the eighty thousand afflictions, which are the eighty thousand *pāramitās*.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "Up to the eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇī* gates, all are utterly pure."

Upon awakening to the sutra, one becomes a Buddha. [The commentary] is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the underlying intent; second, the formal explanation. Regarding the first, there are two sections:
first, explaining the "perfectly illuminating pure awakening" by citing the text and interpreting it through the lens of subject and object;

second, directly explaining it in terms of the essence of the dharma itself. As for the phrase "perfectly illuminating purity," "perfectly illuminating" is itself "purity"; this differs from the previous interpretation.

Because Perfect Illumination illuminates that which is pure, it is said to be unrelated to subject and object. △ The commentary states: "This refers to the three [instances] below, which cite examples to explain the character 'xiang' (aspect/sign).
The first instance of seeing Mañjuśrī occurs in the sixty-first fascicle, at the ancient Buddha-stūpa and temple to the east of Fucheng.
The latter instance of not seeing Mañjuśrī occurs in the seventy-ninth fascicle, where the Sūtra describes how Sudhana relied upon Maitreya.

Sudhana requested an audience with Mañjuśrī; Mañjuśrī extended his right hand from afar across one hundred and ten cities and touched Sudhana’s crown, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening him (he did not see the Buddha’s body, but heard the Dharma).
An ancient master judged this, saying: "Wisdom-illumination is non-dual in aspect" (meaning there is no duality between subject and object).
Regarding the commentary on "Original Enlightenment," the second explanation concerns severing hindrances and attaining the Way by taking this as the cause, which means as follows:
This relies on the perfect illumination of fundamental purity to realize that ignorance is fundamentally empty; this is the true cause for attaining Buddhahood.

If one harbors deluded thoughts within the mind and practices while carrying these delusions, even after many kalpas of toil and labor, it will ultimately fail to achieve the fruit of Buddhahood—just as in the case of the Bodhisattva who accumulated practices, as cited previously.

In the commentary on the Sūtra’s investigation of the false ruler within the second section, part one, there are two parts: first, the general exposition of the intent; second, the detailed explanation according to the sections. Regarding the inquiry in the Sūtra, the commentary has two parts:
first, the inquiry; second, the explanation. Below is the explanation of the text. The commentary states: "The two [points] below clarify the intent. First, it clarifies the faults.
The eighty thousand afflictions and the twelve links of dependent origination will be explained below as appropriate. The commentary [states]: "Non-perception... (Asaṃjñisattva).
Regarding the phrase "and so forth," the *Buddhanāman Sūtra* records the Buddha saying to Śāriputra: "Your teacher Udraka Rāmaputra attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
yet after eighty-four thousand kalpas had passed and his life ended, he could not avoid being reborn as a flying fox.

This was because while practicing this meditative concentration, he was disturbed by the clamor of crows in the forest and the noise of fish near the water. His mind gave rise to anger, and he made a vow: 'May I enter the water and fly through the air to devour them! Once the power of his concentration was exhausted, he received this retribution. (I await a verification of the scriptural text.)
[The commentary] explains this in detail: regarding "the pit of the unconditioned," the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Manifestation [of the Tathāgata]," states:

"On the summit of the Snowy Mountains there is a king of medicinal trees named 'Inexhaustible Root' (ananta-mūla). When its root takes hold, it causes all the roots of the trees in Jambudvīpa to grow;
the same applies to their trunks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits. However, there are two places where it cannot provide the benefit of growth and development, namely..."
Just as one never feels weary of or abandons the deep pits of hell or the water-wheel [of the world], so too is the Great Medicine King Tree of the Tathāgata’s Wisdom (and so forth).
When its root arises, it causes all bodhisattvas to give rise to the root of great compassion that does not abandon sentient beings;

[it has] the deep resolve as its trunk, the pāramitās as its branches, pure precepts and dhūtas as its leaves, the marks and signs of physical adornment as its flowers, and the fruit of the Buddha’s consecration through patience. Only...

In two places, he is unable to bring about growth or benefit: namely, those of the Two Vehicles who have fallen into the vast and deep pit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and those sentient beings who are not vessels for the Dharma because their roots of goodness are destroyed and who are submerged in the waters of great false views and craving.
Nevertheless, he never feels weary of or abandons them. (The commentary states: The author of the *Śāstra* uses this passage regarding the "pit of the unconditioned" to clarify [this point].)
Although the two vehicles have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), they have not yet severed this fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*); this is the "illness" referred to in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
[The commentary] states: "Now, wishing to... and so forth; the second section correctly reveals the intent, and the text is easy to understand.

In the commentary on the sutra, there are two parts to the sub-commentary (*shu*). The second part explains the meaning below, which has three sections: first, explaining the name; second, explaining the primary name.

This [explanation] follows the interpretation of the Dharma-nature school (*Faxing zong*). According to the Dharma-character school (*Faxiang zong*), it says that "illumination" (*ming*) refers to the wisdom of discerning phenomena (*pravicaya-jñāna*);
because this illumination is absent, it is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*). That school holds that ignorance in sentient beings is the fundamental root from beginningless time.
One must cultivate the wisdom that discriminates phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-prajñā*) before it can become illumination;

"The internal core of the six *āmra* fruits (the *tathāgatagarbha* of the two bodies)"; as the sūtra says: "For example, the internal core of an *āmra* fruit is not destroyed;
when planted in the earth, it becomes a great king of trees. In the same way, O son of good family, I observe with my Buddha-eye..."
All sentient beings possess the treasure-store of the Tathāgata within the husk of ignorance, just as a seed exists within its kernel.
Good son, that Tathāgata-garbha is cool, free from feverish affliction, a mass of great wisdom, wondrously quiescent, eternal, and constant;
it is named the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Fully Awakened One. Good son, having thus observed sentient beings, the Tathāgata acts for the sake of the Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas.
In order to purify the Buddha-wisdom, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva elucidates this meaning through the analogy of the mango fruit regarding the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*). The treatise states:

"The afflictions contained within the bodies of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) that can be severed by the wisdom of the first supramundane dharma are called 'afflictions severed by the path of seeing' (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya-kleśa*).
Thus, the verse says: "Just as a seed, separated from its husk, successively produces sprouts and so forth, so too the afflictions severed by the path of seeing [are removed]."

Regarding the phrase "the various stages are produced" (the meaning of this metaphor is that through the Path of Vision, the ordinary being is transformed into a sage; the sacred wisdom is generated and sustains all meritorious qualities, just as when the skin of the mango falls away, the fruit produces sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit).
The "inner kernel" is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature of the two bodies (*kāya*), which has already been explained above, and the rest is likewise so.

Commentary on the Seven Defiled Objects (the *bhāvanā-heya-kleśas*): Regarding the "Golden Image" (the *dharmakāya*), a sutra states: "Suppose there is a person who carries a true golden image and travels to another country.
While journeying along a perilous road, fearing it might be plundered, he wraps it in tattered rags so that no one will recognize it.
On the way, this person suddenly passes away; consequently, the golden image is abandoned in the wilderness, and travelers tread upon it."
It is like one who has attained the divine eye and sees a true golden image within a piece of refuse; he immediately removes it, and all pay him reverence.

In the same way, son of good family, I see that sentient beings, through their various afflictions, wander through birth and death for a long night and immeasurable time, yet the wondrous treasury of the Tathāgata exists within their bodies, solemn and pure, no different from my own.
Therefore, the Buddha preaches the Dharma for sentient beings to sever afflictions and purify the Tathāgata’s wisdom; he further transforms and guides all sentient beings.

The "defiled objects" serve as a metaphor for the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Furthermore, it is said that the afflictions contained within the bodies of noble ones (*ārya*) can be severed by the wisdom of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-jñāna*), which is supramundane (*lokottara*).
Thus, the verse says: "By means of [the wisdom] that destroys the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, [afflictions] are subsumed."
Because one takes up the sublime Noble Path to sever afflictions through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanā-mārga*), it is described as "tattered rags.
Regarding the "eight poor women" (the impurities of the ground) and the "Wheel-Turning King" (the *saṃbhogakāya*):

the Sūtra says, "For example, there was a woman who was poor, lowly, and ugly, loathed by all people, yet she conceived a noble son who was destined to become a Holy Wheel-Turning King and rule over the four continents. This woman did not know [of this]."
Throughout the passage of time, one should constantly maintain the thought of oneself as a lowly person.

Thus, son of good family, the Tathāgata observes that all sentient beings, revolving in birth and death and undergoing various bitter poisons of suffering, possess within their bodies the treasure-store of the Tathāgata, just like that woman who does not realize it.
Therefore, the Tathāgata universally preaches the Dharma for them, saying: "Son of good family, do not..."

Do not disparage yourselves; you all possess Buddha-nature. If you apply yourselves with diligent effort to extinguish all faults and evils, you shall receive the titles of Bodhisattva and Buddha, transforming and delivering immeasurable sentient beings.

Regarding the analogy of the poor woman and the impurities of the ground, the *Treatise* states that these refer to the afflictions subsumed from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage; from the eighth stage upward, they no longer exist.

Regarding the verse stating that the wisdom of the path-cultivation within the stages (*bhūmi*) can sever [defilements]: "The various impurities within the seven stages are like being enveloped by a womb;
once far removed from the womb-encasement, wisdom is non-conceptual and fully matured."

The Commentary states: Regarding the casting of images (the *nirmāṇakāya*) from ninefold molds (the impurities of the pure ground), a sutra says: "For example, it is like a smith casting an image of pure gold.

Once it has been cast and placed upon the ground, the exterior appears scorched black, yet the interior image remains unchanged. When the mold is opened and the image is extracted, its golden color shines brilliantly.
In this same way, O son of good family, the Tathāgata observes that the Buddha-treasury resides within all sentient beings.
Having thus contemplated the body as being fully endowed with its various marks, one extensively explains and reveals that those sentient beings obtain rest and coolness.
With vajra-like wisdom, they shatter the afflictions and open the pure Buddha-body.

Regarding the analogy of the mold for purifying the dross from the ground, it further states that the afflictions contained within the bodies of Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage upward are destroyed by the wisdom of the Vajra-samādhi.
Because they are severed, the verse says: "The various defilements within the three stages are like clay molds; the great wisdom of the Bodhisattvas severs them through the diamond-like samādhi.
Following this, five further metaphors are presented. Above, we have only applied these to the poor man and so forth, but have not yet applied them to the treasure storehouse and so forth;
we shall now apply them. The treatise verse states: "There are two kinds of Buddha-nature: the first is like a treasure hidden in the earth" (this refers to the present case).

The fifth analogy. Second, like the fruit of a tree (the sixth): from beginningless worlds (as mentioned previously), based on the cultivation of the unsurpassed path by means of the intrinsically pure mind (this clarifies that the myriad practices are fundamentally inherent, which is the meaning of "original enlightenment" as internal perfuming within the treatise), one relies upon the two kinds of Buddha-nature (the analogies for the fifth and sixth) to attain the three bodies (the analogies for the seventh, eighth, and ninth).
Because of the first analogy (the treasure storehouse), one knows that there exists the primary Dharmakāya (the myriad virtues).

The basis (*āśraya*) is like a treasure trove; it is the support for clothing, food, the body, the household, and all worldly affairs. By relying on the second metaphor (the *āmra* fruit), one knows that there are two bodies of the Buddha:

the ripening and the unripening stages of the fruit, as explained below. The true Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is pure like an image of pure gold (this seventh metaphor refers to the Dharma-body free from entanglements;

while the previous five metaphors represent the causal nature, this metaphor represents the resultant characteristic, like a finished golden image). Because its nature is immutable, it encompasses the reality of all merits.

(Commentary on the above: Attaining the station of the Great Dharma King is like that of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (the eighth metaphor, representing the Reward Body; that is, the six preceding metaphors represent the causal nature that accomplishes the two bodies, while the eighth and ninth metaphors represent the characteristics of the Reward and Transformation Bodies accomplished thereby).
Relying upon the substance of a cast image, a manifested Buddha-image appears (this is the ninth dharma-illustration). The long discourse states:
"The remaining five metaphors demonstrate the manifestation of birth in those three Buddhas' *dharmakāya*s, because they rely upon the intrinsic nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*."
Because all sentient beings are the treasury [of the Tathāgata], it is said that all sentient beings possess the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Since the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are designated by name and meaning through their three bodies (*trikāya*), these five metaphors can serve as the causes for the three kinds of Buddha-dharmakāya.
For this reason, the nature of the Tathāgata (*tathāgatatva*) is taught; herein, the meaning of "nature" (*dhātu*) is clarified as having the sense of a "cause. Thus it is.
For this reason, a verse in the Sūtra says: "The nature from beginningless time... (*etc.*, the remainder of this passage is omitted below for the sake of providing a complete explanation).

In the Commentary, there are two types of inclusion (*saṃgraha*): first, the inclusion of the essence within the two [aspects]; second, the inclusion of the essence and its function as a single unity. Regarding the inclusion of the essence within the aspects and functions:
this "inclusion" means that the function of the essence itself depends upon the essence of that very function; thus, the essence of that function sustains it.
Regarding the function inherent in the very substance itself, it is not like a chest or similar object that stores other things; rather, it is like the analogy of gold containing vessels.
This means that within pure, uniform gold, myriad vessels are contained, which manifest as soon as the conditions assemble.

This is also the intended meaning of the *Huayan Jinsizi Zhang* (The Golden Lion Chapter of the Avataṃsaka), and is like a bright mirror containing all images; thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* speaks of the "Great Perfect Mirror."

The mental states associated with wisdom can manifest and give rise to the reflections of bodies, lands, and wisdom. △ The commentary further states that the two types of sages include ordinary beings;
this is from the *Tathāgatagarbha-parivarta* of the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*. It says in full:

"As for what is called 'garbha' (store), because all sentient beings are entirely within the wisdom of the Tathāgata, it is named 'garbha. It is designated as such by virtue of the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*)."
Because it is the realm of suchness (*tathatā*), no sentient being whatsoever can ever transcend this realm of suchness;

since all are universally sustained by the Tathāgata, sentient beings are called the "Tathāgata-garbha" (the womb/storehouse of the Tathāgata). Furthermore, there is another meaning—according to the commentary, this constitutes three meanings altogether—namely, that the cause contains the fruit.
This means that while on the stage of the cause, one has already encompassed all the merits of the stage of fruition; therefore, it is called "Buddha-nature."

The treatise states: "As for 'store' (garbha), because it encompasses all merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges while abiding in the stage of the Tathāgata’s attainable nature, it is already fully contained therein.
If one were to say that the nature is only attained when reaching the stage of fruition, then this nature would be impermanent.
Why? Because it would not be something [previously] attained. Therefore, we know it is primordially present; hence, it is called 'permanent'."
The Commentary (Sū) provides three explanations for the phrase "giving birth, thorough understanding, realization, and entry.

Regarding "that which is able to give birth," all teachings maintain that it is only upon ascending to the stages (*bhūmi*) and realizing the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) that one can cultivate and accomplish the various wondrous functions of the merit of the reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Regarding the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, that treatise explains the meaning of "stage" (*bhūmi*) as being "able to give birth" and "able to sustain. It further explains the presiding master of the assembly for the Ten Stages.
Vajragarbha said: "The 'garbha' (matrix/store) is called 'firm' (*dṛḍha*); it is like the core of a tree.

Just as the heartwood of a tree is firm and dense, capable of producing branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit, so too is the wisdom of the stage (*bhūmi-jñāna*), for it can produce the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) [dharmas], and so forth."

The Commentary states: These three [categories] below are assigned to the middle [category]. Regarding the term "the essential substance" (*kètì*), it means that the Dharma-body is fundamentally free from afflictions;

there is nothing capable of obscuring its inherently endowed virtues and functions, as these do not depend on being produced anew. Therefore, it is called "the essential substance. (The above three sections complete the explanation of the names.)

The commentary generally explains the characteristics of the four [aspects] below; first, a general explanation, and second, a specific explanation. Regarding the first, the specific explanation, there are three parts:

first, the opening and closing of the real and the delusory, which refers to how both the real and the delusory each have their own modes of opening and closing, as detailed in the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith*.

Following the initial section on the "Real" (*zhen*) in the commentary, there are two sections concerning "Only Nature" (*weixing*); both the sutras and the treatises contain these two, and the explanation of their meaning is also found within the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* at the end of the commentary.
Regarding the three aspects produced from the "only-mind" (wei-xiang), the first is divided into two, and the second is further divided into four.
As for the unconditioned (wu-wei) within the gate of arising and ceasing, according to the treatise, true suchness (tathatā) also exists within the gate of arising and ceasing;

it is like moisture, which does not necessarily involve waves, yet where there are waves, moisture must necessarily be present. Thus, we know that the unmoving is also contained within the moving. However, [the unconditioned] is not...

Phenomena (*dharma*) are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); unwholesome phenomena are exclusively tainted (*sāsrava*). Wholesome phenomena and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are both tainted and untainted;
furthermore, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are exclusively non-wholesome. Wholesome phenomena and conditioned phenomena mutually interpenetrate as being both [tainted and untainted].

Commentary: Regarding the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) below, there are two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. First, the heading: "First, the true [nature]" and so forth. Second, the explanation, which has two parts:

first, the unchanging [aspect]; second, the arising according to conditions. Regarding the latter, there are two parts: first, the specific; second, the general. First, the specific, which has two parts: first, the commentary on the arising of defilement;

second, the commentary on the pure dependent origination (*viśuddha-pratītyasamutpāda*). Following the latter, there are two parts: first, citing the treatise to introduce the scripture, namely the *Abhidharma*.
In the commentary on the long prose section, the second part explains the *Sūtra* (the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*) by means of the *Sūtra* (the *Abhidharma*). It states:
"As for 'nature' (*dhātu*), it refers to the *tathāgatagarbha*. To speak fully: what is called 'nature' is as stated in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*:
'World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has taught that the *tathāgatagarbha* is the *dharmadhātu*, the supramundane *dharmakāya-garbha*, the supreme-supramundane garbha, and the naturally pure [mind].'"
Because the *dharmakāya-garbha* is the naturally pure *tathāgatagarbha*, the Commentary (*Śāstra*) relies on that treatise, which quotes in full:
"World-Honored One, for this reason, the *tathāgatagarbha* is the basis, the support, and the establishment.

World-Honored One, it is not separate from, not separate from wisdom, uninterrupted, inseparable, non-different, and inconceivable, being endowed with the unconditioned Buddha-qualities. World-Honored One, yet there is also that which is severed and separated."
"Distinct from the external and separate from the wisdom of detachment, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) also depend upon, are sustained by, and are established in the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Regarding the 'various paths,' these are the six realms of birth and death; regarding 'realizing nirvāṇa,' these are the paths of the three vehicles.

Each should be correlated with the scriptural citations provided in the commentary. The scripture states in full: 'Because they depend on the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is birth and death; because they depend on the *tathāgata*..."*
Because it is hidden, one realizes nirvāṇa. Blessed One, if there were no *tathāgatagarbha*, one would not be able to feel weary of suffering or seek after nirvāṇa;

one would neither desire nor aspire for nirvāṇa. What does this clarify? It clarifies that the *tathāgatagarbha* is ultimately the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata, the non-differentiated essence and characteristic of *tathatā*, the ultimate emptiness, and the essence of the *buddhadhātu* within all things.
At that time, one should know that all sentient beings, without exception, abide within this very body. How is this known? It is known by means of the characteristics of the Dharma.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Good son, this nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the essence of phenomena (dharmatva), and the self-nature (svabhāva) are eternally abiding.
Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, this self-nature is pure and has been eternally abiding from the beginning; all sentient beings possess it."

What is the meaning clarified by this *ālayavijñāna*? Based on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), based on the substance of phenomena, based on the correspondence of phenomena, and based on the skillful means of phenomena—whether it be thus or not thus—it is inconceivable.

In all respects, by relying on phenomena, by relying on the measure of phenomena, and by relying on faith in phenomena, one attains mental stability; that [stability] cannot be discriminated as being real or unreal, but relies solely upon faith in the Tathāgata.
Therefore, the verse says: "Relying solely on faith in the Tathāgata, one has faith in the ultimate truth (paramārtha); like those without eyes, one cannot see the solar disk. The commentary states:

"As for the six exhortations to faith following the various [sections], the first clarifies that which should be believed. Regarding the statement 'one must first believe and understand,' this refers to the *Ratnagotravibhāga*."

In the treatise, it is asked: "The meaning of *tathatā*, *buddhadhātu*, and *tathāgatagarbha* is not even within the sphere of the foremost sages—bodhisattvas dwelling on the stage of ultimate non-obstruction—since it is the sphere of the Omniscient One alone.
For what reason, then, is it taught to foolish, deluded worldlings? The answer is given: "For this reason, four verses are briefly stated."
It is said in various sūtras that all internal and external conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are empty, like clouds, dreams, and illusions;
why, then, is it stated here that all sentient beings possess the *tathāgatagarbha*, rather than being described as empty and quiescent?

[The commentary states: The above is still a provisional formulation intended to facilitate the inquiry; the following provides the formal response: "Because they possess a timid mind and treat other sentient beings with contempt."

Because sentient beings cling to false and illusory phenomena, slander the *tathatā* (suchness) and Buddha-nature, and falsely conceive of a self within the body and a person, the existence of Buddha-nature is taught in order to cause them to distance themselves from these five kinds of faults. These four verses are briefly explained by eleven verses (of which eight are cited here).
[This is because] sentient beings do not hear [this teaching], do not resolve to attain bodhicitta, or are perhaps those who are timid and deceive themselves.
Regarding those who, having already generated the bodhicitta in the past or present, give rise to conceited and arrogant views, thinking, "I have generated the bodhicitta;
I am superior to that other bodhisattva"—such arrogant people do not give rise to a mind of right wisdom. This is false conceptualization; they do not know the dharmas as they truly are.
They falsely grasp at the faults of sentient beings, failing to realize that these are adventitious defilements of the mind and that its true nature is pure and devoid of such faults.
Because one grasps at the fault of false appearances while failing to recognize actual merit, one is unable to give rise to the equanimity of self and other.
Upon hearing of that nature of *tathatā*, one gives rise to great heroic power, reverence for the World-Honored One’s wisdom, and great compassion;
these five qualities arise, increase, and become non-retrogressive. Therein is equality, free from all faults, possessing only all manner of merit.
"Virtue consists in regarding all sentient beings as no different from one's own body, thereby swiftly attaining the realization of unsurpassed Buddha-bodhi.
This is what is taught within the "Three Holy Contemplations" (sān shèng guān). [The commentary] states: "Therefore, 'secretly' [and so forth], the second section proves the harm of lack of faith.

[The commentary] states: "Therefore, 'superior' [and so forth], the third section proves the benefit of faithful compliance. This is identical to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*’s contemplation of the reality of the body.

The same applies to the Buddha when viewed through his marks (*lakṣaṇa*). According to the meaning of this passage, it conversely clarifies that if one harbors doubt regarding those [marks] while still bound by afflictions (*saṃkleśa*), then one will likewise harbor doubt regarding the merits of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of all Buddhas once they have transcended those bonds. [Commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*]: The following four sections prove that all practices are fundamentally based upon the *Avataṃsaka*.
Of the nine assemblies of the *Avataṃsaka*, the first assembly is the general and the root; the remaining assemblies are the specific and the branches.
Therefore, this samādhi is the root of all dharmas, for the essence of samādhi is the Tathāgatagarbha. As that sūtra states:

"At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, seated before the Tathāgata (constantly facing the Buddha), upon a lion throne within the Lotus Treasury (symbolizing that the self-nature of the meditative absorption he has entered is unstained and contains the dharmas of fruition), receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, entered a samādhi named..."

The *tathāgatagarbha* of all Buddhas, Vairocana—the body of the Tathāgata whose light shines everywhere—is the great wisdom that is the subject of contemplation; the *tathāgatagarbha* as the body of the Tathāgata is the profound principle that is the object of contemplation.

Although this is equally present in all, it is only through Buddha-wisdom that it is illuminated. Furthermore, "great wisdom" also refers to that which is primordially possessed; because its meaning is the universal illumination of the *dharmadhātu* through true, primordial cognition, it reveals that the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu*) have no separate self-nature apart from the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Therefore, one enters into this. There is another interpretation which states: "Vast" (*viśāla*) means that compassion is boundless; "Great" (*mahat*) means that wisdom is unsurpassed; "Arising and Ceasing" (*janmanirodha*) means that the characteristics of birth have already been exhausted; and "Containing All Virtues" (*garbha*) refers to the inclusion of all merits. This is called the "body of the *tathāgatagarbha*," which is precisely the state of being free from entanglements (*vinirmukta-kośa*).

Regarding the *dharmakāya* from the perspective of its fundamental nature (*prakṛti*), both ordinary beings and sages equally possess it. The *ālayavijñāna* contains all seeds and establishes the various realms of rebirth; as the vast fundamental awakening, its principle and measure are equal to that of a Buddha, hence it is called "Great.

Because it newly arises, it is termed "arising"; because defilement and purity cannot move it, it is termed "resting. The *dharmakāya* while still enmeshed in bondage is called the "Treasury" (*garbha*). Below this, the essence, attributes, and functions are clarified through six pairs.

It universally enters the equality of all Buddhas—this is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha. Therefore, entering the treasury-body is equivalent to having already entered the equality of the Buddhas. [Commentary: Although the following five points clarify the reasons why [this teaching] is difficult to believe...
Upon hearing that the Empress was carrying the embryo of a sovereign, one has no doubt;
yet, upon hearing it said that a poor and ugly woman is carrying the fetus of a wheel-turning monarch (the eighth of the nine previous similes), one refuses to believe it.

It is like a foolish child who, seeing a mani-jewel that does not reflect impure colors and forms, believes it to be pure and bright, yet fails to recognize it when such images actually appear within it.
He was immediately unwilling to believe. ▲ The commentary states that from "I vow" onwards, the six lines are a direct exhortation to believe;

this refers to exhorting those of initial resolve who possess superior faculties (if they were of inferior faculties, one would exhort them to enter the Great Vehicle from the Small, as in the parable of the impoverished son in the *Lotus Sūtra*, waiting for their faculties to ripen before exhorting them). One should abandon the deluded mind that is difficult to abandon (that which is difficult to abandon refers to the objects of the five desires;

this addresses those of superior faculties among ordinary beings. For those of gradual capacity, however, the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles is what is difficult to abandon). One should seek to perceive the wondrous principle that is difficult to see (one's own mind...).

This refers to all the sublime meanings and sublime functions of all virtues within [the Tathāgatagarbha]. Thus, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "There are two things difficult to comprehend: namely, the intrinsically pure mind and that very mind being defiled by afflictions. The commentary explains: "One's own mind and the afflictions constitute these two; both of these are difficult [to understand].

Having thus completed the explanation of the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha, the intended purport of this sūtra is to explain the reason for "brushing away" [all adventitious traces] by taking the self-nature of the Garbha as its basis—its permanence and immutability, which are free from the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). This is precisely [the point].
Among the two aspects of practice, this refers to the gate of *tathatā* (suchness). The term "Tathāgatagarbha" serves as the general heading;

the next two phrases refer to the *śūnyagarbha* (empty treasury), and the final three phrases refer to the *aśūnyagarbha* (non-empty treasury). Hereafter, these will be explained in response to specific difficulties.

The commentary explains the two preceding interpretations and the remaining phrases in two parts: first, the explanation of the "Treasury of Emptiness" (*śūnyagarbha*); second, the explanation of the preceding [passage]. Regarding "that which knows":
in contrast to the aforementioned "object of knowledge" (*jñeya*), which is birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), this refers to the "knowing intelligence" (*jñāna*), the capacity for cognition.

"That which can grasp" calculates that birth-and-death exists; "that which knows" realizes that birth-and-death does not exist. The commentary states: "It cannot be known by intelligence," which, together with the preceding [phrase] "without arising or ceasing," is precisely identical [to the previous point].

A verse from the *Avataṃsaka* says: "That which is able to see" (this refers to the absence of knowing-seeing; as mentioned above, that which perceives is like empty space), "and that which is seen" (this refers to the absence of arising and ceasing;
as mentioned above, knowing is like a flower in the sky), and "the seer" (as mentioned above, the one who knows empty space)—all these are eliminated (summarizing the preceding text).

Not destroying the true Dharma is called the true seer (identical to the three phrases below regarding the nature of the dharma-realm, etc.). The commentary states: "Consciousness and wisdom are both as follows: when delusion is exhausted, principle manifests."
"Both are as such" means that non-thought is itself the self-substance, which is inherently self-aware and not identical to discursive discrimination; therefore, it is called "real.

"Consciousness" refers to the pure, true consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*), not the *ālaya-vijñāna* and so forth. "Radiance" means that the substance of knowing manifests, being free from the darkness of delusion.
"Illumination" means that this very seeing of knowledge is without boundaries or location, and is thus "pervasive. From...

From "The self-substance" (*svabhāva*) onwards, all [the text] is the main body of the *Awakening of Faith* (*Qixin lun*). The commentators follow the preceding two phrases to explain the meaning of "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*);

they then point to the substance that is "not empty" (*aśūnya*) to initiate the meaning of the subsequent three phrases. For this reason, it says, "for the sake of the 'not empty' below," and so forth.

In the commentary, from "Dharmadhātu" (*dharmadhātu*) onwards, there are two explanations of the "not-empty treasury" (*aśūnya-garbha*). Regarding "Buddha-nature" (*buddhadhātu*) and "Dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*), that treatise states: "It exists... [and so on].
Among the category of sentient beings, it is called *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature); among the category of non-sentient things, it is called *dharmatā* (Dharma-nature).
Since *buddhadhātu* is the *tathāgatagarbha*, this is cited as proof. As the commentary states regarding "the creator" and so forth:

the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Awakening of Faith*, the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, and other texts that explain the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha* all contain these passages, which are largely identical with minor differences. Regarding the "two meanings" in the commentary, [they refer to] the Tathāgata...
