In the commentary on the investigation and explanation of the sutra, the sub-commentary (*shu*) is divided into two parts. First, regarding the initial section, the outline of the divisions is presented. Second, the direct explanation of the sutra’s progressive inquiry.

Regarding the phrase "not departing from this" in the sub-commentary, this refers to the essence of Samantabhadra’s practice. In the sutra, within the section concerning those suited to the specific capacity, it says:

"Those who cultivate the Mahāyāna and hear of Perfect Enlightenment. This distinguishes the intended audience; those who do not cultivate the Mahāyāna are clearly not fit vessels to receive and practice this gateway.

Regarding these vessels: even if there are those who practice the Mahāyāna, if they have not yet heard of the Perfect Enlightenment (Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra), they are likewise not vessels.

As previously cited from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, those who have practiced the six perfections for many kalpas are not yet true Bodhisattvas and so forth; therefore, it is now specified that one must possess these two types of qualities.
Regarding "penetrating the natural truth": the preceding chapter explained that the nature of enlightenment is naturally pure and free from birth-and-death and the like.
Because it is not produced, it does not exist.

This refers to the second line of the first section of the commentary on the "Illusionary Illusion" question in the Sūtra. Regarding the general explanation of this section, as for the phrase "this question and so forth":
it was previously stated that "empty flowers are themselves illusory," and the verse says, "all illusions perish and have no location. [Commentary: As for "illusion" (māyā):

The second part consists of two sections explaining the meaning of "illusion" (māyā) in detail. First, regarding the presentation of the general intent: it is said that this is difficult to understand because it does not exist in this land [of China].

The Commentary now explains by opening up the categories according to the following two points. That is to say: the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is like the cloth; the true mind (*tathatā-citta*) is like the magician;

and the discriminating consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*) is like the magical technique. While the phenomena have various distinctions, the magician is one; likewise, while the discriminating consciousness has various distinctions, [it is fundamentally one].
In the single analogy of the "true mind," since it is only the horse that is non-existent, there is no contradiction in the existence of the illusionist’s performance;

likewise, within the correspondence of phenomena, although only the self and dharmas are non-existent, there is no contradiction in the true mind acting as the consciousness that discriminates various things.

Thus, those who are deludedly attached to the horse as real are bystanders, not the illusionist himself. Within the correspondence of phenomena, those who cling to the self and dharmas are the six [consciousnesses].

Regarding the seven mental factors that arise, such as faith, the characteristics of wisdom, and the characteristic of continuity—these are distinct from the intrinsically pure mind (*amala-vijñāna*) and the three subtle states of the *ālaya-vijñāna* according to the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*).

If one wishes to grasp the truth that the true and the false are of one mind without separate external attachments, it is like a magician who has long practiced the arts of illusion; once these illusory arts have become proficient, he can produce them effortlessly at will.
Immediately after the ritual procedure was completed, his mind suddenly became deranged and deluded; he took the conjured object to be real.

Although his mind was deranged, because the power of the illusionary rite was so mature, he involuntarily maintained that perception even as the conjured object did not vanish (just as a dog barking at its own reflection in a well might eventually leap into the well and die).
In the commentary on the section concerning the question of annihilation, there are two parts: first, the direct explanation of this question; second, the citation of scriptural evidence.
Regarding the passage in the sutra that negates non-cultivation, the commentary states: "Not contemplating power and function means merely recollecting the purity of nature."

The *Commentary on the Treatise Requested by the Sūtra* states that the following section precisely conveys the meaning of the aforementioned "not observing the power and function. The *Treatise* says:
"In this way, although the dharma-body of the *tathatā* (suchness) of sentient beings is empty and pure in its essential nature, it is defiled by immeasurable afflictions.
If a person contemplates *tathatā*, even though [afflictions] are immeasurable and pervade all phenomena, they should cultivate everything."
Good conduct serves as the antidote; if a person practices all wholesome dharmas, they will naturally accord with the Dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Regarding the "eight winds," [the commentary] explains that gain, loss, defamation, praise, fame, insignificance, suffering, and pleasure are like the passage in the Preface to the *Śāstra* concerning the "abandonment of the father.
As for "lightning," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that when a beginner hears the Dharma, their initial understanding is like a flash of light in the darkness.
At night, when a flash of lightning momentarily reveals mountains, rivers, people, and things, they immediately return to darkness;

yet, because of this, one has already discerned the objects before one and can reflect upon them through thought. (I do not record the specific text, but cite it for its meaning. Other sources also speak of the "lightning-flash samādhi" (*vidyut-prabha-samādhi*).

Regarding the instruction that "the commentary should be supplemented with 'etc.'": one should state, "I vow to analyze and expound for all sentient beings of the final age what skillful means there are for gradual cultivation," whereby the intended meaning will be made manifest. Regarding the phrase "etc.":
one may say "reveal, show, and analyze," or "analyze and proclaim"—either is acceptable.
In the commentary on the *Sūtra-praśaṃsā*, it is said that [the reflection] is not something received, because the shadow is empty and there is nothing to be received;

nor is it something rejected, because at the time of facing a mirror, the shadow does not exist outside the mirror, but is entirely merged in darkness with it. "Correct reception" (*zhèngshòu*) is the Chinese transliteration of the Sanskrit term for *samādhi*.

In the prose commentary (*dīrgha-pada*) of the Sūtra, the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) is divided into three parts: first, the general exposition of the Sūtra text; second, the detailed explanation of the structural outline (*kośa*);

and third, the specific interpretation of the meaning. Regarding the phrase "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) and so forth, this refers to the *mūla-bodhi* (fundamental awakening) as it follows defilement.

The text further states that the "characteristic of the purification of wisdom" (*jñāna-viśuddhi-lakṣaṇa*) means that, by relying on the power of the Dharma and through the熏習 (*vāsanā*, perfuming) of practice according to reality, one fulfills the skillful means (*upāya*) and thereby destroys [defilements].

The characteristic of the synthetic consciousness (*saṃghāta-vijñāna*) is extinguished (by means of the aforementioned expedient means, one is able to destroy the characteristics of arising and ceasing within the synthetic consciousness, thereby revealing the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing;
because this fundamental ignorance is exhausted, the mind has nothing with which to synthesize, which reveals the meaning of the Dharmakāya as original enlightenment).

The characteristic of the continuous mind is extinguished, and the wisdom of the Dharmakāya manifests in its pure clarity (at this very moment, one is able to extinguish the characteristics of the continuity of karmic signs within the defiled mind, yet without extinguishing the substance of the continuous mind itself; thus, the mind of original enlightenment that follows along with defilement returns to its source, becoming pure, perfect wisdom, which constitutes the meaning of the *sāmbhogika-kāya* as initial enlightenment).

However, this initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) has no separate beginning; it is simply the original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) manifesting in accordance with defilement. Now that the conditions of defilement have ceased, the initial awakening returns to its identity with the original;

therefore, it is called "pure. What is the meaning of this? [Question: As stated above, the movement of that quiescent mind constitutes arising and ceasing. Since arising and ceasing are now exhausted, should not the quiescent mind also cease? [Answer: Because all characteristics of mind and consciousness are entirely ignorance (*avidyā*). [The meaning is:

Defiled minds such as karma are called the "characteristics of consciousness," and these are all characteristics of non-awakening (*a-bodhi*); they are not spoken of in reference to the essence of the mind. An objection is raised: Since it is said that the characteristics of consciousness are all ignorance, it is therefore taught...

If that which is extinguished were to possess a distinct substantial nature separate from True Suchness (*tathatā*), it would follow that the true and the deluded are separate entities; this is the difficulty. Therefore, the following response states:

"The characteristic of ignorance does not depart from the nature of awakening" (just as the characteristic of non-awakening of these various consciousnesses does not depart from the nature of the fundamentally awakened mind that follows defilement).

It is neither destructible nor indestructible. Because this characteristic of ignorance and that nature of fundamental awakening are neither identical nor different—because they are not different, it is not destructible; because they are not identical, it is not indestructible. If one speaks according to the meaning of their non-difference and indestructibility, ignorance is itself illumination. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The nature of illumination and ignorance..."

The absence of duality and the nature of non-duality is itself the true nature (*dharmatā*). If one speaks from the perspective of that which is neither one nor indestructible, it is because ignorance (*avidyā*) can be extinguished. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "By the extinction of ignorance, one attains the lamp of Bodhi.

One should understand the meaning of the extinction of delusion through this principle: just as the water of the great ocean is stirred by the wind, the appearance of the water and the appearance of the wind are inseparable, yet the water is not of a moving nature;
when the wind ceases, the appearance of movement is extinguished, but the moist nature is not destroyed. It is thus.
The self-nature of the pure mind of sentient beings is moved by the wind of ignorance; thus, the mind and ignorance coexist, being formless and inseparable.
Yet, the mind is not of a moving nature, and when ignorance ceases, its continuity is extinguished, for the nature of wisdom is indestructible.
This is the third section: an explanatory commentary following the text.

The sutra’s title “Illusion” is followed by the commentary’s two-part division. Regarding the passage beginning with “defiled phenomena” (*sāsrava*) and continuing through the explanation of the aggregates, bases, and elements, it states that these will be interpreted in detail in the chapter on the “Universal Eye.

The term “etcetera” (*ādi*) refers to the enumeration of all defiled phenomena, including those within the three realms, the nine stages, the twelve links of dependent origination, the twenty-five existences, and so forth.
The citation of the following verse serves to establish the nature of these defiled phenomena. Within this context, the word “middle” (*madhya*) signifies the most [essential].
In Master Yìzàng’s *Commentary on the Heart Sūtra of Prajñā*, he provides two interpretations for the character "heart" (*xin*) within the term "Heart Sūtra.
First, he explains it as the "meaning expressed" (*so-quán yì*), stating that the heart of *prajñā* is the essence (*tǐ*) of all phenomena; therefore, it is called "heart.

Second, he explains it as the "expressing teaching" (*néng-quán jiào*), stating that this half-sheet of scripture is the core among the six hundred fascicles. Here, we adopt the former meaning, as it is truly solid and substantial.

Now, regarding what is called the "substantial core" (*madhya-sāra*): it is like a tree, for its heartwood is the most solid and firm at its center, and thus it is able to grow branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit.

This is as explained in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. Regarding the interpretation of "spiritual understanding" (*śen-jie*), this refers to the explanation found in the *Qixin-lun shu* (Commentary on the Awakening of Faith) by Haidong.
Furthermore, when discussing the mind (*citta*) in general, there are four types. First, the *Huayan-chao* states: in the Sanskrit language, it is *hṛdaya*.

First, the "flesh-ball mind" refers to the heart organ among the five viscera. Second, that which is called "mind" (*citta*) due to its capacity for cognitive reflection (*ālambana*) refers to the eight consciousnesses, as they are all capable of reflecting upon their respective objects.
Third, *manas* refers to the "accumulating and initiating mind," which is the eighth consciousness, because it accumulates all seeds and gives rise to active manifestations (*pravṛtti*).
Fourth, according to the commentary on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, *kanthaka* (translated here as *khanḍa-līḍha*) is rendered as the "solid and real mind."
Regarding the term "solid heart" (*kaṭhina-citta*) analyzed here: if we examine these three terms in their Sanskrit forms—*ghana*, *piṇḍa*, and *khara*—their phonetic qualities are entirely distinct;
they should therefore signify different meanings, such as a mass of flesh, a collection, or solidity. As for the three characters *duo-duo-da*, their phonetic qualities are very similar;
they should likely be the transliteration of a specific term from the Sanskrit of the Five Regions (India), or perhaps represent variations in earlier and later translations.
If there is a minor error in the text, it should logically be the same character "mind" (心). Let the wise examine this carefully:
the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states that the intrinsically pure mind is "stained yet unstained, unstained yet stained," and this refers precisely to this mind.

Therefore, it is said here that this is not the same as the meaning of "object-directed thought" (*ālambana*) or "aggregation and arising. (The physical heart-mass is coarse and superficial; there is no need to exclude it, which is why the commentary does not mention it.)
The Commentary states: "All [the following] extensively explain the meaning of the two [sections]. First, the explanation of the meaning using the sūtras and śāstras of our own school:

first, the direct explanation; first, the explanation using the śāstra. Regarding the statement that "the essence of the mind acts as the cause," the *Original Enlightenment Mind* (*mūla-awakening*) in the śāstra is precisely this *Perfect Enlightenment Wondrous Mind* (*pariniṣpanna-awakening*) of the present sūtra.
That which is "non-enlightenment" (*a-awakening*) in the śāstra is what this verse calls "beginningless illusory ignorance" (*anādikālika-māyā-avidyā*).

According to the treatise, it is said that because of fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), there is non-enlightenment (*a-bodhi*). (The text states: "Because of enlightenment, there is delusion; if one were apart from the nature of enlightenment, there would be no delusion.

This "reliance" is precisely the metaphor for how, based upon the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment, there exists beginningless illusory ignorance. Because of non-enlightenment, three kinds of characteristics arise (which are these various illusory transformations).
To correlate this with the terms "cause" and "condition": it means that by the power of the wind of ignorance, that quiescent mind is moved until—

This most subtle [state] is called the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*), and so on, up to the characteristics of transformation (*pariṇāma*) and manifestation (*vyañjana*). The essence of these three is the fundamental pure mind;
because it is intimately related [to them], it is called the "cause" (as the Sūtra says: "The Dharma-body flows through the five paths," etc.). It is merely moved by ignorance (*avidyā*);

because ignorance is remote [from its essence], it is called the "condition. It is like water becoming waves: the water is the substance of the waves, yet it is simply moved by the wind entering from without. This is precisely that.
If one were to explain the conditions (*pratyaya*) by focusing on a single meaning: based on the three subtleties and six coarsenesses, these are all the characteristics of ignorance (*avidyā*).

The true mind is ultimately pure, neither increasing nor decreasing, and neither changing nor altering; it is merely upon this that ignorance relies to manifest the defiled characteristics of birth and death.
Thus, ignorance appears as if it were the cause, while the pure mind appears as if it were the condition. This is like how various karmas, though caused by afflictions...

Regarding the statement that "afflictions arise," this is explained in terms of retribution; yet, taking karma as the cause and afflictions as the condition, it is like great waves reaching the heavens:
while the nature of water is unmoving, movement appears because wind relies upon the water. This appearance of movement is the characteristic of wind, not the characteristic of water.
While there is a certain meaning in explaining it according to this principle, here we rely on the primary and secondary factors as being proximate.
Because this is a commentary (*śūtra*), it follows the previous meaning for now. Regarding the phrase "the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) serves as the cause," etc.:

fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) conjoining with the true mind (*tathatā-citta*) is termed the karmic consciousness. Because this consciousness possesses the sense of movement and acting as a cause, it is called "karma.

When this consciousness encounters the objects manifested by itself, it gives rise to the six coarse aspects (*ṣaḍ-audārika*), beginning with the characteristic of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of continuity (*anusaṃdhana-lakṣaṇa*). It is like a dream.
When the mind manifests its own objects and those objects confront the mind, attachment arises, and one regards them as real.
This attachment is itself the dreaming mind; however, because attachment arises only when confronted by dream-objects, they are called "conditions" (*pratyaya*).
In the treatise, it is simply stated that "because there are conditions consisting of objects, the six kinds of marks arise again," without mentioning the *karmic-consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*).
Regarding that which acts as a cause, for the time being, it is based on nine aspects in which they arise in succession; the text here is brief, but if explained in full, each has two causes.
These two causes are precisely the two layers of causal conditions established here, and "condition" is also a general term for "cause."

△ Commentary: Therefore, the second section below explains [the three subtle states] by means of the Sūtra. This means that ignorance is the perfumer (the "enabling condition," like wind as the blower), while True Suchness is the perfumed (the "causal condition," like water as the blown object;
when blown upon, it moves). Because of this perfuming, there is transformation into the three subtle states.

Since the Sūtra mentions the coarse to reveal the subtle, and the manifest to reveal the minute, it speaks only of the "manifesting consciousness" (*ādarśa-vijñāna*); however, in reality, all three subtle states are fully present.
Regarding "inconceivable perfuming" (*acintya-vāsanā*): it means that ignorance is able to perfume the *tathatā*, which is a state incapable of being perfumed;
because it perfumes [it] despite this, it is called "inconceivable perfuming. Furthermore, perfuming is itself non-perfuming, and this perfuming of non-perfuming is termed "inconceivable perfuming.

Regarding "inconceivable transformation" (*acintya-pariṇāma*): it means that the *tathatā*-mind, having received the perfuming of ignorance, undergoes transformation despite being inherently unchangeable; therefore, it is called "inconceivable."

The transformation of thought, which is further transformed, is itself non-transformative; this transformation of the non-transformative is called the inconceivable transformation (*acintya-pariṇāma*).
What the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* describes as "being defiled while remaining undefiled" and so forth refers precisely to this perfuming-transformation (*vāsanā-pariṇāma*).

That it is difficult to comprehend is precisely what is meant by "inconceivable" (the meaning of "inconceivable" is that it is difficult to understand). "Grasping various objects" (referring to the aforementioned objective realms acting as conditions) refers to the various things manifested by this manifesting-consciousness (*nirbhāsa-vijñāna*).
The objective realm can further permeate and stir the ocean of the mind, giving rise to the waves of the various *pravṛtti-vijñānas* (namely, the six coarse levels);

as well as the permeation of beginningless false conceptualization (which is the cause of the aforementioned *karma-vijñāna*). Thus, within that ocean of the mind where truth and falsehood are conjoined, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of deluded thought have been permeating without interruption since time immemorial;

because one has never been separated from thought—meaning that while the six coarse and three subtle levels all involve a reciprocal succession of causes and conditions—the *karma-vijñāna* alone [is the ultimate source].
At the beginning, these objects and mental conceptions perfuming and stirring the ocean of the mind give rise to various consciousnesses.

Because the mind’s false conceptions and the objects are coarse and manifest, the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the subsequently arising *vikaḷpa-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of phenomena) are coarse and evident.

The sutra clarifies that the *darśana-vijñāna* (manifesting consciousness) arises by depending on inconceivable perfuming and abides by depending on inconceivable transformation; the *vastu-vijñāna* (consciousness of phenomena) depends upon objects.

Because of the *dhātu*, birth is attained; because of the ocean of mind, abiding is established. If one discusses this according to the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, it only analyzes the conditions for birth and does not discuss the basis for abiding.

Therefore, regarding the subtle [level], it speaks only of the perfuming by ignorance (*avidyā-vaśana*), while regarding the coarse [level], it speaks only of the condition of objective spheres (*viṣaya-pratyaya*).

However, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun) explains the meaning of perfuming based on the provisional teachings of the *Dharmalakṣaṇa* school and has not yet exhausted its ultimate source.
Zhe (Zhizhou) maintains that True Suchness is unchanging and not subject to perfuming (this point will be further examined below within the discussion on the perfuming of defilement and purity).

Here, however, because we rely on the definitive teachings on the Dharma-nature found in the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda*, and the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, there exists the principle of inconceivable perfuming and transformation; only thus does one accord with this sutra.

▲ The Commentary states that the following two layers further clarify the meaning of illusion by correlating them with the preceding five dharmas: the awakened mind is the cloth; ignorance and karmic consciousness are the magician’s arts;
and the various objective realms are the horses. It further says, "It is like flowers in the sky," meaning that existence is non-existent.
The non-discriminative sense-consciousness is like a deluded person who clings to these as having real characteristics. The above citations from various teachings describe the aspect of defilement.

The explanation of the scriptural passage regarding the meaning of "illusion arises from cognition" (*vijñāna*) by way of the mode of arising of phenomena (*dharmotpatti-lakṣaṇa*) is hereby concluded.

However, while this sutra merely states that [illusion] "arises from cognition" without explaining the mode of its arising, it is in the chapter on Mañjuśrī that it says, "Due to this ignorance (*avidyā*), one revolves in saṃsāra," which indicates the root; it is then in the chapter on Maitreya that the branches and their details are fully explained.

It is said that "craving is the cause of desire for life, and life exists because of desire," and so forth, until one successively gives rise to various conditions of opposition and compliance, creating diverse karmas that lead to birth in the realms of hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas, as well as superior wholesome fruits, and so on. [Commentary] Question:

Since the following three sections clarify the obstacles and establish this inquiry, this question follows from the previous passage concerning how the substance of the mind acts as the cause to give rise to the three subtle states and so forth.

The intent of the objection is as follows: "If the true mind gives rise to the three subtle states, it must then be the source of those three subtle states and thus the very essence of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Why, then, does the preceding Mañjuśrī chapter state that 'this ignorance has no real essence,' and so forth?
The answer is quite clear: when ignorance falsely relies upon the true mind to arise, it is merely a false arising.

Since the True Source does not arise, and because it does not arise, how could it be the root-source of delusion? Therefore, the principle is fully exhausted by further clarifying this through the analogy of the first and second months.
Nevertheless, when it says that one is currently deluded regarding the True, the meaning is as follows:

if one speaks from the perspective of delusion, at the very moment one perceives delusion, there is no separate "True" apart from it; what, then, could be called the source? If, however, one speaks from the perspective of the True, then...
Originally, as for non-delusion (*wu-wàng*), with whom does it have its source? When one is dreaming of a butterfly, one sees only the body of the butterfly; there is no separate body of Zhuang Zhou.
If one speaks from the perspective of Zhuang Zhou, then originally there is no body of the butterfly—so with whom would it have a source?

Therefore, it is said that "what appears is currently deluded regarding the Real. The meaning is this: when one is deluded regarding the Real, what appears is currently without reality. If one perceives a reality [within appearances], then...

The phrase "not established" (*bùchéng*) refers to the state of delusion; for now, it is spoken from the perspective of deluded sentiment, as it does not yet address the ultimate truth. Because there is no commentary (*shū*) stating that [delusion] is non-existent, the passage beginning with "The Sūtra says...
is precisely the concluding reference to the scriptural text, used to establish the meaning that the real does not give rise to the false.
This point is a major crux regarding objections within the Buddha-dharma. Master Fǎlì had a verse in which he questioned the scholars of the world, and its meaning is also this same point.
The verse says: "The true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally pure; from where could deluded thoughts arise? (The meaning is:

since it is fundamentally pure like space, what root of delusion could possibly arise? From the real, delusion is born; how can this delusion be stopped? (If the real can produce delusion, then only by removing the real can delusion be removed. Since the real cannot be removed, how can delusion be severed?

Having no beginning implies having no end; if there were an end, there should be a beginning. (One who establishes this principle intends to challenge the Dharma-character school (*Dharmalakṣaṇa*), which holds that afflictions have an end but no beginning. There is no beginning."
Yet there is an end (this being a formal exposition of the teachings of the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school). Long have I harbored bewilderment regarding this principle (concluding with a state of doubt).
I pray that you will reveal the secret and lead me out of birth and death. The Great Dharma Master Li She replied: "The true nature of dharmas is fundamentally pure;

how could delusion ever arise? Delusion does not originate from the True; if there were no delusion, what would there be to cease? Since it is granted that there is neither beginning nor end, how can one demand an end?"

If there is no beginning and no end, who would be so deluded as to fail to understand this principle? Why not proceed toward non-arising (*anutpāda*) instead of praying to be born out of birth-and-death?

(This response fails to recognize the intent of the question; how could Fu Li not know that true nature is fundamentally without arising or ceasing? The underlying meaning of the question was: from what do defiled phenomena produced by conditions arise?

Since their arising has no beginning, how can they have an end? Chan Master Huahui replied: "The Dharma-nature is neither defiled nor pure; truth and falsehood are not like [conventional] principles. (I am merely asking about the origin of the false.)"

Who asks this? To follow reason is to eliminate delusion and seek the truth; how then can this delusion be brought to rest? Since all things are fundamentally non-existent, one needlessly insists on "non-existence" when there is nothing that has not already ceased to exist.

From the beginningless, one perceives existence; from the end, one perceives cessation. Yet this ending is not separate from the beginningless. (This, however, merely serves to reinforce the difficulty rather than answering it.

All phenomena lack intrinsic nature; where there is no intrinsic nature, there is neither birth nor death. (This also shows a complete failure to understand the point of the question. Only after Master Qingliang answered it was the meaning finally clarified.
To the question asked, he replied: "When one is deluded regarding the Truth, false thoughts arise; when one awakens to the Truth, false thoughts cease.

That which is capable of being deluded is not itself the object of delusion—how then could it possess a complete form? (This is because they are neither identical nor different, as illustrated in the treatise by the analogy of the ocean and its waves. Because one has never awakened from the beginning, it is said that delusion is beginningless.
Only when one realizes that the root of delusion is inherently True is there the principle of constancy. If the discriminating mind has not yet perished, by what means can one escape?"

Regarding "birth and death" (the mind does not arise from a single thought; the past and future limits are severed, yet one should not give rise to thought after thought, for thoughts would be infinite).
Commentary: Below, the second section harmonizes the texts of other schools' sūtras and śāstras. Part 6-1: A general statement of the main purport.
"The myriad dharmas are the one mind" means that according to the Dharma-nature school, all defiled and pure phenomena are manifestations of the true mind alone, as in the *Awakening of Faith*.
The statement that the three realms are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) is a principle held by both the schools of Nature (*xing*) and Characteristics (*xiang*).

In the school of Nature, there is also the doctrine that deluded consciousness transforms objects (where "Nature" encompasses both the true and the deluded mind), whereas in the school of Characteristics, it refers exclusively to deluded consciousness. Regarding the "paths of the schools," this refers to the fundamental tenets and trajectories:

from the perspective of the Buddha, there is a distinction between the provisional and the ultimate; from the perspective of human beings, there is a distinction in their emotional dispositions. "Rarely" means seldom. To study according to one [school]...
The school [of thought] maintains that one should not understand anything further beyond what is already known; conversely, they suspect any new learning to be erroneous.

Thus, when what is heard contradicts their own understanding, they reject it and refuse to accept it. One must, however, synthesize and fully describe the meanings and intentions of all schools so as to bring about complete realization.
If this were not done, how could one possibly exhaustively investigate the ultimate goal? [Commentary: Now, regarding the latter two...
To clarify the various teachings separately: those who are deluded regarding the Dharma do not understand that phenomena are empty; this is what is called "attachment to dharmas.

Those who speak of "provisional designations" do not understand *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and instead calculate that external objects exist. They merely say that because one creates individual karma through the mind, one experiences one's own body;

because one creates collective karma through the mind, one experiences the external mountains, rivers, and the physical world (*bhājana-loka*). All that is good or evil is entirely accomplished by the mind.
Therefore, it is said that the "provisional designation" of the *vipāka-ālaya* refers to the eighth consciousness. This is because it is the source of all consciousnesses;

furthermore, "ripening" (*vipāka*) is the fruit of wholesome and unwholesome karma, and since its scope has been the broadest from beginningless time up until the causal stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*), it is selected here.
As for "*ālaya*," it carries the meaning of "clinging and storing," and because its defects are most grave, it is also selected. Both points are as explained below.
The *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) states that the refutation of non-existent objects (*anālambana*) precisely brings forth the meaning of "the single mind" (*ekacitta*).

This means that if one part were the object and another part were the mind, then "oneness" would not be established; however, since the object is merely a transformation of the mind and is therefore also nothing but mind, it is "one.

Question: Although all are mind, there are eight kinds of mind as well as various mental factors (*caitta*), and each has its own objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*). How can they be one?
Question: How can it be said that they are one when they are not identical? Answer: It is simply because there is no separate dharma apart from the mind; this is the meaning of "one.
For example, although a single pine tree has distinct roots and trunks and numerous branches and leaves, all of these are merely the pine itself, and thus it is called "a single pine tree.
Within this, there are three meanings regarding its curvature: first, the mutual existence of both [subject and object], which applies to the eight consciousnesses and all mental factors (*caitta*).

Furthermore, regarding the *nimitta-bhāga* (the objective aspect) that is transformed [by consciousness]—whether one adopts Nanda’s theory of two parts, Dignāga’s three parts, or Dharmapāla’s four parts, as explained in the *Daichao*—there are two ways of subsuming the objective aspect into the subjective:

first, it is common to the "King" (*rājā*) [i.e., the *ālayavijñāna*], meaning that the transformed objective aspect does not arise from a separate seed, but rather arises as consciousness itself carrying its own image;

this is the view of Sthiramati’s "one-part" theory. It is like the sky where there is originally no seed for flowers, yet when the eyes are afflicted by cataracts, the appearance of those flowers arises while carrying their image; the cataracts are the affliction.

Thus, it does not preclude designating [something] as "existent" (such as the *darśana-bhāga* of the mind), while [something else], such as the flower, is entirely non-existent (like the *nimitta-bhāga*).

Third, regarding the inclusion within what is subsumed (*saṃgraha-viniścaya*), this refers exclusively to the eight mind-kings (*citta-rāja*), because mental factors (*caitta*) likewise lack intrinsic nature and exist only by depending on the transformations of the mind-kings. As the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* (composed by Bodhisattva Asaṅga) states:

"The grasper and the grasped," [The former refers to the deluded mind that is capable of grasping, such as greed for wealth, beauty, or anger; the latter should be understood by analogy. The latter refers to wholesome mental factors capable of grasping, such as faith in the Triple Gem or diligence; these should be understood by analogy. This is the section.

Second, "only the light of the mind": (The afflictions such as greed and the wholesome states such as faith are mental factors (*caitta*) that are merely the light and shadow of the mind-king (*cittarāja*); there are no separate mental factors. The light of greed (taking one example;

likewise for hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, wrong views, and the secondary afflictions) and the light of faith (taking the remaining ten as examples of the eleven wholesome factors)—these two lights are not two dharmas. (This correctly establishes that there are no [separate] mental factors.

Regarding the phrase "because the principle is non-dual," it means that while the *tathāgatagarbha* manifests all phenomena by its entire substance following conditions, its intrinsic nature remains unchanged.

Fundamentally unborn and undying, the one mind and its two gates are both without obstruction. This means that when the intrinsically pure nature accords with defilement, the entire substance becomes the conventional;
this is the gate of birth and death. When the nature of defilement is eternally pure, it is the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

This is because these two gates are in fact nothing other than the one mind. It is truly because the characteristics of the mind, though appearing as various kinds, are all empty and false; therefore, they are merely the mind.

Because the mind is fundamentally real, it is one; just as multiple reflections are the characteristics of a mirror while the single clarity is the nature of the mirror, and since the multiple reflections are all empty, there is only the single clarity.
These latter three gates all establish the meaning of the true realization of the One Mind.
The commentary states that "the extinction of defilement and purity" means that the fundamental mind of original purity is inherently devoid of the duality of defilement and purity;

it is only in relation to the impurity of deluded thoughts that it is conventionally designated as "pure. Since delusion is fundamentally empty, purity likewise vanishes. Only the fundamental awakened mind manifests in its clarity and purity.
To refute various numerical categories, it is provisionally called "one. Therefore, this text says: "Various [phenomena] arise from the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*)."

The *Gā* (commentary) also states: "The 'unbroken characteristic' consists of the eight consciousnesses; being without characteristics, it is also without characteristics. This passage is not singular;

it serves as a general rebuttal to those who refute the numerical categories. The intent of the objection is as follows: "One" is a numerical category (*saṃkhyā-dharma*), and number is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Now, since this [reality] is utterly free from defilement and purity and transcends names and numbers, why do you speak of "one"? The answer expresses that it is not two, three, nor even hundreds or thousands of numbers.
Therefore, it is said that "one" is such. The *Dharmapada* states: "One is not even one; this is for the purpose of destroying all numbers.

The commentary explains that when the total encompasses the myriad existences, this is precisely the One Mind. This means that while one has not yet realized that the mind transcends all marks and has awakened to the fact that marks are exhausted and only mind remains, one must see and touch all things as being mind before one fully understands the ultimate nature of the mind. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says, this is truly because [all things]...
Because it is the true mind, three meanings are established: first, the meaning of the mutual inclusion of phenomena through fusion.
This means that since all phenomenal dharmas are entirely manifested from the true mind, a single phenomenon—which is itself the entirety of the mind—pervades all things in accordance with the mind;

and all things—which are themselves the entirety of the mind—enter into a single phenomenon in accordance with the mind. Thus, they revolve and include one another in accordance with the mind, without obstruction. Second, the fusion of phenomena... [text continues]
The meaning of "immediacy" (*ji*) is that because a single phenomenon is the true mind, the mind is immediately all phenomena; at all times, this single phenomenon follows the mind and is also one.
That "all is one" is likewise so. The meaning of "triple-layered interpenetration without end" is that because all things are entirely the mind, they can contain all things;
and because all contained things are also solely the mind, they in turn contain all things.
The "inexhaustible" is inexhaustible because each and every thing is fully endowed with the true mind;

since the mind functions without obstruction, the previous state of the "extinction of appearances" was merely the one mind of the nature. Now, however, each and every phenomenon (*dharma*) is, in its very essence, the one mind itself;
there is no need for further extinction, for since they are fundamentally the mind, they should not be extinguished. Therefore, it is said "it is precisely this," rather than "it is subsumed."

Returning [to the source] by means of these [realms] fulfills the three aforementioned meanings of non-obstruction. However, the distinction between this [present case] and the third and fourth gates above is as follows:

in those three cases, phenomena are subsumed into principle, and the branches are unified with the root; in the fourth, phenomena and branches are both obliterated, leaving only principle and the root.

Here, however, phenomena are entirely identical to principle and the branches are entirely identical to the root; therefore, it is said that there is no distinction between principle and phenomena, or between the root and the branches.
This is different. [The] *Sūtra Commentary* states: "These three preceding and following sections summarize all the teachings. [The] *Sūtra Commentary* continues:

"However, as for the four [points] below, this explains the reason for adhering to specific tenets. One should first ask: "According to what has been explained above, only the Sudden Teaching and the Perfect Teaching are the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) that accords with reality;
how is it that various sūtras and śāstras still contain differing explanations as mentioned previously? This is explained here: "It is because the sūtras..."

This was spoken according to the occasion. Regarding "according to the occasion," as in the section on the "inverse and direct" [teachings], it refers to the capacity of the expressive text (*vyañjana*).

The meaning of the commentary and sub-commentary (*śāstra-vṛtti*)—which explains how the inverse dharma proceeds from one to four in successive stages—is to be understood by taking the intent of these explanations. Question:
Since the scriptural text was a provisional teaching given by the Buddha at that time to suit the specific capacities of various beings, why is it that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa...

Because the treatises composed by various Bodhisattvas to establish their fundamental tenets or to explain the scriptural texts also possess distinctions, it is next stated that "the treatises follow the sūtras universally.
This means that such differences among the capacities of sentient beings exist not only while the Buddha was in the world, but also from after his parinirvāṇa until the present day;
thus, when Bodhisattvas compose treatises, they also follow the fundamental tenets of the sūtras to universally explain the Buddha’s intention.

Treatises on fundamental tenets (*mūla-śāstra*) each accord with a specific category of scripture and correspond to a specific category of spiritual capacity; commentaries (*vyākhyā-śāstra*) each explain a single scripture and likewise follow the purport of whichever scripture they address.

For instance, when the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed treatises on the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), such as those following the *Āgamas*, he delineated the distinct categories of defilement and purity;
when he composed treatises such as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the characteristics and numerical categories were established with certainty. (He also) annotated the *Śata-śāstra*.
The *Treatise on the Manifestation of the Buddha-nature through the Diamond-like Clarity and Emptiness* states that sentient beings are the Dharmakāya Tathāgatagarbha;

the *Commentary on the Ten Stages of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra* explains that the six characteristics are perfectly interfused. Thus, one knows that each [treatise] follows the specific tenet of its respective sūtra.
How could there be the stagnation of dogmatic attachment? As for those who follow these treatises with such attachments, the fault lies with later generations who have transmitted and practiced them.

This is truly because of being narrow-minded and lacking learning, unable to study extensively; upon encountering a single teaching, one immediately claims it to be the perfect and universal truth (*yuan-tong*).

When hearing an explanation that contradicts their own understanding, they reject it and refuse to accept it, instead claiming it is erroneous. Therefore, it is said that they "stubbornly cling to shallow expedients" (*qian-quan*). Shallow expedients mean that each preceding stage is shallower than each succeeding one. Now, the detailed discernment of this matter is provided herein. — *Sūtra Commentary* (Sǔ) **Note:** The character ▲ indicates a section break or a heading in the original source text. The term *qian-quan* (shallow expedients) refers to provisional teachings that are inferior to the ultimate truth. The phrase "the preceding is shallower than the succeeding" reflects the pedagogical hierarchy where earlier stages of practice or doctrine are preparatory and less profound than later ones. The concluding statement "Now, the detailed discernment... is provided herein" introduces the following analytical discussion. The term *yuan-tong* (perfect and universal) is a common translation for *samantabhadra*, signifying the all-encompassing nature of the Buddha-way. The text critiques those who dogmatically cling to limited views and dismiss teachings outside their own narrow framework. The final note regarding *IAST diacritics* has been observed by using them for the Sanskrit term *samantabhadra*. The Chinese characters used are standard for Buddhist scholastic literature. The source text appears to be from a commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* or a related work, given the reference to "shallow expedients. The translation aims to preserve the technical terminology and the critical tone of the original.

Now, in the lower section of this text, there are two parts concerning the reconciliation of the direct and inverse orders. First, the introduction of the intent of the commentary; second, the actual reconciliation. Regarding the latter, there are three points:
first, the inverse exposition of the direct dharma; second, the inverse sequence; and third, the direct dharma. "Inverse sequence" refers to the reverse order of the preceding five gates.

"Direct dharma" refers to the sequence of mental factors as sentient beings, following their delusion regarding truth and the arising of falsehood, proceed from the fundamental source toward the derivative manifestations—just as a single tree [grows from its root].

The roots have trees; from the trees branches grow, and upon the branches flowers and leaves arise. From the fourth [Sudden Teaching] down to the first (Śrāvaka Teaching), because the fifth is the integration of the root and the branches, only the preceding four are discussed here.
"The One Dharma-realm Mind" refers to the Sudden Teaching. "The Tathāgata-garbha" below refers to the Real Teaching.
Furthermore, "by means of the lower" refers to the Provisional Teaching. "Grasping at the inferior" refers to the Śrāvaka.
The Commentary (Sūtra) has two parts. Regarding the second [section], there are two: "conforming to the expression" (*anuloma-vyañjana*) and "reversing the dharma" (*pratiloma-dharma*).

As for conforming to the text: the text is the teaching that expresses [the meaning], as previously listed; it proceeds from the end to the beginning. As for reversing the dharma: the dharma refers to the sequence in which the mental dharmas of sentient beings arise, proceeding from the beginning to the end.
The text has two parts: first, the explicit manifestation of the words; "up to and including" (*yāvat*) means as fully explained above. All of this arises from... [the commentary].
The meaning of the final two [sections] on "binding the mind" is as explained in the commentary. Third, regarding the three capacities for non-obstruction: these three are all without obstruction;

that is, in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), there is no obstruction between the fundamental and the derivative, as also stated above. [The commentary states: "Only mind... and so forth. The final six lines summarize the gains and losses: it is like a person facing a wall;

In the commentary on the Sūtra, Precepts, and Samādhi (2-1), under the section "Śamatha," the explanation of the preceding four lines states that "stopping" (*śamatha*) is the definition of concentration.

During the stage of cultivation, it is called "stopping"; when fully accomplished, it is called "concentration" (*samādhi*). Because all conditions are stilled through stopping, one attains mental concentration.

As for the designation "Tathāgata," although the cultivation is that of an ordinary person, the concentration is the concentration of a Buddha. To "permanently sever conditions" means that the vow is like a reed tethering a goose.

The *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground," says: "If a disciple of the Buddha upholds the prohibitive precepts of the Buddha, they should make this vow:

'I would rather cast this body into a great pit of blazing, fierce fire or onto a mountain of knives than ever violate the sūtras and vinaya of the Buddhas of the three periods by engaging in impure conduct with any woman. Furthermore, they should make this vow:"
It would be better to have one’s body encircled by a thousand layers of glowing iron mesh than to receive any clothing from a faithful donor with a body that has broken the precepts.

Furthermore, one should make this vow: "It would be better for this mouth to swallow glowing iron balls and great torrents of fierce fire for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than to eat even a single morsel of food from a faithful donor with a mouth that has broken the precepts."
Transcending the enjoyment of food and drink of a hundred flavors, he further makes this vow:

"I would rather lie with this body upon a floor of great, fierce fire and glowing iron than ever again receive a hundred kinds of couches and seats from a faithful donor with a body that has broken the precepts.
He further makes this vow: "I would rather have three hundred spears pierce my body and endure this for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than ever again break the precepts."
With this body, he receives from faithful donors the four necessities, including medicines of a hundred flavors, and makes this vow:

"I would rather cast this body into a cauldron of molten iron for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than receive with a body of broken precepts the thousand kinds of dwellings, houses, gardens, and fields offered by faithful donors.
He further makes this vow: "I would rather have this body smashed to pieces with an iron mallet..."

One should cause one’s body, from head to foot, to become like fine dust; yet, never with a body that has broken the precepts, should one accept the respectful prostrations and offerings of faithful donors.

Furthermore, one makes this vow: "I would rather have my two eyes gouged out by hundreds of thousands of hot iron knives and spears than, with a mind that has broken the precepts, look upon the beautiful forms of others. Furthermore, one makes this vow: "I would rather [endure] hundreds of thousands..."
With iron awls they gouge out their ears, yet for one kalpa or two kalpas they never listen to pleasant sounds with a mind that violates the precepts.
Again they make this vow: "I would rather have my nose cut off by a hundred thousand sharp blades than ever smell various fragrances with a mind that violates the precepts.
Again they make this vow: "I would rather have my [tongue] severed by a hundred thousand sharp blades..."
The tongue shall never, with a mind of broken precepts, consume the hundred-flavored pure food of others; furthermore, one makes this vow:
"I would rather have my body severed by a sharp axe than, with a mind of broken precepts, crave pleasant touch.
Furthermore, one makes this vow: "May all sentient beings attain Buddhahood"; for if a Bodhisattva does not make such a vow, they commit an offense.

As for the "two attachments," these are the self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*). "Self" refers to a sovereign; it is like a ruler of a nation who possesses autonomy, and like a minister who is able to exercise decisive power.
Sovereignty is the essence of the self, while governance is its function. Furthermore, sovereignty is innate (*sahaja*), whereas governance is conceptual (*vikalpita*).

That is to say, regarding sentient beings, mind-born beings (*manomaya*), persons (*manuṣya*), those who undergo rebirth (*pudgala*), living beings (*jīva*), those who take birth (*jantu*), individuals (*puruṣa*), and those who act, experience, know, and perceive—when one conceives of these based upon the aggregates (*skandha*) as "self," this is called the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). Yet, [the author] conversely refutes those [positions regarding] the arising of phenomena, and further uses analogies to refute the *Yanmi* (Profound Secrets), which likewise suffers from the fault of being overly broad and inclusive, while simultaneously attempting to encompass both the self and phenomena, as well as human and dharmas, in a perfect synthesis.

Regarding the dharmas of arising, each term used in accordance with conventional expression possesses its own specific meaning; however, because the word "self" (*ātman*) is most intimate, it is now said: "The essential dharma of the self.

To provide a broad explanation, one should consult the *Great Commentary* (*Daisho*) and the *Great Sub-commentary* (*Dakyo*). As for the two kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*): emotional attachment (*kleśa*) conceives of things as existing, whereas wisdom (*jñāna*) illuminates them as empty.

This "emptiness" is simply the absence of that [attachment]; it has no separate substance. Wisdom arises by taking emptiness as its object, serving as the gateway through which one wanders. (Regarding the statement "the self is empty":)

However, because [the self] exists only as a transformation of consciousness, and because a real self cannot be found—since a real self that is either identical to or distinct from the aggregates, or neither identical nor distinct, is in every case irrational (as explained in detail in each instance in the *Dàshù* and *Dàchão*)—it reveals the two aspects of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

These are called the principles of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*). Although their essence possesses characteristics, they are empty in their very nature; it is not that their nature is empty [of something else]. They are taught as the "two emptinesses" based on what they manifest.
In Sanskrit, this is called *śūnyatā*, which here means "emptiness-nature. This is precisely what is meant by the "nature of the two emptinesses."

Regarding the statement that "the manifestation of true reality as emptiness" refers to the nature of the two absences of self (dvi-śūnyatā) spoken of from the perspective of their preeminent capacity, this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound) construction meaning "the nature of the two absences.
To say that "true thusness is empty" does not fully exhaust the principle. The commentary on the phrase "attachment ceases" contains two meanings:

first, it is consistent with all schools that through traversing the various stages and grounds (*bhūmi*), when causes are perfected and fruits are fulfilled, the ten obstacles are exhausted; one realizes the ten aspects of true thusness, which is termed the "manifestation of the noble nature" (*ārya-dharmatā*).
When former afflictions have been exhausted and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have also been eliminated, one attains Equal and Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Brahmā, Śakra, nāgas, and devas all pay homage; with applications as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one is called a Buddha. Second, regarding the accomplishment of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) within this school: when attachment is extinguished and nature manifests, one suddenly becomes identical to the Buddha-realm.

This is the accomplishment of the Contemplation of the Two Emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), which reveals True Suchness (*tathatā*). The application below is the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-vipaśyanā*).

One who has achieved this name is called a Buddha. In the commentary (*śāstra*), the latter two sections open the chapters and provide explanations. First, opening the chapters: "That which breaks attachments" refers to the self and phenomena (*ātman* and *dharma*).
"That which reveals the principle" refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*). That which can break and that which can reveal are the categories of the wisdom of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā-jñāna*).

However, based on the two pairs of subject and object—breaking attachments and revealing the true—there are four dharmas in total. Both the capacity to break and the capacity to reveal are [the wisdom of the two emptinesses].
Because of that wisdom, there are only three dharmas. If we correlate each [aspect] according to delusion and awakening, it should be said:
formerly these were the grasper and the grasped; now they are the refuter and the refuted. Formerly these were the deluded and the object of delusion; now they are the manifestor and the manifested.

Second, following the commentary on the sutra, "Contemplating the Body," Part Two, Section One: Now, regarding the passage beginning with "If one calculates... (夫計下), its general and specific aspects are opened up. If categorized according to the body...

This constitutes a general summary by interchanging the general and the specific. That is to say, one addresses a pervasive objection: "If one speaks of the 'body,' it already comprises the five aggregates;

how can one speak of contemplating the mind as being external to the body? This is resolved through two pairs of general and specific categories—the first pair is concessive (*yǒng*), and the second pair is subversive (*duó*).
Since they interchange as general and specific, both possess a logical basis for resolution; thus, one should not hold them accountable.
[End of section]. △ Now, in the commentary, first, the second part [of the introduction] consists of three sections: (1) stating the intent;

(2) explaining that the body is the root of all cravings, the meaning of which is found in the Maitreya Chapter where it is stated that one must thoroughly investigate the causes of saṃsāra in order to sever craving and so forth;
and (3) citing scriptural texts from four locations to prove the faults of the body under the heading "Purifying the Name. This concludes the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*’s section on skillful means.

This chapter explains (citing the essential meaning for clarification): Because the layman Vimalakīrti manifested himself as being ill through his skillful means, kings, ministers, elders, laymen, brahmins, princes, and thousands of officials all went to inquire after his illness.

To those who came, Vimalakīrti used his own illness as an occasion to preach the Dharma extensively, saying: "O virtuous ones" (hereafter follows the actual exposition of the four contemplations of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self).
The Commentary cites this: "This body is impermanent, powerless, and without solidity; it is a thing that quickly decays and cannot be relied upon" (this is the first contemplation on impermanence).
"It is suffering and affliction, a collection of manifold diseases; O virtuous ones, such a body is not to be trusted by the wise" (the second contemplation on suffering).
"This body is like a mass of foam that cannot be grasped; it is like a flame born from craving."
Illusion arises from perversion; it is like a dream, a false vision. (This is the third contemplation on emptiness.

Next, it is taught that the body is composed of the four great elements, yet has no master (*pṛthivī*), no self (*tejas*), no life-principle (*vāyu*), and no person (*āpa*). Furthermore, it is said to be devoid of cognition, like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles.

(The above constitutes the fourth contemplation on non-self. It concludes by saying: "O virtuous ones, this [body] is something to be weary of and loathe; you should instead delight in the Buddha-body. (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra)
[Regarding] the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, its text is extensive and awaits further investigation for a detailed exposition. As for those who betray kindness (*pratikartṛ*), the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:

"For a long time, I have maintained this body—foul-smelling, filthy, flowing with pus, and unlovely—and have provided it with bedding, clothing, food, drink, elephants, horses, carriages, and precious wealth.
Yet, as a phenomenon subject to transformation and decay, its nature is impermanent; it is difficult to satisfy and difficult to preserve. Although...
"One who constantly receives offerings yet harbors resentment and malice will ultimately abandon me; such a person does not recognize kindness. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states:

"If one examines this body with careful scrutiny, it must return to the place of death. It is difficult to restrain and lacks any sense of reciprocity; its betrayal of kindness is like that of a small child. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* also says:

(The commentary adds this to establish the meaning of betraying kindness: "One who does not cultivate the body cannot contemplate the body, nor can they contemplate the physical form as being non-self."

Within this, one gives rise to attachment to the physical marks of the body and to the self, [thinking] "my body" and so forth, until it becomes a constant enemy—just like a fire one serves or a snake one raises, which, when encountering conditions for its destruction, does not recall at all the kindness of providing food and clothing in the past.

This term "phāṇita" (translated here as "thin curd") refers to the state when one is first in the womb; prior to seven days, it is like thin curd.
The *Aṭṭhakanāgara Sutta* states that "not attaining [self]" means that because the nature of phenomena is empty, there is nothing to be attained.

Regarding the "four selves," this is explained provisionally in terms of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). If one were to rely on the element of earth alone, even a single portion of bone already [constitutes a self].
There should be three hundred and sixty "selves" corresponding to each of the muscles, and it is the same for every one;

the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that within each joint, muscle, and vessel there is a wind with its own distinct name, and by analogy, water and fire are likewise known to exist individually and not as one another;
if each of these were the self, then the self would be infinite.
Regarding the passage "In the commentary on the *Yathābhūta-parīkṣā*, it says 'one sees a ghost at night,' etc.," one should consult the treatise for its exposition.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "It is precisely because of this," the intended meaning is as follows: One's own body is originally also "other," yet due to clinging and conceptualization, it is taken to be the "self" (*ātman*);
thus, it is said that there is a "self. Once it is reckoned as self, then all other bodies and all other phenomena are reckoned as "other. Since it is reckoned as self...
This constitutes the objection raised by the preceding text.

Regarding the passage in the *Sūtra on Contemplating the Mind* commentary, section 2.1, which begins with "The subsequent contemplation... the nature of madness naturally subsides," etc., this is explained according to the two sections cited in the Introduction as the primary interpretation.
Regarding the "causes and conditions" mentioned in the *Sūtra on Investigation and Reflection*, it is as previously cited from the *Aṇḍa-sūtra*.

As for the commentary stating that "the four great elements combine," this was already explained by citing the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*. Regarding the phrase "forming a single form (*rūpa*)": the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:

"First is the *kalala* (i.e., the *kalala* mentioned previously; the Sanskrit terms differ between earlier and later contexts, hence here it is called 'thin curd' or 'congealed butter'; 'first' refers to the completion of seven days). Next, [the *arbuda*] arises."
From the arbuda (herein translated as "bubble") arises the peśī (herein translated as "soft flesh"); from the peśī arises the ghana (herein translated as "solid flesh");

next comes the praśākhā (herein translated as "limbs and joints"), followed by the gradual development of hair, body hair, nails, and so forth, as well as the sensory faculties (*indriya*) and physical forms.

(Other teachings state that the "sixth" and "seventh" refer to the opening of the six consciousnesses; this is precisely what is meant here. In the commentary, the six sense organs are treated as external because the four great elements constitute their very substance.

Because they are substantial, they are called "internal"; because the sense organs (*indriya*) are apertures and gateways, they are called "external. This is said in contrast to their own substance, which consists of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
If contrasted with the six objects (*viṣaya*), then the six sense organs are "internal" and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) are "intermediate.

Now, according to the Sūtra, it says that the six sense organs and the four great elements combine internally and externally to form the body; therefore, this explanation is provided based on the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra*.

It is said that those sentient beings shall all be free from the "self of mind"; since the "self of mind" is fundamentally empty and quiescent, the meaning of explaining the mind here as being the "self" is identical to that [previous teaching].

In the *Sūtra on the Emptiness of Dharmas*, the passage stating that "emptiness is not the extinction of form" is from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*. However, the meaning of the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is great.

Riding upon the initial gateway, there are several doctrinal positions: emptiness because [phenomena] are transformations of consciousness; emptiness because they exist as objects of attachment but lack reality;

emptiness within the absence of reality by analyzing form to clarify the essence of emptiness; emptiness by clarifying that form is empty within emptiness; emptiness because there is no form within emptiness;

emptiness because causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature; emptiness because the attachments of non-Buddhists and the Hīnayāna are not real; and [emptiness regarding] the two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism.
Because what is conceptualized is false and erroneous, it is empty; this is explained in detail with specific citations in the *Dàchāo* (Great Commentary).

thus, the difference in depth and shallowness is evident. Therefore, it was previously said that within the provisional teachings there is no true fruit; if even the contemplation of the Dharma-realm finds no mention [of a fruit], how much less could there be the Buddha-fruit?
From the *Commentary on the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm*, Section II-1, following the sub-section: "The emptiness of self and the quiescence of dharmas.

This means that, based upon the aggregates (*skandha*), the self as it is conceptually imputed is entirely non-existent; it is merely due to the perverse attachments of deluded sentiment that one falsely conceives of it.

Therefore, it is simply called "empty. Although the aggregates, elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and all other phenomena do not exist [independently], their conventional manifestation is not destroyed because there is no grasping [at them as inherently real].
Regarding its characteristic, it is simply said to be "quiescent. As the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "All phenomena, from the very beginning, are eternally of the nature of quiescent extinction.
Because they are of the nature of quiescent extinction, all things are harmoniously integrated; the faculties, consciousnesses, and sense objects are all-pure and pervasively filled.

In the commentary on the scriptural analogy, section three, part one: first, regarding "mani" (摩尼) below, this briefly indicates the characteristics of the analogy. *Maṇi* is here translated as "wish-fulfilling";
for one who obtains this jewel, whatever is desired according to their wishes is invariably fulfilled. As for "blue, yellow, and so forth," these are the primary colors of the five directions;
thus the Sūtra says, "each appears according to its respective direction. Next, section two, part one: second, applying this [analogy] to the Dharma. First, the heading.

The Commentary states: "Regarding the seal below, there are two explanations. First, explaining the seal prior to the two [preceding sections]: directly explaining the statement that the five colors are a metaphor for the five destinies (*gati*).
This has two interpretations. First, interpreting them directly according to the original text: black represents the hells, because of black karma;

blue represents the hungry ghosts (*preta*), because ghosts often have blue faces and because they are emaciated with hunger, bearing a bluish hue; red represents animals (*tiryagyoni*); [and white represents humans and devas].

The *Tiantai Zhiguan* states that the path of blood-stained karma is therefore likened to yellow, representing the human realm; yellow is the color of the center (as the *I Ching* says, "yellow robes" signifies occupying the central position).
The human path does not lie within the pleasures of the heavens, nor does it dwell in the sufferings of the three miserable realms; it occupies the middle ground.
White represents the heavenly realm, as it is evoked by purely wholesome white karma. Second, regarding the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*, [it speaks] of white.

From within the category of form (*rūpa*), "white" is further distinguished; this is assigned to the six destinies (*ṣadgati*). That sutra states: "The mind is like a painter; from its hand emerge five colors:
black, blue, red, yellow, and white—and then 'white-white'. Master Qingliang [Zongmi] assigns these in sequence to the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, and devas.

The three miserable realms (*tṛpatha*) correspond to the preceding [colors]. The remaining "yellow" is assigned to the asuras; the asuras are neither gods nor humans, occupying an intermediate station.
Because it is intermediate, "white" is assigned to humans; because they generally possess good karma, "white-white" is assigned to the heavens.

Since both cause and effect are wholesome [in the heavens], this is also taught in the third stage of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Thus, the lower section of the *Avataṃsaka* uses the metaphor of mistaking a pearl for a colored object to provide scriptural evidence for this view;

the intended meaning is clearly revealed by correlating the sūtra with the present context. Specifically, the first phrase of the sūtra—wherein all phenomena are likened to blue and yellow—correlates the perception of ordinary people with ignorance.
The first two lines of the verse correspond to seeing only blue and yellow; the latter line corresponds to not seeing the substance of the jewel. According to the Commentary:
if the following two [lines] are correlated with the three natures, that which was previously revealed is the *tathatā* (suchness) revealed by the two kinds of emptiness.

Regarding the "previous illusion," the text says, "When the illusion is extinguished, it too is extinguished," and so forth. Regarding the "previous dust and grime," the text says, "When the grime is exhausted, clarity appears. Furthermore...
It says: "One should know that both body and mind are illusory defilements; when the characteristics of these defilements are eternally extinguished, the ten directions are pure.

Regarding the phrase "the characteristics of body and mind being equal," this refers to the period from the time my present body was first formed by the combination of the four great elements until the completion of the contemplation of the two emptinesses.

The commentary states: "To reveal the following two explanations, it clarifies the latter part. Within this, first, it briefly seals the meaning of what preceded in order to initiate the subsequent perfection."
The force of the meaning of "purity" follows this sequence, but here, without further calculation, the meaning of this section is clearly elucidated.
However, the intent of the preceding and subsequent portions of this seal is summarized here; it is both beautiful and subtle, and the flow of the text is very easy to perceive.
One should contemplate this by means of the preceding and following scriptural passages, extending even to [the passage on] "all-pervading purity" and so forth, to bring it forth.
▲ It is very easy and very subtle to explain the preceding three [sections] and the following two metaphors by relating them individually and contrastively;
however, one must again clarify this profound meaning through three further divisions. Only then will the essential textual structure of this sūtra’s core tenet be fully revealed.
The sub-commentary on the *Sūtra* states that the passage concerning "all [phenomena] being equal" and so forth refers to the essence and characteristics of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*).
Since it equally reveals the meaning of the perfect purity of the awakened nature (*bodhi-dhātu*), it is used as a proof for this [text].

When it says they "cannot be defiled," it means that because the nature is pure, even though defiled phenomena appear, those phenomena cannot pollute it. Not only do the appearing defilements fail to defile it, but furthermore—
Because defilement appears, it conversely reveals original purity; just as a mirror reflecting filthy objects conversely reveals the purity of the mirror—how could the filth ever stain the mirror?
This is exactly the same principle. The commentary states: "It is revealed that although perfect enlightenment (pariniṣpanna-bodhi) appears, it is not its fixed reality.

As for "the essence of wisdom being unmoving," because there was originally no defilement and there is now no beginning to impurity, the wisdom of original enlightenment has never moved. Furthermore...
"Though appearing amidst defilement, one is not defiled by it; this is the meaning of immovability, which is fully endowed with the untainted [qualities].
This means that within this original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), the myriad inherent virtues (*dharmas*) are not lacking even by so much as a grain of sand.

Furthermore, because it acts as the internal permeating cause for sentient beings, causing them to give rise to weariness with suffering and the aspiration for liberation, the *Sutra* states in the section on "Erasing Traces": "Erasing traces and entering the profound" is intended for the purpose of entering birth.

Because the Buddha is the ultimate dharma that is equal, conforming to the nature (*dharmatā*), and perfectly pure, he proclaims this to sweep away the traces of prior defilement and purity, delusion and awakening, and the limitations of beginning and end.
This section of the commentary is profoundly deep, wondrous, manifest, and easy to understand;
its excellence may be fully brought forth. [End of] Commentary 2-1: From here upward, the explanatory text shall be matched one-to-one with the commentary.
The meaning of the scriptural text is self-evident; however, its traces will be explained individually within the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) as they appear throughout the text.

Here, I shall first generally clarify the characteristics of the traces to be dispelled—the phenomena of successive arising and ceasing—so that they may become vividly present in one’s mind before proceeding with the detailed exposition;

only then will the explanation be truly flavorful. This is because it was originally taught that "it is an illusion" precisely because sentient beings falsely cling to what is illusory and transformative.

Because sentient beings rely on the teaching to become free from defilement, they are further called "Bodhisattvas. Since these illusory defilements are like colors within a gem, one should know that they are fundamentally non-existent;
thus it is said, "defilements are exhausted. Since the defilements to be abandoned do not exist, how can the wisdom that abandons them be established?
Thus it is said, "the counteractive [removal] is absent. Since the counteractive wisdom does not exist, how can there be a person who gives rise to that wisdom? Thus it is said, "there is none."

Regarding the phrase "as for those who oppose the defilements" (*duì gòu zhě*), since the grasping at depth or shallowness is fundamentally non-existent, how could there be anyone to preach the teaching? Therefore, it is said:
