Regarding the two explanations for the latter two lines of the verse, the first is the refutation of emptiness (*ākāśa*). First, the direct refutation may be understood as follows: Question: We currently perceive that space pervades all places and is devoid of arising, ceasing, or transformation;
furthermore, various sūtras also state that space exists. How can this be refuted? Answer: Within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it is taught that there are briefly two kinds of space:

first, that which is conventionally designated based on the transformations of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*); [the second is the ultimate nature of phenomena]. The former is merely a conceptual construct.

Regarding the conventional designation of "space" and so forth: when one hears the names "space" and so on spoken, there arises for the one who conceptualizes in accordance with them the appearance of space (due to hearing the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak these names, the mind conceptualizes accordingly, and the appearance of space arises as the objective condition). Because of the power of repeated habituation, when the mind and its associates arise, they manifest resembling space;

this manifested appearance remains similar from moment to moment without change, and is thus conventionally designated as "permanent" (the appearance of emptiness thus revealed remains similar from moment to moment).

Because there is no change or alteration, but only a single aspect of vast emptiness, it is metaphorically described as "permanent," "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*), and so forth—just as the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) and other such entities lack any inherent substance and are merely transformations of mind. Second, it is provisionally established based on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*):

namely, the true thusness (*tathatā*) revealed by emptiness and selflessness, which is beyond both existence and non-existence, transcends the paths of mind and speech, and is neither identical to nor different from all phenomena.
(The above generally clarifies the essence of the nature of phenomena. Because this is the ultimate truth of phenomena, it is called [the nature of phenomena].

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—as indicated by the preceding [passage] which clarifies the basis—is called "space" because it is free from all obstructions (this clarifies that which depends [upon the basis]; that is, this very *tathatā* is called "space" because it is free from all obstructions). In a dream, one sees pearls and manifested jewels, as well as one’s own halls, houses, treasuries, and city walls—all of which are empty and non-existent.

therefore, looking in all four directions, there is nothing at all, only open ground—vast, hollow, and a single expanse of emptiness" (this is the emptiness manifested by consciousness).

Why is this so? Because as soon as the mind arises and thoughts stir, one immediately deviates from the essence of the Dharma and loses right mindfulness.
When practice arises and understanding is severed, if understanding were not severed, one would remain long stuck in the mind of conceptual comprehension, and thus practice would not arise.
Therefore, practice is accomplished through understanding; when practice arises, understanding is severed.
The Commentary states: "In the following two pairs of this sutra, the meaning of the scripture is explained by all being termed 'pure.

'Below' refers to the contemplation of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*) up until the manifestation of clarity when defilements are exhausted, with the purity of the *maṇi* jewel serving as the remote expedient (*dūra-upāya*). Regarding the text on 'wiping away traces,' it says 'defilements are exhausted,' which corresponds to the removal of opposition;

that is, there is no longer any opposing defilement, and even the names [of phenomena] are extinguished. Regarding the text on 'extinguishing images,' it says 'one realizes that all illusions are extinguished as images.'"

These are the proximate means (*upāya*), and thus they are identical to the gate of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) in their resolution and severance. "That which is manifested by the awakening to space" refers to the arising of practice;
therefore, it is said that [all things] are extinguished and have no locus of reliance. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"In this context, when people first hear of 'emptiness,' they fear its annihilation. For this reason, it is further stated elsewhere: "It is pure, like the Great Prajñāpāramitā, wherein all things are..."

The *Cloud of Purity* (i.e., the "Chapter on Difficult to Believe and Understand") states: "Subhūti, because form is pure, the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure; because the *prajñāpāramitā* is pure, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*) is pure.

Whether it be the purity of form, the *prajñāpāramitā*, or the knowledge of all modes, they are non-dual, not divided into two, without distinction, and uninterrupted. Thus, through the sequence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the twelve bases and eighteen elements;

up to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment—more than eighty such categories, including all mundane and supramundane phenomena, follow this same principle. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (the *Dapin*) simply says "empty" (directly substituting "emptiness" for "purity").

It is said that all dharmas traversed therein are without distinction. Since both "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) and "purity" (*viśuddhi*) signify the transcendence of all marks (*animitta*), the scripture divided into these seven sections is described as "empty and pure.
This is a dual inclusion: it distinguishes this from an emptiness that is nihilistic annihilation, and it is not a purity characterized by the distinctions of conditioned, untainted phenomena.

Regarding the phrase "if one speaks in terms of the mind," it means that if the mind consists of inverted false imaginings, then [all things]—the seven sections traversed, the sense organs, consciousnesses, objects, and the great elements—are [all such].
All phenomena are invariably existent, yet existence is impure; however, when the mind is free from false conceptualization, these phenomena are all non-existent, and thus they are pure.
Therefore, the Treatise says: "When the mind arises, various phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, various phenomena cease.
This means that because the illusory defilements of the self have been exhausted, the wisdom that observes them also vanishes; having thus merged with awakening, [all is pure].

Because the mind is entirely pure, the *Prajñāpāramitā* states that since the Bodhisattva, through contemplative practice, severs [delusions] within phenomena such as form (*rūpa*), they attain such purity;
thus it is called "purity of form," which can destroy all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding all phenomena.

Third, the formal explanation of the root-consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) in the sutra, which consists of two parts: first, following the preceding section, the explanation of the initial phrase that universally clarifies the cause of purity;

second, the explanation of the subsequent text that specifically manifests purity. Regarding the "cause of purity," this generally pertains to the seven sections; the purity of these seven sections all arises because awakening is perfectly luminous.

Next, following the phrase "in contrast to delusion," the second part explains the latter text to correctly manifest purity, which has three sub-sections: first, a general explanation of purity as being exclusively this [awakening].

The two characters "pure" (*śuddha*) have meanings that apply both generally and specifically. Regarding the general meaning: the mind and the dharmas of the lower faculties and consciousnesses all attain purity because they arise from the perfect clarity of awakening.
Regarding the specific meaning: this alone is called "purity of mind," which distinguishes it from the other dharmas of the faculties and consciousnesses.
These dharmas of the faculties and consciousnesses are called "pure" because they are empty and lack intrinsic nature, like the blue [reflection] within a mirror.
If colors such as yellow possessed a real substance, they would defile the mirror; because they defile the mirror, these blues, yellows, and so forth are termed impure things.
Now, since blues and the like are merely reflections and lack even a fraction of a substantial entity, each is pure.
As previously cited from the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Treatise on Wisdom) and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Great Chapter, and others, it is now said that "the mind... [is pure].

Purity differs from this: just as when there is dust or grime upon the luminous substance of a mirror, not only is the dust and grime impure, but the very substance of the bright mirror itself is also called impure (therefore the Commentary says: "this is like the deluded awakening-mind, within which one grasps at dharmas").
If there is no dust or grime, it is merely reflections; not only are the reflections pure, but the substance of the bright mirror itself also attains the name of purity.

"Pure" (the commentary states: "Now one sees that dharmas and their nature are all empty, etc. means that knowing the mirror is pure is a statement regarding the existence of its substance; this substance is pure, while reflections are without substance.
Only that which is without substance is called "pure. Is this not different [from the previous point]? Regarding the phrase "the seven sections, etc.," it serves as an analogy for what follows.

However, while the analogy applies to the general meaning, it does not apply to the specific distinction of the substance. You should explain this in detail yourself. △ Commentary: Now, unfolding below...
The second explanation concerns the ritual procedure (*vidhi*). This means setting aside for the moment the sequential progression and first explaining the dharmas traversed;

this is the ritual procedure. The phrase "now, for the time being" (*jin qie*) indicates the titles and number of the seven sections to be explained, and does not mean that these constitute only the first chapter.
The "Commentary on the Mind" (*Suxin*) provides a detailed explanation of this chapter below. This chapter refers to the sense-faculties and consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

It is said that by using the general term to introduce the scriptural passage, both the general and the specific are encompassed; the "general" refers to the fundamental mind (*mūlacitta*), while the "specific" refers to the *ālayavijñāna*.

[The commentary] consists of two parts: first, the word-by-word explanation of the faculties and consciousness; second, the inclusion of the seventh and eighth consciousnesses within the term "mind," specifically including the eighth consciousness to explain the character "mind."

Regarding the fifth point, "Defining the Essential Nature by Way of Defilement": To speak of its general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), because it is a synthesis of defilement and purity, when defined by way of its defiled aspect, it corresponds to the eighth [consciousness];
when defined by way of its pure essence, it corresponds to the aforementioned analogy of the mirror’s brightness. [The *Śūchao* states:

"In the *Cheng weishi lun*, etc., the second section establishes the names according to their general characteristics. As for the four types of names, the full text states: 'Thus, although the eighth consciousness exists in all realms of existence...'"
All mental states are fully accomplished, yet they are established with various names according to their specific meanings (for among sentient beings, some possess these names while others do not).
That is to say, it is called "citta" (Sanskrit: *citta*; Chinese: mind) because it is accumulated by the seeds perfumed by various phenomena (*dharma*).

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the meaning of "accumulation" refers to the fact that this consciousness can accumulate and give rise to many types of seeds, or that it can be perfumed within this consciousness; since it has already accumulated all phenomena therein, it is called "mind."

"Vijñāna" (consciousness) is the meaning of "citta" (mind); it is the "mind" within the triad of *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna*. How is this known? Because the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts state that the substance of "mind" (*citta*) cannot be found apart from the third [category], the *ālayavijñāna*. Furthermore, the second chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* also contains the meaning of "mind," though it differs from this [definition].

That [text] refers to a different set of phenomena and speaks from one specific perspective. Alternatively, it is called *ādāna* (Sanskrit), which means "appropriating" (Chinese). This is because it causes the seeds and the various material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) not to perish.

This [function] applies to both ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "It serves as the basis for appropriation (*upādāna*), existing only in ordinary beings. This is spoken according to the single aspect of defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and does not apply universally to all noble ones; however, this [appropriation] also...

It is called the "basis of the faculties" (*indriya-āśraya*), though here it is simply referred to as the "basis" (*āśraya*) based on its preeminent status. Alternatively, it is named the "basis of the knowable" (*jñeya-āśraya*), because it serves as the support for all knowable phenomena, whether defiled or pure.

"Knowable" refers to the three natures (*trisvabhāva*); because this consciousness is their support, it is called the "basis of the knowable. This is precisely what is treated in the first chapter of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the "Chapter on the Basis of the Knowable" (*Jñeyāśraya-paṭala*).

Thus, "knowable" is a specific designation for this ālayavijñāna. Therefore, the *Madhyāntavibhāga* states: "False imagination exists; therein, both [subject and object] are entirely absent. Herein there is only emptiness, and that [emptiness] also exists therein. For this reason, the phenomena of the three natures all depend upon this consciousness to exist. Alternatively, it is called "seed" (*bīja*).

The "son" (the consciousness) is so called because its cognitive capacity is able to universally sustain all seeds of both the mundane and supramundane realms (that is, it serves as the seed for all phenomena;
whereas the first [name], "mind," refers to the sense of seeds being accumulated therein, this present name takes the sense of being able to produce all phenomena).

These various names apply to all stages (this applies to both the contaminated and uncontaminated, whether ordinary beings or noble ones—these are termed "all stages"; within the three stages, they refer specifically to the stage of continuous maintenance). Above.
The preceding commentary has already clarified the details; following that, the treatise states:

"Alternatively, it is called the *ālayavijñāna* because it stores and preserves all factors belonging to the category of defilement so that they are not lost, and because it is grasped as one's own internal self by self-view, self-love, and so forth.

This name applies only to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*), and not to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) or non-regressive Bodhisattvas, for whom [such defilements] do not exist."
It is called the "defiled consciousness" (*kliṣṭa-vijñāna*) because it functions as the storehouse for the grasping of defilements (the meaning of which will be explained below).

Alternatively, it is named the "retributive consciousness" (*vipāka-vijñāna*) because it is the retributive fruit of wholesome and unwholesome karma that brings about birth and death. This intention is to clarify the sense of "drawing forth" the fruit: it is called "retributive" because it is impure and neutral; because it differs from its cause; because it arises from a retributive cause; and because it is produced by a retributive cause.

It is not called "retributive" in the case of the untainted (*anāsrava*), which is wholesome, because it does not differ from its cause nor is it produced by a retributive cause. This name applies only to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and the two vehicles (those in training and those beyond training).

[Question regarding] the Bodhisattva stage (from the tenth stage downward): Why is the Bodhisattva of the Vajra-mind given this name? [Answer: If he has already abandoned [the afflictions], why is he not called a Buddha? Because it is not yet the stage of a Tathāgata;

[the state] still possesses maturation (*vipāka*), and because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) [whereas the Bodhisattva's state is] purely untainted wholesome (*anāsrava-kuśala*). *Commentary:* Regarding the passage "When deluded... and below, there are three explanations for the reason for changing the name.

As for "due to being clung to as a storehouse" (*ālaya*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The first transforming consciousness is named *ālayavijñāna* in the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna."

"Ya" (which in this context means "to store") refers to this consciousness because it possesses the meanings of being that which stores (*ālaya*), that which is stored within (*nidhāna*), and that which is clung to as a self (*ātmagrāha*).

As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "Because it acts as a mutual condition with defiled phenomena, and because it serves as the object of the defiled manas. That is to say, because it acts as a mutual condition with the various defilements, sentient beings cling to it as their internal self.

Because it can maintain the seeds of defilement, it is called "that which is stored" (*nidhāna*); this consciousness is "that which stores" (*ālaya*) because it is the locus where defiled phenomena are perfumed and upon which they depend. Defiled phenomena are called "that which stores" (*ālaya*) because they perfume this consciousness, which is thus "that which is stored. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* further states: "For the sake of the defiled [manas]..."

That which is grasped and stored as an internal self by the seven [consciousnesses] is called the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness). This refers to its mutual functioning as a condition with the defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa*), thereby explaining the relationship between the container and the contained. All contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are termed "defiled phenomena. The phrase "sentient beings and so forth" explains the meaning of "grasping and storing" (*upādāna*).

This refers specifically to the meaning of the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and not the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); otherwise, those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) would also possess this name. It does not grasp others as its own self, nor does it grasp another's self;

thus it is called "one's own internal self. This is the correct explanation of the meaning of *ālaya*. Although its meaning encompasses all three aspects, it is correctly named for the aspect of being "grasped and stored. Otherwise, the two vehicles at the stage of no-more-learning and Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage would also possess this name. If these three conditions are lacking, one cannot receive this name. If that were so, then for the two vehicles prior to the seventh stage...

For those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have entered the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), the attachment of self-love (*ātma-sneha*) should be abandoned; this name [of *ālayavijñāna*] is to be understood as explained in the subsequent passage.

This demonstrates the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—that is, the essential nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*)—of the first transformative consciousness. [Question: If it is said that the *ālayavijñāna* is "the storehouse" (*ālaya*) because it acts as a mutual condition for defilement (*saṃkleśa*), then being the "storer" (*ālayana*) signifies the sense of cause, and being the "stored" (*ālīyate*) signifies the sense of effect.

Apart from cause and effect, how could there be a separate essential nature? [Answer: Because its specific characteristic consists in the grasping and maintaining of cause and effect. (The specific characteristic is the general; cause and effect are the particulars.)

Because it takes the apprehension of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its own essence, "apprehension" (*saṃgraha*) has the meaning of inclusion, and "retention" (*dhāraṇa*) has the meaning of supporting. Question: If that is so, then the self-characteristic (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) must be a conventional existence (*prajñapti-sat*). Answer: Not so.

This is because if the two aspects of cause and effect were combined as a single entity, then the characteristic of the characteristic could be established as conventional; however, since there is no separate aspect of cause and effect apart from the self-characteristic, and the aspects of cause and effect are merely distinct descriptions upon the very substance of the self-characteristic, they are not conventional.

Question: It was previously stated that this consciousness has three states; why, among these three transformations, is the "maturation" (*vipāka*) mentioned there, while in this explanation, the name "storehouse" (*ālaya*) is used instead? Therefore, the commentary next says: "Now, regarding the wisdom of observation... and so forth, which is according to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school.
In both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, one only abandons this designation upon reaching the stage of Arhat (in the Mahāyāna, this is the eighth bhūmi; in the Hīnayāna, it is as may be known).

According to the Final Teaching (Jōgyō), one abandons it immediately upon the initial dwelling of the mind (shohanshinjū). According to the Perfect School (Enshū), this designation never existed in the first place;

it is merely due to false delusion. Therefore, in this Sudden School (Tongo), no stages or positions are established; rather, when the practice of contemplation is perfected, one is entirely identical to the Buddha.
Therefore, it refers only to the mental states associated with awakened wisdom (*bodhi-jñāna*) and does not mention the *ālaya*;
thus, it is said that the name "ālaya" has ceased. This cessation of the name clarifies that its substance (*tattva*) has not ceased to exist.

The same applies to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, which states that because Arhats have completely and finally severed the afflictive obstructions (*kleśa-dausthulya*) within this consciousness, they no longer grasp and store the *ālayavijñāna* as a self.

The internal self thus permanently loses the name "ālaya"; this is described as its abandonment, yet it is not the abandonment of the entire substance of the eighth consciousness. The commentary states:

Because those [beings] have exhausted their afflictions (*kleśa*) to the ultimate degree, it is said they are "permanently ended. Here, however, we take up the case where contemplation has been perfected;

because one does not cling even while in contemplation, it is simply said that the name "sinks away," rather than saying it is "permanent[ly ended]. [The Sub-commentary states: Since the mind... below.

The four [types of] bonds are identical to the stage of the Buddha. That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is called the *ālaya*, while that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is collectively termed the "stainless consciousness" (*amala-vijñāna*).

Therefore, that treatise states immediately following: "Alternatively, it is named the 'stainless consciousness' (*amala-vijñāna*), because it is the support for all most extremely pure, untainted dharmas" (it is exclusively untainted because its essential nature is stainless). This name exists only in the stage of the Tathāgata; there are two [types] among Bodhisattvas.

Because those in the stages of the vehicles and ordinary beings possess contaminated seeds that are susceptible to perfuming, yet have not yet attained the thoroughly pure eighth consciousness—as stated in the sutra:

"The Tathāgata’s stainless consciousness is the pure, uncontaminated realm, liberated from all obstacles, associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom" (this is the verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* on the Tathāgata’s merits). △ [Commentary: The following five points below cite subsequent passages as proof.
This also addresses a general objection, which asks: "The immaculate consciousness (*amala-vijñāna*) belongs to the stage of Buddhahood; how can it be identical [to the state of practice]?

To resolve this through scriptural citation, it is said that in this Sudden Teaching school, when the contemplative practice is perfected, it is entirely identical to Buddhahood. Therefore, the subsequent section states: "Suddenly identical to the Buddha-realm.
Therein lies the doctrine of attaining Buddhahood through six gates, all of which have scriptural authority; these shall be seen in the relevant passages. Furthermore, if...

Regarding the designation "stainless" based on intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), this applies to both ordinary beings and sages; thus, the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* states: "The mind consists of eight consciousnesses, or perhaps nine.
Furthermore, the second fascicle says: "The Tathāgata’s pure storehouse (*tathāgatagarbha*) is also called stainless wisdom (*vimalajñāna*);

it is eternally abiding without beginning or end, and transcends the four propositions (*cātuṣkoṭika*) of verbal expression. Also, the *Niyatāniyata-gotra-śāstra*, in the "Chapter on the Nine Consciousnesses," states: "The first..."

Regarding the ninth, the *amala-vijñāna*, the Tripiṭaka Master Zhendi (who was also the translator of this [text]) explained: "This has two aspects: first, its object of cognition (*ālambana*), which is *tathatā* (suchness);

second, its fundamental awakening (*mūla-awakening*), which is the wisdom of *tathatā*. That which is capable of cognizing is the *aśūnyagarbha* (non-empty treasury), while the object of cognition is the *śūnyagarbha* (empty treasury).
Both are the *tathāgatagarbha*. In the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the 'true consciousness' (*tathatā-vijñāna*) is precisely the stainless consciousness (*vimala-vijñāna*). As stated below.

The *Yinshi* (Commentary on the Introduction) further states that ancient masters also established a ninth consciousness, which Ci'en refuted as being incorrect. It then provides a comprehensive reconciliation, stating:

"However, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* speaks of nine kinds of consciousness; it identifies True Suchness (*tathatā*) as the ninth, naming it the 'Stainless Consciousness' (*amala-vijñāna*). Now, let us further reconcile this:
even if it were indeed True Suchness, it would not contradict what the ancient masters established, because True Suchness is the gate of arising and ceasing."

Furthermore, the *Zhongbenjue* (Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna) treats the one mind as *tathatā*, and it is also stated that the essence of *tathatā* possesses the meaning of "true and real cognition" (*zhenshi shizhi*).

(The remainder is as cited below from Paramārtha’s commentary, which is precisely *tathatā*). This is truly because Ci'en [Kuiji] did not understand *tathatā* within the gate of arising and ceasing (*shengmie men*), and thus he unilaterally refuted it based solely on the tenets of his own school. [End of] Commentary, Part Two, Containing the Second Gate.

Seven: Explaining the Views on the Sense Objects (1) An Analogous Reference to the Remaining Five. The Commentary states: "By means of the following two [sections], the actual analysis is established.
If one speaks according to the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) system, the seventh consciousness exclusively takes the internal as its object and thus does not grasp at a self.

This is because that [system] explains that the eight consciousnesses each have their own distinct substantial essence (*svabhāva*). Here, however, based on the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, the first seven are merely the differentiated functional capacities of the eighth [consciousness]. (As stated in the 'Chapter on Samantabhadra' regarding the eight gates of Mind-Only)."

As already explained [in the middle section], this sutra does not have a formal seventh consciousness; rather, it speaks of the sixth consciousness while implicitly including the eighth. The *Awakening of Faith* describes the sixth consciousness as follows:

"The discrimination of the six sense-objects is called the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). This scripture uses the term "seeing, hearing," and so forth, based on the meaning of their distinct separation.
What is now referred to as "the mind of self that calculates and clings" is the essence of the clinging subject; "seeing all forms and appearances" refers to the self.

"Object" (referring to that which is grasped in conjunction with its grasper) refers to the very essence of the objects such as "views" (*dṛṣṭi*), etc. The Commentary states, "Not merely [the first three]," which clearly demonstrates the meaning of excluding or not excluding a restrictive sense;

this may be understood by consulting the Sūtra. The Commentary states, "Seeking this... and so forth; the fourth section explains the name based on its essence, stating that it is still the mind of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*).

The term "self" (*ātman*) includes both the self and what belongs to the self (*ātmiya*); the distinct name established for it is the object of views (*dṛṣṭi-viṣaya*). This is based on the formal establishment [of the term].
The name "intention" (*manas*) is explained here in relation to what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*);

furthermore, the five [faculties] below are subsumed as a whole from their individual distinctions, as in the case of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which serves as an illustrative example to establish the point (the "self" within the aggregates refers both to the conventional designation and to that which is grasped by ordinary beings). Other meanings will be explained further below.
The commentary merely cites the latter two [sections] to provide the correct explanation of the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). All six are called "faculties" (*indriya*);

the explanation of these names and the enumeration of the six—eye, ear, and so forth—is as extensively cited from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* in the *Dàchǎo*. Regarding why they are all called "faculties," it is as clearly stated in the text of the commentary.
As for the fifth [section], the "explanation of the essential nature" (*svabhāva*), it states that they arise "from their own seeds"; that is, the eye arises from its own eye-seed.
The arising of the manifest eye-faculty and so forth, up to the body, refers to the manifest body-faculty arising from its own seeds.

Regarding the "four great elements" (mahābhūta), this refers to the four great elements that act as the creators (earth, etc. and the four derivative particles (color, odor, taste, and tangibility) that are created by them;
these two types combined constitute eight dharmas that form the substance of the five faculties. As for "pure matter" (rūpa-prasāda), it is characterized by resistance and is invisible.
To distinguish the four objects of the physical sense organs (*mūla-indriya*), there is also a treatise which says: "The eye is like a cluster of grapes; the ear is like a rolled birch bark;

the nose is like a pair of fingernails (the Sūtra says 'a pair of hanging claws'); the tongue is like a crescent moon blade; the body is like the luster of a precious jewel (the *Buddhāvatamsaka-sūtra* says 'the body is like a [yao-ri] drum-head';

the mental faculty is like seeing in a dark chamber). It is not yet clear whether this is correct; the mental faculty is the last one mentioned below. As for the phrase "by means of this," it refers precisely to...
Regarding the meaning of the faculties (*indriya*), following the intent of the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Awakening of Faith*, and other texts:

when the manas takes internal objects as its domain, it is the seventh consciousness (since "manas" is itself a consciousness); when it grasps external objects, it is called the sixth consciousness (since it is the consciousness of the manas).

In the commentary below, the remaining three sections provide the formal explanation of the six consciousnesses. The first sentence establishes the general principle, while the subsequent text is divided into two parts:

first, following the end [of the preceding section], and second, a general correlation with the faculties and objects. Regarding the initial statement, "following the six," etc., this is a general heading indicating that the names of the six consciousnesses are established in accordance with their respective faculties and objects.
Next, the bases (the faculties) and the objects of perception each have six distinct names, differing in their categories.
Because consciousness varies according to those [faculties and objects], it is neither more nor less [in number], nor is it fixed as distinct [from them].

Furthermore, since it is clear that this consciousness is determined to be sixfold by following the faculties and objects, it is evident that when its name is established, it is not based on only one; rather, it receives its name from both the faculty and the object.

The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* also states: "It is called 'consciousness' according to the faculty, and it is called 'consciousness' according to the object," up to "it is called 'blue,' etc. (Master Ji’s commentary says this).

The Commentary states: Since the latter two [types of consciousness] possess [only the sense organ as their basis], one should first ask: "If they are named after their discernment (*vijñapti*), they actually pertain to both the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*);
why then do the various treatises name them according to the sense organ, such as 'eye-consciousness' up to 'mind-consciousness'?

This is answered by the phrase "by possessing, etc. Because [the organ] is superior to the object, they are designated specifically according to the sense organ. Regarding the five meanings, the treatise merely...

For example, it is said that "the five" refers to [the faculties] as the basis (*āśraya*), [consciousness] as what arises from them (*samutthita*), and [the objects] as belonging to them (*pratyāsatti*) and assisting them (*upakāra*), just like the sense-faculties (*indriya*). The second fascicle of the *Abhidharma* states: "If it is called 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*) because it discerns form (*rūpa*), for what reason [is it so called]? [The answer follows: It is called consciousness because it discerns form. Why? Because it is the very nature of consciousness to discern its respective objects. Just as fire is called "fire" because its nature is to burn, so too is consciousness called "consciousness" because its nature is to discern. Furthermore, it is called consciousness because it is the basis for the discernment of objects. Just as one says "a house with pillars" because the pillars are the support of the house, so too is consciousness the support for the discernment of objects. Therefore, it is called consciousness. Regarding the phrase "because it discerns form": "form" refers to the five types of sensory objects—visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. "Discerning" means to distinguish, to differentiate, and to clearly perceive. Because it performs this function of discerning these five objects, it is called consciousness. Furthermore, it is called consciousness because it is the primary agent of discernment. Just as a king is called the "king" because he is the sovereign of his realm, so too is consciousness called "consciousness" because it is the sovereign of the act of discerning.

Moreover, it is called consciousness because it is the support for the discernment of objects. Just as a lamp is called a "lamp" because it supports the illumination of forms, so too is consciousness called "consciousness" because it supports the discernment of objects. Thus, for these reasons, it is called consciousness. As for the question "for what reason": it asks why, among all phenomena, this specific phenomenon is designated by the name "consciousness. The answer is that it is designated as such because it possesses the unique characteristic of discerning objects, which no other phenomenon shares. Therefore, based on this specific activity, it is established as the phenomenon named "consciousness. This concludes the explanation.
Is it that they are called "eye-consciousness" and so forth, but not "form-consciousness" and so forth?

This is because these five types [of explanations] apply to the eye and the other [senses], but not to form and the other [objects]. Among these, the first is consciousness based on the sense organ (*indriya*). It has two meanings:
first, it is called "eye-consciousness" because it is the consciousness within the eye; second, because the consciousness arises depending upon the locus of the eye (this is the seventh case).
And because visual consciousness exists by virtue of its possession [of its basis], this is the third transformation.
For instance, just as mental consciousness follows the seven formless bases within the mind, the mind likewise relies upon those same formless supports; it abides within those formless supports.
Furthermore, because the seventh [consciousness] exists, mental consciousness can exist; it is not that the objective form exists within the consciousness that abides in form.
Since consciousness accompanied by form necessarily arises, we provisionally rely on its coarse characteristics; for those who are blind cannot see.

Thus, although one knows that there is form, consciousness does not necessarily arise [from it alone]. That which is produced by the second sense organ is called "eye-consciousness" because it is produced by the eye.
Just as when the eye is impaired by the disease *kāmalā*, consciousness necessarily undergoes a transformation corresponding to that change in the eye.
All that is seen as blue is taken to be yellow; it is not at the time of the destruction of the object that consciousness is destroyed.
This is precisely what is meant by saying that because this seventh consciousness exists, the sixth consciousness cannot be liberated from its conceptual fetters (*nimitta-bandhana*).

Furthermore, if the seventh consciousness is untainted (*anāsrava*), the sixth must necessarily be untainted (though when the seventh is untainted, it is necessarily induced by the sixth through the severing of afflictions). Third.

From this, one should understand that the seven [faculties] have power over the six, meaning that the seeds of the six follow along with the seeds of the seven.
When the seven seeds arise as manifest activity (*pravṛtti*), the six [consciousnesses] are able to arise because they provide them with power; otherwise, they would certainly not arise.

It is not the case that the seeds of form (*rūpa*) follow the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna*). To the question, "How is this so?"—the answer is: when there is form, it must necessarily be a transformation of consciousness;

just as when there is consciousness, it must necessarily be produced by the sense faculties (*indriya*). How then can the seeds of consciousness fail to arise following the arising of form? The answer is: form is...

Because the sixth consciousness is associated with the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), and because the seventh [consciousness] transforms the outflowing (*sāsrava*) into the outflow-free, the fifth [consciousness] is like the sense faculties.
As it is said: "Because it is the consciousness of the eye, it is called 'eye-consciousness' (*cakṣurvijñāna*). Thus, it is eye-consciousness.

It is like a skillful magician who conjures men and women; although their various faculties appear to move, they are all drawn by a single mechanism (which corresponds to the "one consciousness responding to the six faculties" in the treatise).

Dust and defilements vanish as soon as they are thought of, becoming perfectly luminous, pure, and wondrous. According to the preceding texts, since a single entity gives rise to manifold functions, it is called the "separating consciousness.

"If not" (referring to the preceding section), the following four lines clarify the momentum of the scriptural text. However, this present sutra and treatise do not originally intend to provide such an explanation; rather, they simply wish to...

When the realization of contemplative practice is perfected, awakening becomes perfectly luminous and the mind is immediately pure; as these states follow one after another, they reveal the principle that the mind is entirely pure.
Therefore, the argument must proceed by linking what precedes with what follows.

In the commentary on the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), section two, item one, six, all explain the names [of the objects] below. Among these, first is the general name. The general name for "object" (*viṣaya*) is as can be understood from the commentary.
Furthermore, they are called the "six decays" (*ṣad-dhvaṃsa*; decay of wholesome dharmas) and the "six meaningless things" (*ṣad-anartha*; absence of the meaning of wholesomeness).

These are also explained in reference to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). The commentary states, "Regarding form (*rūpa*) and so forth," which explains the specific names. That which is "taken by the eye" should refer to that which is taken by the eye.
"Name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) refers to that which is grasped by the ear, up to and including that which is grasped by the mind—namely, the six sense objects such as form and so forth.
Since the objects are clarified in relation to the faculties as "form and so forth," the fact that there is only the character *gu* (i.e., "and so forth") in the commentary is intended to be concise.
[The commentary states: "Form has [two aspects] below," which distinguishes the types; generally speaking, the five faculties and the six objects are collectively termed [the eighteen elements].

Regarding form (*rūpa*), according to what is listed in treatises such as the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*, only that which is specifically apprehended by the eye constitutes the "form-object" (*rūpāyatana*) among the six objects.
Furthermore, there are three categories of form based on its visibility and resistance: first, visible and resistant form, which is that which is seen by the eye;
second, invisible and resistant form, which refers to the five sense organs and the four [other] objects—namely, sound, odor, taste, and touch (all of which are invisible, yet possess resistance).
Regarding the three types of form that are invisible and non-obstructive (*anidarśana-apratigha*), these are exclusively forms subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Among these three types of form, only that which is visible to the eye is most prominent; the other two may be understood as being coarse and subtle respectively.

Within this category of form that is visible to the eye alone and is coarse and manifest, there are further three kinds: namely, color-form (*varṇa-rūpa*)—such as blue, yellow, red, white, light, shadow, brightness, and darkness—and shape-form (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*)—such as square, round, coarse, fine, high, low, regular, and irregular.

"Manifest form" (*vijñapti-rūpa*) refers to [actions such as] walking, standing, sitting, lying down, bending, stretching, taking up, and putting down. "And so forth" (*ādi*) regarding sound and the others should be understood to include odor, taste, and touch.

This serves as an analogy for the forms apprehended by the eye and other senses. Furthermore, sound is further categorized as: (1) caused by what is appropriated (*upātta-hetu*), which is sound produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) internally appropriated by the *ālaya-vijñāna*;

(2) caused by what is not appropriated (*anupātta-hetu*), which refers to external great elements such as wind, bells, and gongs; and (3) caused by both the appropriated and the non-appropriated (*ubhaya-hetu*), which refers to both internal and external [elements].

The sounds produced by the four great elements, such as those from striking drums or blowing conch shells; agreeable (that which is desired by the mind), disagreeable (the opposite), and both contrary (the opposite of the two);

heterodox (the doctrines established by non-Buddhists), orthodox teaching (the establishment of doctrine and reasoning that induces realization), authoritative verbal testimony (*āptavāda*) (such as "I see what I see"), and non-authoritative verbal testimony (the opposite of the above);

fragrance—whether excellent, inferior, or neutral—which arises simultaneously with its substance (such as the scent of sandalwood arising together with the wood itself), combined fragrance (arising from a collection of factors), and transformed fragrance (arising only after maturation); and tastes.
The sensations of bitter, sour, sweet, pungent, salty, and bland arise together [intrinsic], through combination [such as food and drink], or through transformation [such as fruits and melons].

These include agreeable and disagreeable tangibles, which possess the four great elements (the basis for the qualities of heaviness, lightness, cold, heat, etc.). Furthermore, there are cold, warmth, roughness, smoothness, hunger, satiety, and so forth, which are perceived exclusively by the mind.
Even those forms included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)—that is, all objects known by the mind—are termed the sphere of mental objects.

Furthermore, for example, among the one hundred dharmas, excluding the ten material forms (*rūpa*) and the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), the remaining eighty-two are all included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Now, from these eighty-two, we further exclude eighty-one and take only that which is categorized as "matter" (*rūpa*) within the sphere of mental objects.

The names and natures of the others are easy to discern, and since they do not possess the meaning of being "objective spheres" (*viṣaya*), they are not taken here. Within this matter of the sphere of mental objects, there is furthermore "extremely subtle matter" (*paramāṇu-rūpa*), which is produced by the total analysis of various forms.

Reaching the ultimate limit of minuteness constitutes this very substance. Because it stands apart from obstruction, it is "extremely remote"; thus, light, darkness, shadows, and reflections are analyzed down to their ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*). That which is "induced by what is received" refers to the discipline (*saṃvara*), non-discipline (*asaṃvara*), and so forth, which are induced and received through the teachings and the preceptor.

That which is "arisen from pervasive conceptualization" refers to the fact that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—among the three natures—is capable of pervasive conceptualization; since objects arise from this, they are said to be "arisen from that. Furthermore, because form arises from that [consciousness], it is also included.

If one were to define the substance [of these phenomena] individually, the six sense objects each constitute their own substance (e.g., visible form constitutes the substance of form), as explained previously regarding the six sense faculties.
As for the examples (such as "the eye is itself the substance"), since their meaning is easy to perceive, the Commentary does not state them explicitly.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra on the four great elements where the Commentary states, "Immediately below, the substance is established; 'not taking,' etc.," this means:

because they do not take up the arising of consciousness, they are not called "faculties" (*indriya*), but are merely called the "internal four great elements. Because they do not attract the mind, they are not called "objects" (*viṣaya*), but are merely... [omitted].
Because they are called the "external four great elements" (mahābhūta), it means taking the substance of the four great elements directly. ▲ Commentary:

Regarding the second section on the characteristics [of the elements] in the *Ratnakūṭa*, the Sūtra states that each of the four great elements has two types. This is a summary of the intended meaning, cited from the original text, which says in full:
"Great King (spoken by the Buddha for King Śuddhodana), there are two kinds of earth element: internal and external. What is the internal earth element? It refers to the body."

Internally, there exists that which is acquired (*upātta*) and appropriated (*upādāna*)—that which is solid and firm (the term "firm" here takes the sense of resistance, for earth has solidity and resistance as its nature)—namely, hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, and so forth. These constitute the internal earth element of the body.
Furthermore, whatever exists externally to the body that is not acquired and not appropriated, and is solid, is called the external earth element.

Regarding the external earth element (the other three great elements follow this pattern one by one; here, "solid" is used as an abbreviation), all teachings state that solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion are the characteristics of the four great elements.

As for the phrase "the body's exterior substance," the full expression is "the substance of wind"; "wind" is named for its swiftness, and "substance" refers to that which is swift. This is the external wind element;
the rest are easily understood.
In the commentary on the *Jingshifajing* (Sutra on the Dharma of Governing the World), section 3-16, regarding the explanation of the meaning of the "gate of arising from the sense bases":

the meaning of "arising" is as stated in the preceding phrase; the meaning of the "gate of the arising of the locus of consciousness" refers to the gate through which the mind-consciousness arises and ceases, enters and exits.

the eye-root constitutes a realm for consciousness, and consciousness constitutes a realm for form, and so forth. As for the "causal meaning": consciousness arises because of the six roots; it is drawn forth by the six objects;

Since the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is clear and discerning, it does not enter into mutual confusion with them; being without self and without master, one does not give rise to karma and thereby attains liberation through this remedy.

Regarding those who cling to a self, the five *sthāpanā* contemplations each remedy a specific affliction; among them, it is said: "For sentient beings who are attached to a self, one teaches the contemplation of the analysis of the elements (*dhātuprabheda*).

By realizing that the elements of the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses are each distinct and separate, and that there is no sovereign master, one understands that there is no self to be clung to.
As for the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*): that which changes and obstructs is form (*rūpa*); that which experiences is sensation (*vedanā*); that which grasps images is perception (*saṃjñā*).
