Rain falls like wagon axles, but the wind checks it so that it does not flow away; it freezes into the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*). Next, the Water Wheel (*apmaṇḍala*) forms first.
After the Brahmā King descends to the lower realms, the wind gradually forms and stirs the pure water to create Mount Sumeru, the seven golden mountains, and so forth;

as sentient beings gradually come to dwell there, the turbid residue becomes the four continents and even the hells, the salt ocean, and the outer perimeter—this is what is called the establishment of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).

When the merit of those born in the second dhyāna is exhausted, they descend to be born in Jambudvīpa. At first, they possess bodily radiance and consume the earth-cake, forest creepers, and wild vines.

However, after the non-glutinous rice became gradually inferior, and the light and the *pṛthivī-parpaṭaka* (earth-cakes) and so forth ceased, there appeared the sun and moon, as well as plowing and sowing.

Because [the food] had become gradually inferior, beings were born into the three miserable realms (*durgati*) out of fear of their transgressions; by practicing virtue, they were born in the three continents, the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and even up to the Brahma world—this is called the *vivartakalpa* (aeon of formation).
Regarding the increase and decrease [of lifespan]: human lifespan begins at eighty thousand years and decreases by one hundred years [per generation].
From one year up to ten years, the lifespan increases again; for every son or daughter born, the lifespan doubles that of the father.

Thus it gradually increases until it reaches eighty thousand years; this is why it is called "increasing and decreasing. "Bifēn" (繽紛) describes a state of disarray or confusion. [Commentary] Question:
The following two sections clarify the refutations and citations of evidence; both layers can be seen as they appear in the text. This section of the commentary explains this.
The latter two explanations of the final two phrases are as in the text.

In the commentary, from "Only now do I know" onwards, the latter two explanations clarify the equality of the primary retribution (正報). First, there is a general commentary that exhaustively explains the scriptural text;

second, there is a specific explanation of the arising of Buddhas. First, there is the statement of intent and the designation of the gates; second, there is the specific explanation according to the gates.
Second, a brief explanation of the first five [schools]: the Sarvāstivāda is the *Sabbatthavāda* school; the Sautrāntika does not hold this view.
As for "only Siddhārtha," it means that other sentient beings lack Buddha-nature and will ultimately have no portion of attaining Buddhahood.

Regarding "three incalculable eons" (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) and so forth, the intent of this teaching clarifies that from the initial generation of the mind, one practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) throughout three incalculable eons.

The five stages of subduing and severing [afflictions], the fulfillment of the ten grounds, and the perfect clarity of the four wisdoms culminate in receiving the office of Buddha-wisdom at the Heaven of Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha), which is termed "attaining perfect enlightenment" (*saṃbodhi*).
Regarding the phrase "the characteristics are exhausted and the nature is manifested": this teaching explains that the fundamental true mind of all sentient beings is originally free from thought;
yet, because they do not know it as it truly is, thoughts suddenly arise—birth, abiding, change, and cessation—and these thoughts are without [intrinsic] existence.

The specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) do not depart from original enlightenment (*mūlajñāna*); through the power of internal and external perfuming, one begins by severing the characteristic of cessation and ultimately reaches the characteristic of arising.

When there is a single thought-moment of resonance, one attains the vision of the mind-nature; this mind is then eternally abiding, which is called the attainment of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).

Regarding the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and so forth mentioned in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the scripture states: "If one is in resonance with such contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), one will not give rise to dualistic interpretations regarding all phenomena."
All Buddha-dharmas quickly manifest before one; at the very moment of the initial resolve for enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*), one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
One knows that all dharmas are the self-nature of the mind, accomplishing the body of wisdom (*jñāna-kāya*) without depending on the awakening of another.

Thus, the commentary explains: "How profound is the Buddha-wisdom! Those who are deluded in their refinement consider it distant. When the mind’s emotions are forgotten and wisdom manifests, it is of one essence."

Yaoshan said: "Since it has been stated that all dharmas are the very nature of the mind, now that the principle is manifested within one's own mind, the nature of the mind is already endowed with boundless virtues.
When the mind is awakened, the principle manifests; when the principle manifests, wisdom becomes perfect.

Like a mirror becoming clear and bright, this occurs neither before nor after, neither new nor old. Not realized through another, it is self-awareness—the realization that all dharmas are [the nature of] the mind."

This is the accomplishment of awakening others through the body of wisdom; it is the fulfillment of awakening through seeing the nature of the mind. How could there be self and other within the mind-nature?
To be tranquil yet able to know is called Right Awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). When one awakens in a single thought-moment, one is called a Buddha.

This means that although from beginningless time we have been deluded and falsely identified with sentient beings, at the moment of awakening in a single thought-moment, the whole body is the Buddha. It is like a dream-body: while dreaming, it is not non-existent, yet upon awakening, [the dream] is realized as such.

Since one’s own body does not depend on further nourishment, the Treatise states: "There is also no distinction between original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) and initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"If one is free from deluded thoughts, all things are spontaneously and unimpededly equal wisdom, which immediately manifests before one.

This is also found in the *Dharmadhātu-viśuddhi-sūtra*. Furthermore, the *Vaipulya-prabhāsa-śuddha-sūtra* states: "Three men approached the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and spoke thus: 'O World-Honored One...'"
"Venerable One, we now have faith and understanding in this Dharma and do not give rise to doubt.
The foremost man addressed the Buddha, saying, "If one were to say, 'I am the Tathāgata,' these words would indeed be a correct statement.

Why is that? Because I do not give rise to doubt regarding this Dharma. (The second man said, "He is the World-Honored One," and the third said, "He is the Buddha"; their words were all the same. At that time, in the assembly, there were a hundred...
The minds of a thousand sentient beings were all agitated and unsettled in their seats, and they all thought: "There are no two Buddhas appearing simultaneously in the world;
why does this man speak such words? Ānanda conveyed the intention of the great assembly to the Buddha.
The Buddha spoke a verse in confirmation, saying: "One who can know the suchness (*tathatā*) of the past, And also knows the suchness of the future, Sees the one [suchness]."
Because all phenomena are thus, he is named Tathāgata; he is not afraid of birth and death, and while dwelling correctly within birth and death, he transforms and delivers all sentient beings.
For this reason, he is named Bhagavān. Having awakened to the fact that ignorance and non-cognition have no inherent nature, he has attained clear wisdom;
therefore, he is named Buddha. The *Bodhisattva Womb Sūtra* (*Pusa chu tai jing*) says: "There may be sentient beings who set out in the morning..."
The various Mahāyāna sūtras state that the mind of the Way attains Buddhahood; their texts are not uniform on this point.

The Chan school of Bodhidharma’s teaching that "the mind is itself Buddha" is precisely this meaning. [Commentary] Sixth: The following two sections provide a complete explanation of the sixth [point].
First, the direct explanation of "originally becoming a Buddha": The Treatise says, "The four marks are simultaneous and all lack independent existence; they are originally equal and identical."

Regarding the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra-vyākhyā*, which explains the subtle and profound meaning: it states that to say there is a Buddha outside the body is not subtle; to say there is a Buddha within the body is also not subtle;
and to say there is neither existence nor non-existence is likewise not subtle. Because sentient beings are themselves the Buddha, it is "subtle and profound" (*weimi*).

The commentary (*shu*) below the passage from the *Huayan* [Sutra] cites two sections of corroborating text, which should be examined according to reason. That commentary poses the following question:

Regarding this, if [the nature] is established as a principle (*tattva*) or as a phenomenon (*dharma*), if it were established as a phenomenon, how could all things be of a single nature or lack nature?
If it were established as a principle, why are there eight aspects? The commentary itself answers: "This is a major point of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;

it is difficult to gain understanding of it unless one confronts the various schools. Now, I shall distinguish this according to the five vehicles and five teachings. However, as for all sentient beings...
If one examines this from the perspective of the teachings for humans and devas, it is endowed with both the self of persons and the self of phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-ātman*).

If one examines it from the perspective of the Hīnayāna teachings, there are only the real dharmas of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which are inherently without self. If one examines it from the perspective of the Mahāyāna’s initial teachings, such as the *Yogācāra* (Faxiang) school, it is said that all is a manifestation of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*).
The *Nirākāra* (Wuxiang) school says that all is illusory existence which is empty; thus, both persons and phenomena are discarded. If one examines it from the perspective of the Great [Vehicle]...

According to the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), because the Tathāgatagarbha alone possesses nature-endowed virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, sentient beings are the Dharmakāya while still enmeshed in afflictions;
thus, "Dharmakāya" and "sentient beings" are one in meaning though different in name (this is spoken according to principle).

According to the Sudden Teaching (Dunjiao) of the Mahāyāna, however, characteristics are fundamentally exhausted and nature is fundamentally manifest; it cannot be said whether one attains Buddhahood or not. If one relies on this school (the Huayan school):

That which was accomplished in the past is also the completion of *nirvāṇa*; this does not refer to the same substance, for it is difficult to claim that what is accomplished here is the very same as what is accomplished there.

Question: If this is so, why is it that sentient beings currently exist who are not themselves Buddhas? Answer: If one examines them from the standpoint of the stage of sentient beings, they do not yet perceive that "mind-only" is itself emptiness;
how then could they see the reality within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*)? It is like one who is confused about the east and calls it the west, remaining firmly attached to the west.

Therefore, if all sensory perceptions (*indriya*) are suddenly shattered, the Dharma-realm manifests perfectly, and there is nothing that is not already accomplished—just as when a person who has awakened realizes that what was "west" is entirely "east.
If this is so, why do the Buddhas still engage in further transformation (*nirmāṇa*)? The answer is: sentient beings do not know it to be thus, which is why transformation is necessary.
Such transformation is ultimate transformation; such transformation is a state where there is no time when one is not transforming. Nevertheless...
Regarding the first of the six gates above: the first gate holds that sentient beings lack the principle of attaining Buddhahood;

the second gate permits only one and a half parts of the five divisions of sentient beings to definitely attain Buddhahood after fulfilling their merit over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; the latter four gates all permit every sentient being to attain Buddhahood.

Among these, the third and fourth hold that when delusion is exhausted and awakening is manifested, this constitutes Buddhahood; the fifth holds that sudden awakening to the absence of delusion is itself [Buddhahood].

The name "Buddha" signifies that from the very beginning there is neither delusion nor enlightenment; one is originally a Buddha. Furthermore, regarding the four intermediate gates, when viewed sequentially, the preceding ones extend while the succeeding ones contract.

Moreover, the first two matters establish the principle, and the subsequent two matters likewise establish the principle, thus forming five [aspects] through principle alone, which together with the principle itself form six—all of which are unimpeded.
*Commentary:* The following three sections of the sutra point to and demonstrate these [six aspects] as they appear in the text.
The commentary on the second section of the first part of the *Shi shi tong zhong* (Commentary on the Essential Agreement with Reality) follows the preceding [text] to explain the first two phrases.

It states that "the dream as the dependent" is a metaphor for the mind that grasps at signs (*nimitta*), seeing saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as things to be loathed or sought after. This explains the scriptural statement that birth and nirvāṇa are like a dream.
That which must serve as the basis for this [dream] is a metaphor for the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhicitta*). This is precisely what is being referred to here.
Because its reality is the nature of equality and indestructibility, the commentary states: "In accordance with reality, they are the same.

Regarding the "spiritual journey," it is told in the historical account of Emperor Wu of the Han: wishing to verify whether the interpreters of dreams were truthful or false, the Emperor summoned them and feigned a question, saying:
"I have dreamed that two roof tiles on the palace terrace transformed into a pair of mandarin ducks and flew away; what omen is this?"
The diviner replied, "There will be a violent death within the palace. Having finished speaking, the supervising official reported that the palace attendants had killed one another.
The Emperor was astonished and said to the diviner, "How did my casual remark come to be so accurately verified?

The diviner replied, "A dream is the wandering of a person's spirit. Your Majesty’s words were like a dream; they were also a manifestation of the resonance between what is seen and heard. This is as explained in the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*.

There are five types of dreams: first, those with an abundance of heat; second, those with an abundance of cold; third, those with an abundance of wind; fourth, those with an abundance of what is seen and heard;

and fifth, those bestowed by celestial deities, as explained at length elsewhere. Here, we shall discuss the fourth type, namely, the influence of what is seen and heard. This refers to the fact that during the daytime, before falling asleep, one encounters various objects through seeing and hearing;
consequently, although the six consciousnesses are dull and indistinct during sleep such that nothing can be clearly discerned, the residual impressions (*vāsanā*) of those sights and sounds persist.
Because the spontaneously arising object of focus is accompanied by sleep, it is called a "dream" due to its being false and inverted.
Regarding the phrase "merely understanding the nature of the dream," while other metaphors involve both themselves and others, the metaphor of the dream alone refers to the essential nature itself.

Thus, the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* (Great Necklace Sūtra) states that in the past there was a Buddha who, wishing to preach the Dharma, caused the great assembly to sleep and preached the Dharma within their dreams to increase their roots of virtue.

The commentary states that the realization of the fruits of the path also signifies that all phenomena are like a great dream; within this great dream, there must surely be the clarity of Great Awakening.
One should know that the following two sections explain the four segments of the latter four categories of the sūtra text, as listed in the commentary.

In the commentary on the prose and verses of the *Sūtra*, the first section concerning the "Initiation of the Practitioner" is treated briefly; this is because while the prose (*gadya*) consists of four segments, the verse (*śloka*) contains only three.
The preceding explanation of the "Universal Eye Chapter" (*Samantanetra-paṭala*) is hereby concluded.

In the *Zhongshu* (Commentary on the Middle) regarding what Jingqing realized, it is stated that the "root of all stages of practice" means that all myriad practices depend upon the genuineness of faith and understanding (*śraddhā-adhimukti*).
Thus, the Sūtra says, "The Tathāgata’s Perfect Enlightenment," and everything following this constitutes the basis (*āśraya*). The "gradual expedients" are that which depends upon [the basis].

By citing the basis to encompass that which depends upon it, [the text] excludes practices devoid of understanding, thereby revealing that [these practices] belong to the midst of sudden enlightenment.
Because practice is gradual, even the gateway of Samantabhadra’s mental application remains open to the ten thousand practices, let alone the case of perfect faith and sudden understanding.
In the commentary following the Great Outline, it states: "The former does not depend on the latter, yet the latter must follow upon the former.

Within the section resolving doubts regarding the difficult points of the Sūtra, the commentary follows the preceding passage because the previous *Puyan* (Universal Eye) chapter stated that "sentient beings are fundamentally perfected."
The Buddhist Path, summarized by its textual exposition, presents three points for the arising of doubt: first, that truth comes first and delusion follows; second, that delusion is taught as truth;

and third, that by restating [the opponent's position] and then conceding it, one incurs infinite fault. These three points are all explained in the commentary (*ṭīkā*) and correlated with the sub-commentary (*vṛtti*).

Regarding the "three difficulties" mentioned above, the following section resolves the intent of these difficulties. As for the phrase "the meaning of attaining Buddhahood is equal," it refers to the natural perfection of the True Nature (*tathatā*).
The Buddha has nothing that is not accomplished; he neither removes false defilements nor adds to true, pure merit, for there is neither increase nor decrease.
Thus, it is the same for sentient beings who have been Buddhas from the very beginning; this is why it is called "equality. Therefore, as stated previously:
"Within the Tathāgatagarbha, there is no arising or ceasing, no knowing or seeing; it is ultimately perfect and pervasive throughout the ten directions. Is this not so?
"Those who should be equal" refers to those who have arisen and those who have not. Because the commentary strives for brevity, it employs only the single character "not" (否).
Since both sentient beings and the Tathāgata are without arising, they should both be non-arising. If afflictions were to arise despite being non-existent, then all things would likewise arise.
As for "the cause contradicting manifest phenomena," this refers to the fact that ordinary beings at the stage of the cause are currently seen to possess greed.
The affliction of the blazing fire of hatred is manifest; how can one say it does not exist? To claim otherwise would be a contradiction.
The two subsequent lines clarify the doubts expressed by Vajragarbha. "Advancing" implies being equal to the Buddhas, while "retreating" implies being equal to ordinary beings;

since both involve the aforementioned faults, neither is tenable. The phrase "there being this" specifically refers to the title of the inquiry. However, in the *Buddhāvatamsaka-sūtra* (or *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*), Pūrṇa... [text fragment ends]

There too, this same objection arises: he says, "If this wondrous enlightenment is fundamentally wondrously enlightened clarity (herein meaning 'originally having attained the Buddha-way'), and is neither increased nor diminished compared to the mind of the Tathāgata, then how did the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena (herein meaning 'subsequently arising ignorance') suddenly come into being?

How is it that the Tathāgatas of today have now attained wondrous, empty, and luminous enlightenment, while the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the habitual taints of conditioned existence [still persist]?"
"When shall they arise again? (This translates as: "When will all afflictions arise again? Taking that [question] and contrasting it with this [text], the meaning becomes clearly intelligible.

In the concluding exhortation of the sutra, the flow [of the argument] is divided into two parts. The first part relies on this; the subsequent section provides a general explanation of the preceding text.

Regarding those passages for which there is no textual record in various scriptures, one should simply refer to the commentaries and transmissions of past and present, as well as the sutras, śāstras, religious doctrines, and practices currently studied and transmitted by the entire community. None [of these] are lacking.
This passage does not mean that Buddhas do not exist at all; for even within the *Uṣṇīṣa Sūtras*, this same question is raised.
It is like a small irrigation weir where the water is so scant that the millstones are left idle—it is called "waterless," yet it is not that there is no water altogether.

As the preface to the *Śāstra* states, "The definitive meaning is hidden in the Dragon Treasury"; thus, when the Buddha speaks of expedient teachings, his statement that sentient beings lack the wisdom of a Buddha is also based on this concealment.

Regarding the statement that "concealment" (*nigūḍha*) refers to the absence of a concealed aspect: this means that when the Buddha preaches the Dharma—whether according to his own intention or the intentions of others—the provisional and the ultimate are difficult to fathom.
This meaning is explained in detail as analyzed in the *Xuántán* (Extended Discourse). Regarding the phrase "the commentary opens the secret treasury":

the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that even ordinary beings bound by all fetters are able to know the Tathāgata’s secret treasury. The phrase "the commentary thereby establishes the title" refers to the title of the sūtra.

It is precisely because one has resolved this doubt that it is called a *nītārtha* (definitive) sūtra. ▲ Regarding the detailed explanation of the latter two [sections], there is a separate interpretation of "doubt" (*vicikitsā*) and "regret" (*kaukṛtya*).

First, the explanation of doubt: Doubt is the root. The text has two parts: first, the general explanation of the four [types of doubt] regarding the phrase "in all [phenomena]" and below, which sets forth its essence and characteristics;
second, the discernment of its function as an obstacle, specifically that it obstructs faith. The phrase "obstructing faith" identifies its activity.
The mind is clear when characterized by faith and turbid when characterized by doubt; thus, it obstructs the category of wholesome qualities.
All types of merit, benefit, skillful virtues, and wholesome dharmas are like precious gems found by a person. If that person lacks hands, they cannot grasp the gems and must return empty-handed.
Faith is like having hands, while doubt is like being handless; therefore, one is unable to take up the jewels of meritorious and wholesome dharmas—this constitutes an obstruction.

All of these are from the commentaries on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), which separately clarify the following two sections; they are distinct explanations based on the *Jñānaprasthāna* (Treatise on Knowledge) as taught by Tiantai.
Regarding the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*): first, sensual desire; second, ill-will; third, sloth and torpor; fourth, restlessness and remorse; fifth, doubt. As for doubt regarding oneself:
one wonders, "I am an ordinary person with dull faculties and heavy obstructions; how can I enter the Noble Path? This is doubt.
The Master [says]: "That person’s three karmas and four modes of deportment are such; how could they possibly benefit me? Or one may doubt, thinking:

"Even if he has attained realization and is thoroughly proficient, how can he be said to teach with his whole heart? Those who doubt the Dharma rely on this [doubt] while practicing; will they surely attain liberation from all suffering and affliction? The Commentary states:
The following three metaphors explain the physician, the medicine, and the patient. Now, the Master... [is compared to] the physician, and the Dharma to the medicine. The Commentary now...
The third section, "The Four Assemblies," states that those who have already [aroused doubt] manifest it because it has already appeared within their mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Those who have not yet [aroused doubt] refer to persons of dull faculties; upon first hearing [the teaching], they merely understand and accept it according to the words, but do not comprehend it and thus give rise to doubt.

Later, when they encounter someone challenging them, or when they reflect for themselves and perceive that the principle seems contradictory, they again fail to reach a resolution and consequently give rise to [doubt].
The Sage, anticipating this matter of doubt, provides various explanations by raising and resolving points of uncertainty at every turn.
This is the intent behind the twenty-seven sections of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāpāramitā Sūtra*, which sever doubts section by section until the end of the scripture.
Thus, Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "From this point onward, all the sūtras demonstrate the severing [of doubts]."

Regarding the arising of doubt (the term "manifestation" indicates its display), the verse states: "Furthermore, severing various doubts and preventing the arising of [such] thoughts. This currently encompasses both cases:

that which was originally asked by Vajragarbha for the sake of sentient beings, and the fact that when sentient beings hear the teaching that they are fundamentally enlightened from the beginning, those of sharp faculties immediately give rise to this doubt (this refers to what has already arisen), while those of dull faculties at that time merely accept it provisionally (this refers to what has not yet arisen). Others [interpret it differently].

One may reflect daily and perhaps begin to doubt; or, because others raise such difficulties, or because of future lives and so forth, one only then begins to give rise to doubt—hence it is said that "all are included.
△ Commentary: However, regarding the two types of cessation mentioned below, when the objects of knowledge arise from the mind, one immediately realizes they are not fixed.
Upon realizing that all phenomena are without anything to be attained, one knows that only True Suchness (tathatā) is the reality of all dharmas.
Those whose natures are such that all others may be understood by analogy—if they doubt the existence of cause and effect, have them contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination;

if they doubt that their own nature possesses infinite merits and wondrous functions, have them contemplate how each of the infinite afflictions is empty and non-existent, whereby defilement is naturally overturned to reveal the true, thus accomplishing all merits as explained in the treatise. ▲ The commentary explains "repentance" in two ways below.

Regarding the mental factor of *kaukṛtya* (remorse) among the six categories of indeterminate (*aniyata*) mental factors—namely, remorse, sleep, vitarka, and vicāra—the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that these are indeterminate with respect to both the wholesome and the defiled.
*Kaukṛtya* refers to "badly done" (*akṛta-karma*). Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the subsequent regret for actions performed;

its function (*karman*) is to obstruct tranquility (*śamatha*). Although, according to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), it is also an obstruction to concentration (*samādhi-nīvaraṇa*), it follows from agitation (*auddhatya*).

Regret and restlessness consist of three types of karma: bodily restlessness involves a fondness for wandering about and engaging in various frivolous games, such that one cannot remain seated even for a moment;

verbal restlessness involves a fondness for chanting and useless, playful discourse; and mental restlessness involves the mind being unrestrained as it clings to worldly arts and various evil thoughts and reflections.

At the time of such restless play, the mind is not yet focused on its object; however, when one subsequently wishes to enter meditative concentration, one then regrets what was previously done, and this anxiety and distress shroud the mind.
Therefore, it is called a "cover" (*nīvaraṇa*). A "cover" is like committing a great and heavy transgression while constantly harboring thoughts of remorse;
the arrow of regret enters the heart, and one subsequently falls into the evil realms. If a person can repent for their transgressions, once repented they should not worry further.

Thus, the mind will be peaceful and happy. One should not harbor constant attachment or, conversely, doubt and regret oneself. There are two reasons for this: first, not knowing that the body and mind are fundamentally empty.
Originally, the Buddha-body is within one's own mind; yet seeking the Buddha outside the mind and accumulating merit by grasping at signs involves much hardship over a long period.

Later, upon awakening that the Buddha resides in one’s own mind, one regrets former vain sufferings, which have only led further astray from the True Principle. As Master Zhi said: "When you attain the Principle and reflect back upon your practices, you will finally realize that your exertion was in vain.
Second, sudden awakening is the realization that the mind is identical to the Buddha-mind; this is my true body, the four great elements.
Regarding all objects of perception as being like adventitious dust, he cast aside his body and surrendered his life, disregarding honor and pleasure;
whether relinquishing fame or wealth, as well as sensory delights such as sound and form, his mind moved toward the Buddha at every turn and his thoughts returned to the source moment by moment.

After practicing in this way for a long time, he took joy only in discarding delusions to accord with the Truth. Before long, he fully realized the functions of a Buddha. Later, he was suddenly questioned by someone based on the inquiry of Vajragarbha.
When refuting [an opponent] or reflecting upon it oneself, if one realizes that these objections can be resolved and cannot be used to turn back [one's resolve], yet instead harbors doubt and regret,
lamenting that one has previously and pointlessly abandoned numerous honors, benefits, and other matters, and wondering whether the Master might not have attained the Buddha-way— this is not right.

In the commentary on the *Sūtra of Praise*, the phrase "the secret treasury (guhyagarbha) of the Tathāgata" is interpreted according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound. Here, "Tathāgata" refers to the person, and "secret treasury" refers to the Dharma;
thus, it means the Dharma is revealed by means of the person. As for the answer provided below, the Sūtra states: "Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are identical in their arising and ceasing;
the wondrous, perfect illumination is free from the cataracts [of delusion]. By displaying this in such a manner, the secret treasury is revealed, which is precisely what was opened by Vajragarbha.

Question: Regarding the fundamental inquiry into these three karmas, they consist of the volition (*cetanā*) that moves the body and initiates speech, as well as the essence of volition itself. As for the "instruments of karma" (*karma-yoga*), these are body, speech, and mind.
That which is non-material manifests as material form, and so forth, all of which is explained extensively in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

In the Commentary (*Śāstra*), the phrase "equal to the sudden [attainment]" corresponds to the perfection of the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) within the first stage of resolve (*prathamacittotpādabhūmi*). This refers to the initial arousal of the bodhicitta.

This refers to the point at which one attains perfect enlightenment; thus, it corresponds to the meaning of "attaining equality with the Buddha" discussed at the end of the "Chapter on the Universal Eye.

Regarding the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*): if faith is resolute, it is termed a "faculty" (*indriya*). This "faculty" has two meanings: first, it maintains its own essence; second, it is capable of growth and development.

In the commentary on the prose section of the Sūtra, there are two parts. First, regarding the fourth lower sub-section, it says: "As for 'the formal exposition' (*samyag-deśanā*), if one were to look only at the Sūtra..."
The text is straightforward: it merely takes up the scriptural passage from the preceding chapter to challenge the Tathāgata, who then provides a comprehensive explanation.
However, if one investigates thoroughly from beginning to end, there is a further profound significance:

from the start of the sūtra until the end of the "Universal Eye" chapter, because the power of realization and wisdom has already been purified, yet because [the practice] has not yet been cultivated, the mind is not yet fully purified; thus, Vajragarbha understands the capacity of the audience.

In response to this inquiry, the Buddha rebuked the view that discriminates [between self and other] regarding the process of saṃsāra and pointed out the fault of not having severed the cycle of existence, thereby awakening [the interlocutor] to what had not been understood.
At the end of the chapter, he exhorted him once more, saying: "Therefore, I say that one must forever sever the root of beginningless saṃsāra.
When Maitreya asked about the root of saṃsāra, the Buddha stated that it is the severing of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) that constitutes the gateway to the pure mind and to wisdom.

When the mind is purified, concentration and wisdom are perfected; only through the power of these two can one attain liberation from both. Therefore, the scriptural text reveals this sublime gateway of practice.
To investigate the root of the doubt that arises: although the essence of this response can be intuitively grasped through the spirit, it is difficult to express in words.

Thus, one first investigates by way of negation (*prati-pra-sam-īkṣ*) to cause one to transcend the characteristics of names and language, and to awaken to that which is free from the characteristics of mental objects.

The meaning of this is profound. Regarding the second section, the formal explanation of the sūtra’s general indication of saṃsāra, the commentary identifies the four aggregates as the "world. As the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"The Tathāgata says that what are called atoms are not atoms; they are called atoms by name. The Tathāgata says that what is called a world is not a world; it is called a world by name.
As for Vasubandhu’s (Wuzhuo) classification of these as form (*rūpa*) and the bodies of sentient beings, he takes them as a collective whole.

The Middle Way Refutation of Corresponding Practice and Abiding (the tenth of the eighteen abidings): Form refers to the aggregate of form and the bodies of sentient beings, which consist of the other four aggregates.
As the Sūtra says, "minute particles" refers to the breaking down of coarse form until reaching the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*).

As the Sūtra says, "worlds" refers to the breaking of the four aggregates through the skillful means of non-attention. The meaning of breaking down coarse form has already been explained in the Chapter on the Emptiness of Form.
That sutra further states later on: "The three-thousandfold world system that is spoken of is not a world-system," and so forth. Vasubandhu explains this in return, saying:
"This refutes the 'name-body' (nāmakāya) of the world-system; for a 'world-system' refers to the world-system of sentient beings. [The author] critiques this, saying:

"While that [explanation by Vasubandhu] speaks of the world-system as being exclusively in terms of sentient beings, the 'world-system' mentioned here in this sutra encompasses both the sentient and the non-sentient."
Therefore, it was stated above that the general designation of "sentient beings and their environment" refers to the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) and the physical world (*bhājana-loka*).

While no one doubts that the physical world constitutes the world, those with limited learning may doubt that sentient beings constitute the world; thus, the *Asaṅga-śāstra* is cited solely as proof for the world of sentient beings.
One might ask: "How does that scripture not contradict this? If it speaks of the 'world,' does it not refer exclusively to the physical world? How can we know for certain? [The answer follows:]...

Because this passage also involves the aspect of emotional affliction (*kleśa*), the commentary answers the subsequent sentence by stating: "If one does not take into account emotional affliction, how could there be saṃsāra?
Moreover, the sutra clearly states that the continuous succession of moments, with their various graspings and relinquishings, is all saṃsāra.

To discern Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vidyā*) while still within saṃsāra is for that nature of Perfect Enlightenment to be identical with the cycle of transmigration, just as, for example, the movement of the eyes [causes the vision of whirling objects], and so forth, up to the application of the analogy."
The conclusion states: "How much more so for the defiled mind of birth and death; how could it be merely designated as 'non-sentient'?
Furthermore, all sūtras and śāstras speak of the sentient world (*sattva-loka*) and the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*). These are merely different names for the same world.
Why then do you believe in these two types of "world" while disbelieving in these two types of "receptacle"? Moreover, the world is also called a "land" (*kṣetra*); a land is defined by its people.
When one's former acquaintances all flee and disperse, one says, "The country has fallen. But is it because the mountains, rivers, and land have collapsed that it is called the fall of a country?

Thus we know that the world includes both the environment and the people. Furthermore, as the Sūtra clearly states in the sixth pair of the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*), regarding the initial transformation:
because the aspect of karma from a single thought-moment transforms into the faculty of seeing, it changes into the objective realm-aspect (*viṣaya-nimitta*). This is the ultimate proof.
At the stage where the ground is fully perfected, one abandons the *vipākavijñāna* (ripening consciousness). Question:
Since attaining the ultimate means exiting saṃsāra, why does the conclusion state that "all are transmigrations"? Answer: These six pairs of phenomena are all objects of conceptualization;

because they are [defined] in relation to the mind that performs the conceptualization, they constitute saṃsāra. Therefore, the objects of conceptualization also undergo transmigration. Now, one calculates that the world had a beginning...
From the arising of transformations from the mind until the attainment of Buddhahood, they finally reach an end; such conceptualization is precisely the view of saṃsāra.
Because those taught through provisional teachings calculate that there is defilement and purity, it is said that "the first transformation ends in realization. This school, however, is not so:
fundamentally, there is no world to be eliminated, nor is there a dharma-realm to be realized. Originally there was no defilement, and now there is no purity.
Therefore, the subsequent scripture states: "Fundamentally, there is neither bodhi nor nirvāṇa; there is neither the attainment of Buddhahood nor the non-attainment of Buddhahood;
there is neither delusive saṃsāra nor the absence of saṃsāra. Based on this principle, how could there be a beginning of initial transformation or an end of ultimate realization?
Thus, in the Real Teaching school (Shōgyōshū), it is said that the Provisional Teachings possess only the scriptural texts but lack actual fruition. [End of] Commentary.

Regarding "the kalpa of abiding" (*sthiti-kalpa*) and so forth, the meanings of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness are as explained previously. Regarding "active manifestation" (*samudācāra*) and so forth, this is spoken of in terms of sentient experience.

"Active manifestation" refers to the time when the mind that performs calculation and its objects correspond. "Subduing" (*vinaya*) means to pacify and subdue the mind so that it does not give rise to thoughts;

since objects do not exist independently at the time when thoughts do not arise, these [terms] all refer to such states, such as the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the state of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

The "perception heavens" (*saṃjñā-deva*) refer to the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and the like. However, among the preceding six pairs, the first two pairs apply to both sentient beings (*sattva*) and the physical world (*bhājana-loka*);
the next three pairs pertain exclusively to the physical world; and this final pair pertains exclusively to sentient beings.

Regarding the phrase "afflictions, karma, and habitual tendencies," there are three successive layers within this that clarify the nature of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). These three layers correspond respectively to afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and [the results thereof].
The "three paths of suffering" refers as follows: the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*) consists of delusion—that is, the root and secondary afflictions such as greed, hatred, and ignorance;

the path of karma (*karma-mārga*) consists of action—that is, wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable [karma]; and the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*) consists of retribution—that is, the bodies received within the three realms.

This explanation here is still based on their successive branches and subordinates; if one were to discuss them according to their fundamental source, it is due to delusion through ignorance (*avidyā*).

True grasping gives rise to delusion, which creates karma and leads to rebirth within the cycle of *saṃsāra*; this meaning is explained in detail in the *Vajraśāstra*. Regarding the term "successive habituation" (*xi-xi*):
"succession" (*xi*) means inheritance, which carries the sense of continuity; "habituation" (*xi*) means perfuming, which carries the sense of practice and learning.

This refers to later moments of consciousness habituating to and inheriting from preceding moments, continuing in succession without end. As for the term "spool" (*lun-lun*), both are employed as metaphors.

The commentary on the meaning of the inexhaustibility of retribution and response states: "It revolves like a wheel. The sub-commentary (*shu-wen*) suggests that one might simply say "revolving" (*lun-zhuan*), as "revolving" (*lun*) carries the sense of sinking;
because it sinks and then emerges again without end or limit, it is called "revolving. However, according to this specific text, the character *lun* (sinking) is not adopted.

Nevertheless, through the repetition of these characters—*lun*, *xi*, *lun*, and *zhuan*—they constitute the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) within the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Regarding the principle that what precedes serves as the cause and what follows serves as the effect, because ignorance arises once again within the body subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death, saṃsāra has no end.
To say that ignorance has no cause and old age and death have no effect is merely stated in terms of a single cycle;
it does not mean that there is no beginning again after the end. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā* states: "Due to the habitual tendencies of various karmas..."

The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the two types of grasping, together with the previous matured fruit (*vipāka*), having already been exhausted, give rise again to further matured fruits—the afflictions of the two types of grasping.
Other [categories] may be understood by analogy. Since both afflictions and karma are all habitual tendencies, this is stated collectively as "the succession of habitual tendencies.

Regarding *kalpa*, this is translated as "time-period" (*kāla-bhāga*); whether it be a great eon (*mahā-kalpa*) or a small eon (*antara-kalpa*), long durations or short durations, down to a single instant (*kṣaṇa*), all are termed "time-periods" for sentient beings.

Since beginningless time, one has experienced eons as numerous as the atoms of a shattered world and eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, wandering in saṃsāra and undergoing suffering in an unending succession that cannot be halted.
May delusion and karma be brought to rest and extinguished, and may birth and death be brought to an end.
"No" means "not so," or "it is not. [In the commentary] "I and what belongs to me": "I" refers to the sentient being.
That which constitutes the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) and serves as the basis for suffering is the body composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*);
the remainder of the text is easily understood. Regarding the scriptural passage concerning seeing real objects in a dream: suppose a person is dreaming while sitting at a window;

upon waking, they see themselves still lying there at that same window. Although the physical locations are all real, what was actually perceived was originally a dream. This is the analogy from the sutra.
Regarding the analogy of "moving the eyes" and so forth within the middle section, there are four pairs of analogies. In the commentary on the first analogy, it says:

"Because the eyes move repeatedly, the water forms waves. This means that when a person moves their eyeballs, or rubs the corners of their eyes with their hands, what they see either tilts, turns, or becomes doubled; all such various rotations occur in this same manner.
Now, the reason for mentioning only water is that water sometimes moves due to causes other than the movement of the eyes; it may ripple through other conditions.
Because those who move their eyes might suspect this movement is spontaneous and fail to recognize it as caused by the eye, whereas other things do not behave thus, only the analogy of water is used.
Next, "the pure visual consciousness" explains the fixed eye; the intent is to take that which is dull and sluggish, unable to act with rapidity.
Upon catching up with it, one sees the fire transform into the appearance of a wheel; therefore, it is called "fixing the eye.
This does not mean that the eye must be rigidly fixed and remain forever immobile to be termed "fixed.

For example, if someone takes a stick and burns its tip to within half an inch of the head, and then immediately rubs and rotates it with their hand, they will see the appearance of a red wheel. If the stick...
As it lengthens and slightly curves, the appearance of the wheel turns and gradually widens;
according to what is seen, it may appear to be three or two feet in circumference. How could a fire that is but half an inch wide suddenly expand?

Thus we know that this is merely because the visual consciousness is dull and sluggish, unable to keep pace with the fire-wheel, and thus it appears as if the entire circumference were ablaze. The Sūtra simply says:

When it is said that "it is the eye," this is a general statement following worldly convention; when it is further stated that "it is consciousness," this is an interpretation of the meaning that must be taken as specifically referring to that which is directly capable of seeing.

Thus, water waves and fire-wheels are merely metaphors for the movement and stillness of the eye; likewise, within the Perfect Enlightenment (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*), seeing ordinary beings or seeing sages is merely the wandering of the deluded mind, and the shifting of the shore or the movement of the moon is identical to the rushing of clouds or the sailing of a boat.

This [passage] is from the "Sshi" (The Swift), which describes the characteristics of rushing and hurried movement. Regarding the phrase "the commentary (*jing*) binds the fingers," the preceding doubt was not yet the answer to the objection.
There was a person who composed a commentary stating: "From 'the world arises and ceases' up to this point answers the first objection;

the metaphor of flowers in the sky answers the second objection; and the metaphor of gold ore answers the third objection. Therefore, he subtly distinguished [these points], but was unable to manifest them [clearly].
Regarding the names: although the subsequent passage from "Even though it is not a direct answer" onwards is also a resolution of an objection, one might fear an objection being raised such as:
"If what was previously stated is not yet an answer to the objection regarding the Buddha’s teaching, what is its intended meaning? Therefore, the subsequent passage resolves this by stating:
"It has already been set forth as the establishment [of the categories], etc."
In the commentary on the section "Explaining the Manifestation of Doubt through Scripture and Simile," the second part, subsection one, two: the simile.
Regarding the second point, the "Direct Explanation of the Scripture’s 'When the Cataract is Removed, the Flowers Disappear,'" the commentary explains the simile of the Buddha as follows:

The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that it is like awakening from a dream, like the opening of a lotus flower, and so forth—these ten meanings have already been explained in the *Xufenchao*. Regarding the commentary on "one emptiness": this refers to the flowers; "one existence" refers to...

Regarding the analogy of the visual impairment (*timira*): according to the principle of the correspondence between the dharma and the analogy, even if the mind is deluded, it is like having a visual impairment; likewise, birth and death are also quiescent, like flowers in the sky.

Within the commentary on the correspondence between the sutra and the dharma, this doubt is identified as being extremely deep, for it not only doubts the literal meaning of the dharma but also falls into error.
The section concerning the slander of the Buddha states that the fault of claiming the Buddha has afflictions (*kleśa*) is not a minor one.

Regarding the passage in the commentary on the "Metaphor of Gold Ore" in the Sūtra, which says, "First, the gold is below; in explaining the metaphorical text, 'melting the stubborn stone,' etc.," one should establish a critical inquiry and state:
within the ore there was originally no gold; by melting the ore, the gold emerges. Within the stubborn stone, there is no gold to be melted.

"The refining of gold should produce this" is an example used to refute the opponent's position. Furthermore, it says, "If gold does not emerge when stones are refined, yet true gold is obtained by refining ore because it was already within the stone, one knows that the gold existed therein. This is a counter-example that establishes one's own thesis. Thus, one should know that true gold is merely manifested through the smelting of ore; it does not come into existence because of the smelting of ore. [The *Shu* (Commentary) applies this principle to the Dharma: [The *Shu* applies the analogy to the Dharma: "The refining of the mind should produce this" is an example used to refute the opponent's position. Furthermore, it says, "If the Buddha-nature does not emerge when afflictions are refined, yet true Buddhahood is attained by refining the afflictions because it was already within the afflictions, one knows that the nature exists therein. This is a counter-example that establishes one's own thesis. Thus, one should know that the true Buddha-nature is merely manifested through the refinement of afflictions; it does not come into existence because of the refinement of afflictions. It is like the relationship between the sun and clouds: the sun is not produced by the clouds, nor is it destroyed by them. It is merely revealed when the clouds disperse. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between gold and ore: gold is not produced by the ore, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the ore is removed. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between water and ice: ice is not produced by the water, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the water melts. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between space and clouds: space is not produced by the clouds, nor is it destroyed by them. It is merely revealed when the clouds disperse. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a mirror and dust: the mirror is not produced by the dust, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the dust is wiped away. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a lamp and darkness: the lamp is not produced by the darkness, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the darkness is dispelled. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a seed and sprouts: the sprouts are not produced by the seed, nor are they destroyed by it. They are merely revealed when the seed germinates. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a pearl and its luster: the luster is not produced by the pearl, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the pearl is polished. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a gem and its brilliance: the brilliance is not produced by the gem, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the gem is cut and polished. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a statue and its form: the form is not produced by the clay, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the clay is removed. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a vessel and its capacity: the capacity is not produced by the vessel, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the vessel is broken. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a person and their wisdom: wisdom is not produced by the person, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the person is enlightened. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a tree and its fruit: the fruit is not produced by the tree, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the fruit ripens. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a mountain and its treasure: the treasure is not produced by the mountain, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the mountain is excavated. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a field and its grain: the grain is not produced by the field, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the harvest is gathered. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a pond and its lotuses: the lotuses are not produced by the pond, nor are they destroyed by it. They are merely revealed when the pond is clear. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a mirror and its reflection: the reflection is not produced by the mirror, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the mirror is clean. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a bell and its sound: the sound is not produced by the bell, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the bell is struck. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a drum and its resonance: the resonance is not produced by the drum, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the drum is beaten. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a fire and its light: the light is not produced by the fire, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the fire is lit. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a cloud and rain: rain is not produced by the cloud, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the cloud pours forth. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a spring and its water: the water is not produced by the spring, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the spring flows. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between a river and its current: the current is not produced by the river, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the river flows. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between the earth and its vegetation: vegetation is not produced by the earth, nor is it destroyed by it. It is merely revealed when the earth is fertile. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It is like the relationship between the sky and its stars: the stars are not produced by the sky, nor are they destroyed by it. They are merely revealed when the sky is clear. Therefore, the Buddha-nature is not produced by the removal of afflictions, nor is it destroyed by their presence; it is merely revealed when afflictions are eliminated. It

The lower two [sections] explain the Dharma and harmonize the two [analogies], the first being the formal application of the commentary. Now, regarding these lower two [sections], they harmonize the two analogies. First, the harmonization of the four [points]: the first is the appearance of the two analogies;

the second is the intent of the commentary explaining the meaning of the two analogies; the third is the clarification that if one were to take only one [analogy], there would be the fault of partiality; and the fourth is the conclusion on the grounds for taking both together. The first is the appearance of the two analogies.

The second is the intent of the commentary explaining the meaning of the two analogies. The third is the clarification that if one were to take only one [analogy], there would be the fault of partiality. The fourth is the conclusion on the grounds for taking both together. Regarding the principle: the fourth is the conclusion on the grounds for taking both together.
It should be understood that the concluding summaries and the explanatory passages for the latter two [sections] below can likewise be understood.
Regarding the passage in the commentary on the *Sūtra*’s section on "creating detachment from thought" which first cites "the awakened mind," etc.:

in various teachings, there is often a dual negation of opposites, such as the phrases "neither true nor false. However, these do not explicitly state what kind of dharma it is that is neither true nor false; they merely [indicate] that it is neither.

Because it negates [the existence of] non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), those of middling and inferior capacity might thereby fall into the view of nihilism. Now, to speak directly and explicitly:
the wondrous, perfect, and enlightened mind has no such real entities as "bodhi" and so forth; this may truly be called the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Regarding "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): bodhi and nirvāṇa are the two fruits of transformation. It is precisely by transforming birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) that one attains nirvāṇa, and by transforming the afflictions...
"Because one attains bodhi through affliction (*kleśa*), this meaning shall be further explained in the lower stages.

[Question: Although the essence is identical to the True, the essence is the body of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*) and its function is bodhi; since this true essence and function are themselves Perfect Enlightenment, how can it be said that they do not exist?
The Commentary answers: 'Although the essence is identical to the True,' etc. This word "essence" (*tǐ*) refers to the whole.
The two dharmas of bodhi and nirvāṇa refer to their own essential natures; it does not speak of the essence as it relates to their functions—let the wise examine this.
Regarding the sūtra’s capacity to produce [the commentary] within the context of the "Bearing Sentiment" section, the sub-sections are divided into two parts, followed by the sequential explanation.
In the *Sūtra*, within the context of the true awakening of the ordinary mind, the "subtle sage" and the "true wise one" refer to the wisdom of the emptiness of birth (*jātī-śūnyatā-jñāna*).

This emptiness of birth is precisely the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). The principle of the subtle sage refers to the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the emptiness of self and person;

it means that at the locus where self and person are empty, one realizes the principle of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), which is not merely a state of non-existence. Therefore, it is called "true suchness. In the topical outline (*kośa*) of the Sūtra, this is designated as "non-substantiality" (*a-vastu*).

"Essence" (tǐ) refers to this mind being fundamentally empty and nameless from the outset; it is called "without essence" because it is not merely that its essence is discussed in contrast to its function and thus found to be non-existent.

In the commentary on the concluding question of the sutra, there are two parts: first, a superficial examination to distinguish and eliminate confusion; second, a thorough resolution of objections. This is the latter.
A certain section of the commentary’s prose is clear and subtle, requiring no further explanation; however, the lecturer must necessarily expound upon the intent of the commentary.

Regarding the presence or absence of the commentary within the chanting of the sutra verses: where the long prose lacks [the commentary], there is reliance on understanding, the arousal of practice, and a concluding inquiry that does not accord with reason;
whereas where the verses lack [the commentary], there is reliance on understanding, the arousal of practice, and a concluding inquiry that does not accord with reason.
A Commentary on the Profound Investigation of the Causes of Saṃsāra, Part Two, Section One, Chapter Three: Explaining the Intent of the Outline. Commentary on the Sūtra Text, Part One:

Celebrating What Precedes. Sub-commentary: Regarding the Five Eyes—First, the Fleshly Eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*): This refers to the pure form within the physical mass of flesh that is able to see forms obstructed from view.
Second, the Divine Eye (*divya-cakṣus*): This is the pure divine eye, drawn forth from the vicinity of the fleshly eye, which sees forms beyond obstructions. Third... [text continues]

The wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) perceives the truth through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) teaches the Dharma and delivers sentient beings through subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).

Regarding the five Buddha-eyes, the first four exist within all Buddhas and are collectively termed the Buddha-eye; furthermore, because the realization of one's nature is perfectly consummate, it is called the Buddha-eye. Thus, an ancient master said:
"The divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) is unobstructed, while the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is obstructed and lacks penetration; the dharma-eye observes only the conventional."
The Wisdom-Eye directly contemplates emptiness, while the Buddha-Eye is like the thousand suns illuminating all things; though their manifestations differ, their essence remains the same.

Other meanings are found in a separate fascicle. Regarding "wondrous faith" (*miao-xin*) in the Commentary: according to the intent of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, not believing in any [provisional] names is called "wondrous faith.

Wondrous faith is the wisdom that is capable of believing, while the eternally abiding [Dharma] is the object of that belief. This present sutra speaks of generating certainty regarding the Great Nirvana.

Because of established faith, it cites the abiding nature of wondrous faith as proof [that the eternally abiding is Great Nirvāṇa]. Alternatively, this mind of wondrous faith is simply able to abide eternally, without retreating or losing [its essence];
thus, both meanings—that delusive thoughts are extinguished and that [the mind] abides eternally—are applicable.
Regarding the phrase "not clinging to the movement of the moon" and so forth: although a metaphor is raised, the intent lies in the Dharma. "Dharma" refers here to the beginning of all worlds.

It refers to the arising and ceasing of the world and so forth. However, although those present at the assembly have attained realization of the Buddha’s teaching, they do not cease to perceive the signs of the world’s arising and ceasing;
rather, they understand that these arise from the transformations of the mind and that these transforming appearances are themselves empty.
Because they do not grasp them or recognize them as real, the Sūtra says, "they no longer follow after them," which does not mean that they do not see them at all before their eyes.
In the *Sūtra on Asking about Severing Saṃsāra*, regarding the phrase "desiring to roam in quiescence" (*śānti*), it is said that because one does not abide in nirvāṇa, one is said to "roam.
In the *Sūtra on Cultivating Compassion and Wisdom*, regarding the commentary’s statement "the dharma-gates are boundless," this corresponds to two of the Four Great Vows.

When a Bodhisattva first resolves their mind [on enlightenment], they must necessarily possess these four; now, practicing the path in reliance upon these vows, how could one possibly be separated from them?
Previously, it was asked regarding the severing of saṃsāra: "I vow to sever all afflictions, though they are boundless. Now, it is asked regarding the cultivation of bodhi:

this is precisely the vow to accomplish the unsurpassed Buddha-way. Since one desires to accomplish the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*), one must extensively study the various Dharma-gates; therefore, in this regard—
In the question, this vow is already subsumed; its entry into the mundane world to save sentient beings is self-evident in the text, and thus the Four Great Vows are fully present.

Regarding the phrase "a little hot water adding ice": hot water is like wisdom and ice is like affliction. If one enters the mundane world with little wisdom to transform and save beings, they will unconsciously develop worldly thoughts themselves.
This is like using a small amount of hot water to melt ice—the hot water itself becomes frozen. Previously, when I was in the capital, I intended to... [text ends]
When entering the mountains, there was once a verse that said: "Throwing hot water into the ice-pool, the ice melts; yet when the ice hardens, the hot water also congeals.
If one throws the ice into the cauldron, the needle and the mustard seed naturally correspond. Having spoken this verse, he entered the mountains until the present day.
Regarding "great compassion born of attachment and views," the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "That sick bodhisattva should further form this thought: 'This illness of mine is not real.'"

There is no such thing as a disease of sentient beings, nor is it real; when one contemplates in this way, if one gives rise to a great compassion based on attachment or views toward sentient beings, one should immediately abandon it.
Why is this? Because a Bodhisattva eliminates adventitious afflictions while giving rise to great compassion;

however, one whose compassion is based on attachment or views will develop a sense of weariness and exhaustion regarding birth and death. If one can remain free from these, [one attains true compassion].

Being free from weariness, wherever one is born, one is not shrouded by craving or views; this extends even to the point where those lacking skillful means are bound by wisdom, while those possessing skillful means are liberated by wisdom.

Regarding the concluding benefits of the sutra, the commentary states that "the mind is like a pure, bright mirror," meaning that the fundamental nature of the minds of all sentient beings is inherently pure.

A bright mirror is not like a mirror stained by dust; rather, it is because the Sixth Patriarch Master Huineng’s eye of wisdom was so pure and clear that he could illuminate [all things], whereas the deluded and confused commoner cannot.
Therefore, the Sixth Patriarch can transmit the seal of the mind (*cittamudrā*); it is not that the Sixth Patriarch’s mind alone is like a pure mirror.
This is merely explained according to conventional truth within the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), as one gradually severs habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The method for this is like wiping away dust until the mirror of the mind is bright;

however, the origin of this verse has already been fully explained in the eighth section of the *Xuántán*, the "Gate of the Graded Stages of Cultivation and Realization. The commentary (*shù*) is identical to the *Lotus Sūtra*, which states:
"Desiring to cause sentient beings to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*). Vasubandhu’s commentary (*ṭīkā*) judges that "opening" signifies the meaning of the unsurpassed.

This refers to the simultaneous opening of the two unsurpassed states of bodhi and nirvāṇa; that is to say, because there is no other matter beyond all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*), it is called "unsurpassed.
Since the "unsurpassed knowledge and vision" mentioned in the present sutra corresponds precisely to this meaning, it is said to be identical.
Regarding the phrase "the pure cycle of saṃsāra" from the commentary on the section praising [the Buddha] in the sutra: if one speaks within the midst of defiled dust, [it is as follows].
To discuss categories within the context of saṃsāra and its various distinctions is merely superficial, for such is the common understanding of ordinary people.

Now, the textual passages of these three chapters have already revealed that ignorance has no real substance; fundamentally, there is no body or mind, nor birth, death, sense organs, or objects—internally or externally, nothing is not pure.
Perfect Enlightenment (Samantabhadra-cakra) shines universally, quiescent and non-dual, extending even to all things.
Sentient beings have been fundamentally enlightened from the beginning; through successive revelations, their principle and wisdom have been clearly manifested.
Now, within this pure clarity, the dharma of saṃsāra is questioned and answered, and within this non-duality, the various categories of differentiation are questioned and answered.
Therefore, this constitutes a profound, secret, and subtle meaning.
The commentary on the *Sūtra on Enduring the Non-arising of Dharmas* (*Anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti-sūtra*) may be consulted for further explanation.

Since dharmas are non-arising, they are likewise without cessation; thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "One does not perceive even the slightest dharma arising or ceasing. Why is this? Because if there is no arising, there is no cessation.
Furthermore, it says: "All dharmas are without arising; all dharmas are without cessation. If one can understand in this way, the Buddhas are ever-present.

In the *Formerly Entrusted Sutra on Entering the Seal through the Power of Faith* (*Xianhu shixin ruyin jing*), there is also the "patience of non-extinction" (*anujñāna-akṣaya-kṣānti*) along with further meanings, as fully detailed in the *Great Commentary* (*Dashu*) and the *Great Sub-commentary* (*Dacao*). In the prose section of the sutra, the commentary divides it into two parts, the first being the sub-section "Tracing the Root and Branches to Effect Severance. Regarding the term "root": [The text continues: ...the root refers to the fundamental ignorance (*avidyā-mūla*). By tracing back to this root, one brings about its severance. This is because all afflictions and outflows arise from the root of ignorance; therefore, if one can sever the root of ignorance, all other afflictions will naturally be extinguished. Furthermore, the "root" here specifically refers to the delusion regarding the nature of reality (*dharmatā-viparyāsa*). Since this delusion is the primary cause for the arising of all subsequent afflictions and karmic formations, the text instructs that one must trace back to this ultimate source to effect its total severance. Thus, by understanding the origin and the derivative manifestations, one is led to cut off the very foundation of cyclic existence. This is the meaning of the phrase "tracing the root and branch to effect severance. The "branch" refers to the various secondary afflictions and karmic actions that manifest based upon that root. By understanding their dependence upon the root, one realizes that they are empty of inherent existence and thereby severs them at their source. This method of practice ensures that the practitioner does not merely suppress superficial symptoms but eradicates the underlying cause. Therefore, the text emphasizes that true liberation requires this thorough investigation into the fundamental nature of the mind and phenomena. This principle is consistent throughout the Mahayana teachings, where the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) serves as the means to uproot the ignorance that sustains the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). As stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā* scriptures, "If one wishes to extinguish all suffering, one must first extinguish all afflictions; and if one wishes to extinguish all afflictions, one must first extinguish ignorance. This is the essential point of the path of cultivation. Thus, the instruction to "trace the root and branch" is a profound directive for practitioners to engage in the analytical wisdom (*prajñā*) that penetrates the ultimate truth. Through such practice, one attains the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*) and enters the seal of the Dharma (*dharmamudrā*). This concludes the explanation of the first sub-section. The second sub-section follows, which addresses the specific methods for severing the secondary afflictions once the root has been identified. [End of excerpt].
That which is the end of craving is precisely the five destinies; this answers the first question. Second, regarding the explanation of the spiritual lineages (*gotra*):
these are the five natures newly perfumed. Through the cultivation of craving and encountering various teachings, distinct spiritual lineages are perfumed and formed.

The intent in instructing others to know this is that they must not follow after the many [diverse paths], but must instead accord with their own minds, taking only the bodhicitta as the foundation. Do not... [the text ends here].
