Regarding the two interpretations of the Dharma as one, the first correctly reveals its essence. Regarding the second interpretation of what is excluded, the Sūtra says: "That which is devoid of cognition and clarity.

Here, "devoid of cognition" is an *apavāda* (negation) and "clarity" is a *vidhi* (affirmation); this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive compound), meaning "the clarity belonging to that which is devoid of cognition.

"Devoid of cognition" is a negation (*paryudāsa*), while "clarity" is an affirmation (*vidhi*) indicating the true nature of numinous luminosity. As for the phrase in the Commentary, "the body and mind that are realized," this refers to the objects of this contemplation.
This differs from the previous contemplation because the previous contemplation took the body and mind as its object of cognition;
thus, there is no "knower" distinct from the mind, nor is there an "experiencer" distinct from the body. Consequently, it subsequently states: "the body touches, the mind conditions," and so forth.
Now, "body-touch" includes the three faculties of nose, tongue, and body, because they all cognize by being conjoined with their respective organs, and these organs belong to the body.

Regarding "the mind taking objects as its condition": this refers to the three consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and mind, because they discern their objects through contact with external things (*bahir-viṣaya*).

"Discrimination arising from this" is a general term for all these consciousnesses. That which "obstructs right knowledge and vision" refers to the essence of the numinous and wondrous mind; this is called "right knowledge and vision.
This is because it was previously stated that "principles obstruct right knowledge and vision," and later it will be said, "perfectly awakening to unsurpassed knowledge and vision. Subsequently:

One should seek those who possess correct knowledge and vision (*samyag-jñāna-darśana*). Therefore, this [text] specifically designates "knowledge and vision" as that which is obstructed, while simultaneously indicating that its essential nature (*svabhāva*) is the luminosity of non-cognition.

Furthermore, because there may be doubt that even "true knowledge" is coarse and shallow based on the phrase "luminosity of non-cognition," it is necessary to completely sublate [all such distinctions];
thus, it is singled out for emphasis. If one were to say that non-knowledge is itself true knowledge, that too would be incorrect.

Since it has already been stated that there is no "awakening" (*jue*), it follows that "that which is awakened to" (*juesheng*) must likewise be non-existent; how then can this school maintain that its doctrine concerns only awakening?
When the lecturer reaches this point, he must certainly provide clear clarification for his students. The commentary (*shu*) correctly reveals the following two explanations of what is signified:

first, "directly revealing the correct" refers to the very essence of the principle that is the primary tenet of this contemplation; therefore, its characteristics are extensively elucidated. Its... [text fragment ends].
Although the phrasing is easy, the method is extremely profound; it must be clearly revealed at the time of explanation.

It cannot be fully exhausted through successive textual commentaries, but is merely indicated according to the text in a concise and abbreviated manner. △ [The] Commentary: From "Now, this... below, there are two parts clarifying the incomparability [of the Buddha].
First, clarifying the incomparability by way of its own essence; the upper and lower sections can be understood as before. "Side" refers to the four directions.
"Center" means that where one is situated, there is no place of abiding; this reveals the absence of a center.

Generally speaking, when we speak of a "center," it is defined by taking the precise location where one’s own body resides as the center, thereby distinguishing east from west and above from below. Now, since the characteristics of body and mind are not grasped, there is neither center nor periphery, nor above nor below.
The Commentary intends to explain that the following two pairs clarify that all phenomena are peerless and do not arise from conditions.

As for "arising," when the conditions for those phenomena converge, they arise; when the conditions separate, they cease. The numinous mind is not like this, and therefore it does not follow [the laws of conditioned arising].
The rest is easy to understand, but I fear you may not yet perceive that Dharma; contemplate it well. [Commentary: Thus, in the following three sections, the ritual of the discourse is explained.
As for the censure of [those who hold] heterodox or Hinayana views: if one were to speak exclusively of emptiness and quiescence, from the perspective of outsiders...

The Way does not recognize the clinging to the nature of darkness as real; rather, it refutes the false reckonings of the Hīnayāna which hold that three or four [unconditioned phenomena] are all truly unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Bhāviveka remained deluded even regarding this, adhering one-sidedly to the meaning of emptiness; therefore, various sūtras and śāstras condemn him as a heterodox follower of the Lesser Vehicle.

All sūtras state that indulgence in emptiness and stagnation in quiescence are the practices of the two vehicles, and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of practitioners of the two vehicles falling into the pit of the unconditioned.
Furthermore, a sutra states: "It would be better to fall [into existence] as large as Mount Sumeru than to fall into emptiness as small as a mustard seed.

The *Yingluo jing* says: "One may delight in practicing the tranquil conduct of a pratyekabuddha. In Master Zhaolun’s *Buzhenkong lun*, he refutes the school of "Original Non-being" (*benwu*), stating:

"As for 'Original Non-being,' they are emotionally attached to non-being; they frequently encounter words and treat non-being as their guest. Therefore, what is not existent is immediately non-existent; it is not that existence itself is non-existent."

"Non-existence of non-existence" means there is no seeking; this is the intent behind establishing the text (seeking the original meaning of the scripture). It simply states that "not existent" does not mean truly existent, and "not non-existent" does not mean truly non-existent.
Why must it be "not existent and non-existent"? This "existence" is not "non-existence," and that "non-existence" is not "this.

This is merely a discourse fond of "non-existence"; how could it be said to accord with the facts of reality or the nature of things? Regarding such views as "knowledge and vision" and so forth... (Note: The final phrase "於知見等者" appears to be an incomplete citation or a transition marker indicating that the preceding critique applies to various specific doctrinal positions.)

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Avataṃsaka*, this is termed the "Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision" (*tathāgata-jñāna-darśana*) based on the illumination and function that are identical to the essence;

within the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, it is called "wondrous clarity," "original clarity," and "perfect clarity. Now, in this scripture and various treatises, it is all termed "awakening" (*bodhi*), whether from the perspective of the essence or from the perspective of its function—each represents a distinct meaning.
Thus, while the establishment of these names and characteristics differs, they are here said to be complete.

By negating the manifest and selecting the dharma, the name "not named" is established; the character "clear" (ming) is forcibly applied. [Commentary: Now, the following four sections conclude and demonstrate the meaning of the sutra;

the text is clear and can be understood as it stands. [Commentary: Regarding the second section, "all obstructions," etc., it explains the transcendence of the basis (*āśraya*) and the distinction from relative counterparts.

This refers to such dualities as body and mind, truth and falsehood, cause and effect, defilement and purity, and ordinary beings versus sages—just as those of the Two Vehicles transcend [such distinctions].
The three realms are contrasted with what lies outside the three realms; Bodhisattvas are contrasted with those who transcend the Two Vehicles, resulting in the distinction between Great and Small;

Buddhas are contrasted with Bodhisattvas who transcend them, resulting in the distinction between cause and fruit; even so for the contaminated and the uncontaminated, and the conditioned and the unconditioned—it is all like this.
Now, when one darkly merges with the numinous mind, none of these distinctions apply; this is called being no inferior to the Buddha.
It is not superior to the ordinary, does not emerge from the mundane world, and does not belong to the three realms (and so forth, with many such examples). For instance,
while the untainted noble ones are unimpeded and tainted ordinary beings are impeded, since [this state] has forever transcended both the realms of the impeded and the unimpeded,
how could it be like the aforementioned phenomena of mutual opposition?
Regarding the passage on "obstructed and unobstructed objects," the commentary contains three points of interpretation for obstructed and unobstructed states:

1. It transcends the two gates of first grasping at stillness and subsequently giving rise to illusions. Because taking the conditions for arising illusions as objects constitutes obstruction, while stillness having no object of focus constitutes non-obstruction, the preceding text states:
"Do not grasp at illusory transformations or various signs of stillness. 2. It transcends both afflictions (*kleśa*) and nirvāṇa. Afflictions are bound... [text fragment] ...to the world.

Bondage constitutes an obstruction, while liberation from *nirvāṇa* constitutes non-obstruction; therefore, the subsequent passage states that afflictions and *nirvāṇa* do not mutually obstruct one another.

Thirdly, the body, mind, sensory objects (*viṣaya*), and realms are collectively termed "obstructions. If one were to define "non-obstruction" merely as the mind’s detachment [from these], it would not apply here in all cases;
rather, because [the practitioner] is detached from them all, it is said they have "transcended" them. This includes both the arising of illusions and afflictions.
"Affliction" constitutes one meaning, while "quiescence" and "nirvāṇa" are taken together as a single meaning to form a pair;
this is the intended sense of the character *shè* (涉) in the preceding phrase and the character *tóng* (同) in the following phrase.

To synthesize the preceding phrase means that one gives rise to illusory wisdom to eliminate illusions, and further desires to transform all illusions and open the gates for the illusory multitude, directing the attention of each and every mental factor.
To stir and weary the mind and its deliberations—even if this involves contemplative wisdom—is still to engage with afflictions; it is likewise an act of disturbance.
For this reason, the intent here is that the arising of illusions constitutes an obstruction of the afflictions, rather than specifically referring to afflictions such as greed and hatred.

As for the connection to the following phrase: it means to single-mindedly pursue stillness, which is identical to the two vehicles’ loathing of birth-and-death and craving for nirvana—an attachment [to quiescence].

Since emptiness, stagnation, stillness, and nirvāṇa are all unimpeded dharmas, and because the aspect of "attaining stillness" (*śānti-lakṣaṇa*) belongs to this category, it is said that they are "the same.
This meaning takes the attainment of stillness as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of nirvāṇa;

it does not separately explain nirvāṇa as the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha-asaṃskṛta*), nor as the extinction of the body and the cessation of wisdom (*jñāna*). Therefore, this pair is distinct from the previous ones, which were explained individually.
The third point concerns "that which belongs to oneself. This refers to all the causes, conditions, and requisites for one's own enjoyment, including houses, fields, gardens, groves, and towers;
or even those villages and districts governed by kings and officials—all such things are termed "belonging to oneself" as articles of enjoyment.
When the practice of contemplation in this gate is perfected and the mind merges with the spiritual source, these [objects] appear vividly...

Nevertheless, as before, there is still no thought of conceptualization—such as grasping or rejecting, or calculating existence and non-existence—and it is shared with those dwelling together in kingdoms and cities.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other treatises state that this trichiliocosm is produced by the collective karma of sentient beings;
noble and base, humans and animals, and all various types of sentient beings rely upon it together to dwell, which is called the "retributive environment" (*niśraya-vipāka*) of one's own body.

Thus, according to their respective karma, there are differences in status—noble or lowly—and experiences—suffering or pleasure—as well as distinctions among species such as birds and beasts; these are termed "individual karmic retribution.
My current intention concerns ordinary people, who are easily perceived, and thus I speak directly of those who "dwell together in nations and towns.
This refers to either a single Jambudvīpa, or a single Aparagoyānī, or a single Great T'ang, or a single Tibetan territory, and so forth—whether broad or narrow.

Whether universal or limited, that which is appropriate to a particular soil and water, produced by local customs, originating from specific mountains and rivers, or transformed by royal law—all may be termed a "world" (*loka-dhātu*).

It is not necessarily the case that it must be a trichiliocosm (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*), for the scope of the human mind when practicing contemplative cultivation need not pervade the entire great thousandfold world-system.
Thus, regarding those who have seen or heard [of such worlds], the commentary briefly cites two examples.

Using one consciousness as an analogy for the others, and citing the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) as an illustration for the mental factors (*caitta*), these various modes of perception and deliberation do not differ from ordinary states when one has not yet cultivated contemplation;
they merely lack the deliberate mental calculation [of a practitioner]. "Passing through the realm of dust" refers to the domain of the sensory objects of the emotions reached thus far.
The commentary on "spiritual illumination" (*lingzhao*) means that the very essence of the spiritual mind possesses the great radiance of wisdom, which pervades...
Because it illuminates the meaning of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), Vairocana is the body of the dharma-realm; in this land [China], his name is translated as "Universal Illumination.
Other terms that have not been explained may be sought according to one's own understanding.

In the commentary on the character *huáng* (鍠), there are two explanations of the analogy (*yù*). First, regarding the "basis of the analogy" (*yù-yī*): this refers to the object upon which the analogy relies.
This is because the physical object is not the illustrative property (*néng-yù-fǎ*), nor is the dharma the illustrated property (*suǒ-yù*); these two are entirely distinct.

However, when the meaning (*yì*) residing in the object resembles the meaning residing in the dharma, it is these two meanings that constitute the illustrative property and the illustrated property. It is like taking a *vajra* [as an illustration].
To use the diamond as a metaphor for *prajñā*: if one grasps at them as two distinct phenomena, there is no connection between them.
That is to say, the diamond has form and characteristics, whereas *prajñā* is formless. The diamond is a tool for discernment, yet how could it ever discern phenomena?

*Prajñā* encompasses all virtues, even down to its wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; the diamond possesses none of these. Nevertheless, we take it as a metaphor solely to express the meaning of being firm and sharp.
"Vajra" refers to that which is so firm that nothing can destroy it, yet it is capable of shattering all things—this is its quality of sharpness (*li*).

One who practices the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is likewise firm and cannot be moved or turned by the celestial Māras, non-Buddhists, afflictions (*kleśa*), ignorance (*avidyā*), or any other obstacles—this is its quality of firmness.
It is capable of severing the afflictions and illuminating the emptiness of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*)—this is its quality of sharpness. However, one should grasp only these two qualities.
Each of these possesses the meanings of "firm" and "sharp," which immediately constitute a metaphor (*dṛṣṭānta*). A metaphor is an illustration through the principle of similarity;

it is used to illustrate and cause understanding. Now, those who wish to examine the holy teachings in their entirety, or who lecture on or listen to their meanings, study them, cultivate meditative wisdom (*dhyāna-prajñā*), or investigate and debate their principles, must clearly understand the intent behind the correspondence between the Dharma and its metaphors. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The wise person, by means of..."

The analogy for attaining understanding is that one does not call a fool "ignorant" [if they are merely confused]. Regarding the uncertainty of the character *shū* (鍠), when investigating its glosses and explanations, this character is not used in the sense of sound;
furthermore, it is not entirely incorrect to adopt its intended meaning, as it can still be interpreted accordingly.

However, because there is doubt regarding the meaning, three interpretations have been preserved. As for "metal, stone, etc.," the "etc. includes copper, iron, and their like, or even within jade and stone, there may be [such qualities].

"Clear and far-reaching" refers to sound; "the characteristics of sound" refers to the appearance and qualities of sound, such as its clarity or turbidity, and its high or low pitch—meaning it resembles these traits.
As for the term "huáng-huáng," one can simply imagine the resonance of striking a bell or a stone chime to understand it.
In the local customs of Bānán, the braying of a donkey is also called the "huáng-huáng" sound; however, that is heavy and dull, unlike the clear and far-reaching reverberation of a bell or chime.
When translating the scriptures, the Indian monk recited the Sanskrit text, while those who understood both languages translated it into the language of Tang (Chinese) and recorded it in writing;
this was called "receiving the pen" (*bishou*). Since the order of words in the Indian language is reversed compared to this [Chinese], it must be rearranged into a literary style (*huíwén*);

furthermore, as that language is plain, it must be polished (*rùn*). Now, regarding what is called "plainness" (*zhuó*): sound is the essence (*tǐ*) and resonance (*huáng*) is the characteristic (*xiàng*); first... [the text continues].
The combined term refers to sound; specifically, "the great bell" (*dàzhōng*) is the explanation given in the *Qièyùn* (Explanations of Pronunciation), which is synonymous with *yóng*. Question:
If this is so, since *huáng* is a material substance, why do you not say "sound within the *huáng*," but instead say "*huáng* within the vessel"?

Therefore, the following response clarifies this point by stating "these various vessels, etc. This means that among those various vessels, there is one particular vessel made of gold (or copper, iron, and so forth) named [the *huáng*].

As for the *huáng* (gong): when striking this gong, the sound emerges from within while the external form is very harmonious; therefore, it is said that by following this principle, one accords with the original text and so forth.

As for "but the scribes and others," it is truly because the two pronunciations *huáng* and *huáng* are entirely identical, and furthermore, both characters are written with the "metal" (*jīn*) radical;
since the two characters *huáng* and *hóng* are also phonetically identical, they are easily confused. As for the "reeds of the *shēng*" (panpipes), there are four [types].
(The appearance is as follows: The *sheng* has seventeen tubes, each tube containing one reed; they differ in length. When blown, the air vibrates through the middle [of the tubes] to produce sound.
If the pitch is not correct, there is a small piece of tin, about the size of a grain of chaff, upon the fan-like mouthpiece;

by shifting it up or down, one adjusts the tonal quality—this is called "tuning" (*diao*). [The character "qing" (please/request) is likely a scribal error for "qing" (clear/pure). This refers to the category of wind instruments such as the *guan* and *yue*.
The *Cien Weishi Shu* (Ci'en’s Commentary on the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi) states: "Because there is wind within, sounds and so forth arise.
Furthermore, the *Laozi Daodejing* says: "The space between heaven and earth is like a bellows; it is empty yet inexhaustible, moving and ever-yielding. (He Shang Gong’s commentary notes:

"The interior of the bellows is empty, therefore it can produce sound and breath; there is no time when it is exhausted. The more it is moved, the more it yields. Wang Bi’s commentary states: "If the bellows maintains its center, it is without end; by discarding the self and entrusting to things, all things find their principle. It emerges from the bellows..."

If the *yè* (flute) has a fixed intention regarding its sound, it will be insufficient to meet the requirements of the player. That explanation addresses two matters; here we take only the *yè*, because it is an object that produces sound. The *tuó* (bellows) refers to types such as bags, bellows, or pouches, which are not objects that produce sound.

These categories—such as pipes, flutes, and transverse flutes—are consistent with the meaning of the analogy in the Sūtra. Regarding the phrase "both are erroneous": this refers to taking the character for *huáng* (簧, reed) as *huāng* (鍠, gong), and taking the *huáng* (黃, yellow) tone as the *héng* (橫, horizontal) tone.
[In the commentary] following the "Correct" section, the second part correctly explains the analogy. Third, although they differ: *huāng* (鐄), *huáng* (簧).
All these are also "penetrating" (tong): the three objects, as well as body and mind, cannot constrain that which issues forth (the sound and the spiritual luminosity).
Furthermore, it does not depart from within oneself, yet one cannot reach it; thus, both the Dharma and the analogy are congruent. The *Sushuo* (Explanatory Notes) states:
The following three citations introduce the interpretations of others. A *jun* is thirty *jin*. A *yong* is a large bell. A *xinglou* is a neighboring watchtower.
Regarding the phrase "the high towers of stars and moon throughout the realm": the term "realm" (huanyu) refers to the division of the world into nations, districts, capitals, and cities;
it need not imply pervading the entire universe. "Self-substance" (ziti) refers to the bell (*yong*), while "others" refer to the towers.

As for the unavoidable doubt, the commentary clarifies that the word "only" (*wei*) indicates striking the bell, yet when returning to the original text to provide a counter-explanation, the term "pipe" (*guan*) is further added.
One immediately recognizes this, yet again suspects that the *yong* (bell) is not the *huang* (the resonance within). Therefore, one further sifts through it with a tube.

Furthermore, even if one does not know that the translations of the scriptures are inconsistent, according to the explanations found in the extant scriptural texts, they are also deficient. For the scripture states: "As when the *huang* within a vessel produces a sound that goes outside.
This implies that the vessel is not the *huang*; rather, it is the *huang* within the vessel. The *huang* is not the sound itself; it is the *huang* that is capable [of producing the sound].

When a sound is produced, is it not manifest that the three aspects [the source, the medium, and the resonance] are each distinct? Now, the commentary states: "A bell of ten thousand *jin*—this is the instrument.
It then says, "Its sound vibrates throughout the world. Is this not omitting the character *huáng* (the resonance) and lacking one layer of meaning?

Regarding the phrase "unable to resolve or penetrate," it further means that the translations and glosses are inconsistent and lack definitive judgment. Furthermore, it asks: what is the definition of *huáng*?
Is it the bell that is the object? Or is it the flute? Furthermore, it does not say they are both objects, nor does it say they are both the sounds of those two objects.
Is it then to be taken as the sound of the bell alone? Is this not a vague and indistinct description?
To be "vague" (*ān-ǎ*) means to be muddled and to contain only the general meaning; the *Qieyun* commentary explains it as being indecisive.
Furthermore, since there is no definitive textual evidence for this, if someone were to challenge you point by point based on the preceding sections, with what words could you respond?
If you encounter one who lectures on that commentary, you may explain it in detail out of compassion;

however, the commentator’s own nature was inclined toward later refinement and lacked depth. His straightforward prose and logical analysis of the scriptural text, while indeed worthy of appreciation, are nonetheless somewhat thin.
As for the profound meanings of the sūtras and śāstras, they do not at all accord with his intent;

consequently, his word-by-word commentary is frequently omitted and incomplete across various sections, nor does he investigate the underlying coherence between preceding and succeeding passages of the sūtra.
Among these, the explanation of this particular section alone is relatively clear and explicit, while the rest remains even more deficient and abbreviated, consisting merely of three phrases each.
Both lines are merely remote [from the point at hand]. In the passages I have cited from that text both before and after, I have selected only those where the principle is immediately applicable;
my aim was to provide corroboration for our shared doctrine of the rational nature (*dharmatā*), while also being unwilling to overlook even a fragment of another’s merit.
Yet, I have never added a single new meaning—the divine principle behind this intention can be understood. My intent is also the same as before.

This is because [the author] previously cited a mistranslation from the *Yijing* and applied it according to his own interpretation; only then, upon examining this text by Master Guo, did it happen to accord with it.

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "still in accordance with the Dharma" (*fahé*), this was possible because the commentary (*shū*) provided a specific correlation between the teaching and the analogy for others;
however, according to the explanations in that *Jì* (Commentary) and the oral traditions of lecturers, such a statement does not exist. — *Shū* (Commentary)

As in the third explanation of the "vessel" analogy, the commentary on the section concerning the "accomplishment of merit" does not adopt [the view of] "illusory transformations" (*māyā-nirmāṇa*) and so forth. Although illusory transformations are empty, they do not destroy their conventional appearance;
however, because one does not grasp at the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that is fundamentally unarisen, it is said to be "quiescent. This simply means not forming a mental intention (*manasikāra*).
Grasping does not obstruct the spontaneous, vivid perception of things as they appear; therefore, one speaks only of "quiescence" (*śānta*) and not of "extinction.
This state of quiescence is fundamentally not a characteristic (*nimitta*); it becomes a characteristic only when grasped by the mind as an object of cognition (*ālambana*).

When one empties the mind and forgets its illumination, no longer grasping it as an object, this characteristic immediately ceases. It is unlike illusory appearances, which continue to manifest spontaneously and clearly.

"Cessation" (nirodha) refers merely to the cessation of the characteristics of these objects of perception; it does not mean that there is a "quiescence" (śānti) which can be ceased, for quiescence signifies the stilling of the mind and is not an objective realm.
Furthermore, this is explained through the method of "substance-overcoming" (kètǐ). Nevertheless, upon the true mind, there are sands and dusts of principles;
yet all of these are but the phenomenal functions (xiàngyòng) that follow conditions. Only quiescent extinction (jímíè) is the principle of the true, essential substance.
Therefore, it is said that on the level of ultimate reality (*tattva*), the quiescence of the two dharmas—illusion and stillness—is the middle way of negation (*paryudāsa*).
Now, the quiescence of the one mind is taught as the middle way of affirmation (*vidhi*). This means that this true mind is, in its very essence, primordially quiescent;

it is not called "quiescent" because it lacks substance during movement, nor is it called "extinguished" because it ceases to exist after having arisen. Thus, it was previously stated: "Perfect Enlightenment universally illumines and is quiescent."
The extinction of non-duality is likewise the "one mind" of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*; therefore, it is said that "it arises within. This concludes by returning to the intent of the scripture:
all are without mind, and each is naturally quiescent. This differs from what was mentioned above; because it is the extinction through quiescence, it is called "arising within.
The phrase "arising within" carries the meaning of the spontaneous accomplishment of the Way.

Regarding the passage "self, others, and so forth," the commentary provides two levels of correlation for self and others: first, taking other people as "others" and one's own mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as "self";

second, taking the mental consciousness itself as "others" (because it arises only by borrowing external conditions) and awakening as "self" (because it is merely the manifestation of original awakening).
As for the phrase "only oneself and so forth," this refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; while that sūtra speaks of the purification of the faculty of mind (*manas*), this [text] speaks of...

The commentary on the "Attainment of Contemplative Wisdom" (*vipaśyanā-jñāna-siddhi*) also explains that the corresponding stages are equivalent. Regarding the phrase "that which is sustained by mere ideation":

just as in a dream, the body, mind, sense faculties, and consciousness are merely sustained by the dream-ideation and possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); this can be understood through the application of the principle of continuity.

The intent of the commentary lies in the fact that these are images easily seen before one's eyes; therefore, it employs the metaphor of empty clouds. If one discusses the intimacy of phenomena and principle (*dharmatā*), [the meaning] becomes clear.
The correspondence between the root and the branches is not as effective as the analogy of a dream.
Regarding the conclusion of the title in the commentary (Sūtra-vyākhyāna), this section provides an explanation of what was concluded.

First, the direct translation and explanation of "dhyāna" (静慮) is as explained previously in the section on the four *dhyānas*. The phrase "not indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) is intended to clarify that it does not exclusively tend toward [a specific state].

Because it is quiescent, submerged in emptiness, and lacks the capacity for discernment, it is called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*); this is not the same as the indeterminate [category] among the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Regarding the equality of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), the sūtras and śāstras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna state that in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) wisdom is predominant, while in the four formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) concentration is predominant;

only in the fourth dhyāna are concentration and wisdom equal. Since dhyāna necessarily includes concentration, whereas concentration does not necessarily include dhyāna, there are eight types of concentration.

Regarding "Chan," there are only four [points]. In the commentary, the subsequent two questions and answers clarify that one who directly reaches the source of the mind does so through neither concentration (*samādhi*) nor wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because it is "neither of the two," they are mutually identical. This meaning is very clear: not grasping at illusory stillness is absolute transcendence;
being unimpeded by obstacles is absolute transcendence; and the fact that afflictions (*kleśa*) and nirvana do not obstruct one another is absolute transcendence. This points to [the ultimate].

The practitioner simply directs the mind in this manner; one who has forgotten emotions does not engage in mental activity at all. To speak of concentration and wisdom is to speak of the "double negation," yet even this is not mentioned.
True and false, arising and ceasing—these are merely relative designations. As for the conclusion regarding their meaning, it is the Buddha’s seal:
this realization of pure, perfect enlightenment belongs to one who has forgotten emotions. Only when one speaks thus can it be called the equality of concentration and wisdom.
Because they are equal, it is called *dhyāna*. It is not that this person says of themselves, "My concentration and wisdom are equal," which is like the *Vajracchedikā* saying:
"That which is called the thirty-two marks is not the thirty-two marks; it is called the thirty-two marks.

"Not possessing a physical body is called possessing a physical body"—all such statements mean that what is "not" is the mind and intellect, while their harmonious accord is what is "is. This is the conclusion of the meaning. At first glance, it appears as if...
That which is "not" and that which is "this name" are contradictory, yet upon realization they are entirely in accord; it is the same within this context as well. [Commentary:
Regarding the three contemplations, the following two sections provide a general judgment via three gates. First, correlating with the preceding scriptural passage to indicate awakening:
"If all Bodhisattvas awaken to the pure, perfect *bodhi*-mind. Regarding the section on Mañjuśrī: he explains that the four great elements and the objects of mental apprehension are like space.
The flowers of the second month and ignorance are like people in a dream; they have no real substance.

The characteristics of the cycle of birth and death, such as body and mind, are not created and thus lack an inherent nature. Because they do not exist, that which can perceive them is also a phenomenon like a flower in the sky.

Since it is ultimately eternally unmoving, there is no arising or ceasing within the Tathāgatagarbha, nor is there any subject-object cognition. Therefore, one knows that what is currently perceived as existing is actually [an illusion].

The "various" [phenomena] arise solely from the fault of stirring the mind; therefore, by practicing *śamatha* (calm abiding) to still the conditions and clarify the thoughts, one now realizes that [reality].
Regarding the practice of Samantabhadra and others, it is taught that one uses illusion to cultivate illusion until illusion is exhausted and awakening is fulfilled.

The illusory minds of sentient beings return to and are extinguished within illusion, such that the four great elements, the sense faculties, consciousnesses, and sensory objects—even the illusory body—are all analyzed and dismantled before the eyes.

Because [the delusions] are extinguished, the illusory mind, the illusory objects, and even the extinction of the illusion are extinguished; as the defilements are exhausted and clarity manifests, one cultivates the contemplation of illusion to eliminate that which is illusory.

Regarding the latter half of the *Puyan* (Universal Eye) and so forth: it explains the analogy of the mani-jewel, wherein the manifestation of forms and the absence of forms occur when defilements are exhausted and opposites are eliminated—namely, the elimination of opposing defilements—and it speaks of "names" because images are extinguished; thus, there is purity without direction and it is boundless.

The void is manifested by awakening; body, mind, faculties, objects, the four great elements, and the three realms are fundamentally pure and immovable, even unto all that is awakened, for they have been fundamentally accomplished as Buddhahood from the beginning.
Within this adamantine treasury, all various distinctions do not interfere with Perfect Awakening (Vajra-garbha).

Even birth-and-death and nirvana, arising and ceasing, and the illumination of awareness, are free from the cataracts of conceptual flowers; thus all dharmas are clearly understood as being severed and extinguished.
Spiritual awakening transcends all dualistic opposition; therefore, it must be free from dependence. The spiritual mind each relies upon this correspondence, for they correspond one-to-one.

Thus, one knows that this practice is the cultivation of that understanding. It is simply because there is sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation that what preceded was general while this is specific.

Those of superior faculties directly express what they have awakened to, and thus do not differentiate; those of middling or inferior capacities find it difficult to reach their minds, so the Buddha follows each accordingly.

The opportunity for realization opens and forms the third stage. When one arrives at the lower stage and eliminates the four marks—including "I" and "mine"—as well as hatred and attachment, one is finally able to enter awakening.
This is precisely what Maitreya practiced during the preceding middle stage: severing the root of saṃsāra.

By relying on the teacher to eliminate afflictions and by not engaging in such unreflective practices, one is finally able to proceed from the state of an ordinary person to that of a sage, following the nature of awakening at every step. This is because of detachment.

Because the four types of illness can only arise when one does not give rise to deluded thoughts, does not extinguish the deluded mind, does not comprehend deluded objects, and does not discern the reality, we know that "Universal Awakening" (*Pujue*) refers to the understanding within the cultivation of "Pure Wisdom" (*Qingjinghui*). *Commentary:* However, the following two sections present differing interpretations.

First, regarding the three characteristics of *Nirvāṇa* in this assembly: as for these "three characteristics," that sutra states (referring to the third [assembly]): [The text continues with the citation from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.]

(These are the ten and the thirty-one characters of the text. Because it is devoid of the ten characteristics (namely: form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, birth, abiding, destruction, male, and female), it is called Great Nirvāṇa.

If a bhikṣu repeatedly cultivates concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and the characteristic of equanimity (which refers to the three characteristics of birth, abiding, and destruction), he then severs the ten characteristics; this concentration is named *samādhi*.

If one grasps at the characteristic of form and cannot contemplate whether the characteristic of form is permanent or impermanent, this is not called *samādhi*; however, if one can contemplate that form is permanent... [the text continues].

The mark of impermanence is called the mark of wisdom (*prajñā*) and samādhi; the observation that all phenomena are equal [in their arising and ceasing]—like the varying speeds of a team of four horses—is called the mark of equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Because the two vehicles possess more concentration (*samādhi*) while Bodhisattvas possess more wisdom, and because the World-Honored One possesses both equally, he clearly perceives the Buddha-nature. To perceive the Buddha-nature is what is called the mark of equanimity.

*Śamatha* is called "that which can extinguish" [the afflictions], and so forth as cited above; therefore, it is called the mark of concentration. *Vipaśyanā* is called "right view," because it is universal seeing, sequential seeing, and seeing of specific characteristics.
This is called wisdom (*prajñā*). That which is called *samādhi* (equanimity) means equality—neither disputing, nor observing, nor acting. This is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).

If a bodhisattva well understands the time for concentration (*samādhi*)—[knowing that] it is not the time for cultivating wisdom when great arrogance arises; the time for wisdom—[knowing that] it is not the time for cultivating concentration because diligence at that time yields no benefit and leads to regret;

and the time for equanimity—[knowing that] one should cultivate equanimity when concentration and wisdom are unequal and thus unsuitable [for other practices]—and likewise knows what is not the time for each [as noted above], this is called practicing the path to enlightenment in common with the Great [Vehicle].

This first stage is named "Cessation" (*śamatha*), wherein one grasps stillness and clarifies the spirit so that the characteristics of meditative concentration increase and excel. (In the other text it says, "merely not grasping at the marks of form," while here it says, "grasping stillness as the practice";

both refer to the objective realm of concentration. Furthermore, the subsequent passage in that text states, "One who cultivates concentration can perceive the marks of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates," whereas here it says, "By clarifying all thoughts, one awakens to the restless agitation of consciousness.

Next, one realizes that sense organs and objects give rise to illusions; by eliminating these illusions, the characteristics of wisdom increase and excel. Finally, when all dependencies are severed and the two are fused, this is entirely identical to what that text calls "equanimity."

This is called the characteristic of equanimity (*upekṣā*). (In this context, "equality" refers to the simultaneous fusion of both [concentration and wisdom], while "equanimity" refers to their absolute transcendence.

As for the slight difference: in that [other] system, concentration comes first, followed by wisdom, and finally equanimity; whereas in this [system], all three gates contain both concentration and wisdom. Although those [three] differ—being concentration first, wisdom second, and so on—they are spoken of according to what is predominant.

How could there truly be a partiality toward concentration or a partiality toward wisdom within the authentic teaching? △ Commentary: The Second Assembly with the World, Part Three of the Tiantai [Commentary].

Observing this, according to the text established in the *Sūtra of the Adornment of the Necklaces* (*Yingluo jing*), it says: "Entering from the conventional into emptiness is called the contemplation of the two truths;
emerging from emptiness into the conventional is called the contemplation of equality. These two contemplations serve as the path of skillful means.

By means of these two contemplations of emptiness, one attains entry into the contemplation of the supreme truth of the Middle Way. When these three contemplations manifest before one, one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*). Tiantai summarizes this as follows: [One].

First is the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional; second is the contemplation of emerging from emptiness into the conventional; and third is the correct contemplation of the Middle Way.

Having already explained these three modes of practice in detail, we shall now discuss how to achieve practice through the mind. By taking the textual passages of the preceding six chapters as a basis, one has already fully manifested the nature of awakening (*bodhi-svabhāva*), refuted false attachments, investigated the natures and characteristics of all phenomena, and distinguished the defilement and purity of the mind and its objects, even extending from the state of an ordinary person...

Having concluded the discussion on entering the noble path, the obstacles and their remedies, the penetration and blockage, the depth and shallowness of severing delusions, and the superiority and inferiority of realized wisdom, this [text] simply aims to cause one to forget emotions, cut off discursive thoughts, obliterate appearances, and merge with the Truth; therefore, it does not establish an object of contemplation.

As for generating understanding through the meaning [of the text], that [tradition] takes *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as its primary principle; it first exhorts one to aspire toward the fruit of Buddhahood and to feel weary of and seek detachment from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Thus...

It praises *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as the gate of transcendence and the gate of entering the Path; it reveals the characteristics of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), which are precisely these three contemplations.

By investigating the true and false natures and characteristics of all phenomena to reveal the meanings of emptiness, the provisional, and so forth, one opens the portals for severing delusions and realizing truth.

Therefore, the relationship between the object of contemplation—the three truths—and the wisdom that contemplates them must be established, for only through their mutual correspondence can the meaning be clarified.
In the commentary on the *Sūtra on Comparative Analysis*, regarding the five precepts and ten precepts: the five precepts for laypeople are: first, not killing; second, not stealing;
third, no sexual misconduct; fourth, not lying; and fifth, not drinking alcohol or eating meat.

The eight precepts add the prohibition against anointing the body with fragrant oils, as well as [the prohibitions against] going to watch performances and using high, wide, or large beds. The ten precepts are the śrāmaṇera precepts, which add [to the eight].
One must not handle raw gold, silver, or wealth, nor may one eat past midday. Regarding the "six supernormal powers" (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), they are as explained in the *Nidāna* (Introductory) section.
Regarding the "eight liberations" (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), they are the eight deliverances (*aṣṭavimokṣa*). To facilitate correspondence with the text, one character has been omitted; thus it is said:
first, possessing internal form, one perceives external forms as impure, the liberation; second, being without internal form, one perceives external forms.

1. The liberation through the perception of the impure; 2. the liberation through the perception of internal formlessness while observing external forms as pure, which one realizes with the body and dwells in fully;
3–6. the liberations of the four bases of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
7. the liberation through the perception of purity, which one realizes with the body and dwells in fully.

Regarding the ten *paryavasthānas*, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The eight *paryavasthānas* are lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), parsimony (*mātsarya*), along with regret (*kaukṛtya*), torpor (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and lethargy (*middha*);

or ten, by adding anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*). Those possessing the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and so forth take the three realms as their object; since one must possess these when entering the state of a noble one (*ārya*) from the level of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they are thus correlated here.

Extracted from the Great Commentary by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Mount Guifeng at the Aranya.

Regarding the question in the *Sūtra* concerning "the one who practices among those who practice," and the commentary’s response, "Is it again one person? and so forth: according to the subsequent commentary, all of these [categories] exist.
Specifically, the first three wheels refer to three persons each possessing one [wheel], while the final wheel refers to one person possessing all three.

As for the intermediate cases of interlacing, they may occur sequentially—as the text says, "first practicing the middle, then the last"—or simultaneously, as the *Sūtra* says, "practicing them together. There are also cases based on [other criteria].

Next (this refers to first practicing *śamatha*, then practicing *samāpatti*, and finally practicing *dhyāna*) or skipping the sequence (first practicing *śamatha*, then practicing *dhyāna*, and so forth).

Within the prose commentary (*gadya*) of the Sūtra, the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) divides the section on the "Correct Exposition" into two parts: the sequential explanation and the following interpretation.

Regarding the enumeration in the Sūtra, the commentary notes that where the meaning is the same as the preceding section, it refers to the beginning of the text on the "Three Contemplations" (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).

This is because, in order to categorize the contemplations as wheels (*cakra*), the text reiterates [the previous point]. A wheel has two meanings: first, the sense of crushing and grinding; second, the sense of revolving and turning. Furthermore, there is the sense of being circular (*vṛtta*).
The meanings of "fulfillment" (*pūrṇa*) and "beginningless and endless" (*anādi-ananta*), etc., are explained extensively in the *Daisho* (Great Commentary).

Regarding the phrase in the *Kankyō Kōra Sho* (Commentary on the Interlacing Net of Contemplation), fascicle 2, section 1-2, which states that the lower division of the contemplations cites the *Ko Sho* (Sincere Commentary) and others:
although these names of contemplation have not yet fully elucidated the intent of the Sūtra, nor have they been able to lead the human mind into the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
However, because the phrasing is elegant and fluent, and many have cherished it, I have preserved it here.

Now, following this [text] as my primary guide for the entire work, I shall also provide an exegesis on the title of the "Contemplation" (*guan*) to harmonize it with the intent of the sutra. Second, the formal exegesis of the sutra text.

The scriptural section on "clarifying the turbid" is an explanation by means of analogy. It means that just as water containing silt and mud must be clarified to become pure, so too is it with the mind:
when there are afflictions (*kleśa*), the defilement of攀緣 (*pān-yuan*, objective clinging) is likewise present. As for "stopping function," this does not merely mean not clinging to various objects;

it also means not giving rise to mental activity, such as observing whether something is illusory or non-illusory. Therefore, the *Jiǎo Shù* (Commentary by Jiǎo) states: "Furthermore, the nature of water is clear and moist; when it irrigates, its essence is revealed."
When merit is directed toward external objects, it becomes turbid and muddy; if one discards it, that which is useful is lost, yet if one retains it, it serves as a means of sustenance.

Just as wine cannot remain pure in a vessel unless it settles and clarifies, flowing water separates into distinct parts: when the mud is removed and the pure water remains, eternal ignorance is severed.
When the marks of clarity are refined and pure, how could this not be realized? Regarding the "seat of the emptiness of dharmas," the Sūtra says: "All dharmas are empty."
Every seat is a place for the summer retreat (*varṣā*). The Bodhisattva constantly dwells in the realm of the emptiness of all phenomena;
entering into quiescence means abiding in ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Based on the principle of quiescence, one should accord with the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*).

Because this Bodhisattva possesses sharp faculties, a tranquil mind, and perfected merit, he realizes the Middle Way within the state of the emptiness of phenomena, without waiting for even the "sickness of emptiness" to be emptied before reaching it.
The Middle Way [teaches] that because this bodhisattva enters emptiness and fundamentally lacks the "sickness" of dwelling in emptiness, one must provide this interpretation;

for, according to the examples in the subsequent text, severing afflictions and entering quiescence are both the phenomenal aspects (*ākāra*) within the practice of non-referential observation (*atyantāpekṣā*).

Regarding the passage in the Sūtra, "Like the butcher Pāṭin, he wields his blade freely," and the statement "By the power of the Buddha," etc.: previously, the illusory assembly was manifested and internal great compassion was aroused.
This refers to the transformation of the world through great wisdom by the power of the Buddha, which is like the various illusory transformations mentioned previously.
The various functions contained within the phrases "conforming to or opposing," "benefiting oneself or others," and "practicing them all" refer exclusively to conforming practice.

Regarding the *dhāraṇī*, the subsequent general explanation of "movement while remaining eternally quiescent" means that tranquil mindfulness and still wisdom are themselves concentration and wisdom (*samādhi* and *prajñā*).

The commentary on the *Sūtra* presents the sounds as emerging from the obstruction; this is the second section, part one, three. Regarding the heading "Presenting": the term "presenting" (*cheng*) is taken from the preceding phrase "the sound emerges externally," which serves as the name for this contemplation.

That is to say, "sound" (*yin*) refers to the resonance of the bells and so forth, while "presenting" (*cheng*) refers to being heard from afar. "Obstruction" (*ai*) refers to the substance of the bell and its tower;

"emerging" (*chu*) means that it cannot be confined or restricted by the physical vessel and material. As for the phrase "vessel and substance": "vessel" (*qi*) refers to the bell and such, while "substance" (*zhi*) refers to the material essence.

"Obstruction dissolving" refers to the flowing through; "striking" refers to the impact of a mallet. According to that commentary (*shu*), it says "responding to the sound according to the *gaṇḍī*," yet here we say "striking" (扣) with the intention of following the meaning of the original metaphor.
Regarding the two explanations of the scriptural meaning starting from "The various... and so on, concerning "boundless" and so forth, there are two points:
first, this illusory realm is the secular world of humans, comprising the differences between past and present, and benefit and harm.
Matters such as these, along with the distinctions between defilement and purity regarding causes and conditions throughout the three periods of time, are vast and boundless, impossible to fathom.
Yet now they must all be gathered together; there is no end to their execution, and no satisfaction in receiving them.
Therefore, it is better to sever all thought, extinguish all traces, and bring everything to rest. The two illusory bodies are empty, having neither limit nor bottom, and thus cannot be exhausted.
The "thorough investigation" (kṣaya) by which the realized one cuts off the mind so that it no longer engages is called "extinction" (nirodha).

Regarding "functions and so forth," as in the previous chapter, the various functions such as the arising of illusory transformations to manifest illusory assemblies, as well as those mentioned in the preceding sections, are now all not taken up.

"Unobtainable" refers to the meaning of the aforementioned emptiness. "Nothing to be observed" signifies the realization of the cessation of observation; this is the meaning of the cessation of observation.
This does not refer to the previously mentioned stillness-object or illusory-object.
Regarding the sutra’s interlacing of the three contemplations, the commentary (Sū) states: "First, the interlacing below corresponds to the number of wheels. Commentary:

Now, each of the following two sections displays the two segments of interlacing; when these two pairs are combined together, it is as follows: taking the stillness-contemplation (*śamatha*) as the primary [contemplation], it is the first...

First, regarding the sequence of one [practice] followed by two: first, tranquility (*śamatha*), then illusion (*māyā*), and finally stillness (*śānti*) (each combining one); second, tranquility, then stillness, and finally illusion (the middle one combining the other two).

Regarding the sequence of three practices: first, tranquility, then illusion, and finally stillness; second, tranquility, then stillness, and finally illusion (the middle one combining the other two). Regarding "first one, then simultaneous":

first tranquility, then simultaneously both illusion and stillness (the simultaneous pair combining the other two). Regarding "first simultaneous, then one": first simultaneously both tranquility, illusion, and stillness, and finally single stillness.

Second, first [the section on] "Equanimity and Stillness" followed by "Single Illusion"; now, taking "Stillness and Observation" as the primary heading, since this is the case, the other two headings should each be treated accordingly.
▲ Commentary: Now, regarding the three subsequent applications of the structural principles, first, the formal explanation of the long division into seven parts:
if one follows the aforementioned structural analysis, it would be appropriate to divide each observation into four segments, and then...
Within each of the [sections] numbered one, two, and four, there are further subdivisions of two;

however, fearing that such a fragmented and piecemeal division might lead to confusion regarding the intent of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*), I have simply divided them into seven long sections. As for why each must be cited individually:

it is because the names of the contemplations each consist of four characters; if two contemplations were combined into a single wheel, there would be eight characters, and if three contemplations were combined into a single wheel, there would be... [twelve characters].

The twelve characters and twenty-one wheel-marks together amount to over two hundred characters written in vain; furthermore, because the phrases are repetitive and arise in confusion, making it difficult to find their sequence, they must be abbreviated.
Regarding "subsequently quiescent" (後寂), in the sutra each instance refers to "quiescent extinction" (寂滅). [Commentary: "Quiescence" (寂) and the following two [terms] distinguish the differences.

Quiescence is the Middle Way; thus, Master Pingala’s preface to the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: ... [text continues] ... *Note: The ellipsis indicates that the original text contains further commentary regarding the distinction between "quiescence" and the subsequent terms.*

Yunji states that these various extremes are called the "Middle," and thus it differs from "quiescence" (*śānti*). This contemplation has already been analyzed in detail in the preceding chapter on "Majesty and Virtue" (*vibhūti*).
Regarding the commentary text, the lower four sections are divided into general and specific categories. Fifth is the word-by-word explanation.
In the first seven wheels of the *Sūtra*, the sub-commentary (*śāstra*) explains the section title "Cultivating Samādhi" as referring to attaining ultimate stillness.
As the *Sūtra* says, "By means of a mind of still wisdom," it speaks directly of establishing the principle of *dhyāna*. In the school of the Vinaya, the precepts (*śīla*) are regarded as a raft;

in the Gate of Meditation (*dhyāna-mukha*), concentration (*samādhi*) is regarded as a vessel. Regarding the phrase "operating the vessel," there are two meanings for its operation: first, [it refers to] oneself...
The first movement is called "transcending the mundane," while the second movement is "universal salvation. If these two intentions were absent, how could it be called "universal"?
Is a boatman who ferries people across not himself remaining on this shore? If he were to remain, it would merely be called "borrowing a boat" and not "ferrying people across.

Upon careful examination, the substance of the boat is precisely *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight); the rest of the text is easy to understand. [End of] Commentary; below, *śamatha* is indicated.
The second section explains the meaning of the scripture.
Regarding the second [verse], the commentary provides two points: first, "The ocean of stillness is as clear as the void" (*zhánhǎi chéngkōng*).

This means that just as waves do not arise in the ocean, it remains profoundly still and unmoving (the accomplishment of tranquil contemplation). The void is free from clouds and mist, vast, pure, and empty; the ocean has no boundaries.

The horizons join the sky in a single hue, and the emptiness penetrates to the bottom of the sea; because the sea contains the aspect of emptiness, it is called "tranquil" (this is the cultivation of the contemplation of stillness).
Therefore, it is said that the waves do not stir; great waves are called *lán*. Since one turns back from the flow of birth and death like waves that do not arise, the water is clear and limpid.
When the merit of the contemplation of stillness is perfected, the numinous mind is quiescently illuminating—this is precisely the nature (*dharmatā*). Therefore, it is called "revealing the nature."

▲ "Sparse and still" (*shujì*). The meaning of the scripture in the following two sections follows from this quiet cultivation. That which is "still" is like water: because it does not move, it is clear and bright;
being clear and bright, it can become a transparent void. The remaining text may be understood accordingly.
Within the three sections of the sutra, the commentary [provides] two [sections], the first of which explains the title of the chapter.

Regarding "Śūra," he is Maheśvara with three eyes, as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; this serves as a metaphor for the three virtues of nirvāṇa, and thus the principle of the three contemplations is likewise made manifest.
The commentary states, "It is stillness," which refers to the meaning of the following two sections of the sutra.

In the commentary on the fourth [chapter], section two, paragraph one, line four, the explanation of the title regarding the "three points" (*tri-bindu*) is also a metaphor for the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) of *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the phrase "the sincere intention and so forth," since the scripture states that names are cultivated simultaneously while it describes them as preceding and succeeding, this merely clarifies the underlying intent of that [scripture].
If we refer to the three points of the letter *I* (𑖀), as represented by the symbol ∴, this scripture states they are neither vertical nor horizontal; such is the case here with these three.
To observe that there is a prior, middle, and posterior is its longitudinal aspect; furthermore, while this is a general outline, a detailed examination would not be strictly applicable.
If there were no benefit or harm [in adopting it], one could not alter it. ▲ This concludes the commentary on the meaning of the next two sections of the sutra.
In the commentary on the fifth fascicle, section 2-1, under the fifth chapter, the headings of the sections are explained.

▲ In the commentary on the sixth fascicle, section 2-1, under the sixth chapter, the headings of the sections are explained; this one also incorporates the "chapter" (pin) title from the preceding section, and both are entirely similar.
▲ In the commentary, under the heading "齊標" (Qiāobiāo), the meanings of two sections of the sutra are explained.

Regarding the commentary on the seventh [chapter], section 2-1-7, under the heading "The Fruit," the subheading "The Tree of Tranquil Samādhi" and so forth means that a mind free from discursive thought (*vīkalpa*) is the foundation of the Way.
Just as a tree [provides fruit], *nirvāṇa* (extinction) is the dharma of ultimate realization;

thus, although one may suddenly accord with and realize *nirvāṇa*, one still practices gradually according to worldly convention for the sake of self-benefit and benefiting others, yet without losing that state of tranquil mindfulness. Therefore, it is said to be like a tree.
"The fruit falls back to the tree and the flowers bloom again"—this also merely captures the general meaning and cannot be taken as a precise account of the beginning and end.
[This concludes] the commentary on the two sections of the sutra following the passage "simultaneously extinguished."

In the commentary on the seventh wheel, section one, subsection one: first, regarding the explanation of the title, "King Wu and others" refers to the *Book of Documents*, which states that King Wu, in accordance with Heaven and responding to the people, rescued the living beings of the world from their plight in the "coating of mud and burning charcoal.
Having no choice but to attack Zhou, once he had conquered him, he returned his horses to the southern slopes of Mount Hua and released his oxen into the wilds of Taolin.

Casting weapons of war into agricultural implements signifies that the world shall no longer employ arms; rather, it indicates the suppression of military force and the cultivation of culture to govern the realm and nourish the myriad people.

Thus, this metaphor illustrates the principle of first employing activity and subsequently resting in stillness. This concludes the commentary on the two subsequent sections of the sutra’s meaning concerning the manifestation of illusion.

The commentary on the "Perfect Cultivation of the Three Contemplations" (Sūtra-yuánxiū-sānguān-shū), Part II-1, subsequently explains the title of the section. The commentary states: "Regarding the 'Perfect' [Contemplation], there are two interpretations of the meaning of the sūtra.

As for the statement that the verses of the sūtra lack the distinction between subject and object in their cultivation while the prose commentary does not, this is because the intent of these verses is identical to that of the long prose sections, despite the differences in their phrasing.
Fearing that [the reader] might not understand the correspondence [between the text and its meaning], I shall explain this at length. The passage on "Perfect Enlightenment" states:
"Pure and originally non-existent, there is neither cultivation nor a cultivator," which means there is no subject or object. At the beginning of the section on the Three Contemplations, it says:

"Regarding all practices, in reality there are no two," yet it does not mention meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) at all. Now, in this verse, it stands alone in saying "arising from meditative concentration. This is because...

To know that the mind is fundamentally quiescent and devoid of the principle of cultivation is itself meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). This is the meaning indicated by the prose section and revealed within the verses;
it is precisely here that the excellence of the method—where the prose presents the dharma and the verses explain its significance—lies.

Regarding the addition of "ropes and so forth" in the commentary, this refers to the episode in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* where Upāli and two bhikṣus perform a ritual confession of their offenses according to the Dharma with Vimalakīrti.
He rebuked them, saying: "Do not further increase the offenses of these two bhikṣus; they should be directly extinguished so as not to disturb their minds. Why is this?
The nature of that offense does not exist within, nor does it exist without, nor does it exist in between.

As the Buddha has said: 'Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure. Furthermore, the mind does not exist within, nor does it exist without."
It does not abide in the middle; as is the mind, so are the defilements of sin, and so are all phenomena—they do not depart from suchness (*tathatā*).
Now, to speak of "adding ropes" means to increase the burden further;
"wounding one who has no wound" refers to when Pūrṇa was previously preaching the Dharma to some newly ordained bhikṣus beneath a tree, and Vimalakīrti again rebuked him.
"Pūrṇa, you should first enter meditative concentration to observe this man’s mind and only then preach the Dharma.
Do not place foul food into a precious vessel; you must know what this bhikṣu is thinking in his heart. Do not equate lapis lazuli with common crystal.
Since you do not know the root-source of sentient beings, do not initiate them with the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings. He himself—
"Do not wound that which is without sores. "If you wish to travel the Great Way, do not show the narrow path.
"Furthermore, as I observe it, the wisdom of the Hīnayāna is feeble and shallow, like a blind man who cannot distinguish the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all sentient beings.
Commentary: Vimalakīrti’s intention was that to preach the Dharma of the Hīnayāna to those who have newly begun their studies is to wound that which is without sores.
This reveals that what is taught here by means of the Mahāyāna Dharma is the intent of this commentary:

to clarify that for one who possesses sudden and perfect realization and understanding, the true nature of awakening is already present and does not require a ritual site, the tying of knots, or other such practices. Were one to require the tying of knots, it would be like inflicting a wound where none exists.

This is the obstacle regarding the middle [stage]. In terms of cultivation and realization, there are differences in how the self is associated with them;

In the commentary on the "Correct Inquiry" section of the Sūtra, regarding which dharmas are defiled: because one initially awakens to the same [nature] as a Buddha yet falsely gives rise to thoughts that return one to the state of an ordinary person, Master Zhìgōng’s verse says:

In the prose commentary (*gadya*) of the Sūtra, there are two sections: first, the main exposition, which includes the sub-section on the classification of the text; second, the word-by-word explanation (*anuvyākhyāna*). The *Triratnabhakti-śāstra* by Vasubandhu states: "To perceive each of the five aggregates as the self-characteristic (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*) is the view of the self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*);

to perceive that the life-force of the self is severed and then reborn in the six realms is the view of the person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*); and to perceive that the body of the self continues in an uninterrupted succession is [the view of permanence]."

Regarding the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-nimitta*)—that is, the numerous transformations of prosperity and decline, suffering and pleasure—one calculates that one's own retributive life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) remains uninterrupted and abides;

this is the mark of a self-sustainer (*ātmabhāva*). The *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-vṛtti* states: "Taking the continuity of one's own substance as the mark of 'self,' and taking what is measured by it as the mark of 'sentient being'.

The other two [marks] have the same intent. However, while Asaṅga speaks of "conceptions" (*saṃjñā*), Maitreya speaks of "marks" (*nimitta*); here, we shall employ both in consultation with one another.

"I" refers to the entirety of non-attachment; "longevity" refers to the entirety of Devaputra (Vasubandhu); the remaining two [terms] unfold and elaborate upon the text to make it easy for others to understand.

The commentary states that this refers to "delusion regarding the realm of consciousness. As for the scriptural explanation, it concerns the realization and awakening to the nature of awareness (*jñatā*).

Proceeding from the coarse to the subtle, one successively eliminates [the four phases]; only when these four phases are entirely eliminated is there finally no more to eliminate. Hence, it is called "delusion regarding the realm of wisdom.

Regarding the phrase in the sub-commentary, "The false self is fundamentally empty," the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Dharmas have no self, for they are free from the defilement of the self. Thus, dharmas are devoid of a self.
Because there is no person and the limits of past and future are severed, the Dharma has no sentient beings; because it is free from the defilements of sentient beings, the Dharma has no life-span;

"Name-suffering" refers to the growth of tainted (*sāsrava*) form and mind; "origin" refers to karma and afflictions; "cessation" refers to tranquility, namely *nirvāṇa*; and "path" refers to the means of deliverance, namely *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and so forth. The three subsequent sets of the Four Truths are explained in detail as clarified in the *Great Commentary* (*Daisho*) and the *Sub-commentary* (*Dakyō*).
This is merely a brief citation of the essential meaning; I have used the preceding [analysis of] arising and ceasing to explain the commentary and cannot provide a prolix narration.

Regarding the statement that "intimate cessation" is due to the former [view], it merely says that one cannot sever it oneself; because there still remains a self that can be severed, it is described according to its superficial characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

As for the afflictions, upon what basis does one wish to sever them? Now, because one realizes that there is no name [for them] to be severed, it is said that they are "intimately severed.

The Sub-commentary on the Separate Explanation of the Four Characteristics, Part Two, Section One, Two: A Detailed Analysis of the Intent. Regarding the phrase "distinct from the ordinary," this refers, as previously stated, to the four characteristics of the objects of deluded consciousness.
"The first fruit eliminates them" refers to the realization of the True Suchness of self-emptiness (*ātma-śūnyatā*) at the stage of the Small Vehicle’s Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
"The Arhat has not yet understood them" means that these four characteristics obstruct Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*); if the Arhat were to understand them, [he would realize it].
Because one should awaken to pure, perfect enlightenment, Tiantai taught that beyond the three realms there are *rajas* (dust) and *asamkhyeya* (sands of the Ganges) levels of ignorance;
this very grasping is their number. It should properly be called "Arhat," but in this text, for the sake of correspondence with the character "greed" (*tan*), it is stated briefly.
Regarding the examination of the self through phenomena: "phenomena" refers to "what belongs to the self" (*ātmīya*), and "what belongs to the self" refers to that which possesses a self.
All objective phenomena and their spheres extend to sentient beings; all things can be seen and known, yet I am unable to see them in reverse.

Therefore, by examining myself through the lens of these objective phenomena and their spheres, I realize that others are not me, and thus I know that I am not another. **Part Two: Detailed Explanation of the Sūtra’s Examination of the Self through Phenomena.** This section is divided into two parts:

first, the statement of the outline’s intent; second, the formal explanation. **First: Statement of the Outline’s Intent.** [This subsection] explains the meaning of the structural outline. **Second: The Formal Explanation.** [This subsection] provides the actual commentary on the text.

In the commentary on the "Raising the Question" section, the phrase "one who possesses awareness knows that all objects and circumstances are not the self, yet this very [awareness] is called the self" is explained as follows:
regarding the term "yanju" (燕居) in the "Explanatory Simile" section, the character *yan* (燕) is pronounced *yàn*, following the usage of the term "yanju" (燕居) found in the *Analects*.
In the *Jiejizhongshu*, it is explained that the essence of awakening (*jue-ti*) is emptiness and stillness; this is the essence (*ti*), which is nirvāṇa.
Awareness (*zhi*) is its function (*yong*), and this awareness is precisely the function of the essence. Nirvāṇa is precisely the essence of awareness, and awareness is precisely nirvāṇa.
Since essence and function are mutually identical, there is no separate essence to be realized. This corresponds to the third section within the five gates of the path of realization (*zhengdao*).
When both subject and object are extinguished, that which is identified as the mark of self (ātman) is precisely false vision; that which is realized as the object of realization is the self.
Since "self" carries the meaning of one's own essence, if one truly realizes the true essence, it is the Dharma-body and the true self;
conversely, if one erroneously realizes a delusive essence, it is ignorance and the delusive self. This analogy is quite clear.
In the commentary on the phrase "Having realized that I have become a person" (經悟我成人), the section following "realized" (悟下) explains the structural outline (*ke*).

In the commentaries and treatises of various schools, whenever the character "person" (*ren*) appears, its substance may refer to one who can realize, one who can grasp, or even the speaker or listener; whether true or false, they are all referred to as "the person" (*zhe*).
It is also like the Sanskrit term *buddha*, which here is translated as "the Awakened One" (*jùzhě*); this refers to a person. If one speaks of *bodhi*, this merely refers to "awakening" (*jué*);
this refers to the Dharma. The categories and examples are like this; those with broad learning should understand it for themselves.

Now, because this turning [of awareness] is even deeper, the perceptions unfold infinitely, all of which constitute subject and object. Is this not far more transcendent than what preceded it? Thus the Sūtra says:

"Awakening to that which is beyond reach" (for "reach" [ji] immediately becomes an "object" [so]). The topical outline says: "Realizing the traces as they arise. The commentary says: "To realize that these are non-existent..."
Because it is established, it is free from the aforementioned errors; furthermore, the statement that "indeterminate [views] grasp at oneness" is all very clear.
