All such cases are of this nature; therefore, it is said they "disagree. As for the sudden gate necessarily containing the gradual, although it speaks of saṃsāra and so forth...

Because it is unconditioned, it has no intrinsic nature; being originally non-existent, it is taught that craving is the root of saṃsāra. Having fully described its faults and defects, one is exhorted to sever it.
Although it is said that sentient beings are primordially enlightened, it is extensively taught that one must arouse the mind, make vows, and diligently cultivate contemplative practice;
therefore, it is said that one must possess the Great Sūtra, which also states: "At the very moment of first arousing the mind..."
Having attained perfect enlightenment, he then fully explains the successive cultivation of the ten abodes and the ten practices, up to the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Regarding the commentary on the *Sūtra’s Response on Merit* (Section 2-14), the lower section analyzes the structure and states the intended meaning.

As for the correlation between hearing the sūtra and the merit bestowed upon others, the *Commentary on the Wise* has already provided its own explanations according to each respective section. Now, from the phrase "Furthermore, as for those who hear" (*fù wén zhě*) onwards, it is repeated.

This explains the meaning of the two sections concerning merit first and wisdom later. Regarding the subsequent section on past causes, which clarifies both merit and wisdom, the Sūtra itself explicitly states:
"planting various merits and wisdoms"; here, "wisdom" (*prajñā*) is synonymous with "knowledge" (*jñāna*). Second, the detailed explanation according to the topical outline.
In the commentary on the "Excellence Revealed in the Sūtra," it says: "As for 'being like a diamond,' it states:

'If a person were to fill the trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, and if another person were to receive, uphold, and even recite a single four-line verse from this sūtra and explain it to others, the merit of the latter would surpass that of the former.
Although the textual examples are similar, there is nevertheless a distinction between their relative superiority and inferiority.

Question: Compared to that [other practice], one must actually receive and uphold [the teaching] to be superior; whereas here, merely hearing its name is already superior. Furthermore, compared to that, one must also explain it to others to be superior;
whereas here, simply having faith in it oneself is superior. Answer: Regarding the initial passage of that sūtra which performs this comparative calculation, it is as stated above.
However, later in that same text, it further uses the sands of many Ganges Rivers to calculate the number of three-thousandfold world systems filled with them.

Even the giving of the seven treasures of the world as alms does not equal upholding and explaining [this teaching]; nor does the giving of one's body and life as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges equal upholding and explaining it.
Is this not, therefore, far superior to the calculation based on the seven treasures of this single world? Answer:
Because that sūtra sequentially resolves twenty-seven doubts, its doctrinal principles and spheres of meaning become increasingly superior; this is what was cited above.
The preceding text has already resolved the doubt that one receives a retributive body (vipākakāya) with grasping up to the seventh level of rebirth;
it has already realized that the retributive body is without grasping. Therefore, its merit surpasses the seven treasures of many world-systems as well as the giving of one's own body and life.
Now, this section merely compares the hearing of the name and the meaning of a single phrase; it does not yet compare the realization of the profound and subtle state.
Because the profound and subtle realm cannot be compared with any worldly phenomena, it is known that what you have asked is entirely of a different category.

"Filling the *kṣetra*" means filling the world. "Serving as a resource for the fruits of outflows" means acting as a supporting condition for the retributive fruits of the six realms of existence associated with outflows, thereby causing the cycle of birth and death within the three realms to never cease and further inviting the gravity of a third rebirth.
It is said thus because it is suffering. The original text states, "that which serves as the material cause for inviting the fruit of outflows (*āsrava*). This phrasing is not precise;

the meaning is that worldly treasures are the means for inviting the fruit of outflows, and the fruit so invited is already fully expressed by these words. To further say "the material cause" (*zī*) here results in a redundancy, as "material cause" (*zī*) already implies the sense of being that which is invited.

The logical force of the sentence is completely inverted. I maintain that "material cause" (*zī*) refers to the conditions (*pratyaya*) that assist and support, specifically assisting and supporting craving.

The statement that "the mind of loving giving invites the fruit of outflows" (āsrava-phala) means that one knows the requisite conditions are what invite [that fruit]; thus, it is rephrased as "serving as the requisite for the fruit of outflows.
This meaning is perfectly consistent with the intent.
Regarding the *Jingdu ren jiaoliang shu* (Commentary on the Sūtra’s Calculation of Saving Beings), section 2.1.2 and below clarifies the underlying intent and provides two explanations of the text.

The Sūtra cites those of inferior and middling capacity; as for those who accumulate merit, consider, for instance, that if one succeeds in persuading a single person to abstain from alcohol and meat or to observe the five precepts, the resulting merit is already vast.
How much more so for the eight precepts, the ten precepts, and even taking the full ordination upon leaving the household life—their merit is already difficult to describe.
How much more so for a hundred Ganges Rivers, and the fine grains of sand within each of those rivers?
If one were to count each grain of sand as representing one person, and were to cause that many people to all attain arhatship, the merit of this could only be calculated by a Buddha;
who else could fathom its limit? Therefore, it is said "it can be known, it can be known" to mean the utmost possible extent, not that its specific numerical quantity is known.
In the *Commentary on the Manifestation of the Supreme*, it is stated that the essence of emptiness is not empty; this means that the spiritual discernment (*lingjian*) is not obscured.
Thus, taking the empty *tathāgatagarbha* as the "half-verse," possessing both aspects constitutes the "full verse. Alternatively, regarding the "impermanence and true permanence":

to realize that all phenomena are entirely suffering, empty, and impermanent is the half-verse; to perceive the eternally abiding reality within that state of emptiness and impermanence is the full verse.
It is only when one realizes the Dharma-body of the fundamental awakening that it is complete; thus, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the rākṣasa recites half a verse, saying:

"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing. He later further says: "When arising and ceasing have ceased, tranquility is bliss"—only then is it complete.

Furthermore, contemplating the impurity of the body and so forth constitutes the four foundations of mindfulness as the "half-dharmakāya," whereas the permanence and bliss [of the Dharma-body] constitute the fullness.
If we consider this according to the sutra itself: because the illusory body ceases, the illusory mind also ceases; because the illusory mind ceases, the illusory objects also cease;

because the illusory objects cease, the cessation of illusion also ceases—this constitutes the half-verse. Because the cessation of illusion ceases, that which is not illusory does not cease; it is like polishing a mirror:
when the grime is exhausted, the brightness appears—this constitutes the full verse. Question: If this is so, then this...
Question: You claim that the analysis of half a verse is identical to the Hīnayāna or the provisional teachings of the Mahāyāna;

how can its merit be so immeasurable? Answer: Because we have already established Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*) as our primary tenet, and because the destruction of ignorance is like awakening from a dream, it is only within this intrinsically pure and perfect enlightenment that the teachings of impermanence and so forth are expounded; therefore, one first realizes the Perfect Enlightenment of the Tathāgata.
Only after becoming stainless does one then explain that the various illusory transformations of beginningless ignorance all arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment;
this is the principle of the school that reveals the nature. This treatise also states: "Because of relying on enlightenment, there is delusion.
Although this is but half a verse, it already far surpasses the entirety of all other teachings; for this reason, its merit is difficult to calculate.

Having stayed overnight, upon returning he examined the *Zhongshu* (Commentary on the Middle), sections 213 and below, which clarify the underlying intent. Regarding the second part, the "Explanation of the Text," it follows the sequence of the sutra.

As for the phrase in the *Zhongshu*, "The textual momentum is like that of the *Vajracchedikā*," that sutra says: "After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, in the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit;
they will be able to give rise to faith in these chapters and phrases and take them as reality. You should know..."
Such a person has not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas (the inverse implication);
rather, they have planted all manner of roots of goodness under immeasurable thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of Buddhas (the direct clarification).
Because this is a commentary on the *Sūtra on Protecting and Sustaining*, the "sūtra" mentioned refers to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.

"Delighting in birth-and-death" means being attached to wealth and pleasure, relying on one's own strength and vigor, and constantly taking pleasure in conforming to others; these are the karmas of birth-and-death. "Adhering to various views" refers to false wisdom (*mithyā-jñāna*).
Therefore, it is cited as evidence, for the *Ratnaketu-parivarta* (or *Yingluo jing*) states: "Delighting in the practice of competition is the conduct of Māra; delighting in views is [the same]."
This is not the practice of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Regarding the passage in the midst of the assembly of Heavenly Kings where the commentary identifies the requester as the host, it is as explained in the initial section of the *Xuántán* (Extended Discourse), citing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Regarding the "one *yojana*" mentioned in the midst of the assembly of Ghost Kings (*preta-rāja*), the old translation states it is forty *li*, while the new translation states it is ten.

Six *li*. In the commentary, from "I reflect upon myself" (*zìwéi*) onwards is the third major section: "Celebratory Praise and Dedication" (*qìngzàn huíxiàng*). This has three parts: first, celebration; second, [dedication]; third, [the specific dedication]. First, "celebration" refers to lamenting the past.

"Delusion" (*mí*) means ignorance (*avidyā*). "The ocean of mind" (*xīnhǎi*): "mind" is the subject and "ocean" is the metaphor; it corresponds to "birth and death" (*saṃsāra*) in the subsequent sentence.

Waves are the phenomenon (*dharma*) and the ocean is the metaphor (*upamā*). This means that when the wind blows upon the sea, waves are formed; likewise, when ignorance deludes the mind, birth and death (*saṃsāra*) are produced. Thus, the Treatise says:

"Just as the water of the great ocean is stirred by the wind, the appearance of the water and the appearance of the wind are not separate from one another, yet the nature of the water is not movement.
If the wind ceases, the appearance of movement ceases, but the moist nature is not destroyed. It is like this.
The intrinsic nature of the mind of these sentient beings is pure; however, moved by the wind of ignorance, the mind coexists with ignorance.

Though they are formless and inseparable from one another, the mind is not of a moving nature. If ignorance ceases, the continuity [of the mind] is extinguished, yet the nature of wisdom remains indestructible.
According to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, the wind is used as a metaphor for objective conditions (*viṣaya*); the text states: "The ocean of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is constant."
The great waves stirred by the winds of objective realms surge through the abysses of the ocean without end.

The *Śāstra* says that ignorance refers to the cause (*hetu*), while the *Sūtra* says that objective realms refer to the conditions (*pratyaya*). Because cause and condition are fully present, they cause the pure mind to move, forming the waves of birth and death.
As for "drifting and sinking," the human and celestial realms are the drifting, while the three miserable paths are the sinking; it is like a person falling [into the water].
It is like a whirlpool in water that once sinks to the bottom, floats to the surface for a moment, but upon emerging cannot stay afloat and sinks back down again;

this may be understood through each corresponding analogy. As for the appearance of Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust and grains of sand, from beginningless time the Buddhas, out of their compassion and pity for sentient beings who are deluded and fallen, have appeared in the human world; if one were to calculate their number, it would be like wiping away the entire world.
The number of atoms in the realms is likewise equal to all the sands within the Ganges River;
as there are such Ganges Rivers, each with its own fine grains of sand, I lament that I lack the karmic affinity with the Buddha. When the Buddha appears in this world, I am born in another;
when the Buddha appears in various worlds, I am born in this one; or perhaps he appears at the very time I am present.

Whether I am in the three miserable realms or in other difficult places such as the Northern Continent, even if I should briefly obtain a human body, the Buddha and his teachings may have already ceased to exist;
or, even if the Dharma has not yet ceased, I may neither hear it nor believe it, and thus be unable to resolve my mind toward awakening—
just like a blind turtle that has fallen into the ocean and cannot find its way out, while in the sea there is a floating log with a single hole just large enough for the turtle to pass through.
Suppose a blind turtle with a shell were to surface once every hundred years, and suppose there were a single floating log with a single hole in it drifting upon the ocean.
Even if the turtle were to enter that hole, it would likely drift back out to sea; thus, the meeting of a hundred thousand such blind turtles and a floating log is impossible.

Just as the blind turtle and the floating log do not meet, so too have ordinary beings and the *Dharmapada*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and other teachings failed to encounter one another until now. To say that a Buddha appears among human beings is merely a remedy for this ailment.
That which is heavy involves partial anxiety. The retributions of the six realms of existence are mostly produced by those in the human body of Jambudvīpa.

The cultivation of the untainted karma of the Three Vehicles through the arousal of the resolve likewise occurs within the human body; this is because humans possess intense discrimination and abundant capacity for reflection.
The suffering in the six heavens is slight, and the eight difficult conditions act as barriers; thus, those capable of receiving transformation are found only among humans.

Commentary: How fortunate! Below, there are two expressions of joy. If we consider the teachings encountered thus far—the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and several other sūtras and śāstras that reveal the nature through the perfect and sudden teachings—then for now, my primary joy concerns this very sūtra. Regarding the "thousandfold doubts":
previously, within the teachings on the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, I resolved to practice for several years; I sought to have countless doubts resolved.

Later, having encountered a true and virtuous spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) of the Southern School of Chan, I have severed all doubts regarding the fundamental path of delusion and enlightenment, and of sinking and rising from the beginning to the end.

However, concerning the various distinct gateways—such as the mind and objects, the origin and the culmination, cultivation and realization, the stages of practice, and the immeasurable doors of meaning—as well as the provisional and ultimate teachings, I have not yet attained full resolution. This has occurred whenever, through reflection and contemplation, or due to...

When one searches through the various sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras, encountering passages that appear contradictory, convoluted intentions, or points of confusion and doubt, the intellect becomes obstructed—just as water blown by the wind freezes into ice and can no longer flow. The depression and distress of the mind and heart are likewise like this.
If one personally studies and gradually resolves each point of this teaching, it will be like ice in the sunlight.
Because it is drenched by the heat of boiling water, it is said to be like ice melting; as for "investigation and reflection" and so forth, this serves as a counter-verification of past causes.

If one had not encountered various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) over successive lifetimes to hear the teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and thereby perfumed the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), how could one now, upon seeing this wondrous scripture, immediately attain realization and understanding?
How could it be that one attains such faith and understanding merely after hearing it in one, two, three, four, or five lifetimes?
One who is able to awaken to and enter this nature and characteristic— where the true and the false are harmoniously integrated, the ordinary and the sagely mutually penetrate,

and the root and the branches are sovereignly free from confusion or disorder; where each of the myriad gates and ten thousand meanings is fully accomplished without doubt or stagnation, and where one is rightly free from heterodoxy—

should be known as one who has accumulated the熏習 (vāsanā) of hearing over successive lifetimes and has encountered spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) over many births, and is thus finally able to achieve thorough penetration.
This profound and ultimate teaching concerns the gateways of meaning such as "the text diverges while the intent is pervasive.

Indeed, I have frequently contemplated this meaning—whether through the entire night in stillness, throughout the day in leisurely seclusion, or while traveling alone for the full length of a journey—imagining it within my heart.

I am deeply grateful that, over many lifetimes, various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) have guided, exhorted, and instructed me until I reached this point; furthermore, [this matter] is detailed [in the following].
Reflecting deeply, I consider that in the time prior to several lifetimes, when I first encountered a virtuous friend, I must have been difficult to lead toward faith.
Clinging stubbornly to various views, I uttered all manner of irrational words and displayed my skill and eloquence solely for the purpose of resistance.

It was only through the compassionate mindfulness and awakening of that virtuous friend—fearing that I might damage the teachings or fall further into ruin—that he exhausted his heart and strength to employ skillful means for my rescue and deliverance.
After such a number of lifetimes, one finally becomes willing to believe and accept; yet, though able to believe and comply, one has not yet attained realization.
Furthermore, through the various skillful means, parables, and instructions of virtuous friends, one is led to a thorough understanding. This process continues for several more lifetimes.

Although one understands immediately upon hearing the words, afterwards one merely reverts to former habits and complacency; thus, one still does not give rise to the thought that this [Dharma] is difficult to encounter, nor does one maintain it in every moment of mind.
In seeking learning, one often merely exhausts the strength and mind of virtuous friends; only through long-term exhortation and encouragement can one gradually progress.

Furthermore, throughout several lifetimes, one may superficially enjoy studying the principles of verbal teachings, yet fail to examine the mind in relation to sensory objects and fail to awaken to and subdue deluded thoughts or emotional attachments.
Whenever hearing virtuous friends explain profound meanings, one listens with joy and receives them [with pleasure].

When one hears that the application of the mind is deviating from the Way, one does not rejoice; instead, one suspects the virtuous friend, or doubts whether they have ulterior motives, or places trust in the words of others.

Such various gateways to obstructing the Way—from the initial generation of the mind until now—have involved worldly and crooked reflections and conceptualizations of their kind numbering in the thousands, tens of thousands, and millions. One must [recognize] these matters.
In each instance, I was compassionately spared from abandonment by virtuous friends who, through hundreds of means and thousands of examinations, gradually guided and led me;
only now in this present life have I been able to transcend so many such obstacles and bottlenecks on the path.
Whenever I had leisure in secluded places, reflecting upon the events of many lifetimes, tears flowed down to my neck and choked my throat and chest, as I often spoke in a low voice.
Weeping and lamenting that we cannot see you often, we shall remember each and every virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) we encounter,

prostrating with utmost sincerity and repaying their kindness in various ways. Consequently, we shall vow in every thought-moment that in our future lives we may meet each of them again, and furthermore,
attain the knowledge of past lives (jātismara-jñāna) so that we may recognize each one clearly and exhaustively offer our bodies and minds in worship to repay their profound benevolence.
Thus, not knowing what else to do, I have briefly recorded this to show my fellow practitioners, so that they may know my carriage has already overturned and that others should change their course.
In the commentary, regarding the two eulogies for the lamentation over the末代 (mòdài, "latter age") at the end of the upper section, it is stated in each of the twelve bodhisattvas' inquiries:

This vow is for the sake of bodhisattvas and sentient beings of the final age. Regarding "beginning" and "end": the beginning refers to Mañjuśrī’s inquiry into the fundamental stage of the causal ground;
the end refers to the Bodhisattva of Perfect Enlightenment’s inquiry into the cultivation and realization of the three contemplations.

If one were to explain this in a single session for those of superior faculties, the Chapter on Pure Wisdom would describe the characteristics of ordinary and sagely cause and effect as they accord with the nature of enlightenment.
This concludes the section on the sequence. "Sequence" refers to those who, having understood the teachings, resolve their minds to directly enter the Mahāyāna;
for them, one must first inquire upon what dharma they rely to generate the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), and what constitutes its primary cause.

Because Mañjuśrī asks based on this, the Buddha explains that the pure mind of *pariniṣpanna-bodhi* (Perfect Enlightenment) is primordially present and serves as the universal retention (*dhāraṇī*) of all phenomena, both defiled and pure. This is the essence of all things.
The source of all phenomena arises from ignorance; because one falsely identifies this body and mind as the self, there is cyclic existence.
Furthermore, since ignorance is fundamentally non-existent, there is likewise no one who attains enlightenment. One returns to the Tathāgatagarbha, which is ultimately perfect and complete.
Next, having awakened to this state, one naturally understands the principle of practicing according to the site of awakening. However, pure awareness is inherently present and does not increase.
Since ignorance is fundamentally non-existent and cannot be diminished, there is nothing to be eliminated or severed; thus, it would not accord with cultivation.

Yet, if one does not cultivate, one will perpetually dwell within illusion. The meanings of "cultivating" and "not cultivating" are verbally contradictory yet identical in intent; one must certainly understand this. Therefore, based on this, Samantabhadra asks the Buddha:
although the body, mind, and the wisdom of cultivation are all like illusions, it is not precluded that one may cultivate by means of illusory wisdom.
When the illusory body and mind are exhausted, illusory wisdom also ceases; the nature of awakening is perfect and full, without arising or ceasing.

Having realized this principle, one must naturally understand the skillful means for its cultivation: how to conceive the intention and how to direct the mind so that the practice of contemplation is accomplished.
Therefore, Universal Eye (Samantacakṣus) received this and questioned the Buddha, who taught that one leaves illusion behind through right mindfulness.
As a preliminary expedient (*pūrvāṅga-upāya*), one quiets all conditions (*śamatha*, here translated as "stopping"); firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts; dwells peacefully among the assembly;

and constantly sits in meditation within a quiet chamber. One should perpetually contemplate and individually eliminate [clinging to] the four great elements, the sense organs, consciousnesses, and sensory objects.

Within these, both the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) and the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) are found to be non-existent. Thus, one realizes the true nature manifested by the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), and furthermore, even the distinction between cultivation and awakening is obliterated.
The images of marks also cease; the awakened mind is pure, and all things are likewise so—without self and without other, equal, unmoving, and pervading the entire dharma-realm.
Regarding the two types of objects, there is neither love nor hatred, even unto the point that all sentient beings have fundamentally attained the Buddha-way.
Having heard this teaching, those whose faculties are somewhat inferior naturally come to doubt: "If they have been enlightened from the very beginning, how could it be otherwise?"

Because the present [state] and that of the Buddha differ vastly in excellence—being separated by a distance as vast as heaven and earth—the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, knowing the [Buddha’s] intent, questioned him accordingly.

The Buddha’s teaching arose from observing the revolving mind of sentient beings within Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-ābhisaṃbodhi*): it appears to have circulation, yet in reality, the essence of enlightenment is fundamentally unmoving.
It is like a boat moving, whereby the two banks appear to shift; yet in reality, the banks do not move at all. Since this principle has been established, [the following ensues].
Through this doubt, one finally realizes that it is due to the mind of saṃsāra that one perceives the flow of Perfect Enlightenment;
thus, by the nature of things, this mind must be severed. Next, however, this mind of saṃsāra and its appearances flow on spontaneously, beyond one's own control.
Not knowing which dharma is the root of saṃsāra, one remains unable to cut it off or bring it to an end. Maitreya relies upon this [realization].
He then asked the Buddha: "Since you have taught that craving is the root, karma is created and retribution is received in an endless succession.
Even if one relies on the teachings of the Three Vehicles for cultivation, if the fundamental ignorance is not eliminated, it will ultimately be difficult to enter awakening.

Next, one must realize this and resolve to sever craving, giving rise to a superior mind and making pure vows to abide in the Perfect Enlightenment of the Buddha and seek out virtuous friends. Thus he spoke.
Falling into false views, one then cultivates true stillness and deluded principles; though the intent may seem comprehensive, it is natural that one must know what to rely upon for cultivation.

Since one proceeds from the initial resolve to the fruit of Buddhahood always relying on Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-ābhisaṃbodhi*), all that is done and enacted must constantly be in accord with it.
If there is no distinction between ordinary beings and sages once one accords with Perfect Enlightenment, how can there still be gradations and differences in the stages and levels?
Because all are in accord with undifferentiated awakening, pure wisdom relies upon this to inquire of the Buddha.

The Buddha explains that the ten stages of faith, the three levels of worthiness, the ten bhūmis, and the fruit of Buddhahood each follow the nature of awakening and possess their respective modes of practice. Thus, the dharma-meaning of a single lifetime—from beginning to end—is complete and perfect.
However, the faculties and natures of sentient beings are manifold and diverse; they may be superior, middling, or inferior; they may be active, still, or at rest.
One may either accord with the Way through spontaneous ease, or realize the principle through focused concentration;

just as a city has four gates through which one enters from any direction, how can skillful means universally accommodate all capacities? Therefore, the Bodhisattva Mahātejas asked this of the Buddha, who replied:
"In the reality of all practices there are truly no two; the number of skillful means that accord with it is immeasurable. Thus, they are perfected.
Regarding the distinctions of the nature of what is gathered and its orientation, there are three types, namely *śamatha* and so forth.

Next, having heard that these three contemplations are distinct gateways for entering according to the suitability of individual faculties, it is naturally necessary to know whether one person practices all three together, or whether three people each practice one, two, or three, or whether they are practiced singly or in combination. Thus, [the text] explains the sounds.
Having raised this question, the Buddha explained the twenty-five cycles (*pañcaviṃśati-cakra*), all of which are permitted.

Subsequently, once one understands the gateway to the meditative practices (*vipaśyanā*) to be cultivated, it is natural that some may, despite practicing according to the Dharma with undivided mental attention, fail to achieve success in their practice.

Such a person may then doubt the intrinsic purity of the awakened nature (*bodhicitta*), thinking: "This is due to delusion and inversion, and thus does not correspond [to reality]; now that I have attained sudden awakening, I shall again rely upon..."
Having entered the gateway, how can one practice it so as to be unable to realize entry? Therefore, Pure Karma raised a question:

"The Buddha taught that because of the continuous succession of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time—consisting of attachments to a self (*ātman*), a person (*pudgala*), sentient beings (*sattva*), and a life-span (*jīva*)—one does not enter awakening.

This non-awakening opposes and rejects all who would seek to enter. Subsequently, once it was known that the mark of self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*) lies latent, difficult to discern and difficult to eliminate, one must rely upon the wholesome.
Regarding the gate of accumulating merit through friendship, one should diligently cultivate the resolve and strive to sever [afflictions],

for it is a natural law that one must know what kind of person is a true spiritual friend worthy of reliance. Furthermore, as a natural law, there is a class of people who, because they have resolved to practice and sever [afflictions] with diligence,
either engage in various activities to strive for early realization, or fear that the arising of such thoughts will cause them to lose their way, and thus remain entirely passive.
Some practitioners may merely cease false thoughts, while others seek to eliminate the sense faculties and their objects;

the Bodhisattva Pujue (Universal Awakening) recognizes this and poses a question, to which the Buddha replies by teaching the method for removing subtle ailments by relying upon an enlightened master.

Having completed the exposition of the Dharma-gate for those of middling capacity, there remains another class of people—those of inferior capacity who nevertheless possess great resolve and are determined to seek [enlightenment].
Those who seek realization must employ formal dharmas and constraints to be able to overcome their obstacles and achieve success;

therefore, the Bodhisattva of Perfect Enlightenment, following this principle, questioned the Buddha regarding the methods for establishing a three-period *dharmāśālā* (meditation hall) and applying effort and practice, as well as the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*).

He asked whether one should cultivate them individually, collectively, or by alternating between them, and what to do when such cultivation does not yield results, including instructions on performing repentance rituals (*pūjā-vidhi*) and so forth.

Next, the main body of the treatise consists of three sections: first, the necessity of knowing the methods for protecting, upholding, practicing, and cultivating these teachings so that they may circulate without interruption;

second, the questions posed by Bhadrapāla and the Buddha’s responses regarding the title of the sutra, the Buddhas who preach and protect the sutra, and the comparative merit of upholding the teaching; and third, the protection provided by various heavenly deities.
It is called "sequence" because it is for the sake of the great assembly to practice and uphold [the teachings]. As for "consultation," this refers to the Buddha’s praise of Mañjuśrī, saying:

"You are indeed able to consult the Tathāgata regarding the Dharma-practice of the causal stage for all Bodhisattvas. Regarding "Nengren" (能仁), the Sanskrit term is Śākya, which means "Able One" (Nengren).
As for "responsive resonance" (yinggan), the assembly of Bodhisattvas who pose the questions is that which "resonates" (gan), and the Buddha is that which "responds" (ying).

The Buddha who is perceived is that which responds; the bodhisattvas are those to whom one responds. That which is called the "source of the mind" (*xin-yuan*) is the wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment (*yuanjue miaoxin*), which is the source of all phenomena.
One may say that the mind itself is the source, hence it is named the "source of the mind. Alternatively, the mind is that which cuts off, while the defiled and pure minds are that which is cut off;
thus, the source of the mind is the awakened nature (*jue-xing*), the true mind. This is the source of the mind, and is therefore named as such.

Regarding the two interpretations—that "mind-source" (*xin-yuan*) is first an *upapada-karmadhāraya* (descriptive compound) and subsequently a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound)—both are applicable to this sutra.
This is because all the various distinct dharmas and meanings explained from the beginning to the end of the text are each established in reliance upon the pure mind of Perfect Enlightenment;

thus it is said that [the teaching] accords with it. As for "no obstruction between the fundamental and the derivative," while some Mahayana teachings may exclusively expound emptiness and quiescence—
The principle of *tathatā* (suchness) is quiescent, without cultivation or realization, without subject or object;

it is beyond the reach of wisdom and consciousness, cut off from the path of language, and extinguished where the movements of the mind operate. This speaks only of the fundamental source while negating the derivative branches.

Alternatively, it may be taught categorically that all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have relied upon the eight consciousnesses for their mutual perfuming, thereby giving rise to both the defiled and the pure through transformation.
All phenomena, whether sentient or insentient, arise from ignorance; thus, one gives rise to delusions, creates karma, and undergoes retribution without end.
If one does not encounter a Buddha, one is certainly an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) with no means to achieve equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

If one encounters the Buddha’s teaching, one generates the aspiration for awakening, gives rise to faith, and cultivates the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and myriad practices, or the practices of the two vehicles (*dvi-yāna*), gradually entering therein and each attaining their respective fruition within three lifetimes according to their own vehicle.
To claim that one only attains Buddhahood after sixty kalpas or three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas describes only the end while obscuring the beginning.

This present sutra fully and clearly reveals both the beginning and the end: the Unsurpassed Dharma King possesses Great Perfect Enlightenment (*mahā-vimala-bodhi*), yet ignorance is fundamentally non-existent;
even the knowledge of its non-existence is like flowers in the sky. Within the Tathāgata-garbha, there is no arising, ceasing, knowing, or seeing.
Even up to the wondrous, perfect, and enlightened mind, there is fundamentally no such thing as bodhi or nirvana;

nor is there the attainment of Buddhahood or its non-attainment, nor is there deluded saṃsāra or the absence of saṃsāra. Instances of this kind cannot be fully enumerated, for they are all the fundamental nature.

Furthermore, there are the various manifestations of deluded conduct, the various modes of spiritual practice, and the stages, positions, and levels of those practices—these are all contemplations of the fundamental nature.
The rules for the practice of the various paths at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) are such that it would be difficult to cite every instance exhaustively;

these are all "branches. What is spoken of as branches is precisely the branch of the root, never obstructing the root; what is spoken of as the root is precisely the root of the branches, never obstructing the branches.
Therefore, it is said that "root and branch are without obstruction. These words regarding non-obstruction were requested by Vajragarbha.
I only pray that you will not abandon your unimpeded great compassion and open the secret treasury for all bodhisattvas.

Just as when a Great *Cai* (Assembly) is held, monks and nuns from near and far come and are immediately provided for without further obstruction—even practitioners, children, the poor, and the sick are all permitted without hindrance—this is called the "Unobstructed Assembly" (*wu-cha zhai*). This sutra is likewise so; it is for the great bodhisattvas of the *bhūmi*.

From those prior to the stages of the Bodhisattva path up to the final age—whether at the gateway for beginners or regarding the depth of their intent in practice—it is like the water of a great ocean that does not refuse even small streams;
since asuras, mosquitoes, and gadflies may all drink from it until they are fully satisfied, it is called "unrestricted" (*wu-cha*).

"Sudden" (*dun*) refers to the suddenness of the pedagogical method (*hua-yi*); this means that even if one were to speak only of eradicating traces and departing from signs, it would still not be [called sudden].
The *Dun gu fa gu jing* (Sudden Dharma Drum Sūtra) states that all sūtras on emptiness are "incomplete teachings" (*savyavaccheda*) because they do not exhaustively explain the principle.

Furthermore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states that emptiness is the "initial gate" (*mukha*) of the Mahāyāna. If one were to speak only of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*), and positions, this would also not constitute the "sudden," as it would fail to reach the ultimate source of truth.
This present sūtra, however, explains both the beginning and the end as being mutually identical and unimpeded; therefore, it is called "sudden."
This is an exposition.
The commentary (*shu*) has already extracted the latter three dedications from various sūtras, vinayas, śāstras, commentaries, and miscellaneous essential and wondrous secret instructions.
To "strike the true stillness" means to turn back and contemplate one's own mind, illuminating the principle by relying on the place of awakening and the place of vision.

In composing this commentary, there are two underlying intentions: first, because it gathers various explanations, it differs from certain schools of Chan that describe the principle solely in terms of the mind without verifying it against the holy teachings as a definitive standard;

second, because it seeks to strike the silence [of the ultimate], it differs from those who merely study texts and commentaries, who simply collate old phrases and compile treatises and commentaries by changing their headings.
At the conclusion of the *Yì* (Book of Changes), it is stated that I have composed commentaries (*zhāngshù*).

Now, taking the sacred teachings as a clear mirror to illuminate one’s own mind, and taking one’s own mind as a lamp of wisdom to illuminate the profound purport of the scriptures, it is said: "Gathering the exegesis to strike at the silence," and so forth.
The phrase "striking at the silence" refers to what is said in the *Zǐshū*: "Striking at the silent void to seek the underlying meaning. Although this accords with the sacred intent...
One surveys all the various teachings without employing them exhaustively, nor does one merely select those with which one is personally familiar;
rather, one employs whichever accords with the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*) when the Sage preached this sutra. Thus, it is said that "one follows the Sage’s intent according to what is appropriate.
This "text" refers to this very sutra. Regarding the dedication of merit toward sentient beings: the objects of such dedication possess three aspects.

This means that because the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality) of the bodhi of sentient beings—according to the intent of the sutra—is present within every gate for sentient beings of the final age, I have followed the sutra by designating "sentient beings" [as the object].
Furthermore, among those who practice the Mahāyāna, there are those in whom great compassion predominates and those in whom great wisdom predominates;

however, as my own temperament and faculties are dull and weak, I feel much pity for those of inferior capacity, and thus I dedicate these merits toward sentient beings so that we may together enter the light.
The "Concealing Light" (zàngguāng) treasury is precisely the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). It lacks only the word "bodhi," yet this is contained within the character "enter" (rù);
because that which can enter is wisdom, it corresponds to bodhi.
*Commentary on the Brief Exposition of the Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*, Scroll Twelve (End).

The enlightened nature is perfectly luminous, responding wondrously to conditions in myriad ways; delusions and karma are empty and still, yet they arise and transform in profusion as a single essence.
Within change there is the unchanging; movement and stillness are truly profound and mysterious.

Thus it is said that while causes and conditions gather and disperse, the true principle remains eternally constant. Neither awakening nor delusion, it is primordially complete—this is the Sage of the Dharma-realm.
This is indeed the wondrous, awakened, and pure true essence. Now, those who enter the stream of the holy path must first recognize this vital message;
only then will they attain mastery in all directions, acting spontaneously according to the occasion.
Thus, the boundless ocean of Samantabhadra’s practices and the nature of Vairocana are not different—how could there be any fixed framework or uniformity? It is for this reason that...

Having already undertaken this task, how could I dare not promptly solicit contributions to carve these woodblocks for the *Commentary on the Concise Commentary on the Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* by the Chan Master Guifeng Dinghui, so that it may circulate forever?
Is this not what is meant by "above, aligning with the compassionate heart of all Buddhas; below, harmonizing with the sorrowful yearning of sentient beings"?
It is my great fortune to have encountered venerable seniors and eminent masters who have graciously bestowed their compassion upon me.

If you exercise compassion and forgiveness, not only will the seeds of the Buddha be preserved and the fragrant lineage continued, but it will also allow the Great Master of Samādhi and Prajñā to stretch forth his hands in dance and broaden his smile from afar.
Furthermore, if those of the Chan and Lecture schools do not stubbornly deceive themselves, they will avoid being an object of derision;
thus, not only will the three obstructions be realized as empty and their self-nature be pure, but it will also allow—
Sentient beings within the Dharma-realm, regarding the physical bodies inherited from their parents, find that Perfect Enlightenment shines universally, quiescent and non-dual;

they suddenly perceive the worlds of all Buddhas arising and ceasing in disorder, neither identical nor separate, where the environment and its inhabitants are equal, having been Buddhas from the very beginning—this is precisely the transcendent liberation from sense organs and objects, the solitary radiance of the numinous light. At that time...
Respectfully recorded by the scholar-recluse Fan Biyong of Wudingxuan on the occasion of the Mid-Autumn Festival in the year Jihai,
the seventeenth year of the Yongle era.
